en: Now begins the third chapter.

In the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter, titled "The Means" (Sādhana), there is the consideration of the movement [of the soul] and its return, as well as the investigation into the determination of dispassion (vairāgya).
Immediately following that is the section concerning the attainment [of the next state] (tadanantarapratipattyadhikaraṇa), Sūtras 1–7.
Now begins the third chapter:
I worship that Leader of Sītā, whom those endowed with dispassion, who discern the meaning of "That" and "Thou," and who are self-controlled, attain through spiritual means. (1)
START BsCom_3,1.1.1 1 The section concerning the attainment of the next state (tadantarapratipatti): Sūtra 1–7.
Upon the attainment of that [next state], he departs enveloped [by the subtle elements], according to the question and the explanation. (BBs_3,1.1)

In the second chapter, the contradiction with tradition (*smṛti*) and reasoning (*nyāya*) regarding the vision of Brahman prescribed in the Vedānta has been resolved; the worthlessness of rival doctrines has been elaborated upon;
and the contradictions among the scriptural texts (*śruti*) have been refuted.
And therein it was stated that the principles distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), which serve as its instruments, are born from Brahman.

Now, [the following topics will be discussed]: the manner of the individual soul’s journey through transmigratory existence when conditioned by those instruments; its various states; the true nature of Brahman; the distinction and non-distinction of forms of knowledge (*vidyā*); the inclusion and non-inclusion of qualities (*guṇa*); the accomplishment of the human goal through perfect vision (*samyagdarśana*); and the classification of the injunctions regarding the means to perfect vision.
The non-fixity of the fruits of liberation and other such matters will be examined in the third chapter, along with whatever else arises incidentally.
Therein, first, in the first quarter (pāda), the various paths of worldly existence (saṃsāra) are demonstrated by means of the Pañcāgni-vidyā for the purpose of generating dispassion (vairāgya),
as indicated by the concluding statement, "Therefore, one should feel aversion."

It has been understood that the individual soul (jīva), accompanied by the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) as its minister, along with the senses and the mind, and taking hold of ignorance (avidyā), karma, and the impressions of previous experience (pūrvaprajñā), leaves its former body and attains another body;

this is known from the scriptural texts situated within the context of transmigratory existence, beginning with "Then these vital breaths gather around him" and ending with "He fashions for himself another new and more beautiful form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1–4).
And because the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit must occur,
it is now considered whether that body goes forth unenveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) as seeds, or rather enveloped by them.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
"He is not embraced" means:
why? Because, unlike the appropriation of the instruments of action, the appropriation of the elements is not mentioned [in scripture], as in:
"Taking these particles of light to himself... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1).
For in this passage, the term "mere elements of light" (tejomātrā) refers to the inclusion of the sense organs,
because the eyes and other organs are mentioned in the remainder of the sentence;
there is no such mention of the inclusion of the mere material elements (bhūtamātra).
Furthermore, the elemental constituents (bhūtamātrā) are easily available everywhere;
they exist right where the body is to be commenced. Therefore, their being led [from one place to another] would be purposeless. Consequently, it follows that [the soul] departs unenveloped.

This being the case, the Teacher reads: "In the transition to another state, he goes enveloped. This means that in the transition to another state—that is, in the acquisition of another body—he goes, meaning he travels, enveloped by the subtle elements which constitute the seed of the body.
Why? Because of both the question and the explanation.
For instance, there is the question: "Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3).

And the detailed explanation in the response shows five oblations—consisting of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen—in the five fires of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman, concluding: "Thus, indeed, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9.1).

Therefore, it is understood that the individual soul (*jīva*), enveloped by water, moves on as it departs. But is it not shown by another scriptural text that [the soul] does not abandon the previous body until it has reached the next body, as in the case of a leech: "Just as a caterpillar" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.3)? Even in that case, there is no contradiction, for what is compared to the leech is merely the lengthening of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the body to be attained—which is presented by karma—while the soul remains enveloped by water.

Thus, since the manner of attaining another body has been declared by Śruti, there arise various conceptual constructions originating from human intellect, such as: "In the attainment of another body, the pervasive sense organs and the self obtain their functional activity there through the influence of karma," or "There,
the self alone obtains its functional activity."
The sense organs, however, arise as entirely new ones in each respective place of enjoyment, just like the body;
or rather, the mind alone might settle upon the place of enjoyment.
Or else, the individual soul (jīva) itself, having leaped out from one body, attains another body, just as a parrot flies from one tree to another.
All such [views] as these are to be disregarded, because they contradict the Śruti. (Note:
The means of perception include renunciation and so forth;
this concludes the incidental refutation of the body as the self.)
The meditation on the five—the day, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman—as fires constitutes the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).
"Karma" refers to what is called merit and demerit;
"prior wisdom" (*pūrvaprajñā*) refers to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births.
The "prolongation" of cultivation refers to its having the future body as its object.
"Mere" [consciousness] is the conception of the Buddhists;
"mind" is the conception of the Vaiśeṣikas.

The Digambara conception of the *jīva* is included by the mention of the first [conception], that of the Lokāyatas. [The soul] departs enveloped at the time of entering another body, according to both the question and the answer.
Having restated what has been discussed, he states the subject matter of the third chapter with the words "In the second," and so forth.

There is a relationship of cause and effect between these two [chapters]: once the meaning of the Vedānta texts is established as non-contradictory, there arises the occasion for an inquiry into the means of attaining knowledge of that [meaning].

Furthermore, once the subtle body (*liṅga*) and its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are established, there follows an inquiry into the transmigratory state of the individual soul (*jīva*) as conditioned by them; thus, there is a logical connection between the sections (*pāda*) as well.
In this regard, detachment is treated in the first chapter;
in the second, the meaning of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) and the reality of Brahman are explained through the description of states such as dreaming;
and in the third, the meaning of the Great Sentence (vākyārtha) and the meditations (upāsanā) for that purpose are investigated.
He states the meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "from right vision" (*samyagdarśanāt*).
The means of vision are renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and so forth.
Regarding the fruit, which is the nature of liberation, there is an absence of any rule of gradation as there is in the case of heaven; that is to say, it is of a single uniform nature.
The refutation of the body as the self follows as a secondary topic.
The meditation on the five—namely, the sky, rain, earth, man, and woman—as being fires constitutes the Pañcāgni-vidyā (the knowledge of the five fires).

Since there is misfortune in the form of coming and going through the cycle of action, the scripture states at the conclusion of the Pañcāgni-vidyā that one should cultivate "jugupsā"—that is, disgust, aversion, and detachment—toward the fruit of action; thus, it is presented here for the purpose of generating dispassion (*vairāgya*).
This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).
In the first aphorism of the treatise (*śāstra*), dispassion (*vairāgya*) produced by the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal was stated;
here, for the sake of strengthening that, dispassion produced by the contemplation of the afflictions of going and returning is stated—thus there is no tautology.
He states the subject matter of the discussion: "the individual soul" (jīva).
"Ignorance" (avidyā) is well-known;
if the reading is "knowledge" (vidyā), then meditative worship (upāsanā) is to be understood.
Karma is that which is called dharma and adharma; prior wisdom is the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) from previous births.
The meaning is that, at the time of death, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) become unified with the individual soul (*jīva*) in the heart.
"Form" refers to the body; "subtle elements" refers to the portions of the fivefold-composed elements that undergo transformation into the subsequent body.
This is because all the topical sections (adhikaraṇas) constitute an inquiry into the means for attaining knowledge of the meaning of Vedānta.
The connections with the scriptures (*śruti*) and the treatises (*śāstra*) are as follows: because this results in dispassion (*vairāgya*), it has a connection with this section (*pāda*).

In the preceding section, the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) was stated for the sake of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); here, that very transaction is being investigated. Thus, the relationship between the result and its consequence (*phala-phalibhāva*) constitutes the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*). Here, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [it is argued] that there is no movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) without a substratum.
There is no dispassion;
for according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), dispassion consists in the departure of the vital breath from its support in the elements—this is the difference in result.
The "measures of light" (*tejomātrā*) are the eyes and other senses.

The ellipsis [of the sentence] is "he sees" and "he smells. King Pravāhaṇa’s question to Śvetaketu is: "Do you know how water, when offered in the five fires and offered as the fifth oblation, becomes designated by the word 'person' (puruṣa) and transforms into the nature of a person?"
And when he did not know the answer to that, the King said to his father: "In that world, Gautama, this is indeed the fire; there, the water called faith is the oblation.
In this world, at the Agnihotra sacrifice, the waters in the form of curds and other substances, offered with faith, become connected to the sacrificer;
having reached the heavenly world, they abide in the form of a divine body known as Soma, and at the conclusion of the ritual, they flow forth."

It has been established that when water is offered into the rain-cloud, it takes the form of rain; from there, it takes the form of food on earth; and when offered into a person, it takes the form of semen; and when offered into a woman, those waters—designated by the term "person" (*puruṣa*)—become male in nature.
Now, one might object: it is illogical to claim that after leaving this body and traveling with the waters, one subsequently attains another body.

One might object that this contradicts the Śruti, which states: "Just as a leech, having grasped another blade of grass, lets go of the previous blade, so the individual soul (jīva), having grasped another body, lets go of the previous body. To this, he provides the resolution: "In that case also... The meaning of the Śruti is that even here [in this life], by means of the contemplation "I am a god" and so forth, one grasps the future body dependent upon karma and thereby lets go of the previous body; therefore, there is no contradiction.
The "extension" of meditation refers to its having the future body as its object.

The individual soul (jīva), conditioned by limiting adjuncts like the space within a jar, goes to another world by means of its subtle adjuncts; this is the method stated in the *Pañcāgni-śruti*. Because other conceptions contradict this, they are all to be disregarded—this is the logical connection.
He states the Sāṅkhya conception with the words "of the all-pervading ones."
He states the Sugata’s (Buddhist) conception with the words "of the solitary [self]":

the meaning is that the self, which consists of a continuum of non-conceptual cognition, acquires a function called conceptual cognition of sound and so forth in another body. He states the Kāṇāda (Vaiśeṣika) conception with the word "mind."
The mind alone goes toward another body, while the sense organs are newly produced; thus he states the Digambara conception: "the soul" (jīva). //1//
[Objection: But does it not follow from the cited question and answer that [the soul] departs enveloped by water alone?
Because of the force of hearing the incorrect word [in the text],
how can it be asserted in a general sense that [the soul] departs enveloped by all subtle elements? To this, he recites the following reply:
"But because [water] consists of three elements and is predominant. The word "but" (tu) cuts off the doubt that was raised.
For water consists of three elements, according to the scriptural teaching on the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).
When those [elements] that constitute the origin are accepted, the other two elements must also necessarily be accepted;
for the body consists of the three [elements], since the effects of all three—fire, water, and earth—are perceived therein.
Furthermore, it consists of the three because it has three constituents (dhātu), namely the three: wind, bile, and phlegm.
It is not possible for that [body] to be produced by water alone, setting aside the other elements;
therefore, this expression "water consisting of a person" (āpaḥ puruṣavacasaḥ) is dependent on the predominance [of water].
In both the question and the answer, the word "water" does not refer to exclusivity.
For in all bodies, an abundance of liquid substances such as plasma and blood is observed.
[Objection: But is it not the case that the earth-element (pārthiva-dhātu) is perceived as most predominant in bodies?
[Response: This is not a fault.
There will also be an abundance of water even in comparison to other [elements].
Furthermore, an abundance of fluidity is observed even in the seed of the body, which is characterized by semen and blood;
and karma is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) in the commencement of another body.
Furthermore, rituals such as the Agnihotra depend upon liquid substances like soma, clarified butter, and milk;
and it will be stated that the waters, which are inherent in those rituals and denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā), are offered along with the rituals into the fire called the heavenly world.
Therefore, too, the abundance of water is well-established.
And because of their predominance, it is faultless to understand that by the word "water" all the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), which are the seeds of the body, are intended. // 2 //

[Objection: Is it not improper to say that the body consists of three elements because the three effects of digestion (pāka), moisture (sveda), and odor-color-form (gandha-rūpa) are perceived? For the body actually consists of the five elements, since both vital air (prāṇa) and space (avakāśa) are also perceived. Anticipating this lack of conviction, he offers another explanation with the words "Furthermore" (punar ca). The grammatical connection is as follows: because they sustain the body, they are called *dhātus*; and because it possesses these three *dhātus*, it is said to consist of three elements (*tryātmaka*).

The sense is that if the body were composed solely of water (*kevalābja*), then *vāta* (wind) and *pitta* (bile), which are respectively of the nature of air (*vāyavya*) and fire (*taijasa*), would not exist.
Water is predominant when compared to the other elements.
Furthermore, because the actions (*karman*) that cause the body are predominantly aqueous, the other elements are indicated by them; thus he says, "And action," and so forth. //2//
And because of the departure of the vital breath (prāṇa). BBs 3.1.3.

Furthermore, the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) upon the attainment of another body is declared by such scriptural passages as: "When he departs, the *prāṇa* departs after him; when the *prāṇa* departs, all the vital breaths depart after it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Since that movement of the vital breaths is not possible without a substratum, it is understood that their movement is necessitated by the movement of those other elements which serve as their substratum and are conjoined with them. Even though these [elements] are sinless, their movement is inferred from the movement of the vital breaths.
For the vital breaths, being without a support, never go anywhere nor do they remain anywhere, since we observe them in one who is living. // 3 //

Regarding the departure [of the soul], he states that the vital breaths (prāṇas) have as their substratum the five elements which are the seeds of the body, because they are of the nature of vital breath, just like the vital breath residing in a living body; thus: "And because of the movement of the breath" (Sūtra 3).
If it be argued that [the soul does not go] because of the scriptural statement regarding its going to Agni and others, we say no, because that is figurative. 3.1.4.
It might be argued as follows:

the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not indeed depart together with the living soul (*jīva*) upon the attainment of another body, because of scriptural statements regarding their movement into fire and other elements.

For scripture shows that at the time of death, the vital breaths such as speech go to the deities such as fire: "When this person has died, his speech goes into fire, his breath into the wind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).
If it is argued that this is so because of such passages [as those cited], we say no;
for it is figurative.
The scriptural statement regarding the departure of speech and the other senses into fire and the other elements is secondary (gauṇī), as they are not observed in the hair.
For it is thus recorded there in the scripture: "The herbs [become] the body hairs; the trees [become] the head hairs.
Indeed, it is not possible that the body hairs and head hairs, having leaped up, go to the herbs and the trees.
Furthermore, the departure of the individual soul (jīva) is not possible if the limiting adjunct of the vital breaths (prāṇa) is excluded;
nor is experience in another body tenable without the vital breaths.
Moreover, the departure of the vital breaths together with the individual soul is clearly declared elsewhere in the Śruti.

Therefore, with respect merely to the cessation of their assistance at the time of death, it is figuratively stated that speech and the other organs go to Agni and the other deities, who are the presiding deities of speech and the rest and who provide assistance to them.

Note: In passages such as "When he departs from there," etc., one might suspect that the movement of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is unestablished; therefore, the author refutes this by stating "fire, etc.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because [the movement] of the herbs and trees is not observed."
The meaning is that they cause the body hairs to stand on end.

The meaning is that if the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) into fire and the other elements were taken as primary, it would be impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to undergo departure and experience [of results]; therefore, because of the clear scriptural statement, "All the vital breaths depart after [the soul]," and because of the mention of their dissolution in hair and so forth being figurative, [the former] must be understood as figurative.
If it be argued that [the waters] are not mentioned in the first [libation], we say no, for they are indeed [implied] because of the logical consistency.
It might be asked:
"How then [is it known] that 'in the fifth libation the waters come to be called man' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3)?"
This cannot be determined;
for there is no mention of water in the first fire at all.
For here, the five fires beginning with the heavenly world are taught as the receptacles for the five oblations.

And with reference to them, beginning with "That world indeed, O Gautamas, is the fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1), it is taught that "In this very fire, the gods offer faith as an oblation" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.2), whereby faith is presented as the substance to be offered.
Water is not heard of there as being the substance for the oblation (*haumya-dravya*).

Even if one were to imagine that water serves as the substance for the oblation in the four subsequent fires beginning with Parjanya, let it be so imagined; for in those cases, it is logical that Soma and other substances offered as oblations consist largely of water.
If it is argued: "In the first fire, it is a rash assertion to discard the *śraddhā* (faith) mentioned in the scripture and instead postulate waters (*āpas*) that are not mentioned;
for *śraddhā* is a specific kind of mental conviction, as established by its conventional usage.
Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that waters attain the state of a person in the fifth oblation."
This is not a fault;
because even there, in the first fire, those very waters are intended by the word "śraddhā" (faith). Why? Because it is logically consistent.
For in this way, by connecting the beginning, middle, and end, this single coherent statement is established without confusion;
otherwise, however, when the manner in which water comes to be called "man" at the fifth oblation has been asked,
if one were to introduce "faith" (śraddhā) as the sacrificial substance in the place of the first oblation during the occasion of the reply, then the question would be rendered inconsistent.

Otherwise, there would be no syntactic unity with the response, "But it is at the fifth oblation that the waters come to be called 'man'"; moreover, by concluding thus, [the text] demonstrates this very point.
Furthermore, the effects of faith—namely soma, rain, and so forth—are observed to become gross and consist predominantly of water.
And that [liquid] is the logical reason for faith being water;
for the effect must correspond to its cause.

Furthermore, the factor called faith cannot be extracted from its substrate—whether it be the mind or the individual soul—as a property to be offered, like the heart and other organs from a sacrificial animal; therefore, the waters themselves are designated by the word "faith."
They would be so;
moreover, the word "śraddhā" is applicable to water, as seen in Vedic usage: "Water, indeed, is śraddhā."
Since the waters, which constitute the seed of the body, attain a state of subtlety and assume a form similar to faith (*śraddhā*), they may be designated by the term "faith.
Just as a man possessing the prowess of a lion is called a "lion," so too the word "faith" is appropriately applied to the waters because of their association with actions preceded by faith.
It is like the word "bed" (mañca) being applied to the men [on it].

Furthermore, the application of the word "faith" (śraddhā) is appropriate because it is the cause of faith, according to the Vedic scripture: "The waters indeed bow down to him with faith for the sake of meritorious action. // 5 // [FN:
The term *saṃgāna* occurs in such passages as "When he departs... and so forth.]
The waters, not drying up, from another source,
bow down and bring forth for this sacrificer.

Having stated the course of the waters when they are joined with other elements, and having raised an objection regarding their being designated by the term "person" (puruṣavacastva), he provides the resolution beginning with "In the first [case].

Anticipating the objection that the word "first" is redundant because the waters are not mentioned in connection with the subsequent fires either, he says "Even if..."— meaning that while there is mention of them later on because soma, rain, food, and semen are of the nature of water, such is not the case in the first instance.

The meaning of the objection is this: once it is established that water (*āpaḥ*) constitutes the oblations in the five fires, it would follow that they attain the state of being called "man" (*puruṣavacastva*) at the fifth oblation; however, that is not established because they do not constitute oblations in the first fire. For only if water is understood by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*) does a single coherent sentence result, through the consistency of the question, the answer, and the conclusion, which thus share a single purpose.
If, however, water were not taken up in the four fires, then one would have to say "at the fourth oblation" because water constitutes the oblation;
therefore, since the word "at the fifth" is heard both in the question and the conclusion,
the purpose of the resolution is that water alone must be understood even in the first fire.
"Anapah" means other than water.
"This very [is it]"—
the meaning is that this shows the word *śraddhā* has the sense of water (*āpah*).
He states another meaning for the word "upapatti" (arising): "the effect of faith.

The meaning is that through such passages as "from that oblation of faith, soma arises," it is heard in scripture that faith, soma, and so forth, are successive transformations of one another; therefore, because faith is a transformation of fluidity, it possesses the nature of water, and because primary faith—which consists of conviction—cannot logically be an oblation itself.

Having explained the primary denotation (*vṛtti*) of the word *śraddhā* (faith) in water by way of its quality of subtlety, [the author] states the relationship—either as a commonality of action or as a cause—for the sake of explaining the secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*). He says: "preceded by faith" (*śraddhāpūrvaka*), meaning for this sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
The meaning of the Vedic text is that waters, for the purpose of bathing and so forth, bow toward faith—that is, they produce it. //5//
If it be argued that this is not so because [the path] is not mentioned in scripture, we say no; for those who perform sacrifices and other rites are known [to travel by it].
Now, it might be argued that although by means of the two replies water indeed attains the form of a person through the sequence beginning with faith at the fifth oblation,
the individual souls (jīvas) do not depart enveloped by that [water],
because this is not stated in the scripture.

If it is argued that this is incorrect because there is no sound here to indicate that the souls are enveloped by water as they are, and therefore the statement "he goes forth enveloped" is unjustified—
this is not a fault.
Why? Because performers of sacrifices and other rites are recognized [in the text].

Beginning with, "Now, those who in this world worship through sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts—they pass into the smoke" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6), the text describes the attainment of the moon by the performers of sacrifices and other rites via the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) starting from smoke, stating: "From space they reach the moon; that is King Soma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.4).

These very same [waters] are understood here as well, because of the similarity of the scriptural statement: "In this very fire, the gods offer faith; from that oblation, King Soma arises" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.2).

Furthermore, the substances such as curd and milk, which serve as the means for performing rites like the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa, are visibly water itself, owing to their preponderance of liquid matter.
Those subtle oblations, which are the unmanifest forms (*apūrvarūpa*) of the offerings poured into the *āhavanīya* fire, take hold of those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*.
And at the end, the officiating priests offer their bodies into the final fire according to the funeral rite, saying: "This person [goes] to the heavenly world, *svāhā*!

Thereupon, those waters—which consist of the oblations, are conjoined with actions preceded by faith, and exist in the form of the unmanifest—take hold of those performers of the *iṣṭi* and other rites.

That living beings, enveloped [by faith], are led to this world for the purpose of yielding fruit—this is what is expressed here by the term "offering" (*juhoti*), as in the passage: "They offer faith" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.9).

Likewise, in the Agnihotra, through the supplementary passage consisting of the explanation of the six questions, beginning with "These two offerings, once offered, depart," the attainment of another world for the commencement of the fruit of the Agnihotra oblations is described.
This has been demonstrated.

Therefore, it follows that the living beings (jīvas), enveloped by the waters consisting of oblations, hasten toward the enjoyment of the fruits of their own karma. // 6 // [FN: By means of the *naidhana*, that is, the funeral rite known as *antyeṣṭi*.]

"May he go to heaven"—this is the meaning of the mantra. Having introduced the destination of the waters, [the author] resolves the question regarding the destination of living beings by means of water through the passage beginning with "Now moreover" (athāpi). Having stated that King Soma arises from the oblation of faith offered into the fire of the heavenly world, the remainder of the passage identifies those who perform sacrifices and other rites—having reached the moon from the ether via the path of smoke and so forth—as "this King Soma."

Therefore, the meaning is that in this statement regarding the oblation of faith (*śraddhā-huti*), the departure of the living beings who perform sacrifices and other rites—along with the waters denoted by the word "faith"—is understood due to the commonality of the term *somarāja* (king Soma).

By stating their connection with the subtle, quintuplicated waters whose nature is the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of the ritual substance, he explains their joint departure in the passage beginning with "And of them, the Agnihotra...
The word *nidhana* means death; it refers to the performance of the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) occasioned by that death.
The meaning of the mantra is: "May this sacrificer go to heaven.
To show that water in the form of the offered substance also goes [to heaven], he cites another scriptural passage, beginning with "And likewise."

In the section concerning the Agnihotra, Janaka addressed Yājñavalkya with six questions: "But indeed, you do not know the departure of these two evening and morning oblations, nor their movement, nor their foundation, nor their satisfaction, nor their return, nor the world that rises up to meet them. The King himself provided the explanation for these: "When these two oblations are offered, they depart."

This has been established by the remainder of the passage: "Going from the intermediate space through the door to heaven, they make heaven itself their foundation; they satisfy heaven, and from there they return again; then, when offered upon the earth in man and woman, they arise in the form of a man. //6//
But how, then, is this departure for those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious deeds asserted to be for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their own karma?

To the extent that [the texts] show those who have ascended by the path characterized by smoke to become food for the moon, there is another scriptural passage on the same subject: "This is King Soma; that is the food of the gods, and the gods eat them" (Chāndogya), and "Having reached the moon, they become food; there the gods eat them just as they do King Soma, saying, 'Swell up! Wane away! (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2.16).
Thus, these two scriptural passages refer to the same matter.
And it is not possible for those being devoured by the gods to experience enjoyment, as if they were being eaten by tigers and the like.
Therefore, he recites the following reply: "Or [the term 'enjoyment'] is figurative, because of their lack of self-knowledge; for thus scripture shows. (BBs 3.1.7)
The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to exclude the previously mentioned objection.
Their status as food is figurative, not primary;
for if their being food were primary, then injunctive texts concerning qualification, such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," would be untenable.
If there were no enjoyment for those who perform sacrifices and other rites in the lunar orb, why would those entitled to such rites perform actions involving great effort, such as sacrifices?
Furthermore, the word "food" (anna) is seen to be used figuratively even for things that are not literal food, on the basis of their common quality of being a cause of enjoyment;
for example, it is said, "the subjects are the food of kings," and "livestock are the food of the subjects."

Therefore, the "eating" intended for these [beings] by the gods is their dwelling in happiness with those who have performed sacrifices and other meritorious deeds—who have entered into a subordinate status just as one's beloved wife, sons, friends, and servants do—and not the chewing or swallowing [of them] like sweetmeats and the like.
As it is said: "The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.6.1).
And thus [the text] precludes the gods from the activity of chewing and so forth.

Furthermore, for those performers of rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* who have entered into a subordinate state toward the gods, enjoyment is possible—just as it is for the attendants who subsist upon a king.
And because they do not know the Self, it is logical that the performers of rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* become objects of enjoyment for the gods.

For thus the Śruti shows that those who do not know the Self are objects of enjoyment for the gods: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he is like a beast to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).

And even in this world, by pleasing the gods through rituals such as sacrifices, he serves them like a beast; likewise, subsisting upon them and enjoying the fruits prescribed by them, he serves the gods like a beast.
It is being gone to.

There is another explanation for the statement, "Because they do not know the Self, it is so shown": for these performers of sacrifices and other rites (*iṣṭādikārin*) are merely performers of ritual actions; they are not practitioners of the combined performance of knowledge and action.

Here, the "knowledge of the five fires" is figuratively designated as "knowledge of the Self" due to the context. And because these performers of sacrifices lack the knowledge of the five fires, their status as food is presented through figurative praise in order to extol the knowledge of the five fires.
For it is the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) that is intended to be taught here, as is understood from the purport of the passage.
Thus, another scriptural text (*śruti*) shows the existence of enjoyment in the lunar orb: "Having experienced greatness in the world of Soma, he returns again" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.4).

Likewise, another scriptural passage also shows the attainment of enjoyment by those who perform sacrifices and the like, as they dwell together with the gods: "Now, a hundredfold the bliss of the Pitṛs who have won their worlds is equal to one bliss of the Karma-devas—those who attain the state of divinity through their ritual acts" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.33).
Thus, since the statement regarding their becoming food is figurative, it is understood that the individual souls of those who perform sacrifices and the like enter here [into the body of the eater].
Therefore, it is rightly said that [the soul] ascends enveloped. [Note:
*Adhikāra* means that by which a person is qualified or connected with an injunction; it is the desire for a result.
Just as an animal is an object of enjoyment, so too the ignorant one—meaning one who possesses the notion of duality—is an object of enjoyment for the gods.]
Now, he raises an objection regarding what the subsequent Sūtra will refute, beginning with "How? and so forth.

To dispel the misconception that the status of being food belongs here to the moon named Soma rather than to those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭāpūrta*, he cites another Śruti passage: "They [make] him the moon.

Just as in a sacrifice, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) repeatedly cause the Soma situated in the cup to swell by saying "Swell! (using the imperative *loṭ* for the repetition of the action), and having repeatedly caused it to swell and repeatedly diminished it, they consume it.

The meaning is that in this way the gods consume those who perform undesirable acts (aniṣṭādikārin) by making them into the form of food. "Adhikāra" means that by which a person is authorized—that is, connected with a ritual injunction; it refers to the desire for a result.
The intention is that the status of being "food" is figurative, in order to avoid rendering the scripture purposeless.
To the question, "By what fault are they objects of enjoyment for the gods?", he says: "And because of being non-knowers of the Self" (*anātmavittvāt*).
The meaning is that, just as an animal is an object of enjoyment, so too the ignorant person who possesses the notion of duality is an object of enjoyment for the gods.

Having explained a portion of the Sūtra by emphasizing the primary sense of the word *ātman*, he offers another interpretation—stating that the five fires under discussion are metaphorically designated as the "Self" by the author of the Sūtra—beginning with the words "non-Self," etc. (*anātma*...).
He explains the remainder of the Sūtra—*tathā hi* (for thus it is)—to show that being food is not primary for the purpose of praising knowledge;
for it is established that detachment arises from such a consideration of the course [of transmigratory existence]. //7//
END BsCom_3,1.1.7 START BsCom_3,1.2.8 2.
The Section Concerning the Passing Away of What Has Been Performed (Kṛtātyayādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 8–11.
"When the performed [deeds] have passed away, one returns possessed of residual karma (anuśaya), according to what was seen and remembered, both by the same way and not so.

Regarding those performers of sacrifices and other meritorious acts who have ascended to the lunar orb by the path of smoke and so forth, it is traditionally taught that after they have experienced their enjoyments, there is a descent from there: "Having dwelt there as long as their [karmic] residue lasts, they then return again by this very same road."

Starting from the passage, "Thus indeed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5), up until the point where it says that those of pleasant conduct attain the womb of Brāhmaṇas and others, while those of foul conduct attain the womb of dogs and others—
therein this is considered: do they descend without residual karma (*niranuśaya*), having exhausted all their performed actions, or rather with residual karma (*sānuśaya*)?
What, then, is the initial position?
That they are free from latent dispositions (*niranuśaya*).
Why? Because of the qualification "as long as there is a falling away" (*yāvat-saṃpātam*).
By the term *saṃpāta*, the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is meant here—[that] by which one descends from this world to that world for the purpose of experiencing the fruits [of action].
And the expression "having dwelt as long as the *saṃpāta*" shows that the entirety of that performed [karma] has been exhausted right there. As it is said:
"When that of theirs comes to an end" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.16).
And this very point is demonstrated by another scriptural passage as well.
It might be argued:
"I shall assume that one enjoys only so much karma as is to be experienced in that world."
It cannot be imagined that "whatever" refers to anything other than [the specific acts] mentioned elsewhere:
"Whatever he does here in this world, having reached the end of that karma,
he returns again from that world to this world for the sake of karma" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
For thus another scriptural passage, by means of the non-specific reference "whatever [he does]," shows the exhaustion here [in this world] of all karma performed in this life.
Moreover, death is the manifestor of karma whose fruit has not yet begun;
for it is impossible for that which is obstructed by karma whose fruit has already begun before death to be manifested.
And because there is no distinction [between them], that [knowledge] manifests everything whatsoever whose fruit has not yet begun;
for when the cause is common, the effect cannot be uncommon.
Indeed, it is not tenable to say that when a lamp is present without distinction, a jar is manifested but a cloth is not.

Therefore, when it is argued that they descend without any residual karma (*anuśaya*), we reply: "Upon the exhaustion of what has been performed, one possesses residual karma. That mass of karma by which they ascended to the moon for the sake of experiencing the fruit is exhausted through that experience;

their body, which was commenced in the moon for the purpose of such experience, vanishes like the solidity of clarified butter through contact with the fire of grief upon seeing the exhaustion of that experience.

Then, when the exhaustion of the performed karma—such as sacrifices and the like—has occurred through the enjoyment of its fruits, they descend into this world still accompanied by residual karma (*sānuśaya*).
For what reason?
He says: "On account of what is seen and on account of tradition."

For thus a direct scriptural text (śruti) shows the descent of those accompanied by residual karma (sānuśaya): "Now, those here whose conduct has been pleasant, it is likely that they will attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya;
but those here whose conduct has been foul, it is likely that they will attain a foul womb—the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig..."
"or into the womb of a Caṇḍāla" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7).
He will explain that by the word "conduct" (caraṇa), residual karma (anuśaya) is indicated.
Furthermore, this experience of enjoyment, distinguished as high or low, is seen to be determined by birth itself.

Because the occurrence of [results] cannot be accidental, this indicates the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), since scripture generally establishes that prosperity and misfortune have good and evil deeds as their causes.
Furthermore, the *Smṛti* states: "The castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after death experience the fruit of their actions, and then, by what remains..."

"Those who possess distinguished birthplace, caste, family, form, lifespan, learning, conduct, happiness, and intelligence obtain [such] a birth"—this shows that the descent belongs only to those with residual karma (*sānuśaya*). But what, then, is this so-called "residual karma"?
Some say that it is a certain remainder of the karma performed for the sake of heaven whose fruit has already been partially experienced, like oil clinging to a vessel.
For just as an oil vessel being emptied is not emptied of its contents entirely, but some residue of oil remains adhering to the vessel, so too it is with the latent disposition (*anuśaya*).
[Objection: Since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is contrary to its effect, it is not logical for it to remain in a state of residue once its fruit has been experienced.
[Response: This is not a fault.
For we do not assert that the fruit of karma has been fully experienced in its entirety.
[Objection: But surely he has ascended to the lunar sphere for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his karma without remainder? [Reply: Certainly.

Nevertheless, because of the mere remainder of very little karma, one is not permitted to remain there. It is said that just as a certain servant, having approached the royal court with all the requisites for service, becomes depleted of many of those requisites due to a long absence and, possessing only a parasol, sandals, and so forth, is unable to remain at the royal court.
Thus, it is argued that the lunar disk cannot remain sustained by the mere persistence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Yet this is not plausible;

for it has already been stated that the continued existence of a remainder of karma once its fruit has been experienced while residing in heaven is impossible, because such a remainder would contradict the very nature of its effect.
But surely this is incorrect;
for it cannot be that every single action whose fruit is heaven will have its fruit already exhausted.
This [objection] is not sound.

It is said that an action performed for the sake of heaven produces its entire heavenly fruit only for one who remains in heaven, but does not produce even a small portion of that fruit for one who has fallen from heaven.
Such a conceptualization is not tenable for those for whom scripture (*śabda*) is the sole authority.
However, in the case of an oil vessel, the persistence of a small residue of oil is plausible, as it is observed through direct perception.
Likewise, it is observed that for a servant, a small portion of his implements continues [after death];

however, in this case, no such persistence of even a fragment of the karma that has heaven as its fruit is observed, nor can it be postulated, because that would contradict the scriptural teaching that heaven is the fruit [of that karma].
And this must necessarily be understood in this way.
It is not the case that *anuśaya* (residual karma) is a portion of a work such as an *iṣṭi* sacrifice—which has heaven as its fruit—that persists like oil remaining on a vessel;

for if one were to assume that a certain portion of that very same well-performed work, such as an *iṣṭi*, by which one experienced heaven, constitutes the *anuśaya*, then the *anuśaya* would be exclusively pleasant and never the opposite.
In that case, this scriptural passage concerning the classification of *anuśayas* would be contradicted: "Now, those here whose conduct was pleasant..."
[And it is said: "Now those of foul conduct" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7).

Therefore, when the collection of actions whose fruit belongs to the next world has been exhausted through enjoyment, the remainder—the other collection of actions whose fruit belongs to this world—is the *anuśaya* (residual karma); those possessing that descend [to earth].

As for what was stated—that because of the reference to "whatever" without distinction, they descend free from *anuśaya* after reaching the end of all action performed here through the enjoyment of its fruit—that is not so.
This is not so;
for the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) has already been established.
It is understood that whatever action performed here has a fruit in the next world, once its enjoyment has begun, all of it is exhausted through the experience of that fruit.

As for what was also stated— that death, because it is without distinction, manifests all karma whose fruit has not yet begun, such that by some karma a fruit is commenced in the next world and by some in this one— that too has been refuted. Furthermore, it must be explained by what reason death is asserted to be the manifestor of karma whose fruit has not yet begun.
Just as, prior to death, the emergence of the activity of other [karmas] is impossible because they are obstructed by karma whose fruit has already begun,

so too at the time of death, since it is impossible for many karmas with contradictory fruits to begin their fruition simultaneously, the emergence of the activity of a weak [karma] is impossible when it is obstructed by a stronger one.

For it cannot be said that, merely by virtue of the commonality of having results not yet begun, multiple karmas whose fruits are to be experienced in different births manifest simultaneously at a single death and initiate a single birth;
this would contradict the principle that each karma has its own specific, determined fruit. Nor can it be said that at the time of death some karma manifests while another is destroyed.
Because it would contradict the principle that [karma] has an inevitable fruit;
for the destruction of karmas is not possible without causes such as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
Smṛti also shows that another karma, when obstructed by karma with a contrary fruit, persists for a long time: "Sometimes a well-performed deed remains here, buried deep."

"Being crushed in *saṃsāra*, one is released from as much suffering as possible"— this is of such a nature [as the teaching]. Furthermore, if all karma whose fruit has not yet begun were manifested at a single death and thereby initiated only a single birth,

then, because no further qualification for rebirth would be perceived in the realms of heaven, hell, or animal wombs, and because dharma and adharma would not arise due to the absence of a cause, a subsequent birth could not occur.
Furthermore, the scriptural tradition that each individual act, such as the killing of a Brahmin, serves as the cause for multiple births would be contradicted.
Moreover, it is impossible to conceive of any cause other than the scripture for understanding the nature, results, and means of dharma and adharma.
Nor is death a possible manifestor of actions with visible results, such as the *kārīrī* sacrifice; thus, this hypothesis that death is a manifestor is also non-comprehensive.
The analogy of the lamp has also been refuted by demonstrating precisely the relative strength and weakness of karma;
this should be understood as being like the manifestation or non-manifestation of gross and subtle forms.
For just as a lamp, despite being equally present [to both], manifests a gross form but not a subtle one.
Thus, although all the accumulated karma whose fruits have not yet begun is equally present at the time of death, it brings forth the operation of the powerful karma and not that of the weak.
Therefore, this admission that all karma is manifested [at death] is untenable, as it contradicts scripture, tradition, and logic.
Furthermore, the fear that "if residual karma exists, there would be the consequence of no liberation" is misplaced.
Because it is heard in scripture that there is the destruction of all karma through right vision (*samyagdarśana*),
it is therefore established that those who descend do so while still possessing residual impressions (*anuśaya*).
And as they descend, they descend both in the same manner and in a different manner as they ascended.
"Yathetam" means "in the manner in which they came";
"anevam" means "in the opposite manner.

Since smoke and space are mentioned as being traversed on the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) during the descent, and because of the word "yathetam," it is understood that [the ascent] was "in the manner in which they came."
Because [the sūtra] does not mention "night" and so forth, and because "clouds" and so forth are added as supplementary specifications, the opposite is also understood.
[Note: *anuśaya* is karma;
that is karma.]

"Returns" means it becomes exhausted. "Manifestation" means being oriented toward the fruit. Among those living beings descending there, the phrase "those of pleasant conduct, of meritorious deeds" refers to this [world], the land of karma; the word "nearby" (ābhyāśas) means that it is necessarily so.
*Kapūya* means evil. *Ricyamānaṃ* means being separated or deprived.
Now, he describes the arrival that occurs between different states of existence with the phrase *kṛtātyaye*.
The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is immediate succession following the completion of the karma to be experienced.
The construction is as follows: the scriptural passage beginning with "yathaitam" and ending with "śvādiyoniṃ" is what is traditionally taught (āmnāyate).
Regarding this, he states the doubt by saying "tatra," because of the qualification "yāvat-sampātam" and the statement "ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ."
Latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are karma;

the distinction here is that according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because there is no karma, there is no restriction on rebirth, and thus detachment (*vairāgya*) is not firm; whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because karma exists, there is a restriction on rebirth, and thus detachment is firm.

The meaning is that when the karma of those performers of sacrifices and other rites comes to an end—that is, when it is completely exhausted—then they return; thus, even by another scriptural passage, it is stated that the entire karma is experienced in the world of the moon. He says "not so" because it is not proper to restrict the scope of the word "as long as" (yāvat), as that would contradict the other scriptural passage.

The meaning of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) is this: whatever action this person performs here in this world, having obtained its final fruit in the next world, he returns again for the sake of action.

Having stated the scriptural authority regarding the absence of action, he states the logical argument (*yukti*) with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). Manifestation (*abhivyakti*) means being oriented toward the fruit.

The meaning is that because all karma manifested at death necessarily results in experience in the next world, there would be an absence of karma [in this life]. When it is argued that descent occurs solely from what is called "conduct" (*caraṇa*), he explains the thesis of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "by which" (*yena*). Among those living beings descending there, those who in this land of action (*karmabhūmi*) have "pleasant conduct"—that is, those of meritorious deeds who partake of a meritorious womb—that is the case; "abhyāśo ha" means "certainly indeed."
*Kapūya* means evil.
Having stated the literal meaning of the word *dṛṣṭa*, he states another meaning: "And it is seen" (*dṛṣṭaśca*).

Through such scriptural passages as, "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action and evil by evil action," it is understood that pleasure and pain have merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) as their causes.

Furthermore, the proof of the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is as follows: the enjoyment observed from birth onwards has karma as its cause, because it is enjoyment, just like the enjoyment in heaven;
for if the opposite were the case, the reason would be absent, leading to the undesirable consequence that enjoyment is accidental. This is the meaning.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: those belonging to the stages of life (āśramiṇaḥ), having remembered their hermitages (āśramāḥ) and having died (pretya)—that is, having passed away—experience the fruit of their actions (karmaphala) in another world; then, by means of the remainder (śeṣeṇa)—meaning by the action other than that which has been experienced, known as "residual karma" (anuśaya)—they undergo rebirth.
Those [worlds] are described as such because they possess ten qualities, beginning with specific locations (deśa) and ending with intelligence (medhā).
*Śruta* is knowledge,
and *vṛtta* is conduct.
He asks— "But who..."— in order to state his own intended underlying intention (*anuśaya*).

He states the explanation of a certain school of thought (ekadeśin) with the words beginning "some say" (*kecit*): when there is enjoyment in heaven of the karma that has been performed, the remnant (*leśa*) of the karma already experienced is the *anuśaya*; one descends while possessing that, because a residue of oil is observed in a vessel, and because of the Smṛti statement, "Then [one descends] by means of the remainder.
[The phrase] "being emptied" (*ricyamāna*) means being deprived of its oil.
One might object: "Since karma is destroyed by experience, it is not logical for a residue (leśa) to remain. This is the doubt expressed by the word "nanu.
The sense of the rebuttal is that destruction would occur only when there has been experience of the entirety of the karma; however, such complete experience has not yet occurred.
He raises the objection that "it is incorrect to say that experience does not arise" with the words "nanu" (but surely).
He answers that "experience has arisen with a remainder" with the words beginning with "bāḍham" (certainly).
He refutes this explanation of the "partialist" (ekadeśin) with the words "na ca" (and not).

The meaning is that the scripture, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," enjoins ritual action for the sake of experiencing heaven; therefore, if the remainder of that [action] were the cause of mortal experience, there would be a contradiction with the scripture.

Furthermore, he says "And necessarily" to show that if one descends from the remainder of the action that caused heaven, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural teaching regarding the attainment of a foul womb.
He states his own intended latent tendency (anuśaya) with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He refutes the seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by repeating it with the words beginning "That which...
(*yad*); the construction is that it is understood from the sentence "having exhausted [them], they return again" or "having reached the end."

The sense is that a restriction of the general terms "whatever" (*yat kiñcit*) and "as far as the completion [of life]" (*yāvat-sampātam*) to the realm of the hereafter is logical, because there is a contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding "pleasant and foul conduct" (*ramaṇīya-pūya-caraṇa*), which— supported by the evidence of experienced enjoyments from birth onwards— is intent upon qualifying specific actions belonging to this world and subsequent residues (*aihika-anuśaya*).
It is incorrect to claim that death is the manifestor of all karma.
He says "that too" because it would contradict the scriptural statement regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have been explained.
And because there is an obstruction by powerful karma that has already begun its fruition (*ārabdhakarma*), there is no manifestation of all karma; thus he says, "Moreover," and so forth.
The sense is that there is no cause for that [destruction] to be the manifestor of all karma.
Considering this as a question, he offers a response with the words, "That which has begun... (*ārabdha*).

He provides the resolution with the words "Just as... (*yathā*): because even a powerful [karman] that has not yet begun [to bear fruit] acts as an obstacle, there is no manifestation for the sake of yielding the fruit of every [karman].

Anticipating the objection that all karmas might manifest because they are equally unmanifested fruits, he explains that it is impossible for mutually contradictory results—such as bodies leading to heaven or hell—to originate from a single body; this is expressed by the words "For not... (*na hi*).
Then, fearing that weak karman might simply be destroyed, he says "Nor also... (*nāpi*).

"The statement that 'action is not exhausted without being experienced' is an absolute general rule; however, that rule is set aside by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), knowledge of Brahman, and meditation, but not by mere death—this is the meaning.
He states "Smṛti" as the authority for the fact that weak karma is not destroyed by death.

Having rejected the position that karma is destroyed [by death], he points out another defect in the position that all previously performed karma is manifested [at the time of death], saying "And if..."
The meaning is that because all karma would be exhausted through experience in a single birth as a god or other being, there would be no further birth;
yet, due to the absence of knowledge, there would be no liberation—thus, an ignorant god would be in a miserable intermediate state. [As it is said:
"Of dogs, pigs, donkeys, and camels; of cows, goats, sheep, deer, and birds..."

"Furthermore, because of contradictions with such Smṛti texts as, 'The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of Caṇḍālas and Pulkasas,' it is not the case that all karmas initiate a single birth; thus he says, 'Brahma... [and so on].
Now, one might ask: how can a single action have multiple births as its fruit?
He says "not so" because it has not been observed.
Furthermore, even if death were a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), should it be postulated as the manifestor of all karma, or the manifestor of only some karma?
It cannot be the first, because in this world, actions such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice—which have their results in this very life—cannot possibly be manifested by death; thus he says "not so."
Refuting the second [point], he dismantles the example stated by the opponent with the words "pradīpa" (lamp) and so forth.

The meaning is that, like a lamp for forms, death is not the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of any karma whatsoever; rather, when there is an absence of obstruction by a powerful karma, a weak [karma] is manifested.
Thus, by not accepting that death is the manifestor [of karma], the example of the lamp has been refuted; yet, even if it were accepted, it would be a favorable example, as he says: "gross," etc.
The remainder of the sense is that because the subtle [karma] is unmanifested in form, the manifestation of all karma at the time of death is not established.

Thus, he concludes the refutation of the view that the entire collection of karma (*sarvakarmasaṅgha*) initiates a single birth—that is, that the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is "pertaining to one existence" (*aikabhavika*)—with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The meaning is that because of the existence of unmanifested karma, as established by the scriptural statement regarding conduct (*caraṇa*), by the Smṛti texts such as "Then by the remainder" (*tataḥ śeṣeṇa*), and by the logical principle of "obstruction by a stronger [force]" (*prabalapratibandhāt*).
To the objection that the "pertaining to one existence" must be accepted because liberation would otherwise be untenable, he replies with the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*).
He explains the remainder of the Sūtra with the words beginning "And they," etc.
The path of descent is heard in this way: "Having dwelt there as long as their merits endure, they then return again by this very same path, just as they came—to space;
from space to air; having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud."

Having come into being, it rains; these here are born as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. Indeed, it is from this state that it is most difficult to escape. For whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the semen, he becomes that very thing again.
Thus, those whose conduct here has been pleasant attain a pleasant womb.

Having stated that they return by this path in the same manner as they went—that is, by the path beginning with smoke—it was thought that the night and so forth situated on the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) consisting of smoke and the rest had not been mentioned, while additional elements such as the clouds and so forth had been mentioned; therefore, the author of the Sūtras said, "as they went and not so.
The meaning of the remaining Śruti passage will become clear later. //8//
"If it be argued that [the term 'foot'] refers to the act of going,
[we reply:
No, for Kārṣṇājini maintains that it is used in a figurative sense."
It might be argued that there is a scriptural passage cited to establish the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*), namely: "Those here whose conduct was pleasant... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7).
However, that passage indeed demonstrates rebirth in a different womb due to one's conduct (*caraṇa*) and so forth, not due to residual karma.
Conduct (*caraṇa*) is one thing and latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is another. Conduct, behavior (*cāritra*), practice (*ācāra*), and morality (*śīla*) are synonymous.
Latent disposition, however, refers to karma that remains beyond the karma whose fruit has already been experienced.

Furthermore, the Śruti designates the performance of action by way of distinction: "As one acts, as one behaves, so does one become" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5), and "Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, not others;
those good deeds which are ours should be observed by you" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.11.2).

If it is argued that the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*) is not established because of the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of another womb based on one's conduct (*caraṇa*), this is not a valid objection;
for the teacher Kārṣṇājini considers that this mention of conduct is intended merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the residual karma. // 9 //

Now, the author of the Sūtras explains the word *caraṇa* as it occurs in the Śruti, by way of an objection: "If it be said [that the qualification is] from conduct (*caraṇāt*)... In the Smṛti it is stated: "Non-malice toward all beings in action, thought, and speech;

kindness and knowledge—this the wise know to be character (*śīla*). Thus, non-malice and the rest, which constitute character in the form of knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, are declared to be auxiliary to all ritual acts (*sarvakarmāṅga*). The word *caraṇa* is the indicator of that [character], which is subordinate to the principal act.

The view of Kārṣṇājini is that [the term "residual karma" (anuśaya)] indicates rites such as those prescribed in the Śruti; since the subsequent state of the action itself is what is called dharma and adharma—the *apūrva*—the residual impression (*anuśaya*) known as *apūrva* is established through the very indication of the action, as it is non-different from it. //9//
If it is argued that [the Veda] would be purposeless, we say no, because it depends upon that. 3.1.10.
This might be asked:
why, then, is the latent disposition (*anuśaya*), which is etymological, indicated by the word "conduct" (*caraṇa*), while setting aside the literal sense of "moral conduct" (*śīla*)?
Is it not the case that the fruit of moral conduct itself—whether enjoined or prohibited, and whether virtuous or non-virtuous in form—will be the attainment of a good or bad rebirth?
If it is argued that one must necessarily admit some fruit for moral conduct (*śīla*),
otherwise it would follow that it is utterly useless, we reply:
this is not a fault.
Why? Because of its dependence on that.
For the collection of rites such as the *iṣṭi* sacrifice depends upon conduct (*caraṇa*).

Indeed, no one devoid of good conduct could be qualified [for such rites], according to Smṛti texts such as: "The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of conduct. Thus, even though conduct serves the purpose of the person, it is not without significance.
For when a collection of actions such as sacrifices begins to produce its fruit, conduct dependent upon those very actions will initiate some degree of excellence therein;
and it is well-established in Śruti and Smṛti that action accomplishes all purposes.
Therefore, the view of Kārṣṇājini is that action alone—characterized by conduct and existing as a latent residue (anuśaya)—is the cause for entering a new birth.
For when an action is possible, it is not logical to resort to a different means such as moral discipline (*śīla*) and so forth;
for one who is able to flee on his feet ought not to run by crawling on his knees. // 10 //
He states that very point through the resolution of a doubt by means of the Sūtra beginning with "If it be argued that [the injunctions] would be purposeless" (*ānarthakyam iti cet*).
Having raised the objection that since the literal meaning denoted by the word *caraṇa* itself can be grasped, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate, he says "But surely" (*nanu*).
Prohibited conduct (*pratiṣiddhaṃ śīlam*) consists of anger, falsehood, and so forth.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for moral conduct (*śīla*) to be fruitless, he states "and necessarily" (*avaśyaṃ ca*) to show that the attainment of birth in the womb of the learned (*śrutayonyāpatti*) is the fruit of that very conduct, and not of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

According to the *Smṛti*, the Vedas and the rituals whose purpose they serve do not bear fruit without proper conduct; thus, because conduct is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to ritual action, there is no expectation of a separate fruit, as it is rendered purposeful by the fruit of the primary rite (*aṅgin*).
Nor should it be said that the result is merely the attainment of a particular birth as a limb [of the sacrifice];

for since a subsidiary element cannot possess a fruit of its own, it is impossible to take the word "conduct" (*ācāra*) in its primary sense, and thus metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is appropriate—this is the sense of the resolution.

Furthermore, he states, "Even if it were for the sake of man," meaning that even if conduct, like bathing and so forth, were for the sake of man by way of being a human purification (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), there would still be no contradiction.
The meaning is that, like the meditations connected with the limbs [of the sacrifice], conduct (ācāra) possesses its own purpose.

Anticipating the objection that "rebirth into a womb might then result from conduct alone, known as moral character (śīla)," he says "And action" (karma ca), because such a view would contradict scriptural passages such as, "Verily, by a meritorious deed one becomes meritorious. "Pārayamāṇaḥ" means capable. //10//
"But Bādari [says] that it is indeed good and evil deeds. (BS 3.1.11)
The teacher Bādari, however, maintains that it is good and evil deeds alone that are signified by the word *caraṇa*.
*Caraṇa*, *anuṣṭhāna*, and *karman* are not different in meaning;
for indeed, the root *car* is seen to be used without distinction for action (*karman*) in general.
For those who perform meritorious action characterized by sacrifice and so forth, worldly people say, "This great-souled one practices dharma.
Furthermore, conduct (*ācāra*) is indeed a specific form of dharma;
the designation of them as distinct is also justified by the analogy of the "Brahmin and the wandering mendicant" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*).

Therefore, the conclusion is that those of "pleasant conduct" are performers of praiseworthy actions, while those of "wicked conduct" are performers of censurable actions. (11) [Note: This is also an application of the maxim of the cow and the bull.
Although character—consisting of non-anger and so forth—is of the nature of general duty and thus not distinct from action in its specific form, nevertheless...

The terms *caraṇa* and *ācāra* denote only ritual action (*karman*) and do not signify moral conduct (*śīla*); thus, there is no occasion for metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He states Bādari’s view, which is the primary established conclusion (*mukhya-siddhānta*), beginning with "sukṛta" (well-done). He concludes the meaning of the word *caraṇa* with "ācāro 'pi" (conduct also).
If conduct (*ācāra*) itself is identical to action (*karman*), how can there be a statement of distinction such as "according to what one does" (*yathākārī*)? To this he says:

"The designation of distinction. From the word *ācāra* when used without a prefix, the specific form of "good conduct" (*sadācāra*) shines forth. Therefore, the word *yathākārī*, which denotes action in general and is mentioned in conjunction with that [term], refers to other specific types [of conduct]. Likewise, [the phrase] "blameless actions" (*anavadyāni karmāṇi*) is used in a general sense.
The distinction is that our own well-performed deeds are superior;
therefore, it is established that detachment arises from the contemplation of the inevitable recurrence [of rebirth] due to the force of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). //11//
END BsCom_3,1.3.11 START BsCom_3,1.3.12 3.
The Section Concerning the Results of Unrighteous Acts, etc. (Sūtras 12–21)
And it is also heard in scripture regarding those who perform undesirable deeds.
It has been stated that "those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious acts go to the moon";
now it is considered whether those others who perform undesirable deeds also go to the moon or not.
Regarding this, they first say: it is not the case that only those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious deeds go to the moon.
Why?
Because it is heard in scripture that even those who do not perform sacrifices and other such acts must go to the lunar orb.
For the Kauṣītakins record this without distinction: "Whoever indeed departs from this world, they all go to the moon" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.2).
This is because of the restriction regarding the number of oblations in the phrase "at the fifth oblation," since otherwise everyone would simply ascend to the moon.
If it is argued that it is not logical for those who perform sacrifices and others to have the same destination, we say no;
because others lack enjoyment in the lunar orb. // 12 //

Having thus described detachment by reflecting on the going and coming of those whose nature is meritorious, he now describes it by reflecting on that same process for sinners with the words: "Even for those who perform undesirable acts," etc.

Since there is a doubt arising from the non-specific scriptural statement, "Whoever they may be," and from the scriptural statement, "Vaivasvata is the gathering place of men," he explains the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra—beginning with "Therein," etc.—by way of a connection consisting in the challenge to the established rule [of the first section].
The meaning of the Vedic text is: "Propitiate Yama, who is the proper destination for sinful people, with an oblation.

According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since there is no restrictive rule that the journey to the moon belongs exclusively to those possessing merit, the result [of this teaching] is the realization of the futility of merit and the strengthening of detachment from sin.
In the Siddhānta, it is held that even the sight of the world of the moon does not exist for sinners; thus, the fruit [of this teaching] is the meaningfulness of merit and the firmness of dispassion.

Since there is a rule that the commencement of a body occurs in the fifth fire, it must be stated that even sinners reach the first fire, which is the heavenly world (dyuloka); thus he says, "the commencement of a body.
The sense is that although sinners lack the enjoyment of heaven, they still proceed to the moon because there is no other path. //12//
But in the case of Saṃyamana, the others experience [the fruits of their deeds] there; from that, there is ascent and descent, as seen from the observation of their course. (3.1.13)
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that all go to the moon.
Why is this so?
For the ascent to the moon is solely for the sake of enjoyment, neither without purpose nor merely for the sake of descending;
just as someone climbs a tree solely for the sake of gathering flowers and fruit, neither without purpose nor merely for the sake of falling.
It has been stated that there is no enjoyment for those who perform undesirable deeds while on the moon;
therefore, only those who perform desirable deeds ascend to the moon, and not others.
They, however, having entered Saṃyamana, the abode of Yama, and having experienced the torments of Yama corresponding to their own evil deeds, descend again to this very world.
In this manner, their ascent and descent occur.
Why? Because their destiny is observed [in scripture].

For instance, a scriptural passage similar to the words of Yama shows that those who perform undesirable acts are subject to Yama's authority: "The way to the hereafter does not reveal itself to the fool, who is deluded by the infatuation for wealth and is heedless."
"One who thinks, 'This world exists, there is no other,' falls again and again under my power" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.6).
Furthermore, there are many such signs of falling under Yama's control, such as "Vaivasvata, the gathering place of people. // 13 //
He explains the sūtra of the established conclusion with the words "the word 'tu' (but)," and so forth.

The construction of the sūtra should be understood as follows: having experienced the torments inflicted by Yama in the world of Yama (Yamaloka) during their confinement, they descend; thus there are both ascent and descent.
"Of those who have exerted themselves" means of those who have departed after death.
That which is properly attained in the hereafter is *saṃparāya*, meaning the next world; the means to that is *sāṃparāya*.
It does not shine for the fool—the ignorant person—especially one deluded by attachment to wealth and thus committing negligence out of delusion.

And that fool—who is conceited, thinking "this world of women, wealth, and so forth exists, but the next world does not exist"—falls under my power, that is, under the power of Yama; such is the meaning.

The intention is that, by the force of specific Śruti and Smṛti texts stating that sinners fall under Yama's control, the non-specific Śruti passage beginning with "whosoever they may be" (*ye vai ke ca*) should be interpreted as referring specifically to those who perform sacrifices and other rites. //13//
And they remember it as well. (BS 3.1.14)

Moreover, cultured authorities such as Manu, Vyāsa, and others remember, in the Nāciketa narrative and other texts, that the ripening of evil karma occurs under the authority of Yama in the city of Saṃyamana.
The commentary on these three sūtras is easy to understand. // 14 // // 15 // // 16 //
Moreover, there are seven. (BBs 3.1.15)
Furthermore, the seven hells, headed by Raurava, are recorded by the authors of the Purāṇas as the ground for experiencing the fruits of evil deeds.
It is those who perform undesirable acts and so forth who reach them; what possibility is there, then, for them to reach the moon? This is the intended meaning. // 15 //
Objection: Is it not contradictory that those who have committed evil deeds experience torments dependent upon Yama?
As for the claim that in those hells such as Raurava and others, various presiding authorities like Citragupta and so forth are recorded in tradition, he says:
"No; even there, because of his (Yama's) activity, there is no contradiction. (BBs 3.1.16)
There is no contradiction even in those seven hells, because it is accepted that Yama himself performs the function of presiding over them;
for Citragupta and the others are recorded in tradition as being presiding authorities only when appointed by Yama.
"But [the phrase] 'of knowledge and action' is used because they are the subjects under discussion. (BS 3.1.17)
