In the *Pañcāgnividyā*, at the time of answering the question, "Do you know why that world is not filled? (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.3.3), the following is heard: "Now, those beings who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small, repeatedly returning creatures;
'be born and die'—this is the third station, and for this reason that world is not filled" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.8).
In this context, "of these two paths" refers to knowledge and action.
Why?
Because they are the subjects under discussion.
For knowledge and action are the means for attaining the two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the fathers—under discussion here.

By the words "Those who know thus," the path of the gods to be attained through knowledge has been proclaimed; and by the words "Sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1, 3), [the path of the fathers is indicated].

Thus, by means of that [performance of ritual action], the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) is proclaimed as that which is to be practiced. Regarding its procedure, it is heard in scripture: "Now, neither by one of these two paths. What is meant by this is as follows: those who are not qualified for the path of the gods (devayāna) through the means of knowledge (vidyā), nor for the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) through ritual action (karman), for them there is this third path, characterized by small creatures, from which there is a return again and again.
Thus it is said.
For this reason as well, the moon is not reached by those who perform undesirable actions and the like.
This might be so.
The claim that they too, having ascended the lunar disk, will descend from it and enter the state of small creatures—
that also is not the case,
because such an ascent would be purposeless.

Moreover, if all those who strive were to reach the world of the moon, that world would become completely filled by those striving; consequently, the response given would be contradictory to the question.
For the response ought to be such that this world is not filled.
If it is argued that its non-filling is established because of the admission of descent (avaroha), we say no.
Because it is not so stated [in scripture].
It is true that incompleteness could also be established on the basis of descending;
however, scripture demonstrates incompleteness by mentioning a third place: "This is the third place; therefore, that world is not filled" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8).
Therefore, it is logical that there is no completion [of the journey] simply because of non-ascension;
for if descent were common even to those who perform sacrifices and other rites, the mention of a "third place" would result in being purposeless.
The word "but" (tu), however, cuts away the suspicion arising from statements in other Śākhās that there is movement to all [places].
This being the case, in the scriptural passage belonging to another recension, the word "all" remains relative to those who are qualified [for the rite]:
"Whoever indeed depart from this world, they all go to the moon alone. (17)
As for what was said—that because there is no other path, even sinners attain the state of the moon—that is not so;
for there is a scriptural mention of a third path, as he says: "Of knowledge and action... (Vidya-karmaṇoḥ).
In the Śruti, the word *atha* (then) serves to introduce the exposition of the third path immediately after the description of the two paths.

Those persons who are not endowed with either of these two means—knowledge and ritual action—which are the instruments for the two paths, become beings situated on the third path, which consists of the cycle of birth and death;
[this is expressed] by the imperative mood (*loṭ*) indicating a recurring action.
The meaning of the Śruti is that because there is no movement toward the moon for those evildoers, the world of the moon is not filled.
"In the case of attainment" (pratipattau) means in the case of the means of reaching [the goal].

Furthermore, the logical connection is as follows: if that world were filled by sinners descending from the moon, then the response [of the scripture], "And yet it is not filled," would result in a contradiction.

He says, "Not so, because it is not heard [in the text]," meaning that the non-filling of the world due to descent should not be assumed, as that would entail the abandonment of what is actually heard in scripture.
He says, "Of the descent," because the descent itself is stated in scripture to be the third place.

The meaning is that the repetition is redundant because it has already been established by implication that those who perform sacrifices and the like (iṣṭādikārin) descend, based on the statement regarding the descent of those very performers; for they "return again to this path.

Furthermore, since the phrase "of these two" would contradict the introduction of a different path and contradict the word "third," it should be understood that the word "place" (sthāna) indicates the "path" (mārga). //17//
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that all ought to go to the moon in order to obtain a new body— this is now addressed.
Regarding the argument that it is so because of the fixed number of oblations in the statement "at the fifth oblation," that is answered:
No, because it is not perceived as such in the third [oblation]. (BBs 3.1.18)
The restriction of the number of oblations to five need not be observed for the sake of attaining the third place.
Why? Because it is so perceived;
for, even without a fixed number of oblations, attainment of the third place is perceived in the manner described: "Be born and die—this is the third place" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8).

Thus it is said; moreover, in the passage, "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3), the number of oblations is proclaimed as the cause for a human body, not as the cause for the bodies of insects, moths, and so forth.

Because the word *puruṣa* denotes the human species; furthermore, it is taught that water attains the designation "human" at the fifth oblation, but it is not prohibited from attaining the designation "human" at any oblation other than the fifth, as that would entail the fault of a single sentence having two contradictory meanings.
In that regard, for those in whom ascent and descent are possible, the body will arise at the fifth libation;
for others, however, the body is commenced by means of waters infused with other elements, even without the sequence of libations.

Having thus refuted the two seeds of the prima facie argument—namely, the scriptural statement without qualification and the absence of any other path—he introduces the sūtra beginning with "yat punar... (as for that which... in order to refute the third seed.

The meaning is that there is no regard for the number of oblations, because for those devoid of knowledge and ritual action, constant birth and death are observed through the scriptural passage "Be born as a worm, a moth, etc.," in the form of worms, insects, and so forth.
He says "apica" (moreover) to show that this is also the case on account of the word "puruṣa."
He states with the words "Moreover" (*apica*) and so forth that there is no fixed rule regarding the number of oblations even for a human body;
the meaning is that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if two distinct meanings in the form of injunction and prohibition were present. //18//
Moreover, it is also recorded in common worldly usage: BBs_3,1.19.
Moreover, it is recorded in the world that Droṇa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others, as well as Sītā, Draupadī, and others, were not born from a womb;
among them, for Droṇa and the others, there was no oblation consisting of a woman.
But for Dhṛṣṭadyumna and others, neither of the two oblations—one pertaining to a woman and one to a man—exists.
Just as there is no regard for the number of oblations in that case, so it will be elsewhere as well.
It is a common worldly belief that even the crane conceives a fetus without the emission of semen. // 19 //
To confirm the memory regarding the lack of restriction, there is the sūtra: "It is also remembered" (smaryate 'pi).
That by which something is observed is called "loka"; this refers to the *Mahābhārata* and other such works. He also states the primary meaning: "balākā" [is used here]. //19//
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (3.1.20)

Moreover, since among the fourfold collection of living beings—namely those born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, and from a sprout—it is observed that those born from sweat and from a sprout arise even without sexual intercourse (*grāmyadharma*), there is no regard for the number of oblations;
the same will be the case elsewhere as well. (20) [FN: *jīvaja* means born from a womb.]
"Udbhijja" refers to trees and the like.

He explains the Sūtra by relying on the Śruti passage: "And those born from eggs, those born from a womb, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.2), stating: "Moreover" (api ca).
The meaning is that this applies elsewhere as well, even to those who perform undesirable acts and so forth. //20//
Now, an objection is raised: "Of these beings, there are indeed only three origins: the egg-born, the viviparous, and the soil-born" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.1).

In this context, only a threefold collection of beings is heard; how then is a fourfold nature of the collection of beings asserted? To this it is replied: the third term includes those born from heat and moisture. (BBs 3.1.21)

In the passage, "born from an egg, born from a living being, and born from a sprout" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.1), it should be understood that the third term, "born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*), itself includes those born from sweat (*svedaja*);
for both sweat-born and sprout-born beings are equally characterized by their origin through the breaking forth [of life] from earth and water.

However, since the emergence of mobile beings (*jaṅgama*) is distinct from the emergence of stationary beings (*sthāvara*), there is no contradiction in the statement elsewhere regarding the distinction between those born of moisture (*svedaja*) and those born of sprouting (*udbhijja*). [The author] introduces the Sūtra beginning with "Now, [the objection]" (*nanu*) as a response to the following doubt: "How is a fourfold classification stated by this Śruti, when another Śruti restricts it to only three, thus creating a contradiction? *Note: "Born of moisture" (*saṃśokaja*) means born of sweat.* [The Sūtra: But there is no contradiction, because of the difference in the emergence of the stationary and the mobile. (2.1.21) [Commentary: There is no contradiction. Why? Because the emergence of mobile beings is indeed different from the emergence of stationary beings; therefore, the discussion of the distinction between those born of moisture and those born of sprouting in other places remains consistent. *Note: "Born of moisture" (*saṃśokaja*) means born of sweat.* By this Śruti, how is a fourfold nature stated, given the contradiction with the restrictive declaration in another Śruti that there are only three? It is in response to this doubt that he takes up the Sūtra with the words "Now, [the objection]" (*nanu*), etc.

The distinction is as follows: viviparous (jīvaja) refers to humans and the like; those born by breaking through the earth refer to trees and the like; and those born by piercing through water refer to mobile beings such as lice and the like.
Sorrow is perspiration. //21//
Topic 4: Attaining the State of Being Like [the Deity] (Sābhāvyāpatti-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 22.
"Attainment of its own nature [occurs] because of the logical possibility.

(BBs 3.1.22) It has been stated that those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* ascend to the moon, dwell there for as long as their karma lasts, and then descend from there with a remainder of their residual karma (*sānuśaya*).
Now, the manner of that descent is examined.
In this regard, there is this scriptural passage concerning the descent: "Then they return again by this very same path as they came—to space;

from space, to air; having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud; having become a cloud, he rains down" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5). Regarding this, a doubt arises: do those descending attain the actual nature of space and the other elements, or do they attain a similarity to space and the others?
In that regard, they first establish that [the Self] has the very nature of space and so forth as it is attained [in deep sleep].
Why? Because such is the scriptural statement;
otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
And when there is a choice between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), direct scriptural statement is the logical one, not indirect indication.
Thus, the words "having become air, he becomes smoke," and so forth, are appropriately understood as referring to the actual acquisition of those respective forms.
Therefore, there is the attainment of the very nature of ether and the other elements.
This being the case, we reply: they attain equality with ether and the other elements.

When that body composed of water, which was produced for the sake of experience in the lunar orb, dissolves upon the exhaustion of that experience, it becomes subtle and equal to ether; from there it comes under the power of the wind, and then it is joined with smoke and the subsequent stages.
This very point is stated by the passage beginning with, "From here as they came, to space; from space, to air" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5). Why is this so?
Because it is logically consistent;
for it is only in this way that this is consistent,
since the actual existence of one thing as another is not logically possible.
Furthermore, once the true nature of space has been attained, a descent through the sequence of air and so forth is not possible.
Moreover, because space is all-pervasive and thus eternally connected [to the self], no other connection with it is tenable apart from the attainment of similarity to it.
And when the primary sense of a scriptural statement is untenable, it is indeed proper to resort to a figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, in this context, the very attainment of equality with space and so forth is metaphorically designated as "the state of being space and so forth. // 22 //

5. The Section on Not Too Long (Nāticirādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 23: Having thus examined the going and returning of sinners, [the author] now states the specific detail regarding the descent of those who perform sacrifices and other rites: "The attainment of similarity [of form], because of that possibility; they return by the same way as they came, and not otherwise. According to the manner already described, they return again by the path of smoke and so forth, exactly as they had come.
Having ceased their activity and being freed from the body at the end of their karma, those possessing latent dispositions (anuśayin) go to space and become like space.
Immediately after becoming like space, they become condensed and endowed with an extremely subtle liṅga; being led here and there by the wind, they become like the wind.
That aggregate of latent dispositions, having become like the wind, becomes like smoke when joined with smoke.
Having become like smoke, it becomes like a cloud.
A cloud (*abhra*) is so called because it bears water (*apo bibharti*);

a rain-cloud (*megha*) is so called because it sprinkles or pours down (*mehati siñcati*), being the agent of rain. Having become like that [cloud], it enters the earth by way of the streams of rain and becomes rice, barley, and so forth—this is the meaning of the scriptural passage according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The two preceding arguments should be understood as seeds of doubt:

in the former case, since two paths were mentioned and this is stated to be the third, it is appropriate that the word "place" (sthāna) indicates the "path"; however, in the present case, in common usage such as "milk becomes curd," the verb "becomes" (bhavati) is primary in the sense of attaining the nature of a transformation.

The connection with the counter-example is that there is no seed characterized by the attainment of similarity. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the primary meaning of the scriptural text is the result.

The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "In this way," etc., on the grounds that it is impossible for those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) to attain the nature of the previously established ether and so forth; therefore, [the text] refers to a mere resemblance (*lakṣaṇā*).
The meaning of the words of the sūtra is as follows: *sābhāvya* is the state (*bhāva*) of having a common nature (*dharma*); that is, similarity (*sāmya*).
"For it is thus" means that this very process of becoming is established precisely in the form of such similarity.

He states that the definition of similarity is also established by the impossibility of the latent dispositions (*anuśayins*) emerging from space and so forth otherwise, saying: "having the nature of space" (*ākāśasvarūpa*).
Anticipating the objection that it might be defined as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), he says: "due to omnipresence" (*vibhutvāt*).
The meaning is that if it were defined as conjunction, it would result in a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the scriptural mention of the verb *bhavati*.
He concludes the discussion on detachment by reflecting that "in the descent [to lower births], there is a leveling with various types of beings"; thus he says, "Therefore... (22).
Not after a very long time, because of a specific distinction. (BS 3.1.23)
In that regard, concerning the cognition of space and so forth prior to the cognition of rice and other such things, there arises a doubt:
does [the object] remain for a long time through similarity with each preceding moment before attaining similarity with the succeeding one, or for only a short time?
In this matter, there is no fixed rule, because of the absence of a scripture that establishes such a rule.
This being the case, he says: "not after a long time.
Having remained for a very short time in the state of space and so forth, they fall upon this earth along with showers of rain. Why is this so?

Because of the observation of a distinction; for, immediately after the attainment of the state of rice and so forth, [the text] specifies: "From there, indeed, it is more difficult to emerge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6).
The letter *ta* in this Vedic grammatical derivation should be understood as elided.
The meaning is that the exit from this state of being rice and so forth is more difficult to fall away from, more difficult to emerge from, and more painful than before.
Thus, by demonstrating here the difficulty of emerging from suffering, he shows the ease of emerging from it in the preceding states.
This distinction between pleasure and pain is caused by the shortness or length of the time before one falls [from the womb].
Because the body has not yet been formed during that interval, experience is impossible.
Therefore, prior to attaining the state of rice and so forth, the descent [into the womb] would occur in a very short time. // 23 //

Not long after [the statement regarding similarity]. Having relied upon the aforementioned similarity, the author raises a doubt based on the observation in the world that those who travel take either a long or short time to reach their destination, and thus presents the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*).
The result of the prima facie view is that, due to a lack of fixed rule, the attainment of a new womb may sometimes be delayed.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, the distinction is that because of their existence as rice, barley, and so forth, there is a delayed exit for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*); whereas due to their existence as ether and so forth, there is a swift exit. Thus, through the contemplation that the attainment of a womb occurs without delay, there arises a firmness of detachment (*vairāgya*). This is the discernment. Now, one might object: since the existence of those with residual karma in ether and so forth is pleasant, while in rice, barley, and so forth it is painful, it appears from the word "painful" that the exit is not delayed, but rather occurs quickly; therefore, he says: "And this is merely a distinction between pleasure and pain."
The limit is time. //23//
END BsCom_3,1.5.23 START BsCom_3,1.6.24 6.
The Section Concerning the Superintendence by Another (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 24–27.
Because, as before, there is a statement regarding those [beings] presided over by others;
on that very ascent, immediately after the raining down, it is recited: "Then they are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6).

In this regard, there is a doubt: during this period, do the *anuśayins* (those possessing latent impressions) become partakers of the pleasure and pain of the stationary state, having entered the genus of stationary beings; or rather, do they merely undergo contact with stationary bodies presided over by other *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls)? What, then, is the initial position?
Those who have entered the class of stationary beings (sthāvara) become possessors of that pleasure and pain and are endowed with latent dispositions (anuśayin). Why is this so?

Because birth (janman) is established as having its primary meaning [in this context], and because the state of being a stationary being is well-known in both Śruti and Smṛti as a locus for experiencing [the results of karma].
Because it is logically established that the class of actions consisting of ritual efforts such as animal sacrifice results in undesirable fruits,
this birth of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) as rice and other grains is indeed primary,
just like their birth as dogs and other animals.

Just as birth among dogs, pigs, or *caṇḍālas* for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) is primarily characterized by being accompanied by their respective pleasure and pain, so too do those with residual karma undergo mere contact within rice plants and the like; it is not that they experience the pleasure and pain associated with those states.
Thus it is also with birth as rice and so forth.

This being the case, we reply: when the rice and other grains are presided over by other living beings, those possessed of residual karma (anuśayins) undergo mere contact with them; they do not become partakers of their pleasure or pain.
It is as before:
just as the state of being wind, smoke, and so forth, for those with residual karma, is merely a state of conjunction with them.
In this way, even the state of being rice and so forth is merely a conjunction with stationary beings that have attained birth. Why is this so?
Because here too, there is a description exactly like that [of the previous case].
What is this "state of being like that" (tadvadbhāva) of the expression?
It is the mention [of something] without reference to an operative action (karmavyāpāra).
Just as in the case of space and so forth, up to the end of "raining," one does not perceive any operative action at all, so it is also with respect to the birth of rice and other such things.
Therefore, there is no experience of pleasure or pain for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) in this state.
However, where the text intends to refer to the experience of pleasure and pain, it points to the operation of karma, as in the passages "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct.

Furthermore, if the birth of those possessing residual karma in rice and other grains were taken in its primary sense, then when the rice and so forth are being reaped, threshed, cooked, and eaten, the residual selves identifying with them would have to depart.
For it is well known that when a living being identifies with a body, it departs when that body is afflicted.
In that case, the state of being a "seeder of semen" (the progenitor) would not be predicated of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) upon their becoming rice and so forth;
therefore, there is for the possessors of residual karma merely a conjunction with the rice and other plants presided over by another [soul].

By this, one may refute the claim that "birth" (janman) has its primary meaning [in the case of plants], as well as the claim that the state of being a stationary being (sthāvarabhāva) is a locus for experience.
Nor do we deny that the state of being a stationary being is a locus for experience;
let it be a locus of experience for other creatures who have attained the state of stationary beings through the power of their demerit (apuṇya).
However, we maintain that those possessing residual karma (anuśayin) who descend from the moon do not experience the state of stationary beings (sthāvara). // 24 //
The sequence of the topics is to be understood from other statements, from the sequence of the scriptural text (*śrutikrama*), and from the sequence of their meanings (*arthakrama*).
The meaning of the scriptural passage here is that those possessed of latent tendencies (*anuśayin*), having fallen upon this earth by way of showers of rain, are born as rice and so forth.
Regarding this, he states a doubt based on the scriptural text "they are born here" and because of the previously mentioned similarity to the elements beginning with space and ending with rain;
the phrase "tattra" means "in this interval," that is, immediately after the similarity to rain.
It is not appropriate to interpret the word *durniṣprapatara* as indicating a long duration for the process of emerging.

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the connection of an objection—namely, that "exit [from the body] occurs with difficulty" because it is the primary possibility—starting with the words "What, then... (*kiṃ tāvat*).

The distinction here is as follows: in this prima facie view, there is a great effort required by the qualified seeker to avoid becoming stationary; whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is ease of effort merely to avoid the simple conjunction with rice and so forth, as well as a firmness of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Now, one might object: "Birth for living beings occurs through the production of a body, not inherently; moreover, things such as rice and the like do not possess the nature of a body. To this, he says:
"Of the state of being stationary," referring to the scriptural passage beginning with, "Some enter into stationary objects."

"The man goes to the state of an immobile being due to the defects of actions born of the body"—such is the Smṛti. Now, one might object: since those in heaven lack sin, how can they attain the state of an immobile being? To this, he says: "As animals," etc.

The Sāṅkhyas say that the meaning of words such as "eating the remnants of Soma" and "drinking liquor" refers to the consumption of what remains after the ritual; and since even acts like ritual slaughter possess the general quality of being "slaughter," it is not contradictory for them to produce a latent demerit (*duritāpūrva*) by virtue of being prohibited by scriptural injunctions such as "one should not kill. Furthermore, the state of becoming rice and so forth for those with residual karma (*anuśayin*) mentioned here is not something produced anew, because it is stated here without reference to any specific action.
He establishes the final position (siddhānta) with the words "Thus [the objection] having been raised," etc., stating that it is like the previously mentioned states of ether and so forth.

The term "as before" (pūrvavat) has been explained both as an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) and as a constituent part of the reason (hetu). Furthermore, he provides a counter-example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta) regarding what is referred to here in this context as a specific action, namely "that birth," with the words "But where... (yatra tu).

Furthermore, in the supplementary passage, "For whoever eats the food, and whoever sheds the seed into the woman, that very thing he becomes," the connection of the group of those with residual karma (anuśayin) who have entered into rice and other grains with the man who sheds the seed is heard to occur by way of the food; since this would otherwise be impossible, the scriptural mention of birth cannot be taken in its primary sense. This is what [the author] states with the words beginning "Moreover" (apica).

The meaning is that, since the liberation of embodied beings necessarily occurs upon the destruction of the body in the form of rice and so forth, there would be no union with a seed-discharging being (retassig-yoga).
"By this" refers to the aforementioned inference and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

The meaning is that one should respond to the objection—that the primary sense of the scriptural statement "it is born" and the fact that rice and other grains serve as the locus for the experience of those with residual karma (*anuśayin*)—by stating the following.

Now, an objection may be raised: "If the status of rice and other grains as loci of experience is not admitted, would this not contradict the previously cited authority of Śruti, Smṛti, and common consensus? To this, he says: "And not... (24).
If it be argued that [the world] is impure, we say no, because of the Word (Śabda). 3.1.25.

As for the further argument that because sacrificial ritual action (*ādhvarika-karma*) is impure due to its connection with the injury of animals and so forth, an undesirable fruit is also possible for it— and therefore, let the primary birth of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) as rice and other grains occur, making a figurative interpretation therein useless— that is refuted: No, because the knowledge of dharma and adharma is based upon scripture (*śāstra*).

The treatise alone is the cause for the cognition that "this is dharma" and "this is adharma," because those two are beyond the reach of the senses and because their causes are not restricted by place, time, or circumstance.
A particular dharma which is practiced in a certain place, at a certain time, and under certain circumstances becomes adharma when performed under different places, times, and circumstances.
Therefore, apart from the scripture (*śāstra*), no one possesses knowledge regarding what constitutes dharma and adharma.
Since the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice—consisting of acts such as killing and favoring—is determined by the scripture to be dharma, how can it be said to be impure? [Objection:
But surely the scripture itself, in the injunction "one must not harm any living beings," makes known that harming living beings is adharma.
"Certainly;
that is the general rule (utsarga), while the exception (apavāda) is: 'One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.'"
Furthermore, there is a fixed determination of the scope for both general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*).
Therefore, Vedic action is pure, because it is practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and because it is not censured.
Therefore, it is not appropriate for its fruit to be birth as an immobile being;
nor can birth as rice and so forth be like birth as a dog and so forth,
for that [latter] is spoken with reference to those who have committed foul deeds, whereas here there is no such specific qualification.

Therefore, for those who have fallen from the lunar orb and are subject to rebirth, their becoming rice and so forth is merely a state of contact with rice and other grains; this is what is figuratively designated as "becoming that. (25)
He elaborates on the meaning of the Sūtra— "Vedic action is not impure because it is enjoined by the Śāstra"— with the words beginning "This is Dharma. The meaning is that the conclusion—

that the Agnihotra performed in a pure place at dawn or dusk for the purpose of livelihood and so forth constitutes Dharma, whereas the same act performed in an impure place at midnight for the purpose of death and so forth becomes Adharma— is achievable solely through the Śāstra.
To this he replies: "And from scripture.
Now, one might object: it is not proper here for the general rule (utsarga) that "whatever is violence is unrighteousness" to be set aside by a specific injunction;

for just as the Śyena sacrifice—which is prohibited by the rule "one should not practice malevolent magic"—is understood to serve the purpose of the person, there is no contradiction in prohibited violence and the like serving as an auxiliary to the sacrifice.
Regarding this, he says: "In the case of general rules and exceptions.

This is the meaning: in all instances of optional (kāmya) ritual action, engagement in the aspect of the instrument (karaṇa-aṃśa) arises from passion (rāga), whereas engagement in the subsidiaries (aṅga) arises from injunction (vidhi); such is the established position.

And thus, even though the ritual act known as the Śyena is prohibited, activity toward it would still occur due to the intensity of passion; however, in the case of violence that is an auxiliary to a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga-hiṃsā*), activity must be said to proceed from the injunction itself.
Now, if that injunction were not to sublate the fact that [violence] is a cause of harm—which is established by general rule—then it could not be an instigator of action;
or, if it were an instigator, the injunction would lead to what is harmful.

Therefore, the injunction (vidhi), being without scope [elsewhere], establishes the general rule (utsarga)—which has scope [in other matters]—as restricted to cases of non-prescribed injury and the like.
This statement was made by assuming that the prohibitive scripture (niṣedha-śāstra) operates on the basis of the commonality of "being injury" (hiṃsātva) and so forth.

In reality, however, since that [prohibition] pertains to injury prompted by passion (rāga-prāpta), it does not apply to injury performed under scriptural injunction (vaidha-hiṃsā); thus, one should understand that there is no occasion for the suspicion of impurity (aśuddhatva) regarding such [prescribed] injury.
The construction is: "It is not the case that its fruit is a corresponding form of suffering.
It has been stated here that in the state of being rice and so forth, there is no specific entitlement (*adhikāra*), nor is there any reference to karma. //25//
Now follows the connection with the shedder of semen. (BS 3.1.26)

For this reason as well, their becoming rice and so forth is merely a state of contact with them, because immediately after the state of being rice and so forth, the state of being one who emits semen is taught for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*): "For whoever eats the food and whoever emits the semen, he becomes that very thing again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6).
And in this context, a literal state of being one who emits semen is not possible.
For one who has been born for a long time and has reached youth becomes a "seeder" (retaḥsigin).
How, then, could that state of being a seeder—being free from figurative usage—be attained by a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) that has not followed along with the food currently being consumed?
In this regard, one must necessarily admit that the state of being a seeder consists precisely in the connection with a seeder.
In the same way, the state of being rice and so forth is merely the conjunction with rice and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction. // 26 //
Now, after the state of rice and so forth, the state of being one who emits semen is heard in the scripture.

In that case, since those with residual karma (anuśayin) residing in food cannot logically be agents of the emission of semen, it must be understood as mere conjunction; likewise, in the opening statement as well, only conjunction is to be accepted.
Thinking that otherwise there would be a contradiction between the opening and the concluding statements, it was said: "Thus there is no contradiction. //26//
From the womb, the body [is produced]. (BS 3.1.27)

Furthermore, the scripture states that immediately after the state of being a seed-sower, when the semen has been discharged into the womb, a body superior to the womb is born for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) to experience the fruits of that karma— namely, the passage beginning, "Now, those here whose conduct was pleasant" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.7). From this also, it is understood that at the stage of becoming rice and so forth during the descent, that very body is not endowed with pleasure and pain.
Therefore, it is established that the birth of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) consists merely in their conjunction with rice and other such grains. // 27 //
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that because the scripture speaks of the body as arising from the womb, those possessed of residual karma (*anuśayin*) do not have rice and other grains as their bodies.

Thus, concluding the meaning of the chapter (Pāda), he summarizes: "Thus it is established," on the grounds that by reflecting on how the cycle of going and returning for those who perform ritual actions (*karmiṇaḥ*) is difficult to escape, dispassion toward the fruits of action—which is the means to the knowledge of reality—is established.

This concludes the first [section] of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Govinda Bhagavatpāda.

Third Chapter, Second Section / [In this section: An investigation into the purification of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*] 1. The Section on the Twilight Devotions (Sandhyādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 1–6.
"In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says.

(BBs 3.2.1) Having previously, in the section concerning the departed, illustrated the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) and detailed the various paths of the individual soul's transmigratory journey,
the different states of that very soul are now being detailed.

Regarding this, they cite the following: beginning with "When he falls asleep" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9), it continues, "There are no chariots there, no draft animals, and no roads, yet he creates chariots, draft animals, and roads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10), and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is the creation in dream, like that in the waking state, ultimately real, or is it composed of illusion?
In this regard, it is first established that the creation during the intermediate state is of a real nature.
By "intermediate state" (*saṃdhya*), one refers to dream, as seen from its usage in the Veda: "The third state is the intermediate state, the state of dream" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9).
It is called *saṃdhyam* because it occurs at the junction (*saṃdhi*) between two states of the world, or between the states of waking and deep sleep.
In that intermediate state, the creation must indeed be real in nature.

Why? Because the authoritative scripture (*śruti*), being a means of valid knowledge, declares thus: "Then he creates chariots, horses for the chariots, and roads," and so forth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10).
For it is understood exactly thus from the concluding summary that "he indeed is the agent. // 1 //
"In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says.

He states the connection between the two chapters in the form of a relationship between cause and effect—namely, that the discrimination between the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam*, which is to be accomplished through the detachment already described, is the means for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*)—in the words "That which was transcended," etc.
Precisely because this chapter consists of an inquiry into the means [of knowledge], its connection to this [fourth] chapter [is established].

In this chapter (*pāda*), prior to the section beginning with "Not even from the standpoint of place" (*na sthānato 'pi*), the referent of the term *jijñāsitatva* (the object of inquiry) is first analyzed by way of its states (*avasthā*); starting from that point until the end of the chapter, there is an analysis of the referent of the term *tat* (that), which is the subject to be enjoined.
Within that, the waking state was previously defined through an investigation into going and returning; immediately following that, the dream state—

Having taken up what is stated in the Śruti as the subject matter, and expressing a doubt based on the mention of the creation of chariots and so forth in that dream state as well as the mention of their absence, he applies the sūtra of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "In this regard, there is a doubt," and so on.

The meaning of the doubt is as follows: are the chariots and other objects in a dream possessed of empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-sattā*), like the chariots and other objects in the waking state, or are they merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell?
It should be understood that this is because the ultimate reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) was negated in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*.

Regarding this, the result is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the distinction of the individual soul (*jīva*) from the dream state is not established, just as it is not in the waking state;

whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), its self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) is established through the distinction [of the soul] as the witness (*sākṣin*) of the objects of perception which are merely apparent.

For one who is about to die, because all the senses have been withdrawn, there is no longer experience of this world; yet, while remembering this world through mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there occurs by the force of karma a dream in the heart consisting of the manifestation of the next world through the mind.
This is the "intermediate dream" (*saṃdhya-svapna*), which occurs at the junction between the two worlds.
Thus says the Śruti: "Standing in that intermediate place, he beholds both these places—this world and the place of the next world."

Out of dissatisfaction with the view that this dream is merely occasional, it is stated that the eternal dream exists at the junction of waking and deep sleep (*prabodha-saṃprasāda*). Others, however, maintain that because the dream touches upon both worlds by its very definition— since it possesses the characteristic of the other world (*paraloka*) insofar as it involves direct perception of forms and so forth not produced by mortal eyes and the like, and possesses the characteristic of the mortal world (*martyaloka*) insofar as it involves such perception not produced by divine eyes and the like— it partakes of both realms.
They explain that the state of being a junction between two worlds belongs to the dream itself, just as a path touching two villages is the junction between them.
Not only does scripture establish the empirical reality of the objects in dreams, but he states that it is also because they have an agent: "For he is the agent" (1).
And some [maintain] that the creator is the son and so forth. (BBs 3.2.2)

Moreover, some followers of other Vedic branches (śākhins) declare that in this very intermediate state, the Self is the creator of desires, as it is said: "This Person who wakes while others sleep, fashioning desire after desire" (KaU 5.8).
And here, "desires" (kāmāḥ) refers to sons and so forth, because they are objects of desire (kāmyante).
[Objection: But surely, by the word *kāma*, only specific desires would be denoted. [Reply: No;
for after beginning with "Choose sons and grandsons who shall live a hundred years" (KaU 1.23), it concludes at the end: "I make you the enjoyer of all desires" (KaU 1.24).
This is because the word "desire" (*kāma*) is employed there in reference to sons and other such things mentioned in the context;
furthermore, we understand from both the context and the remainder of the passage that this creator is the Wise One (*prājña*).
For this is the instrument of the Wise One, as stated in: "Other than dharma, other than adharma... (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.14).
And so forth; moreover, the supplementary portion of the passage concerning that very subject also states: "That indeed is the pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal;

upon it all worlds rest, and no one transcends it" (KaU 5.8). Since the creation effected by the Prājña is understood to be real in nature when based on the waking state, the creation based on the dream state must likewise be real.

And thus the Śruti says: "Now, indeed, they say that this [dream state] is the very region of waking; for whatever one sees while awake, those same things one sees while asleep" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14).
This declares the identical principle governing both dreaming and waking. Therefore, the creation in the intermediate state is indeed real in nature. // 2 //

Furthermore, he states the meaning of the sūtra with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth: "And moreover, the objects of dreams are real, because they are created by an intelligent being, like space and so on."
Fearing that [the term] might be taken in its conventional sense, he refutes it with the words "But surely," etc.
The meaning is: that which remains awake while the instruments (senses) are asleep and inactive—that alone is the pure, self-luminous Brahman.
[This is so] because of the dream's [correspondence] with the objects of the waking state.

He states that the purpose of the scriptural declarations regarding their occupying the same location and the declarations regarding their non-difference is to establish their reality: "Now, indeed, they say... (2).
This being the case, he replies: [as follows].
"But it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not fully manifested.
The word "but" sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that what was stated—that creation in the intermediate state (saṃdhye) is ultimately real—is correct.
The creation in the intermediate state (saṃdhyā) is indeed an illusion; there is not even a scent of ultimate reality in it.
Why? Because its essential nature is not manifested in its entirety.
For the dream state does not have its essential nature manifested through the characteristics of an ultimately real entity in its entirety.
Furthermore, what is intended here by "completeness"? It is the non-contradiction regarding place, time, and causal conditions.
For place, time, causal conditions, and non-contradiction pertaining to objects that are ultimate reality cannot possibly exist in a dream.
To begin with, a suitable place for chariots and such things does not exist in a dream.
For otherwise, chariots and other such things would find no space within the confined regions of the body.
It might be argued:
"One will perceive dreams outside the body, because one perceives objects located in distant places."
Moreover, scripture shows that dream occurs outside the body: "Having moved about outside his nest as an immortal, he goes wherever he desires as an immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12).
Furthermore, the distinction between the cognitions of staying and going would not be consistent if the living being had not departed [from the body].
No, it is said;
for it is not possible for a sleeping person to have the capacity to travel to and return from a place separated by hundreds of yojanas in a mere moment.

Moreover, in some cases, he reports a dream that lacks a return, saying: "Today, while lying down and overcome by sleep, I went to the Pañcāla country in a dream, and having awakened here, [I am back]."
If he were to depart from the body, he would awaken among the Pañcālas; yet he does not awaken there, but rather awakens right here among the Kurus.

Furthermore, those standing nearby see that very body by which he imagines himself traveling to another place as remaining in the very place where he lay down. And the other places he sees in his dream do not exist in the manner in which he perceives them.
If, while running about, he were to perceive [the world] as a real entity, just as when waking, he would apprehend Māra as being truly existent.

Moreover, Scripture demonstrates that the dream occurs within the body itself, beginning with "When he moves about in the state of dreaming" and concluding with "He moves about at will within his own body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.18).

Therefore, because it contradicts both Scripture and logical reasoning, the scriptural passage concerning "outside the nest" must be interpreted figuratively as meaning "having moved as if outside the nest, the immortal one [moves]."
For that which, though dwelling within the body, does not perform any function by means of it, is as if outside the body.
Such being the case, even the distinction between the conditions of staying and moving must be admitted as a mere deception.
Furthermore, there is a discrepancy regarding time in dreams: one who has fallen asleep at night perceives it as day in the land of Bhārata.
Likewise, in a dream that lasts for only a moment, one sometimes passes through many series of years.
Furthermore, no signs (nimitta) suitable for cognition or action exist in a dream;
for, due to the withdrawal of the instruments of perception, one possesses no eyes or other senses for the apprehension of chariots and such things.
Furthermore, how could he have the capacity to produce chariots and such things in a mere twinkling of an eye, or even from wood?
Moreover, these chariots and other objects seen in dreams are sublated upon waking;
indeed, they are easily sublated within the dream state itself.
Because deviation [from consistency] is observed at both the beginning and the end:
for that which is determined in a dream as "this is a chariot" becomes a human being in an instant, and that which is determined as "this is a human being" becomes a tree in an instant.

Furthermore, the scripture clearly declares the non-existence of chariots and so forth in a dream: "There are no chariots there, no horses yoked to chariots, and no roads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10), and so on.
Therefore, the vision of a dream is merely an illusion. (3) [Note:
*saṃvṛte* means "in the conventional"; *saṃkīrṇaḥ* means "confused"; *paryetum* means "to go about" or "to travel"].
[The opponent argues that dream chariots and the like] could arise [from elsewhere] or come from outside.

The author establishes his own position—that dream chariots and such are merely appearances—by means of the word "but" (*tu*) and so forth, since they are observed even without the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) established for waking chariots and the like, just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

It is stated in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya that ignorance (*avidyā*), which resides in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), exists in the individual soul (*jīva*) as well by virtue of being delimited by the nature of consciousness; this [ignorance] is *māyā* in the form of chariots and so forth.

By the word "only" (*mātra*), in order to indicate the non-difference between illusion (*māyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), the exclusion of empirical reality—which consists in being unsublated as long as the cognizer exists—is stated.

Here, "wholeness" (*kārtsnya*) refers to the state of being produced by whatever causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is established in the waking state; this is the property of the waking object, which is an effect of ultimate reality.
The pervader of truth explains its absence in a dream with the words beginning "not indeed" (*na tāvat*), etc.;
"in a confined space" means in a crowded place, and "to traverse" means to go.
The awakened person causes those standing nearby to hear [this], so that they may come to understand it correctly; this is the sense.
"In such a way that it would be like a dream" means that at whatever time he moves by means of the state of dreaming, he moves as he pleases within his own body;
"as if outside" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that the immortal Self, as if outside its nest—the body—having moved about according to its desire, i.e., as it pleases, goes forth and sports.
He states the reason for this with the words "for he who":
the meaning is that, by virtue of the quality of being free from identification with the body, although situated within the body, he is said to be "outside," as if he were external to it.

This being so, the meaning is that by both scripture and reasoning, the dream exists within [the body] itself. "Vipralambha" means delusion. Having stated the absence of a suitable place, he states the absence of time with the word "kāla.
Here, it is said that even during the time of night, it is day in other regions such as Ketumāla; thus it is called "Bhārata."

The purport of the Sūtra is that, regarding the previous inferences based on the example of objects seen while awake, the state of being produced by a preceding cognition and the state of being incapable of sublation constitute the limiting conditions (upādhi). //3//
For [the subtle body] is indicated by scripture, and those who know it declare this as well. (BS 3.2.4)
If it is argued that because [the dream] is mere illusion, there is not even a trace of ultimate reality in a dream, we say:
no;
for a dream is indeed indicative of future good and evil fortune.

For it is heard thus: "When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for the sake of desired objects, one should know that there will be prosperity in accordance with that dream-vision" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.9).
Likewise, by such dreams as "he sees a black man with black teeth; he kills him," the scripture declares that a short life remains.
And those who study the science of dream interpretation declare: "Mounting an elephant and such things in a dream are auspicious, while riding a donkey and such things are inauspicious.
Furthermore, they maintain that certain dreams, caused by specific mantras, deities, or substances, possess a scent of truth.
Even in those cases, let it be granted that the object indicated may indeed be real; yet...
The intention is that for a dream-communicator, however, there is indeed falsity regarding the sight of women and so forth, because it is sublated.
Therefore, it is logical that the dream is merely illusion (*māyāmātra*).
As for what was stated, "For it says," since this is the case, that [scriptural passage] must be explained as being figurative (*bhākta*).
Just as it is said that "the plough draws the oxen and so forth" merely because it is the instrumental cause,
and not because the plough itself directly draws the oxen;
in the same way, because he is merely the instrumental cause, it is said that "the sleeper creates chariots and so forth," and that "he is the agent."
It is not, however, that the sleeping person creates chariots and so forth by means of direct perception itself.

Rather, it must be said that his status as a cause consists in his being the agent of the good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) which serve as the causes for those [experiences], since one observes joy, terror, and the like upon the appearance of chariots and such.

Furthermore, because the Self’s nature as self-luminous (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) is difficult to discern during the waking state due to contact with objects and sense organs and the intermingling with lights such as the sun, the dream state is introduced in order to discern that.

In this regard, if the statement regarding the creation of chariots and so forth were taken literally according to the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), then the self-luminosity [of the soul] would not be established.

Therefore, the statement concerning the absence of chariots and so forth must be understood according to the direct scriptural statement, whereas the statement concerning the creation of chariots and so forth must be explained as being figurative (*bhakti*). By this, the scriptural mention of "emanation" (*nirmāṇa*) is also explained.
As for what was also said—that "they declare this [self] to be the conscious creator"—that too is incorrect;

for in another scriptural passage it says: "Having himself struck down [the body], having himself created [the dream world], he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9).
Thus, because the activity of the individual soul (jīva) is heard [in scripture];
here too, in the passage "He who wakes among those who sleep" (KaU 5.8), this very soul, as is well known, is celebrated as the creator of desires.

However, by means of the remainder of that passage, that very *śukram* (the pure light) is taught to be *brahman*, setting aside its state as the individual soul (*jīva*) and establishing its nature as *brahman*— just as in the case of "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and other such texts— and thus there is no contradiction with the context of *brahman*.
Nor do we deny the activity of the *prājña* (the conscious self) even in dreams.
Because he is the Lord of all, it is logically consistent that he is the presiding controller over all states;
however, what is being established here is merely that this creation based on the twilight periods is not ultimately real, unlike the creation of space and so forth.
Furthermore, even the creation of space and the rest does not possess absolute reality.

For it has been established in the sūtra, "The non-difference from That [Brahman] follows from such terms as 'originating' and so forth" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14), that the entire phenomenal world is merely māyā;
however, prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self, the phenomenal world consisting of ether and the rest exists in a fixed form.
However, since the phenomenal expansion based on the twilight state is sublated every day, this specific nature of the twilight state as being mere illusion has been declared. // 4 //

He explains another Sūtra—beginning with "māyā" and so on—as a response to the objection that if a dream were merely an illusion, then even the object indicated by it would not be real. [The objection is:
"If dreams are indicators of reality through mantras, divine grace, or the use of medicinal herbs, they must themselves be real. To this he says: "In that case too, let it be granted.
The underlying sense is that even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, which causes true joy, is never observed to be real.

Just as the plough becomes the cause of the livelihood of cows and other animals through the medium of agriculture, so too the dreamer becomes the cause of the creation of the dream through the medium of his *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit);

it is not, however, a case of being the direct creator of the dream—like a potter with respect to a jar—as has already been stated regarding the absence of causal materials and the presence of contradiction. This is what is expressed by the passage beginning with "yad uktam" (as has been said).
Thus, the sense is that since dream lacks a primary agent, the reason [adduced] is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Furthermore, he states "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that the reality of dreams is not tenable because it contradicts the purport of the Śruti;
*vyatikara* means confusion or intermixture.
The meaning is "by the scripture's intent";
the sense is that there is no distinction from the waking state.
He states the conclusion with the words "therefore."
"By this" means by way of being figurative (*bhākta*).

Furthermore, as for the reason stated in the second sūtra— that the dream state has the wise one (*prājña*) as its agent— is that established by scripture (*śruti*), or is it established because the wise one is the Lord of all?
He says "not so today" with the words beginning "even what was said," etc.;
having himself paralyzed the waking body, making it motionless,
or having himself fashioned it through latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The meaning is that one experiences the dream by means of one's own light—that is, by the activity of one's own intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) and by one's own radiance, which is the consciousness of one's true nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*).

It is not only in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* that the individual soul (*jīva*) is heard to be the agent of dreaming; he states "here too" to show that this is also the case in the *Kaṭhaka*. To the objection that there would be a contradiction with the context concerning Brahman if the individual soul were mentioned here, he says: "But of that [soul]... [referring to the subsequent text].
Having thus refuted that the reason is established by scripture, he accepts the second alternative with the words "na cāsmābhiḥ" (nor by us).

Then, raising the objection that the dream must be real because its cause is established, he considers the alternatives as to whether this reality is empirical (*vyāvahārika*) or ultimate (*pāramārthika*); and since sublation is observed at the time of worldly transaction, he states "pāramārthikas tu" (but the ultimate one... to show that the first [alternative] is not the case.
Regarding the second [point], he states "nor... (na ca) to show that the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavaikalya).
Anticipating the objection, "What then is the distinction here between a dream and waking?", he states "previously... (prāk) to indicate its nature as a mere appearance (prātibhāsikatva). //4//
But [the Self] is concealed by meditation on the Supreme; for from that [concealment] arise its bondage and its opposite.
Now, it might be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed a mere part (*aṃśa*) of the Supreme Self, like a spark from a fire.
This being the case, just as fire and its sparks possess the same powers of burning and illuminating, so too do the individual soul and the Lord possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty.
Consequently, by virtue of the individual soul's knowledge and sovereignty, the creation of chariots and other objects in dreams will be produced through mere volition (*sāṃkalpikī*).

To this it is replied: even though there exists a relationship of part and whole between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), the fact that the individual soul possesses qualities contrary to those of the Lord is directly perceived.
Does it follow, then, that the individual soul possesses no qualities whatsoever in common with the Lord?
It is not that they do not exist at all.
Although it exists, it is concealed by the intervention of ignorance and other such factors.

That which is thus concealed becomes manifest— just as the power of vision, when obscured by cataracts, is restored through the efficacy of medicine— to some perfected individual who has exerted effort in meditating upon the Supreme Lord and whose darkness has been dispelled by the grace of the Lord.
It is not by their own inherent nature that all living beings [experience this];
why? Because from that cause, namely Īśvara, the bondage and liberation of this individual soul (jīva) occur.
Bondage arises from the lack of thorough knowledge of the true nature of Īśvara, while liberation arises from the thorough knowledge of His true nature.

And thus says the Śruti: "Having known God, there is the falling away of all bonds; with the afflictions exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death. Through meditating upon Him, upon the dissolution of the body, there is the third [state]: universal sovereignty, being alone and having attained all desires" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11).
Such are the passages beginning with this. // 5 //

Having raised the objection that it was incorrect to state that a dream is an illusion because of the absence of a previously prepared causal complex— since a real creation can occur even through mere true volition (satyasaṅkalpa)— the author explains the Sūtra while resolving that doubt with the words "Now,
it might be argued," and so forth.

The meaning of the resolution is that while for one of true volition the creation resulting from volition becomes real, the unreality of the volition of an individual soul (jīva) is directly perceived.
Then, one might raise the objection: "In that case, because of possessing contradictory attributes, the individual soul (jīva) cannot possibly possess the nature of the Lord (Īśvara).

To this he replies: "It is not that [the nature] does not exist; rather, it exists but is veiled, and it is manifested again to someone through the grace of the Lord. He explains: "It is not non-existent" means that for one whose darkness has been dispelled, who is free from sin, who is perfected, and characterized by [powers] such as atomization (aṇimā).

Having known and directly realized the Lord as "I am indeed Brahman," there occurs the removal—that is, the destruction—of all fetters, namely the afflictions such as ignorance; one becomes of that very nature.

And with the afflictions destroyed, there is the dissolution of the bondage consisting of birth and death, which are their effects; thus the fruit of the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) has been stated.
He now states the fruit of the knowledge of the qualified (saguṇa): "Of him... [tasya].

By meditating with a sense of "I-ness" directed toward another [the deity], with a view toward liberation from bondage, or with a view toward the two types of loss mentioned by Manu, there arises—upon the fall of the mortal body and the attainment of a perfected body—the third state, which is universal sovereignty in the form of *aṇimā* and so forth. Subsequently, through the knowledge of the Self, one becomes solitary (*kevala*), free from duality (*dvaita-śūnya*), and one whose desires are fulfilled (*āpta-kāma*), having attained the bliss of self-luminosity (*svayañ-jyotiḥ*). This is the meaning of "gradual liberation" (*krama-mukti*). //5//
Or rather, that [non-perception] also occurs due to the connection with a body. (BBs 3.2.6)
Why, then, does the individual soul (jīva), being indeed a portion of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured?
It would be more logical for knowledge and sovereignty to remain unobscured, just as the power to burn and the capacity to illuminate are not obscured in a spark of fire.
To this, it is replied:
This is indeed true;

however, that concealment of the individual soul's knowledge and sovereignty arises from its connection with a body—that is, from its association with the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, sensations, and so forth.

There is an analogy for this: just as the power of burning and illuminating, though inherent in fire, becomes concealed when it is produced from a fire-drill (araṇi), or as it is concealed when the fire is covered by ashes.

Thus, due to the connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body produced by name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which are themselves established by ignorance (avidyā), there occurs for the individual soul (jīva) the concealment of its knowledge and sovereignty caused by the error of non-discrimination from that [ignorance].

The word "or" (vā) is intended to exclude the doubt that the jīva and the Lord (īśvara) might be different. Now, one might object: let this very jīva be the Lord himself, since its knowledge and sovereignty are merely obscured; what is the use of postulating a connection with the body?
This is not so;

for the distinctness of the individual soul (*jīva*) from the Lord (*īśvara*) is not tenable, since the text begins with "That divinity thought" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.3.2) and continues with "having entered by means of this living self" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.3.2).

Because the individual soul (*jīva*) is referred to by the word "Self" [in the passage], and because [the scripture] teaches the identity of the Self with the Lord to the individual soul in the words:
"That is the Truth, that is the Self; That art thou, O Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.4).
Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed non-different from the Lord; however, due to its association with the body, its knowledge and sovereignty become concealed.
Consequently, it is not possible for the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream to be produced by the mere will of the individual soul.
Furthermore, if the creation of chariots and so forth in a dream were produced by will, no one would ever experience an undesirable dream.
For no one intends anything undesirable.

As for what was said—that the scriptural mention of the waking state establishes the reality of the dream—that statement of equality does not intend to assert actual reality, because that would contradict the self-luminosity [of the Self]. Moreover, the absence of chariots and so forth in the dream has been shown by the scripture itself.

However, because the dream is constructed from the latent impressions (vāsanā) originating from the waking state, that [scriptural statement] intends to convey its appearance as being similar to that [waking reality].
Therefore, it is logically established that the dream is mere illusion (māyāmātra). // 6 //
The aphorism is intended to explain that the cause for the concealment of the aforementioned sovereignty is the identification with the body;
to refute the doubt regarding this, he states: "Why?
Having accepted that there is no real obscuration, he establishes the imagined obscuration with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth.

Having raised the objection that it is better to assume the soul's distinctness from the Lord than to assume the existence of an obscuration while accepting its lordship, [the author] refutes it by means of scripture, beginning with "But surely" (nanu).

If light and so forth were real even in a dream, then the self-luminosity of the Self would be as indistinct as in the waking state; however, if they are merely illusory (prātibhāsika), then even in the absence of light, sense organs, and the like, the immediate manifestation of the object is established clearly as belonging solely to the light of the Self.
Therefore, the statement regarding the similarity of place and so forth refers to the intention that a dream appears as equal to the waking state; such is the meaning. //6//
END BsCom_3,2.2.6 START BsCom_3,2.2.7 2.
The Section Concerning the Absence of That (tadabhāvādhikaraṇam); Sūtras 7–8.
The absence [of that dream experience] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of scriptural statements to that effect.
(BBs 3.2.7) The state of dreaming has been examined; now the state of deep sleep is being examined.
In this regard, there are the following scriptural passages concerning the subject of deep sleep.
In one place it is heard: "When, being thus asleep and composed, he does not perceive any dream, then he has entered into these channels" (Chāndogya 8.6.3).

In another place, however, after enumerating the channels, it is heard: "Having descended by means of them, he rests in the pericardium" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1.19). Likewise, in another place, after enumerating the channels, it is said: "He is in those [channels] when, being asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one with this very breath" (Kauṣītaki 4.19).
Likewise, in another place: "He lies in that space which is within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17).
Similarly elsewhere: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1);
and also: "Embraced by the conscious Self, he knows nothing without nor within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: are these channels and so forth distinct places for deep sleep, independent of one another, or is there a single place for deep sleep that exists through mutual dependence? What, then, is the initial position? That they are distinct.
Why? Because they have the same purpose.
For things that serve a single purpose, such as rice and barley, mutual dependence is never observed;

however, the fact that the channels and so forth serve a single purpose is seen in deep sleep, as it is said: "He has entered into the channels" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3) and "He lies in the pericardium."
And because the use of the locative case is identical in various such instances [as Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19], one might object:
"But if this were so, the locative case is not seen used in the passage: 'Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
This is not a fault.
Even there, the meaning of the locative case is understood;

for the remainder of the passage states that the living being seeking a dwelling-place approaches the Existent: "Not finding another abode, it takes refuge in breath alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2), since the word "breath" refers back to the Existent which is the subject under discussion there.
And the locative case (*āyatana*) signifies the sense of the seventh case;
indeed, the use of the seventh case is also seen in that supplementary passage: "Having entered into Being, they do not know: 'We have entered into Being'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2).
Furthermore, deep sleep, characterized by the cessation of specific cognition, is not distinguished in any respect [as being different from this state].
Therefore, because the channels (nāḍīs) and the other [locations] serve a single purpose, one or another of these locations is approached for sleep by way of option at different times.
This being the position reached, it is established: "The absence of that occurs in the channels and in the Self.
"The absence of that" means the absence of that aforementioned dreaming, i.e., deep sleep (suṣupta).
The meaning is that one approaches these—the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth—along with the self (ātman), by way of conjunction (samuccaya), and not by way of option (vikalpa).
Why? Because of the scriptural statement (tacchruteḥ).

For instance, in various places, the status of all these—the channels and so forth—as the locus of deep sleep (suṣupti) is heard in scripture; and that [status] is properly subsumed under conjunction.
For if these were alternative options (*vikalpa*), there would be a contradiction.
Now, it might be argued that an option between the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth is possible because they have the same purpose, just as in the case of rice and barley;
but this is not so, as we shall explain.
The fact that multiple meanings or a combination [of options] can be expressed by the mention of a single case-ending does not follow merely from such a mention;
for we observe the use of a single case-ending even when there are multiple meanings or a combination, as in examples such as "he sleeps in the palace" and "he sleeps on the couch.
Thus, here too, the combination of sleeping in the channels, in the pericardium, and in Brahman is logically consistent.
And so the Śruti says: "Then this happens when one who is asleep sees no dream at all; then he becomes one with this very prāṇa" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 4.19).
This scripture declares the conjunction of the channels and the prāṇa during deep sleep, because they are presented in a single sentence.
Furthermore, that the prāṇa is Brahman has been established in the sūtra: "The prāṇa [is Brahman], because of the subsequent agreement" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.28).

Even where the text speaks of the channels (*nāḍī*) as if they were independent, presenting them as the place of sleep— namely, "At that time, he has entered into these channels" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3)—
there too, since there is no denial of Brahman, which is well-known from other passages, it is understood that he abides in Brahman itself by means of the channels.
And even so, the use of the locative case for the channels is not contradicted.
Even one who approaches Brahman by way of the channels has indeed already entered those channels;
for he who goes to the ocean by means of the Ganges has already gone into the Ganges.
Moreover, since the path to the world of Brahman consisting of rays and channels is intended here, the mention of "entering" is for the purpose of praising the channels.
Having stated, "He has entered into the channels" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3), the text praises the channels by saying, "No evil whatsoever touches him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3).

And he states the reason for the absence of contact with evil: the meaning is that one whose organs are pervaded by the "heat" known as *pitta* residing in the channels does not perceive external objects.
Alternatively, the term "heat" (*tejas*) is a designation for Brahman itself, as in another scriptural passage: "Brahman indeed is heat indeed" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7).

Thus, because the word "light" (*tejaḥ*) has been explained as referring to Brahman, the meaning is that one is indeed united with Brahman at that time by way of the channels (*nāḍī*); therefore, no evil touches him.

Furthermore, union with Brahman is established as the cause for the absence of contact with evil, as it is said: "All evils turn back from there, for this world of Brahman is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).

From such scriptural passages as these, and this being so, it is established that there is a combination of the channels with Brahman—which is well-known from other passages as the locus of deep sleep—as their underlying support.

Likewise, since the pericardium (*purītat*) is also mentioned in the context of the exposition of Brahman, its status as a locus of sleep is understood to be consistent with that [Brahman]: "He lies in that space which is within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17).

Thus, with reference to this very state of sleep in the space of the heart, it is said here: "He lies in the pericardium" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19). By "pericardium" (purītat) is meant the membrane surrounding the heart; even though he is actually lying within the space of the heart, he can be said to lie in the pericardium.
Even one residing within a city surrounded by walls is said to reside "in the wall.
Furthermore, the nature of Brahman has been established for the space within the heart in the sūtra: "The small [space] [is Brahman], because of the subsequent [texts]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.14).
Likewise, there is also a conjunction of the channels and the pericardium, as stated: "Having descended by means of them, he rests in the pericardium" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19).
This is understood from their being mentioned within a single sentence;
furthermore, the status of Brahman is well-established for both the "Being" (sat) and the "intelligent one" (prājña).
Thus, in these scriptural passages, only three places of deep sleep are proclaimed: the channels (nāḍyaḥ), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman.
Even there, the channels (nāḍīs) and the pericardium (purītat) are merely gateways;

Brahman alone is the single place of deep sleep. Furthermore, the channels and the pericardium serve only as the support for the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva), since its organs function therein.

Indeed, apart from its connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), no substratum for the individual soul (jīva) is possible by itself, because it is non-different from Brahman and is established in its own majesty.
