Furthermore, even its status as having Brahman as its substratum during deep sleep is not stated with the intention of implying a distinction between container and contained; rather, it is stated with the intention of identity (tādātmya).
For it says: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own (svam apītaḥ)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
By the word *sva*, the Self (ātman) is denoted; the meaning is that one who has attained his own true nature (*svarūpa*) is asleep.
Moreover, there is never a time when the individual soul (jīva) is not in union with Brahman, because its own essential nature (svarūpa) is imperishable.

However, with reference to the states of dreaming and waking—where, due to contact with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it appears as if it has assumed another form—it will be explained that upon the cessation of those adjuncts in deep sleep, it attains its own true nature.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that in the state of sleep the soul sometimes becomes united with Being (sat) and sometimes does not.
Furthermore, even if one accepts the hypothesis of a location, deep sleep (*suṣupta*)—characterized by the absence of specific cognitions—is not distinguished in any way among those [locations].
In that state, it is logical that one who has become united with Being (*sat*) does not cognize, because of its oneness;
as the Śruti says: "What could he know, and through what? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that [the self] moves within the channels, no cause for the lack of cognition on the part of one who is lying down can be discerned, because the scope of difference is the condition, as the scripture states: "But where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.31).
Now, one might object that even for that which has difference as its scope, causes such as extreme distance could be the reason for non-cognition.
"Certainly;
it would be so if the individual soul were admitted to be intrinsically limited,
just as Viṣṇumitra, being away on a journey, does not see his own home."

However, there is no limitation of the individual soul (jīva) apart from its limiting adjuncts (upādhi). If it were argued that the cause for not knowing—such as extreme distance and so forth—is located solely within the adjunct, even then, since the adjunct has been stilled, it is logical that the soul, having become one with Being, does not know. Furthermore, we do not here intend to establish a combination of the channels (nāḍīs) and other factors as being equally [independent causes].
There is no purpose served by this knowledge that "the channels are the place of sleep" or "it is the pericardium";
for no fruit dependent upon this knowledge is heard of in scripture,
nor is this knowledge taught as a subsidiary part of anything that possesses a fruit.
We shall now demonstrate that Brahman is the non-departing place of sleep.

There is a purpose for this knowledge: it serves to ascertain the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman, and to ascertain its state of being free from the activities of the dreaming and waking states.
Therefore, the Self alone is the place of sleep.

Thus, when the external organs have ceased their activity, having reflected upon the dream state— which consists of the play of ignorance ignited by mental impressions— for the sake of demonstrating the self-luminosity of the Self as the witness, he now investigates deep sleep, which consists of the dissolution of the mind in the state of dreaming, through the connection of the correlative and the counter-correlative: "Its absence [is] in the channels and in the Self, because of the scriptural statement."

This "sleeping" (svapana) occurs in such a manner that at the time one is asleep— meaning deeply asleep (*suṣupta*), with all [faculties] withdrawn, the external organs set aside, and because of the dissolution of the mind, there is a complete absorption (*samprasanna*)— this is the meaning.

Having stated the location of the channels (*nāḍī*) during sleep, he states the scriptural texts concerning the conjunction of the channels and the heart (*purītat*), as well as the channels and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), in the passage beginning with "elsewhere."
He cites the scriptural passages concerning the Supreme Self alone with the words "And so elsewhere," and so forth.

He states the doubt arising from the use of the locative case regarding the channels (*nāḍī*), the *purītat*, and Brahman, as well as from the scriptural mention of their combination, with the word "Therein" (*tatra*).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because of the optionality of the locations, there is no definitive conclusion that the individual soul (*jīva*) is one with Brahman.

In the established doctrine (siddhānta), the distinction is that [the soul] goes through the channels (nāḍīs) to the pericardium (purītat) and then rests in Brahman itself within the heart; this is the conclusion because of their conjunction (samuccaya). An objection is raised: "The mutual independence of rice and barley as being for the purpose of a single sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is observed, but how can there be such independent location for the channels and so forth with respect to the single state of deep sleep? To this he says: "And of the channels, etc. The meaning of the doubt is that since Brahman exists [as the locus], the third case-ending (instrumental) is used in the scripture rather than the seventh (locative).
He says, "This is not a fault," because from the word *āyatana* (abode), the sense of the locative case—namely, the state of being a substratum—is understood.

The meaning is that the individual soul (*jīva*), exhausted in the other two states [waking and dreaming], approaches the True Brahman called *prāṇa*, which is the place of rest, during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Since the locative hearing conveys an independent substratum, one must accept an option (*vikalpa*) [regarding the abode]; thus, the status of the channels (*nāḍīs*) and so forth as the location may sometimes be combined [with *prāṇa*]. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts on combination (*samuccaya*). This is the meaning of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He establishes the conclusion with the words "thus it follows.
In the Sūtra, the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including the pericardium (*purītat*).

If the channels were the place of deep sleep, then the pericardium would not be the place; thus, there would be a contradiction of the scriptural statement regarding the location in that alternative view.
He says that this is not logical, stating: "For there is an option among these," because the sense is that an option between rice and barley arises only as a last resort (*agatyā*).
As for the claim that the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth have a single result based on the hearing of the locative case (*saptamī-śruti*), [that is incorrect].
To this he says "no," for it is not so: "na hyeka... [and so forth].
Although there is a difference in the results—the purpose of the palace being to support the couch, while the purpose of the couch is lying down—a single case-ending is nevertheless observed.
Furthermore, because they serve as means for sleeping through the conditions of being separated or not separated [from the body], there is a combination;
likewise here too, since the soul's sleep occurs in Brahman alone by way of its movement through the channels (nāḍīs) and the pericardium (purītat), there is a combination—this is the meaning.
He states that there is a mutual combination of the channels and the vital breath (prāṇa) because they are both mentioned in a single sentence, saying: "In a single sentence... (ekavākyeti).

"The meaning of the locative case is merely the state of being a substratum, not independence; therefore, the locative does not contradict the notion of conjunction," he says with the words "And even so...
The meaning is: "even in the case of conjunction.

Here, regarding the scriptural mention of the channels (*nāḍī*), it is not intended that the sleeper's sleep occurs within the channels themselves, because the purpose is to praise the path consisting of the channels connected to the rays; thus he says "Moreover... (*api ca*).

The meaning is that because there is an absence of perceiving objects through bile (*pitta*), there is an absence of pleasure and pain, and thus there is no contact with the evil (*pāpman*) whose nature consists of those causes.
Alternatively, he says "or" to indicate that there is no contact with evil due to the attainment of Brahman, which is free from evil (*apahatapāpman*).
Regarding this interpretation, he states the advantage: "And this being so... (*evaṃ ca sati*).
The meaning is that a combination [of the two paths] is resorted to, based on the scriptural text: "Then he becomes one with them; then he becomes one in this very breath.

Just as there is a combination of the channels (nāḍīs) and Brahman during sleep by way of a subordinate and a primary relationship, so too is there a combination of the pericardium (purītat) and Brahman; this he states with the words beginning "In the same way," etc.
Having begun with "He lies in the ether, which is Brahman," it is subsequently stated: "Having descended through those [channels], he lies in the pericardium."
And thus, since it is established that [the soul] goes to the heart through the channels and rests in Brahman, there is a combination [of the two paths]; so he says, "Thus, the channels...

Because of the scriptural statements regarding both Being (*sat*) and the Intelligent One (*prājña*)—"He becomes united with Being" and "He is embraced by the Intelligent One"—there are five places of sleep; therefore he says, "Of Being and the Intelligent One.

Furthermore, in the case of rice and barley, an option is appropriate because they are each capable of producing the single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) required for the Darśa and other sacrifices independently of one another.

However, since the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth lack the capacity to serve as the substratum for the soul during deep sleep independently of Brahman, there can be no option [between them and Brahman]; thus he says: "Moreover, the channels...

It must be stated that the channels and the pericardium, which are the supports for the subtle body (*liṅga*)—the limiting adjuncts—are the substrata for the soul as conditioned by those adjuncts through a mediated succession;
yet even that is not possible in deep sleep.
The meaning is "due to the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts" (*upādhilayāt*).

Now, one might object: even Brahman cannot be the primary locus of the individual soul (*jīva*) because of their non-difference. To this he says: "being the substratum of Brahman. The point is that while the soul abides in Brahman through non-difference, for a soul whose limiting adjuncts have dissolved in the channels (*nāḍī*) and the pericardium (*purītat*), mere existence is not possible; therefore, since there is no capacity for a single purpose [in both], there can be no option (*vikalpa*).

He says "Moreover" (apica) because, since the limiting adjuncts that differentiate the individual soul (*jīva*) have dissolved during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it is not logical to conceive of any distinction from its natural state of non-difference from Brahman.

Furthermore, even by one who asserts that deep sleep occurs in any one of the various locations such as the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth, it must be admitted that the state of deep sleep is not thereby differentiated;
yet that cannot be maintained. Thus he says, "Moreover, regarding the location" (apica sthāna).
The absence of distinction is indeed the cause for the absence of the cognition of distinction;
however, the meaning is that for the individual soul (jīva) who has entered the channel, because it remains in a state of distinction, there is no instrument for the non-cognition of distinction.
He raises a doubt regarding the cause for the non-cognition of duality even while in a state of duality: "But [it is] distinction... and so forth.
The state of being distant from the object of sight for the seer is either natural or adventitious due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Regarding these, having restated the first position along with an illustration, he replies with the words beginning "Certainly" (*bāḍham*);
having restated the second, he refutes it with the words "It belongs only to the adjunct" (*upādhigatam eva*).

If the soul were separated from its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) while in the channels and so forth during sleep, there would be the undesirable consequence of knowing certain nearby objects; thus, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) would be contradicted.

However, since the soul cannot abide elsewhere when the adjuncts have dissolved, one must conclude that sleep occurs in Brahman itself—this is the meaning. Having thus rejected the alternative views, he refutes the idea of an equal combination (*samuccaya*) of the channels, the pericardium, and Brahman as being fruitless, and concludes by establishing their combination through the relationship of subordinate and principal—beginning with the words "Nor do we... and so on.
Therefore, awakening arises from this. BBs 3.2.8.

And because the Self alone is the place of sleep, for that very reason, awakening from this Self occurs as if eternally; this is taught in the section concerning sleep through the reply to the question, "Whence did he come? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.16), namely: "Just as small sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths [emerge]," and so on, as well as:
"Having come from Being, they do not know that they are coming from Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.10.2).

If, however, these states were being conceptualized as the place of deep sleep, [the scripture] would have taught that one awakens from the channels at some times, from the pericardium at others, and from the Self at yet others;
therefore, for this reason also, the Self alone is the place of deep sleep.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement regarding the soul's emergence from Brahman, the author of the Sūtras states that Brahman alone is the locus of deep sleep: "Therefore, [the soul's] awakening [is from Him)" (BrSū 3.2.9).
The meaning is that since the channels (nāḍīs) and the pericardium (purītat) are never heard of as the point of departure for emergence, they cannot be the locus of deep sleep.

Therefore, since the soul is non-different from Brahman when its limiting adjuncts (upādhis) have dissolved, the difference is merely adventitious; thus it is established that the non-difference of the meaning of the Viveka-vākya is proven. //8//
Section 3: The Topic Concerning Ritual Action, Recollection, Sound, and Injunction (Sūtra 9) *End of BsCom_3.2.2.8;

*Karmānusmṛti-śabda-vidhi-adhikaraṇam* / Sūtra 9.

"But that very [person] [returns], on account of the remembrance of action, the scriptural word, and the injunction" (BBs 3.2.9). Regarding that attainment of Being (*sat-sampatti*), it is considered whether the one who awakens is the very same person who had attained Being, or whether it is either he or another.
On this point, the initial position is that there is no fixed rule.
Why? For when a drop of water is thrown into a mass of water, it then becomes that very mass of water; and upon being drawn out again, it is difficult to establish that it is that same drop of water.
Likewise, one who is asleep has attained oneness with the Supreme and becomes serene; thus, he himself ought not to be able to rise again.

Therefore, having reached the position that either that same Lord or some other individual soul (jīva) awakens, the author says this: "But that very same soul, having fallen [into sleep] and attained its natural state, rises again, and not another."
Why?
Because of the recollection of karma, [the recollection of] words, and the rules of grammar;
I shall demonstrate the reason by analyzing them.
Since one is observed to perform the remainder of a ritual action, that same person must be the one who rises [from the state of dissolution] and not another.
For instance, it is observed that on the following day, one performs the remainder of a ritual action that was commenced on the previous day;
and it is not possible for one person to be authorized to perform the completion of a ritual action that was only half-finished by another.
Because this would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
Therefore, it is understood that the very same person who was the agent of a single action on the previous day is the agent on the subsequent day.

For this reason as well, it is that very same person who arises; for the recollection later of what was previously experienced—expressed as "I saw this on that past day"—would not be possible if someone else had arisen.
For one who has seen something cannot remember it if he were another;
furthermore, the recollection of the self in the form "I am that very person" would not be possible if a different self had arisen.
Moreover, it is understood from the sacred texts that the very same [self] arises again.

For thus it is said: "Again, according to the rule and according to its origin, it rushes forth toward the state of waking" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.16); "All creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2);
"Whatever they may be here—whether a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—they become that again."
Such words as these, read in the context of sleep and awakening, would not find consistency if there were the arising of a different self;
this is likewise understood from the injunctions for ritual action and knowledge,
for otherwise those injunctions for action and knowledge would be rendered purposeless.
For if the rising were from something else, it would follow that one is liberated merely upon falling asleep.
If this were the case, tell me, what would be accomplished by action or knowledge that bears fruit at a later time?

Furthermore, on the view that the rising is from something else, if the individual soul (jīva) were to rise while still engaged in activity in another body, it would entail the consequence of the cessation of activity in the former location.
Furthermore, if one who has fallen asleep there were to wake up [elsewhere], that conceptualization would be purposeless.

For he who falls asleep in a certain body wakes up in that very same body; if one who has fallen asleep in one body were to wake up in another, what benefit would there be in such a conceptualization? Moreover, if one who is liberated were to wake up, it would follow that liberation has an end.
Furthermore, for one whose ignorance has ceased, a re-arising is logically impossible;
by this, the re-arising of the Lord (Īśvara) is refuted,
because his ignorance is eternally ceased.

Furthermore, under the view that [the self] arises from the forest [of causes], there would be the unavoidable consequences of experiencing the results of actions not performed (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of the results of actions performed (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*).
Therefore, it is that very same [self] which arises, and not another.

As for what was further stated—that just as a drop of water cast into a mass of water cannot be extracted, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), having become merged [in Brahman], ought not to emerge—[that is not so].
That is refuted as follows:
It is logical that in that case a drop of water cannot be extracted because of the absence of a cause for separation;
however, here there exists a cause for separation—namely, karma and ignorance—and thus there is a difference.
Moreover, it is observed that even milk and water, which are difficult to distinguish for those of our kind, are separated by a swan when mixed together.
Furthermore, there exists no such thing as a "living soul" (jīva) distinct from the Supreme, which could be separated from the Being—as a drop of water is separated from a mass of water.
Indeed, it has been explained more than once that it is the very Being itself which is called the "living soul" due to its contact with limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
This being the case, as long as the persistence of bondage resides in a single limiting adjunct (upādhi), there is the designation of a single soul;
however, when the persistence of bondage resides in another limiting adjunct, there is the designation of a different soul.
Since this very same limiting adjunct persists through sleep and waking according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout, it is logical that this same soul awakens. // 9 //

"But that very same [jīva] [returns], on account of the remembrance of actions, remembrance of words, and scriptural injunctions. Since there is doubt—arising from the observation that upon the destruction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in deep sleep, there is no remembrance of actions or words—it might be argued that the previously stated position, "Brahman alone is the locus of deep sleep because of the scriptural teaching of the jīva’s rising from Brahman," is untenable. This is because it is possible for someone other than the one who slept to rise, and thus the channels (*nāḍīs*) and so forth could also be the locus of deep sleep. With this objection as the point of transition, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—"In the absence of a restrictive rule, there is no fixed rule"—beginning with the words "Of that [deep sleep], moreover... and so on.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), knowledge is useless because liberation in the form of non-return is established by deep sleep alone;

however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since one who exists as the Self of Brahman while it remains unknown is necessarily bound to arise again through the power of ignorance, there is a need for knowledge to destroy that ignorance—this is the result [of the discussion]. The phrase "or the Lord" was stated to strengthen the rule regarding the lack of restriction [as to who may attain liberation].
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is simply that "it is either he or another.

The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "But it is he indeed" (*sa eva tu*), etc., on the grounds that without knowledge there can be no absolute destruction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*); thus, the individual soul (*jīva*), which was associated with a particular intellect during deep sleep and remained in a causal state, arises again associated with that very same intellect which possesses the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from the experience of various karmas.

The over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) consists in the consequence that a single sacrifice, such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, whether half-performed or fully performed by one person, would result in having multiple sacrificers.
Having stated the traditional teaching (*smṛti*), he states the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) indicated by the word "again" (*anu*): "I am that [same person].
*Ayana* means going; *āya* is the act of coming.
The womb (*yoni*) is the location of each respective sense organ.
The meaning of the Vedic text is that one returns to the various wombs in order to awaken, according to the specific destiny that has been determined.
The statement "he does not find [the way]" indicates the necessity of the sleeper's rising from sleep due to the presence of ignorance.
The meaning is that those who exist in the previous awakening are the very same ones who exist in the subsequent awakening.

He explains the injunction with the word "karma" (action); the meaning is that it is determined that "he alone arises. Right here, he states another argument not found in the sūtra itself, beginning with "apica" (furthermore).

The meaning is that if [the body] were to arise from something else, pleasure and so forth would not be the effects of prior karma; thus, there would be the acquisition of pleasure and so forth not earned, and the destruction of karma performed by a living being during a previous state of sleep.
He refutes the example cited by the opponent through the disparity [of the case], starting with "But as for that which...
Thinking that the Lord, depending on the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of living beings, performs even that discrimination which is impossible for people like us, he states the example: "And it is seen..."
And because the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from Brahman, there is a disparity with the example of a drop of water; thus he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*).

Anticipating the objection that if there is non-difference, the question of whether "that one" or "another" arises has no room for consideration, he says, "This being so," [meaning] that the consideration arises because the individual souls are distinct due to the distinctions in their intellects (*buddhi*).

Since, upon waking from deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the intellect is destroyed, the daily empirical usage of a single soul would not be possible due to the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the intellect; therefore, he says, "He is this very same person."
The meaning is that a single limiting adjunct (upādhi) exists in both gross and subtle forms. //9//

The Section Concerning the Half-Completion of the State of Being Stunned (mugdha). Sūtra 10.
The state of the fainting person is a partial attainment [of death], because of what remains.
There is a state called "fainting," which common people describe as being "in a swoon.
Regarding the investigation of what its condition is, it is said: [it is a partial attainment of death].
There are three well-known states for the individual soul (jīva) while residing in the body: waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
the fourth is its departure from the body.
However, no fifth state of the soul is known to exist in either Śruti or Smṛti.

Therefore, since it follows that fainting must be one of the four states [of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death], we reply: first of all, the person in a state of fainting cannot be in the waking state, for he does not perceive objects through the senses.
It might be argued as follows:

The deluded person will be like the analogy of the arrow-maker: just as the arrow-maker, though awake, does not perceive other objects because his mind is attached to the arrows, so too the deluded person, though awake, does not perceive other objects because his mind is preoccupied with experiencing the pain produced by the impact of the mallet and so forth.
This is not so.
Because of the absence of volition (*acetayamānatvāt*).
For an arrow-maker, with his mind preoccupied, says: "I was perceiving only the arrow for all this time.
But one who has fainted, upon regaining consciousness, says: "I was cast into blind darkness for all this time; nothing at all was perceived by me."
Even for one who is awake, the body is maintained even when the mind is attached to a single object;
however, the body of one who is swooning falls to the ground.
Therefore, such a person is neither awake nor does he see dreams, because he is devoid of consciousness.
Nor is he dead, because of the presence of breath and warmth.

For when a person has fainted, those who are uncertain whether "this one is dead" or "not dead" feel the region of the heart to determine whether warmth exists or not, and they feel the region of the nose to determine whether breath exists or not. If they do not perceive the existence of breath and warmth, then concluding "this one is dead," they carry him to the forest for cremation.

But if they regain either the vital breath or warmth, then, concluding that "this person is not dead," they administer medical treatment to restore consciousness; and because of their rising again, it is understood that he has not gone to the realm of destiny (diṣṭa),
for no one returns from the kingdom of Yama.
"Let it be, then, that the one in deep sleep [is the Self], because of being unconscious and because of immortality. No, because of the difference in characteristics.
One who is swooning sometimes does not breathe for even a long time; his body trembles, his face is terrifying, and his eyes are wide open.
One who is in deep sleep has a serene face and breathes repeatedly at regular intervals; his eyes remain closed, and his body does not tremble.
They can awaken a person in deep sleep merely by a light touch of the hand, but they cannot awaken one who is in a state of swoon even with the blow of a mallet.
Furthermore, there is a difference in the causes of delusion and sleep:
delusion has its cause in the striking of a pestle and the like, whereas sleep has its cause in fatigue and the like.

Furthermore, in the world there is no common consensus that "one who is unconscious is asleep. By process of elimination, we understand that unconsciousness is a state of partial attainment (ardhasampatti):
one has attained [the state of sleep] because of the absence of consciousness, yet one has not fully attained it because of the difference from the other [state of deep sleep].
But how can it be said that "half-attainment" constitutes a state of insensibility?

For regarding one who is asleep, the Śruti has stated: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), and "In this state, a thief is no longer a thief" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22).
"Neither day nor night cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds [cross it]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1), and so forth.
For the attainment of good and evil deeds by the individual soul (jīva) occurs through the production of the cognitions of happiness and suffering.
And yet, neither the cognition of happiness nor the cognition of suffering exists in deep sleep.
Even in the state of swoon (*mugdha*), those two signs of cognition are not found at all.

Therefore, due to the cessation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), there must be a complete attainment [of identity with Brahman] in the state of swoon as well, and not a partial attainment.
To this it is replied: we do not say that for the individual soul (*jīva*) there is a partial attainment of identity with Brahman in the state of swoon.

What then? We say that the state of being "stupefied" (mugdhatva) belongs half to the side of deep sleep and half to the side of another state [of consciousness]. And the similarity and difference of stupor with sleep have already been shown;
furthermore, this is the gateway to death.
When his karma still has a remainder, then speech and mind return [to him];
but when his karma is without remainder, then breath and warmth depart.
Therefore, the knowers of Brahman maintain that there is a partial attainment [of liberation].
As for what was said— that no fifth state is well-known—
this is not a fault;
it may simply be that this particular state is not well-known at certain times.
Moreover, this [classification] is well-established in the world and in the *Āyurveda*;
and because the attainment of half [of the conditions] is accepted, the fifth [cause] is not counted, which is thus faultless. // 10 //

Having distinguished the Self from the three states, he distinguishes it from the state of swoon (*mūrchā*): "In the case of one who has fainted, there is a partial attainment [of the other states], because of the remainder.
[The opponent asks: Is swoon included within the well-known states, or is it a fifth state? [The reply:
Since the four states are established and because swoon differs from them, there is doubt; yet for one who has awakened through the recognition "I am that very person," [the Self is known].

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the connection of the example—that fainting (*mūrchā*) is included within deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—based on the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that it is indeed deep sleep because the absence of specific cognition is no different [in both states], just as there is no difference [between them] regarding being asleep. He says: "First, there are three... In this prima facie view, the result is the failure of effort to achieve the discrimination of the Self from fainting, which is distinct from the well-known states.

In the Siddhānta (the final conclusion), the distinction is that there is a persistence of separate effort; demonstrating this by way of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he establishes the conclusion with the words "Not indeed," and so forth.
The meaning is: "even when awake" (*jāgrad api*) means even while in the state of wakefulness.

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating the disparity through the words "No," and so forth, noting that the person in question possesses sensory cognition of objects and the maintenance of the body, whereas the one who is swooning (*mugdha*) does not.
Having stated the distinction between fainting and waking, he states the distinction from sleep and death with the words beginning "Nor... (*nāpi*).
They "touch" (*ālabhante*) means they grasp.
"Diṣṭam" means death.
He says "no" because, although there is some similarity between deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and fainting (*mūrchā*), there is a difference due to many points of dissimilarity.

Having stated the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), he states the difference in their causes (*nimitta*). He further says "nor" because recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is also not established [in the case of fainting].

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: through the previously stated similarities and dissimilarities, the state of being "half-attained" (*ardhasampatti*) is established; the person in a swoon (*mugdha*) is not in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), because he is not endowed with all the characteristics of deep sleep, nor is he dead, because he is not endowed with all the characteristics of the state of death; rather, he has entered a different state.

Regarding this Sūtra, one who is confused—thinking that the "half-attainment" of the individual soul (*jīva*) by Brahman is being described here—raises the objection: "How so? (i.e., how can this be?).
The scriptural statement that one who is asleep has attained identity with Being (*sat*) is intended to mean the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Since this absence of limiting adjuncts applies to me even when I am in a state of swoon (*mugdha*), the meaning is that there is indeed a complete attainment [of Being].

Having raised the objection as to how there can be a re-emergence from sleep if there is no connection with karma at the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says "For in the case of the individual soul" (*jīve hi*) to explain that the statement of non-connection is made because of the absence of its effects.
Brahman, having accepted the notion of complete attainment [of death], refutes it by saying, "We do not say so.

For the state of being "half-dead" (mugdhatva) is possessed of a partial attainment of sleep through its similarity to the property of unconsciousness and so forth, and it is possessed of a partial attainment of death through its similarity to trembling and so forth; such is the meaning of "partial attainment."
He states "and the door" to show that there is a difference from deep sleep for this reason as well.
Having conceded its lack of renown, he says "and it is well-known" to show that it is indeed established in common usage.
*Āyurveda* is the science of medicine.

Anticipating the objection, "How can there be a dispute regarding what is well-known?", he says "half" (ardha), meaning that people have the notion of its being included therein because of the partial attainment of the characteristics of deep sleep and death. //10//

The Section Concerning the Two-fold Characteristics (Ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 11–21.
The Supreme possesses neither of the two characteristics even from the standpoint of its location, for it is so everywhere.
Now, the true nature of that Brahman with which the individual soul merges during deep sleep and other states due to the cessation of limiting adjuncts is determined on the basis of scripture.

There are scriptural passages concerning Brahman that possess both characteristics, such as: "He whose work is all, whose desire is all, who is all fragrance, who is all taste" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2).

Those passages such as "It is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8) possess specific characteristics, while those beginning with "neither gross nor subtle" possess characteristics of the absence of specific qualities.
In these scriptural passages, is Brahman to be understood as possessing both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*), or as possessing only one of the two?
Even if it possesses only one, is it with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) or without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*)? This is what is being investigated.

On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Brahman must possess both characteristics, in order to accord with the scriptural texts that present both sets of characteristics. To this we reply: first of all, it is not logically possible for the supreme Brahman to possess both characteristics by its very nature.
For it is impossible to maintain that a single entity possesses both specific qualities such as form and the opposite of those qualities by its own nature, because of their contradiction.
Suppose, then, that this is due to "position," meaning through connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as earth;
even that is not tenable.
For even through association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is impossible for a thing that possesses one nature to possess a different nature.

Indeed, a crystal, though naturally transparent, does not become non-transparent through association with limiting adjuncts such as lac; this is because the conviction of its non-transparency is merely an illusion, and because limiting adjuncts are themselves presented by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, even when adopting either of the two characteristics [of being with or without qualities], Brahman must be understood as being devoid of all distinctions and free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), and not its opposite.
For in all passages intended to establish the true nature of Brahman—such as "without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15;
Muktikā Upaniṣad 2.72)—Brahman is taught precisely as that which has all distinctions cast aside.

FN: "Place" (*sthāna*) refers to a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); because of connection with it, one might otherwise think that the referent of "Thou" (*tvam-artha*) is stained by all states. Desiring to demonstrate that it is unstained by any state whatsoever, [the author] first states its featurelessness: "Not even from the standpoint of place does the Supreme possess a dual characteristic, for it is everywhere so.

He states the contextual connection (*avasara-saṃgati*) for the inquiry into the nature of Brahman immediately following the cessation of the desire to know the meaning of the term "Thou" (*tvam-pada-artha*), which was the subject of the initial statement: "By which... (*yena*).

The meaning is that there exist scriptural texts (*śrutis*) characterized by both marks (*ubhayaliṅga*), which indicate—that is, make known—both featurelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*) and the possession of features (*saviśeṣatva*); these serve as the seeds of doubt.

Just as the state of being "stupefied" (*mugdhatva*) possesses the dual nature of both contradictory states, namely deep sleep and death, so too, on the basis of the authority of scripture, Brahman is to be meditated upon as possessing a dual nature; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that Brahman is to be known as exclusively featureless and of a single form, beginning with the word "evam" (thus).
Is this state of having both forms intrinsic?
Or is it that Brahman is intrinsically devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), while attributes such as "possessing all fragrances" are real only through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)?
Or rather, is Brahman itself inherently possessed of distinctions (*saviśeṣa*)?
Therein, having set aside the first [position] and restated the second, he refutes it with the words "Let it be so, then.
"Location" (*sthāna*) refers to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). It is a particularity (*viśeṣa*) in Brahman.
The meaning is that [the distinction] is imagined because it is adventitious (*aupādhika*), like the redness of a crystal.

Even when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is real, it is observed that what is produced by it is false; how much more so, then, must it be said that the distinction produced by limiting adjuncts is false, since those adjuncts themselves are false in the case of Brahman? Thus he says: "of the limiting adjuncts" (*upādhīnām*). He refutes the third [position] with: "and therefore" (*ataśca*).
The meaning is: "because every distinction is merely imagined. And he says "for everywhere" (sarvatra hi) because the scriptural texts of negation are likewise [to be understood in this way]. //11//
If it is argued that [the whole] does not exist because of the difference [of its parts], we say no, because each [part] is not said to be that [the whole]. (BBs 3.2.12)

Now, it might be argued that what was stated— that Brahman is indeed without conceptual differentiation (nirvikalpa) and possesses only a single characteristic (ekaliṅga), and does not possess both characteristics either by its own nature or from the standpoint of its states— is untenable. Why?
Because of difference;
for distinct forms of Brahman are taught for each respective Vidyā.

Such as: "Brahman has four quarters," "Brahman has sixteen parts," "Brahman characterized by being dwarf-like (vāmanī), etc.," and "Brahman denoted by the term Vaiśvānara, whose body is the three worlds"—these and others of this kind.
Therefore, it must also be admitted that Brahman possesses specific qualities.
Now, as for the objection that it is impossible for Brahman to possess both sets of characteristics,
this too is not a contradiction.
If it is argued that this is because the distinction of forms is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
for otherwise the scripture concerning distinctions would result in being without a subject matter,
we say: no.
Why?
Because it does not state that [Brahman] is different in each case.
For the scripture declares that Brahman is indeed non-different despite the differences in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): "And he who is here in this earth... [and so forth].
"The person consisting of light, consisting of immortality, who is this corporeal person within the self— this very one is that which is this Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.1),
and so forth. Therefore, it cannot be asserted that Brahman possesses a connection with diverse forms according to scripture.
Because difference exists for the purpose of meditation, the intended meaning (tātparya) lies in non-difference.
"Difference" (bheda) is that which is differentiated, i.e., a particularity (viśeṣa).

He explains the doubt—that even though there is a scriptural statement regarding the absence of particularities, since particularities are also mentioned in scripture, reality might possess both forms—by saying, "Nevertheless, it might be so."
He recalls the previously mentioned contradiction with the words, "But has it not been said?

The meaning of the resolution is that there is no contradiction because we accept a distinction of forms based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the sake of the authority of the scriptural texts concerning difference.

Is this distinction of forms residing solely in the adjuncts merely attributed (*upacaryate*) to Brahman for the purpose of meditation, or does a real and non-contradictory distinction of form arise in Brahman through its connection with the adjuncts?
In the first case, our desired conclusion is established; as for the second, he refutes it by means of the scriptural texts on non-difference, saying: "We say, no. //12//
Moreover, some maintain this very view. (BBs 3.2.13)

Moreover, having first censured the perception of difference, certain followers of a Vedic school transmit the perception of non-difference itself: "By the mind alone is this to be attained; there is not the slightest diversity here.
He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity" (KaU 4.11).
Likewise, others also say: "Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—all that is threefold is my Brahman" (ŚveU 1.12).
Thus, it is taught that this entire manifold world, characterized by the objects of experience, the experiencer, and the controller, has Brahman as its sole intrinsic nature. // 13 //

Furthermore, by stating that the reality is without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) through a censure of duality (*dvaita*) followed by the teaching of non-duality (*advaita*), he explains the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (*apica*).

The meaning is: having reflected upon—the enjoyer (*bhoktā*), which is the individual soul (*jīva*); the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), such as sound and so forth; and the impeller (*preritāra*) of those two, which is the Lord (*īśvara*)—one should know that all that has been declared by Me is the threefold Brahman alone. //13//

But how is it that, when there exist Vedic texts concerning Brahman that teach it as having form and others that teach it as being without form, Brahman is determined to be indeed without form and not the opposite?
To this he replies:
"For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because it is the primary reality.
(BBs 3.2.14) Brahman is to be understood as being devoid of forms such as color and shape, and not as possessing form and so forth.
Why?
Because that is its primary characteristic:
"Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).

"Soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15; Muktika Upaniṣad 2.72); "That which is called space is the revealer of name and form; that within which these two reside is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1);
"For the divine Person is formless, both internal and external, and unborn" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).

In the passage, "This is that Brahman—without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior; this self is Brahman; he [the self] has become all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), and similar statements, it has been established in the sūtra *tattu samanvayāt* (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.4) that these texts have as their primary purport the reality of Brahman as the Self devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), and not any other matter.
Therefore, in sentences of this kind, Brahman must be understood exactly as it is heard in the text, as being indeed formless (*nirākāra*).

However, other scriptural passages concerning Brahman as possessing attributes do not have that [Brahman] as their primary subject; rather, they have the injunctions for meditation as their primary subject. Therefore, when there is no contradiction, one must rely on them exactly as they are heard in the text.
But when a contradiction exists, those passages whose primary subject is that [Brahman] are more authoritative than those whose primary subject is something else.
This is the reason for the definitive conclusion:
that even though both types of scriptural texts exist, Brahman is determined to be formless alone, and not the opposite. // 14 //

An objection is raised: "How then [is this so]? given that there exist two kinds of scriptural texts; what is the determining factor for the absence of distinction? He states the answer: "The principle that 'in a conflict between a text whose primary purpose is that [subject] and one whose primary purpose is something else, the former is stronger' is the determining factor. Thus he says: "Just as formless [Brahman]. Having raised the doubt that even if there is no intent regarding form in passages concerned with meditation (*upāsanā*), form might still be established—as in the case of the physical forms of deities—he replies: "Because they are absent in those [texts]," meaning that such a view is not tenable due to the contradiction with the scriptures whose primary purpose is the non-dual, undifferentiated reality (*niṣprapañca*). //14//
What, then, is the status of those scriptural passages concerning objects that possess form? To this, he says:
"And like light, [the teaching of Brahman's forms] is not purposeless" (BBs 3.2.15).

Just as light—whether solar or lunar—pervading space appears to assume the states of straightness, curvature, and so forth when it comes into contact with limiting adjuncts such as a finger that assumes those states, even so Brahman, through its connection with limiting adjuncts such as the earth, appears to assume their form. Thus, the instruction regarding specific forms of Brahman based on those adjuncts for the purpose of meditation is not contradictory.
In this way, there will be no futility even for those sentences whose subject matter is Brahman as possessing forms (*sākāra*).

Indeed, it is not reasonable to maintain that some Vedic sentences possess meaning while others are meaningless, since there is no difference in their status as authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[Objection: Even so, does this not contradict what was previously asserted—that Brahman does not possess both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) even through connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)?
We say no,
because it is impossible for that which is caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to be an inherent property of the reality itself,
and because those adjuncts are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*).
And we have stated in various places that it is only when innate ignorance (avidyā) exists that the engagement with worldly and Vedic conventions occurs. 15.

Furthermore, because they have scope for application within the imagined duality (*kalpitadvaite*), the scriptural passages concerning the world of manifestation (*saprapañca*) are weak; thus he says, "And like light" (*prakāśavacca*). Now, one might ask: why is it described that sentences regarding forms possess a subject matter consisting of omnipresence and so forth—which are imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—when rather their futility (*vaiyarthyam*) should be stated?
To this he replies: "For [it is not the case] with Vedic sentences... (*na hi vedavākyānām iti*).
"Even so" means: even if the scriptures are established as having both forms by accepting the aforementioned manner [of explanation].
It was stated previously that the reality of both forms is not true, because the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are imagined and what is conditioned by them (aupādhika) lacks ultimate reality.

Now, he states, "We say no," to show that there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows, even while accepting both forms—that truth is non-differentiation and falsity is differentiation.

Having raised the objection that if duality were false, then because it would be sublated by knowledge, practical activities such as meditation (*upāsanā*) would not be possible, he says, "It is true," meaning that such activity exists precisely prior to that sublation. //15//
And it says: "It is merely that" (tanmātra). (BsCom_3,2.16)

And the Śruti says that Brahman is pure consciousness alone, devoid of any distinct form and free from all distinctions: "Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

This is what is meant: there is no form of this Self other than consciousness, whether internally or externally; it is just like salt, which is nothing but an uninterrupted mass of salty taste and possesses no other taste. Thus it is. In such passages as these, it is likewise recorded in the Smṛti that Nārāyaṇa, assuming a universal form, said to Nārada: "O Nārada, this is indeed a māyā created by me, whereby you see me endowed with the qualities of all beings; you ought not to know me in this way."
FN: "Beyond" (adhi) means other; "tranquil" (upaśāntaḥ) means one from whom duality has been cast out.

Furthermore, since Brahman is taught in the Śruti and Smṛti by means of the negation of the supreme [world], he says "and it shows" to indicate that Brahman is devoid of phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañca).
Now, the meaning is that immediately after the statement regarding duality, the instruction "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) is given because it is the cause of knowledge.
To him—who was persistent, saying, "Sir, teach me further, teach me again"—the Teacher spoke, abandoning silence, when asked for a second and third time:
[He is] "tranquil," meaning one from whom duality has been removed.
Therefore, his silence itself is the answer; thus, the word "ataḥ" in the Sūtra has that meaning. It is "beginningless" (anādimat) because it is not an effect that has a beginning.

It is "existent" (sat) because it is perceivable by the senses, and "non-existent" (asat) because it is imperceptible; the meaning is that [the Self] is not [so characterized] because it is self-luminous.
That you see me as having a physical form endowed with all elemental qualities such as divine fragrance and so forth—that is *māyā*.
Therefore, you ought not to see me as the Blessed One possessing duality; the meaning is that, in reality, I am beyond duality. //17//
And for this very reason, there is a comparison [of the soul] with the reflection of the sun and so forth. (BS 3.2.18)

And precisely because this Self is of the nature of consciousness, devoid of distinctions, transcending speech and mind, and to be taught only through the negation of the other, it is for this very reason that the scriptures on liberation employ similes such as "like the sun in water," with the intention of referring to its appearance of possessing distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). As it is said: "For just as the unborn light, the sun, though one, enters into many different waters; so does the Self, though one, appear manifold."
"By means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the unborn Self, the Lord, appears as differentiated within the fields (*kṣetra*).
And: "For the single Self of all beings, residing in every being, is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water" (Brahmabindu Upaniṣad 12).
In such passages as these. // 18 //

Furthermore, just as attributes such as difference and motion attributed to the sun and moon are merely imagined through limiting adjuncts (upādhi) like water, so too are they for the Self; this is stated on the basis of scriptural illustrations that the Reality is devoid of distinctions.
For this very reason, the scripture provides a comparison: the suffix *-ka* in the term *sūryaka* is used to indicate that the sun appears as a mere reflection in its form as residing in water.
Just as this luminous Vivasvat, though inherently one, appears manifold when following the waters divided by the differences of jars.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "In this way, this unborn Self, the God who is self-luminous, though one, becomes differentiated in form as it follows after various fields (kṣetra) through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Māyā. //18//
Here, an objection is raised:

"But because it is not perceived like [the reflection] in water, it is not so. (BBs 3.2.19) It is not appropriate here to say that [Brahman] is like the sun in water and so forth, because it is not perceived in that manner.

For in the case of the sun and other such material objects, a material reflection is perceived as distinct from them and located in a distant place; therefore, the arising of a reflection of the sun and so forth is logical in those cases.
The Self is not material, nor are its limiting adjuncts (upādhis) separate from it or located in a distant place, because [the Self] is all-pervading and non-different from everything;
therefore, this illustration is inappropriate. // 19 //
Regarding this, the sūtra raising a doubt about the discrepancy with the stated analogy concerning the Self is: "Like water" (ambuvat).

The meaning is that because the Self is formless and because there is no proximate limiting adjunct (upādhi), a distinction of reflections within the intellect and other faculties through Māyā is not tenable. //19//
