[The opponent argues: "In this way, the state of participating in increase and decrease [of the parts] is appropriate because both are included and thus consistent. [The author replies:
"However, this illustration is indeed suitable because the intended aspect exists;
for it is impossible for anyone to demonstrate total similarity between an illustration (dṛṣṭānta) and its subject (dārṣṭāntika) by excluding some intended aspect."
For if there were complete identity between all things, the very distinction between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) would be destroyed.
Nor is this presentation of examples such as the sun in water or a reflection made out of one's own fancy;
rather, the mere purpose of these examples already established in the treatise is being set forth.
What, then, is intended here by "similarity" (*sārūpya*)?
It is said: it is the participation in increase and decrease.
For the reflection of the sun in water increases when the water increases, decreases when the water decreases, and moves when the water moves.
Just as [the sun] is said to be divided when there is a division in the water, thus following the properties of the water, yet in reality the sun does not possess such a state;

so too, although Brahman is in reality unchanging and of a single nature, it appears, as it were, to undergo the properties of its limiting adjuncts—such as increase and decrease—due to being contained within adjuncts like the body.
Thus, because of the correspondence between both the illustration and the illustrated, there is no contradiction. // 20 //

By including the substrate (*upādhi*) within [the reflection], the intended portion here is the possession of those properties imagined therein; thus, by way of that similarity, the sūtra provides the resolution: "In accordance with increase and decrease" (*vṛddhihāsabhāk*).
To the objection—"Even if there is similarity in the example, how can a reflection of a formless self (*nīrūpātman*) be imagined through one's own intellect?"—he says: "And this is not [so].
The meaning is that it is heard [in scripture], it is not imagined.
To the question, "What is the purpose of presenting the illustration of the sun and so forth for one who has heard [the teaching]? he says: "By the scripture," etc.
The meaning is that the result is the non-distinctness (nirviśeṣatva) of the Self. "Non-contradiction" means the absence of disparity.
In the inference "The self is devoid of reflection because it is a formless substance, like air," there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to space (ākāśa).
The point is that because the reflection of the sky is seen even in a small amount of water, the distance of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is sometimes irrelevant. //20//
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (BBs 3.2.21)

Moreover, Śruti demonstrates the entry of the supreme Brahman alone into the limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth: "He made himself threefold; he made himself biped and quadruped. Having become a bird, he entered the bodies" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.18);
and also: "Having entered by means of this living self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
Therefore, this is logical: "And for this very reason, it is without form, like the sun and so forth" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.18).

Consequently, it is established that Brahman possesses only the single characteristic of being free from conceptual differentiation (*nirvikalpa*), and not both characteristics nor a contrary characteristic.
On this point, some propose two separate topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).
First, [the question is]: Is Brahman of a single form, with all manifoldness entirely subsided, or is it endowed with manifold forms like the world of manifestation?

Second, however, once its state of having all manifoldness subsided is established, is Brahman characterized by existence (*sallakṣaṇa*), or characterized by consciousness (*bodhalakṣaṇa*), or characterized by both?
On this point, we say: in every respect, the commencement of a separate section is useless.

If this effort is intended to refute the multiplicity of attributes in the supreme Brahman, then since that must already have been refuted by the preceding section beginning with "Not even from the standpoint of place" (na sthānato 'pi), this subsequent section beginning with "And like light" (prakāśavacca) would be entirely redundant.

Nor can it be said that Brahman has only the characteristic of existence (*sallakṣaṇa*) and not the characteristic of consciousness (*bodhalakṣaṇa*), for that would entail the absurdity of scriptural passages such as "Brahman is a mass of pure consciousness" being rendered meaningless. Furthermore, how could Brahman, if devoid of consciousness, be taught as the Self of the conscious individual soul (*jīva*)?

Nor can it be said that Brahman has the characteristic of consciousness alone and not the characteristic of existence, for that would entail the absurdity of rendering such scriptural passages as "It is to be apprehended simply as 'It is'" (Phaṭṭha 6.13) meaningless;
or else, how could a consciousness devoid of existence be admitted?
Nor can it be said that Brahman possesses both characteristics [existence and consciousness],
for that would entail a contradiction with what was previously accepted.

For one who asserts that Brahman is endowed with a consciousness distinct from existence and an existence distinct from consciousness, that very same "possessed-of-multiplicity" (saprapañcatva) of Brahman which was refuted in the preceding section follows as a consequence.
It would follow [that this is the case].
If it is argued that there is no fault because it is so stated in scripture, we say no;
for it is logically impossible for a single entity to possess multiple intrinsic natures.
Now, if it were argued that existence itself is consciousness and consciousness itself is existence, such that there is no mutual exclusion between these two,

even so, the alternative inquiry— whether Brahman is characterized by existence, or characterized by consciousness, or characterized by both— would remain entirely without a basis. However, we have interpreted the Sūtras as having a single unified subject matter.

Furthermore, since there are conflicting views regarding Brahman in the Vedic scriptures—some presenting it as having form and others as being formless—once the formless Brahman is accepted, the status of the other scriptures must necessarily be explained.
To that end, the sūtras beginning with "prakāśavat ca" (and like light) become more meaningful.

Even if it is argued that those scriptures which speak of form are intended solely for the realization of the formless Brahman by means of dissolving the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and do not have a separate meaning of their own, that too does not appear to be correct.
How so?

For certain elaborations are mentioned in the context of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), such as: "For his bay horses are a hundred, indeed; these are the bay horses; he is indeed thousands, many and infinite" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).

These and other such passages have the purpose of dissolution [of distinctions], as is evident from the concluding statement: "This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).

On the other hand, those elaborations which are mentioned in the context of meditative worship (*upāsana*)—such as "consisting of mind, having breath for its head, and having light for its form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2)—[are intended for the sake of meditation].
Therefore, it is not logical that these [passages] have the purpose of dissolution [of the world],
because they are connected precisely with the injunction for meditation under discussion, such as "He should form a resolve" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).

Furthermore, since it is possible to understand that qualities of this kind serve the purpose of meditation based on the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), it is not tenable to assume through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that they serve the purpose of dissolution.

Moreover, if all [qualities] were common to the purpose of dissolution, the statement providing the reason for determination— namely, *Brahma-sūtra* 3.2.14, "For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because it is the principal"— would have no scope.
Furthermore, it is clearly understood that their fruits are as taught: in some cases the destruction of evil, in some the attainment of sovereignty, and in others gradual liberation.

Therefore, it is logical that the meditative passages (*upāsanā-vākya*) and the passages concerning Brahman (*brahma-vākya*) are distinct; they cannot constitute a single unified statement (*ekavākyatva*).
Moreover, one must explain how these could possibly be conceived as forming a single statement.

If it is argued that this is because a single injunction (*niyoga*) is understood [in both], as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, we say no;
for there is an absence of injunction in the sentences concerning Brahman.

Indeed, it has been established in detail in the commentary on *Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.4 (*tattu samanvayāt*) that the sentences concerning Brahman terminate in the mere reality of things (*vastumātra*) and do not teach an injunction.
It must be stated what the object of the injunction (*niyoga*) intended here is;
for a person being enjoined by the command "Do! is enjoined toward some specific activity of his own.
[Objection: But surely the dissolution of the manifold world of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*) will be the object of yoga.

For as long as the manifold of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*) has not been dissolved, the realization of the reality of Brahman does not occur; therefore, the manifold of duality, which stands as an obstacle to the realization of the reality of Brahman, must be dissolved. Just as a sacrifice is taught to be performed by one desiring heaven, so too is the dissolution of the manifold taught for one desiring liberation (*apavarga*). And just as one who wishes to perceive the true nature of a jar or similar object situated in darkness must first remove the darkness that stands as its opposite, [so too must one dissolve the manifold].
Thus, by one desiring to realize the reality of Brahman, the phenomenal world (prapañca), which stands as its opposite, must be dissolved.
For the phenomenal world has the nature of Brahman, but Brahman does not have the nature of the phenomenal world;
therefore, through the dissolution of the phenomenal world of names and forms, the realization of the reality of Brahman occurs.
On this point we ask: what is this so-called dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)?

Is the dissolution of phenomenal proliferation to be effected like the melting away of the hardness of ghee through contact with the heat of fire; or rather, is the phenomenal proliferation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) within Brahman—which is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), like the appearance of many moons caused by a visual defect when there is but one moon—to be dissolved away by knowledge (*vidyā*)?

In that regard, if it were said that this phenomenal expansion— consisting of the internal characteristics of the body and so forth, as well as the external characteristics of the earth and so forth— must first be dissolved by knowledge, then since it would be impossible for a mere human being to dissolve it, the instruction for its dissolution would have an unattainable object.
Furthermore, if by the liberation of a single person the dissolution of earth and the other elements were effected, then the world would now have become empty of earth and the rest.
Or, if you should say that this phenomenal world, superimposed upon the one Brahman through ignorance, is dissolved by knowledge;
then Brahman alone must be made known by the rejection of the phenomenal world superimposed through ignorance, as "Brahman is indeed one without a second."
"That is the Truth; That is the Self; That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7)—when this has been made known, knowledge arises spontaneously, and by that, ignorance is sublated.
Consequently, this entire phenomenal expansion of names and forms, superimposed by ignorance, dissolves like the expansion of a dream.

But even if it were said a hundred times, "Perform the knowledge of Brahman and the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca) within the unmanifested Brahman," neither the knowledge of Brahman nor the dissolution of the phenomenal world would arise.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, once Brahman has been made known, there could be an injunction (niyoga) regarding the object of that knowledge or regarding the object of the dissolution of the phenomenal world? [Reply: No.
For both [the realization of Brahman and the dissolution of the world] are established simply by the knowledge that Brahman is the self, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

Indeed, by the mere manifestation of the true nature of the rope, there occurs both the cognition of its true nature and the dissolution of the world of snakes and so forth superimposed through ignorance (*avidyā*).
And what has already been accomplished is not performed again.

Furthermore, as for that which is understood as the so-called "individual soul" (jīva) during the state of phenomenal manifestation (prapañca)— whether it belongs to the side of phenomenal manifestation itself or to the side of Brahman— in the first alternative, since the individual soul is dissolved along with the earth and other elements through the teaching of the non-phenomenal reality of Brahman, to whom could an injunction regarding the dissolution of phenomenal manifestation be addressed? Or to whom could liberation be said to be attained by remaining steadfast in that injunction?

In the second [chapter] as well, it is established that Brahman alone is the nature of the individual soul (jīva), which is by its very essence not subject to injunctions, while "jīvahood" is merely produced by ignorance; thus, since there is no one to be enjoined within Brahman, there is an absolute absence of injunction.

Furthermore, even words such as "should be seen" (draṣṭavya) and so forth, which are found in the context of the higher knowledge (paravidyā), primarily aim at directing one toward reality and do not primarily enjoin the act of cognizing reality itself.
Even in common worldly usage, in instructions of this kind such as "see this" or "hear this," one is told to simply apply one's attention (*praṇidhāna*), not to actually produce the cognition itself.

Even for one who is oriented toward the object of knowledge, cognition sometimes arises and sometimes does not arise; therefore, one who wishes to make that object known must demonstrate the very object of knowledge to him.
Once that has been demonstrated, cognition arises spontaneously, according to the object and according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, even for one who is instructed, a cognition contrary to the facts cannot occur regarding an object already established otherwise by another means of valid cognition.
If, however, one were to produce a cognition thinking "I am commanded" when it is otherwise, that would not be a cognition; rather, it would be a mental action.
If it were to arise otherwise by itself, it would simply be an error.
Cognition, moreover, is produced by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and has as its object things as they truly are; it cannot be made to function otherwise even by a hundred commands.
Nor can it be prevented even by a prohibition;
for that [nature] is not dependent on a person,
but rather depends solely upon the thing itself.
For this reason as well, there is an absence of *niyoga*.

Furthermore, if the Veda were to terminate solely in *niyoga*, then that which has been accepted—the fact that the individual soul (*jīva*) has Brahman as its self, which is not subject to injunction—would be rendered without any means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇaka*).

If, on the other hand, the scripture itself were to declare that the soul has Brahman as its self—which is not subject to injunction—and also enjoin a person toward the realization thereof, then the single scripture concerning Brahman would have two purposes and thus possess contradictory purposes.

Furthermore, [the faults of] abandoning what is heard and imagining what is not heard would follow; and if there were a focus on injunction (*niyoga*), such defects as liberation being an unseen fruit like the fruits of ritual action, its impermanence, and so forth, could not be avoided by anyone.
Therefore, the sentences concerning Brahman have as their goal only that which is already understood, and do not have injunction as their goal.
Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) based on the cognition of a single injunction (*niyoga*).

Furthermore, even if the existence of an injunction were admitted in the sentences concerning Brahman, that singularity would be unestablished between those teachings that describe the world as devoid of manifoldness (*niṣprapañca*) and those that describe it as possessing manifoldness (*saprapañca*).

For when a difference in injunctions is understood through means of knowledge such as the use of different words and so forth, it is impossible to maintain that there is one and the same injunction everywhere.

In the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, unity is appropriate because there is no difference in the aspect of qualification (*adhikārāṃśa*). However, here, in the injunctions regarding the qualified and unqualified [Brahman], there is no single aspect of qualification whatsoever.
For qualities such as "consisting of light" (*bhārūpatā*) and so forth do not assist in the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-pravilaya*).
Nor does the dissolution of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) assist the qualities such as the nature of light,
because they are mutually contradictory;
for it is not possible to reconcile the total dissolution of all conceptual proliferation with the dependence upon a portion of that same proliferation within a single substratum (dharmin).
Therefore, the division we have stated regarding the teachings on those with forms and those without forms is the more logical one. // 21 // [FN:
For this Lord who has attained the state of a living being (*jīva*), there are ten *haris*—either sense-objects or the senses.
To him who seeks knowledge...]
A word whose meaning is distinct from the sentence-meaning is a "different word" (śabdāntara).
Furthermore, because of the scriptural mention of "entry," there is a sublation of the aforementioned inference; thus says the author of the Sūtras:
"And because [it] is seen."

He made bipeds—human bodies and the like—first; having made quadrupeds first, that Lord, becoming a bird—that is, possessing a subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)—entered the cities before the manifestation of the eyes and other senses. Even though he has entered the cities, he is still the "Person" (puruṣa), meaning he remains full. His nature as a bird should be understood from the description of the subtle body as having wings and so forth in the Taittirīyaka Upaniṣad.
Thus, concluding his own view that Brahman is without distinction because difference and so forth are merely imagined through the nature of a reflection, he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He introduces the interpretation of the "partialist" (*ekadeśin*) with the words, "In this regard" (*atra*).
The section beginning with "Not even from a different location" (*na sthānato 'pi*) constitutes a single topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*).

In that regard, once Brahman’s state of being free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*) is established, a doubt arises as to what the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman is; it is with reference to this doubt that the second section begins, starting with the words "And like light" (*prakāśavacca*).
Brahman is not merely of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), but is also like light and of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).
Why? Because of its non-redundancy (*avaiyarthyāt*).

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that Brahman possesses two forms because both scriptural passages—"Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" and "Being alone, my dear"—are meaningful [only if it has these two aspects], the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states: "And the scripture says that it is only that.
The scripture declares that Brahman is pure Being (*sanmātra*), because knowledge does not exceed its existence.
This [passage] refutes the second position with the words "here we...

Having raised the alternatives as to whether the fruit of the second position is the negation of Brahman’s manifold nature (*anekarūpatva*), or the negation of its nature as consciousness (*bodharūpatva*), or the negation of its existence (*sattā*), the author elaborates on its total futility and states that it is redundant in the first case with the words "if, for a start... (*yadi tāvad*).

He says "nor" (na ca) to show that the second [alternative] is not [the case]. He asks "or how" (kathaṃ vā) because, if the nature of Brahman as consciousness were rejected, it would be insentient, and thus there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts on the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva).
He says "nor also" (nāpi) to show that the third [alternative] is not [the case].
He asks "How so? because if existence were excluded, consciousness would become a mere nothingness.
Nor should it be argued that consciousness is not a nothingness because it is not distinct from existence;
for if the referents of the words "existence" (sat) and "consciousness" (bodha) were not distinct, they would result in being synonyms.

Having thus refuted the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the absence of a result, he refutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "nor also" (*nāpi*). He states the very reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) with the word "existence" (*sattā*);
"distinctness" (*vyāvṛttatva*) means difference (*bhinnatva*).

The meaning is that because it would contradict the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that [Brahman] has a single nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it possesses both distinct natures cannot arise. He raises the objection that it does arise on the strength of scriptural testimony regarding both [natures], saying: "Because it is so heard" (*śrutatvāt*). He replies: "No," for it is not logical—even by means of a hundred scriptures—to suspect non-difference with a single Brahman between two things whose existence and cognition are mutually distinct, like Mount Meru and the Vindhya mountains.
Is there a difference between existence (*sattā*) and true consciousness (*sad-bodha*), or not?

Regarding the first case, it has been stated that since even the scripture would then be subject to the impossibility of having contradictory meanings, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) cannot arise.
Now, he raises the second alternative: "Or rather, [existence] is indeed [true consciousness]."

The meaning is that although there is a difference between the denotative meanings (*vācyārtha*) of the two words "Being" (*sat*) and "Awakening" (*bodha*), the identity of their indicated referent (*lakṣyaikya*) is established because they are accepted as having an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*).
It would be improper for the indivisible meaning to be treated as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), since it is actually the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Furthermore, he states "even so" (*tathāpi*) to show that even the doubt raised here is inappropriate.

Regarding the question of how the sūtras are to be interpreted under the view that they constitute a single topical section (*ekādhikaraṇapakṣa*), he says: "The sūtras... He further states: "Moreover... The sense is that because the subsequent sūtras have as their purpose the [explanation of] the movement necessarily required [by the preceding], they form a single syntactical unit with what precedes; therefore, there is no division of the topical sections.
It has been stated that our own position is that the goal of the scriptural texts concerning specific forms (*ākāra*) is the imagined form (*kalpitākāra*);

however, those who advocate for the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañcavilayavādin*) say that the goal of such scriptural texts on forms as "consisting of mind, having breath as its body, whose desires are true" is the dissolution of those forms into their opposites.
What, then, is the meaning of "consisting of mind"?
The meaning is that [the Self] is devoid of any limiting adjunct (upādhi) other than the mind.
Thus, by the phrase "body of vital breath" (prāṇa-śarīra), since limiting adjuncts other than the vital breath are negated, the non-existence of even the mind is established.
In this way, all words refer only to the formless Brahman; having thus restated that view, he refutes it with the words beginning "yadapi" (as for what was said...).

Do the words denoting forms (*ākāra*) occurring in the context of the knowable Brahman have the purpose of negation, or do they also apply to those occurring in the context of meditative worship (*upāsanā*)?
Regarding this, he accepts the first position with the words "For those which...

For this Lord who has attained the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), there are ten *harayaḥ*—so called because they carry away objects—which are the ten sense organs; and in view of the various classes of living beings, these are hundreds and thousands. Anticipating the doubt that these might be distinct from the Lord, he says: "This [is He]..."
The meaning is that "the Lord alone" refers to Hari.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "But those who... [and so on].

He states "And by scripture" [etc. because, when the primary sense of words such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) can possibly refer to [His] qualities, even an indirect indication through negation (niṣedhalakṣaṇā) is not appropriate.

Furthermore, since there is a twofold scriptural tradition regarding both having form (*sākāra*) and being formless (*anākāra*), the doubt arises as to what the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) is for the conclusion that Brahman is indeed formless; it is for the purpose of stating that the restrictive principle (*niyāmaka*)—namely, that the scriptures such as "not coarse" (*asthūla*) etc., have the intention (*tātparya*) of negating form—that this Sūtra becomes meaningful.

However, if all the scriptures were intended solely for negation, such a doubt would not arise, and thus a restrictive Sūtra would be redundant; this is what he means by saying "and of all [the scriptures]... (*sarveṣāṃ ca*).

Now, having raised the objection that since sentences concerning meditation (upāsana) lack a fruit in their own primary sense, they must be subordinate to prohibitory sentences that possess a fruit, [the author] replies—stating "the fruit also"—that because a fruit is indeed heard [in these passages], they are not subordinate to anything else. Furthermore, he states "and how? to show that there is no single-sentence unity (ekavākyatā) due to the absence of a single purpose.
He then raises the doubt regarding a single purpose with the word "one."

Just as there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) among the sentences concerning the subsidiaries and the primary rites due to the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*) known as the supreme *apūrva* that possesses a fruit, so too—because there exists a single object in the form of an injunction whose content is the dissolution of the phenomenal world for one desiring the realization of reality—there is syntactic unity among all the sentences, whether they possess a formal structure or lack one. He refutes this by means of the non-establishment of the injunction, saying: "No."
He raises an objection regarding the object [of knowledge]: "But surely, [in the case of] duality...

[The term] *pratyanīka* means an obstacle. [An objection is raised: "Surely, upon the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), there would be the dissolution of Brahman as well, because of their non-difference. To this he replies: "For the phenomenal world has the very nature of Brahman."

For the cause is the very nature of the effect; therefore, even upon the destruction of the effect, there is no dissolution of the cause, because clay is still perceived even when the jar has been destroyed—this is the meaning.
Having raised the alternative that there is a dissolution of the world-either as something real or as something imagined—he refutes the first with the words "In that case, if first... and so on.

Because the destruction of truth occurs through knowledge, and because it is impossible to destroy the entirety of duality by means of a pestle or other such instruments, this injunction has an unattainable object, like the injunction to swallow the sky;
furthermore, it would follow that the liberation of all would occur through the liberation of Śuka and others—this is the meaning.
He refutes the second [view] by restating it with the words "Now, if... and so forth.

The meaning is that since the dissolution of ignorance and its resulting phenomenal world (prapañca) is accomplished through the very knowledge produced by the instruction (upadeśa), an injunction (niyoga) is entirely useless.
Furthermore, regarding the injunction for the knowledge of Brahman and so forth, does it apply when Brahman is unknown or when it is known?
It is not the first case, because it would be impossible; thus he says: "But if [Brahman] has not been made known."

He raises a second objection with "But surely" (nanu). He replies with "No" (na), stating that since Brahman is known through instruction alone, the direct realization and the sublation of duality are established; therefore, an injunction is useless, because it is impossible to perform by means of an injunction what has already been accomplished.

Having thus stated the absence of an injunction due to the absence of such an object, he states its absence also due to the absence of a person to be enjoined (niyojya) with the words "And the person to be enjoined as well."

The meaning is that Brahman is included within phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*). In the first case, because the individual soul (*jīva*) would perish, the application of an injunction (*vidhi*) is impossible; in the second case, there is no established person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

In that case, what is the status of the injunctive suffixes (*vidhipratyaya*) regarding knowledge? To this he says: "The words such as 'it is to be seen' (*draṣṭavya*)," and so forth. Now, one might object: why discard the directly heard knowledge and instead postulate an injunction for the operation of its means? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even for one who is oriented toward the object of knowledge," because knowledge is not something to be accomplished by human effort (*puruṣakṛtisādhya*). Furthermore, for one who maintains that there is an injunction regarding knowledge, Brahman—the object of knowledge—must necessarily be made known by the Vedāntas; for without the comprehension of the object, an injunction cannot be understood.
And thus, he states that because knowledge arises through the Vedāntas alone, injunctions are purposeless, with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
This means: with reference to that seeker of knowledge.
Now, one might argue that an injunction is meaningful for the purpose of modifying the knowledge once it has arisen.
"No," he says, "nor [is it so]. Now, one might object:

even though the cognition "the woman is not fire" arises from the means of valid perception (pratyakṣa), it is seen to be altered by an injunction such as "one should meditate on her as fire. To this, he says: "If..."
If a cognition of something otherwise were achievable through effort, it would be a mere action;

if it occurs without effort, it is simply an error. Therefore, since knowledge cannot be established by means of an injunction in the absence of a means of valid cognition, the injunction regarding knowledge—which is dependent upon the object of valid cognition—is false; this is the meaning. He states "moreover" (*kiñcānyat*) because there is another refutation for those who maintain the existence of injunctions within the Vedāntas.

Having raised the objection that the Upanishadic statements possess authority regarding the union with Brahman as the Self, [the author] refutes this by stating "Now, moreover" (*atha...*) and so forth, on the grounds that there would be a split in the sentence due to a difference in meaning, and a lack of authority due to the contradiction in meaning. Furthermore, he states that while Brahman is heard in the Vedanta, an injunction (*vidhi*) is not; and if one were to postulate such an injunction, it would follow that liberation is produced by ritual action, which entails its being non-eternal and subject to degrees of excellence. He concludes by stating the result: "And if there were a focus on an injunction... (*niyogaparatāyāṃ ca...*) and "Therefore... (*ataśca*).
Now, having provisionally accepted the injunction (*niyoga*) as a bold argument (*prauḍhavāda*), he refutes its unity with the words "even if [it] were admitted.

Just as there is a difference in words expressing distinct actions—such as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and "he gives" (*dadāti*)—so too here there is a difference in words, namely "one knows" (*veda*) and "one meditates" (*upāsīta*).

By these means of proof—the distinction between the forms of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) and the qualified (*saguṇa*), the distinction of context (*prakaraṇa*), and the distinction between the fruits of liberation (*mukti*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)—the meaning is that there is a difference in the injunctions concerning the knowledge of the attributeless and the meditation on the qualified.
How, then, is there a unity of injunction (*niyoga*) in sentences concerning both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*) rites?
To this he says: "prayāja...

The meaning is that because a single person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is entitled to both the principal rite together with its subsidiaries, there is a unity of sentence due to the unity of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) which is the fruit to be accomplished by them.
Even here, one might argue that because the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) and the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman share a single locus of authority, there must be a unity of injunction;
to this he says "not so" (*na tv iha*).

Because seekers differ according to whether they desire liberation or worldly prosperity, and because two knowledges whose objects are mutually contradictory cannot stand in the relation of principal and subordinate, there is no unity of injunction.
Nor should it be said that the injunction regarding knowledge devoid of attributes (nirguṇavidyā) is unique because knowledge with attributes (saguṇavidyā) is not accepted [as subject to injunction];
oh, how contrary is the scholarship of your honor,
to claim that there is an injunction for a knowledge that is fit for obstruction, yet no injunction for that which is fit for injunction!

Therefore, the conclusion that sentences describing forms (sākāra-vākyas) attain syntactic unity with the sentences describing the attributeless (nirguṇa-vākyas) by means of the dissolution of those forms is a false position; rather, their "course" is toward an imagined form, since prosperity is achieved through meditation upon them, whereas the attributeless sentences have the ultimate reality as their objective. Thus he concludes, "Therefore," [stating] that the distinction we have stated is indeed the more correct one. //21//

The Section Concerning the Limited Nature of the Primal Cause (Prakṛtaitāvattvādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 22–30.
"For [the text] denies the finitude of that which has been described as the natural state; thereafter, it speaks further.

Having begun with, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1), and having divided the five great elements into two groups, [it speaks of] the essence consisting of flavor, which is designated by the word *puruṣa*.
After showing forms such as those dyed with saffron and others, it is further recited: "Now, therefore, follows the instruction: 'Not this, not this.
For there is nothing else higher than this 'not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).
In this regard, we desire to know what the object of this negation is.
For here, no specific thing to be negated is perceived such that one could say, "This is that.
However, by the word *iti*, some object of negation is indeed implied here; this is because the use of the negative particle (*nañ*) is directed toward the phrase "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

It is observed that when the word *iti* is employed, depending on another word and referring to what is proximate, it functions similarly to the word *evam* (thus), as in such examples as "Thus, indeed, the teacher used to say," and so forth.
And here, by the force of the context, two forms of Brahman along with their manifold elaborations are present; these are the two forms of that Brahman.
Regarding this, a doubt arises in us: does this negation negate both the forms and that which possesses the forms, or only one of them?
Even if it negates only one, then does it negate Brahman while leaving the forms remaining, or does it negate the forms while leaving Brahman remaining?

In this regard, we suspect that because there is no distinction in their being the subject under discussion, both [negations] are intended to be prohibitions. Furthermore, since two negations are present due to the twice-occurrence of the word "not" (na),
it is our understanding that by one of them the form of Brahman along with its manifold world (saprapañca) is prohibited, and by the other, Brahman as possessing form (rūpavat) is prohibited.
Alternatively, it is Brahman itself that is denied as possessing form; for since Brahman transcends speech and mind, its existence is not ordinarily conceivable, and thus it is fit to be denied.
However, the manifold of forms (rūpa-prapañca) is not fit to be denied, as it falls within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge.
The repetition [of the negation] is for the sake of showing reverence.
This being the case, we reply:
first of all, the negation of both is not tenable, as it would entail the consequence of nihilism (śūnyavāda).
For something is negated only by taking recourse to some ultimate reality, just as a snake and the like are negated in relation to a rope and so forth.
And that [negation] is possible only when some entity remains as a residue;
but if both are negated, what other entity could remain as a residue?

Furthermore, if another entity is not left as a residue while one attempts to negate the other, then because that [remaining entity] cannot be negated, it would follow that it alone possesses ultimate reality, and thus the negation becomes untenable.
Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable, because it would contradict the introductory statement, "I shall tell you of Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and so forth; [for it is said:
"He becomes non-existent indeed."
Because this contradicts such condemnations as, "If one knows Brahman as non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1),
[the truth is that] "It should be perceived as indeed existing" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.13).
This is because it would contradict such definitive assertions and lead to the undesirable consequence of subverting all the Vedānta scriptures. Furthermore,
even the statement that Brahman transcends speech and mind is not intended to signify its non-existence.

For it is not the case that, after Brahman has been established in the Vedāntas with such great effort through passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1) and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), its non-existence would then be asserted once again.

For there is the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off"; however, this is merely the method of exposition, according to the passage: "From whence words return, together with the mind, having failed to reach it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1).

This is what is meant: Brahman is that which transcends speech and mind, does not fall within the sphere of objects, is the innermost self (pratyagātman), and is by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free.
Therefore, it must be accepted that [the scripture] negates the manifold expansion of forms belonging to Brahman and leaves Brahman as the remainder.
This very point is stated in the sūtra: "For it negates the extent of what has been previously described."
This word negates that form of Brahman which has been under discussion—namely, this much, limited by quantity, characterized as both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*).

For that [form] was introduced and elaborated in the preceding text with reference to the divine (*adhidaivata*) and the corporeal (*adhyātma*); and it is precisely from that [form] that another form arises, characterized by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), consisting of the essence of the formless, denoted by the word "Person" (*puruṣa*), and dependent upon the subtle body (*liṅgātman*).
This has been demonstrated through similes such as those involving great crowds [of people],
because it is impossible for the formless essence of the Puruṣa to possess a form perceptible by the eye.

Thus, it is understood that this form of Brahman, along with its manifold elaborations (*saprapañca*), is presented to the negative particle (*nañ*)— the negator— by means of the word "iti" (*iti-karaṇa*), which serves as a proximate object of reference.

In the preceding text, Brahman was indicated by the genitive case as a qualifier of form, not as the primary subject itself. Once its two forms have been elaborated upon, this inquiry into the true nature of that which possesses those forms is commenced with the words: "Now, therefore, the instruction is: 'Not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).
It is determined therein that this is the communication of the true nature of Brahman through the negation of its superimposed forms.
For this entire aggregate of effects has its locus therein, and thus it is negated by "not this, not this.

And it is logical that the non-existence of the effect is established through such negations as "a mere modification of speech" and so forth; however, Brahman is not negated by "not this, not this," because it is the very root of all conceptualization of agency.

Nor should this objection be raised: "How is it that the scripture itself, having shown two forms, then prohibits them again, as in the saying, 'It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off'?
For this scripture does not point out the two forms of Brahman as objects to be established [as ultimate reality].
This is faultless: these two forms, well-known in the world, are referred to as being imagined upon Brahman for the purpose of negation and for the purpose of establishing the nature of pure Brahman.

And these two negations negate both the formed and the formless according to the principle of respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Alternatively, the former negation negates the aggregate of elements, while the latter negates the aggregate of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Alternatively, this is a repetition—"not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6)—meaning that whatever may be imagined, all that is not Brahman. For if a negation were made of only a limited number of things, the inquiry would arise: "If this is not Brahman, what else could be Brahman?"

But when there is the repetition [of the negative particle], because the entire range of objects is negated, the inquiry ceases with the realization that Brahman is the inner self (pratyagātman), which is not an object [of cognition].

Therefore, the conclusion is that [the scripture] negates only the phenomenal world (prapañca) imagined upon Brahman, while leaving Brahman itself intact. For this reason as well, this alone is the correct conclusion.
Because of that very negation, he speaks further: "There is something else beyond" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).
For if the negation were made as a mere non-existence, why would he say, "There is something else beyond"?
In this regard, the construction of the words is as follows: having pointed out Brahman by saying "not this, not this," he then explains that very instruction.
What is the meaning of "not this, not this" (neti neti)?
It means that there is nothing other than this Brahman; therefore it is said "not this, not this," but the meaning is certainly not that Brahman itself does not exist.
And it shows that there is another, supreme, unprohibited Brahman which exists.
When, however, the syllables are construed in this way— "not indeed from this [instruction] as 'not this, not this' (neti neti)"—
meaning that there is no further instruction regarding Brahman other than the teaching consisting in the negation of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca),
then the phrase "and he says more than that" is to be applied to the subject of the name.
Furthermore, regarding the designation: "The truth of truth; for the vital breaths are truth, and he is their truth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20)—this indeed speaks thus.
And that [designation] becomes consistent when the negation culminates in Brahman.
But if the negation were to terminate in non-existence (abhāva), how could it be said that "the Truth of Truths" exists?
Therefore, we conclude that this negation terminates in Brahman, not in non-existence. [Note:
The three elements—earth, water, and fire—are "mūrtam" (possessing form).]
Air and space are formless; thus, by way of these two groups, [the text] speaks of them.
*Mahārājana* is turmeric.

Having stated that Brahman is pure consciousness without distinction, it declares its nature as "Being" (*sat*) as the ultimate limit for all negations: "For it denies the extent of what is manifested in nature, and then it declares further."

Having stated the two groups— namely, that the triad of earth, water, and fire is corporeal (mūrta), while the pair of air and ether is incorporeal (amūrta)— it is taught that the essence of the two incorporeal elements is the "instrumental self" (karaṇātman) Hiranyagarbha, who is described as "this person in this solar orb and this person in the right eye."
Its dream-forms, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), are manifold and described through similes such as "like saffron-dyed cloth," "like white woolen cloth," and "like the indragopa insect.
In this context, *māhārajana* refers to turmeric; cloth dyed with that is *māhārajana*.
"Pāṇḍvādika" refers to white woolen blankets and the like.

However, some explain that by treating the Vedic statement as an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa), they show that the five subtle elements are formless (amūrta) while the five gross elements produced by quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) are formed (mūrta); thus, by the mention of the "essence of the formless," the fact that the organs are composed of all five elements (pāñcabhautikatva) is established.
Now, following the description of the manifold world consisting of six categories,
the meaning is that instruction is given by means of the negation "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), because the aforementioned superimposition is for the purpose of negation.
He states the meaning of the word "not" (*na*) with the words "for not" (*nahi*).
The meaning is that because there is nothing other than this Self, it is described as "not this, not this" (neti neti).
According to the established doctrine, the purpose of the scriptural statement "the Supreme Brahman exists" is to refute [an absolute] emptiness; such is the meaning of the Śruti.
Here, the author expresses a doubt regarding the specific object of negation with the words beginning "In that regard, what is its... and so forth.
The meaning is that the application of the negative particle (*nañ*), specifically the letter *a*, functions to negate a thing presented by the word *iti*.

When the word *iti* provides the general object of negation and there arises an expectation for its specific nature, the context reveals that both the two forms and the embodied Brahman are the objects of negation;
having thus stated the doubt, [the author proceeds] with the connection of the objection that the previously mentioned attributeless Brahman does not exist.
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In that case, because of the context...

The result is that under the prima facie view, since the referent of the word *tat* (that) is absent, the non-difference of the sentence-meaning is not established; whereas under the final view (*siddhānta*), it is established.

Since a negation without a substratum is never observed, a universal negation is not tenable; expressing dissatisfaction with this, he states "Or rather" (*athavā*) to indicate that Brahman is negated within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

He says "But repetition" (*abhyāsastu*) because there would be tautology of the two negative particles (*na-kāra*) if only a single Brahman were negated. He begins the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) even before the sūtra itself, saying "Thus" (*evam*).

To the one who says that the consequence of emptiness is accepted, he replies: "For something... (*kiñcid dhi*). The meaning is that "that" refers to the negation. Since there would be no basis remaining, the cause for the form of valid cognition (*pramā*) would be absent; thus, the meaning of the negative sentence could not be a valid cognition. This is because, in the world, it is observed that a negation such as "this is not here" is always a valid cognition only when it possesses a basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*). This is the meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the general rule that "whatever appears is real," its exception (*apavāda*) consists in the valid cognition of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) which lacks the object of that appearance; for by means of this [cognition], one determines that the prior appearance was an error, thereby negating the existence of the object.

He states, "And if nothing remains," because if the exception is not admitted, the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) would—by virtue of the general rule—result in being real, making its negation untenable.

Having stated that the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) is illogical since neither error nor its negation is possible without the reality of the substratum, he refutes another position of the opponent with the words, "Nor..."

The sense is that the negation of duality—attained through worldly means of knowledge based on the conceit of the body as the self—is appropriate, but not of Brahman as cognized by the Vedānta. Regarding the claim that Brahman is fit for negation because it transcends speech and mind, he says: "Speech and mind...

He states "for the purpose of instruction" [in response] to the question: if the transcendence of speech and so forth regarding Brahman is not for the sake of negation, then for what purpose was that stated?
He applies the Sūtra to the meaning already stated with the words "This very [is... and so forth.
The meaning is that because the two forms alone were introduced as primary in the passage, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman," the negation is expressed as "not this.

An objection is raised: "But since Brahman also was mentioned here as primary in the statement, 'The Person in the solar orb,' is it not so? Anticipating this, he says, "That which is produced from that [alone]," on the grounds that the "Person" is the *liṅga-ātman* (the subtle body), because the Śruti speaks of it as being the essence of the formless (*amūrta-rasa*)—which implies it is produced from the elements—and because the Śruti describes its nature as being like a dream.

The non-difference between form and the formal has been stated. Now, one might ask: why is form consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*) alone used as the point of comparison? Why could it not be the well-known [ordinary] form itself? To this he says: "of the immaterial essence" (*amūrtarasasya*).
Since these two types of form are the primary subjects under discussion, he states the conclusion: "that" (*tad*). The meaning is that it is presented as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

The sense is that, in reality, there is no negation of Brahman on the basis of its primacy, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of negating the king in the statement, "The king has no servant. Furthermore, since Brahman is the subject to be established, it cannot be negated; thus he says, "And when [the world] has been elaborated... Now, one might object: even if something is negated with respect to Brahman, its existence elsewhere is possible; so how can it be considered merely imagined (kalpita)? To this he says, "That is its locus."
The meaning is that what has been negated in relation to the substrate (upādāna) cannot abide elsewhere.
As for the objection that the negation of duality contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, he says in response: "And it is logical," and so forth.

For it was established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* that the validity of perception and other means of knowledge is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and not a revealer of ultimate reality (*tattvāvedaka*);
therefore, the sense is that there is no contradiction because [the world] is negated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).
Now, one might object: since it is a real entity (*vastutvāt*), let there be a negation of Brahman as well, just as there is of non-duality.
He says "no," [expressing] "not thus.
The meaning is that because [the Self] is the witness of both the existence and non-existence of duality, its negation is impossible.
The passage beginning with "nor" (*na ca*) and so forth is of clear meaning.
Regarding what was said—that by means of the two negations both form (*rūpa*) and the formal Brahman (*rūpin*) are negated—he says: "And these two...

The principle that when there is equality in number between the subjects (*uddeśya*) and the predicates (*vidheya*), they are connected respectively, is established by Pāṇini’s sūtra: *yathāsaṅkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*. Therefore, here, with reference to the two forms...
The meaning is that it is a prescription following two negations.
Regarding the alternative of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), he states the distinction: "because all visible things are negated, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is stilled.
The meaning is that if there were a specific negation such as "it is not the formed (*mūrta*), nor is it the formless (*amūrta*)," the desire to know would not be stilled.
He explains the remainder of the Sūtra with the words "itaśca" (and for this reason).

The meaning is that, because a negation would otherwise be untenable, it is understood that Brahman exists; furthermore, the Śruti explicitly declares, "There is another [Brahman] beyond. And as for the word "tat" (that):
The meaning is that Brahman is what remains;
the rest is clear. //22//
For scripture declares that it is unmanifest. (BS 3.2.23)
If that Supreme Brahman exists, which is other than the prohibited multitude of phenomenal manifestations (*prapañca*), why is it not perceived?
It is said in reply: It is unmanifest (*avyakta*) and cannot be grasped by the senses, because it is the witness of all that is visible.
For thus says the Śruti: "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other gods, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8).
"This is that Self described as 'not this, not this,' which is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26);
"That which is invisible and ungraspable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6);
"For when he [the wise man] finds refuge in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and without support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1), and so forth.
Smṛti also states: "This is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.25), and so forth. // 23 //
Indeed, he explains the aphorism—"That which is [not perceived] because of what has been denied"—in order to dispel the doubt that Brahman does not exist because it is ungraspable.
The meaning is that it is unmanifest and ungraspable by the senses due to the absence of form and other qualities, but not because of non-existence.
The grammatical connection is: "It is not grasped by other gods," i.e., by the other senses. //23//
Moreover, [the existence of the Self] is established through perception and inference in the state of successful realization. (BS 3.2.24)
Moreover, at the time of *saṃrādhana*, yogins perceive this very Self as unmanifest and with all phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) cast aside.
And *saṃrādhana* is the practice of devotion, meditation, focused intent (*praṇidhāna*), and so forth.
But how is it known that they perceive [it] at the time of *saṃrādhana*?
The meaning is "by means of perception and inference, as well as by Śruti and Smṛti.
For instance, the Śruti says: "He pierced the sense-organs outward; therefore, one looks outward and not at the inner self.
But some wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inward Self with his eyes turned back" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.1).
And likewise [the scripture says]: "When his being is purified by the clarity of knowledge, then, meditating, he beholds Him who is partless" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8).
Smṛti also states: "Those who are sleepless, who have conquered their breath, who are contented, and whose senses are restrained..."
Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who practice yoga behold as light.

"And yogis behold that eternal Blessed One," and so forth. [FN: The Self-existent Lord, having made the senses—which are directed outward and do not grasp the Self—withdrawn, has shone forth; he whose vision is turned inward has restrained his senses.]
Free from sleep and free from darkness;
the practitioner is one who meditates;
the Self attainable through yoga is the self of yoga.

Then, he explains the sūtra as an answer to the doubt, "When, then, is it to be grasped? with the words, "Moreover, this... The word "ca" (moreover) has the sense of "but. It means that it is not grasped by the senses, but rather through *saṃrādhana*—that is, by means of a mind refined by the scriptures.
*Praṇidhāna* is the firm placement or establishment of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) within the mind through devotion and meditation;
the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to recitation, prostration, and the like.
*Svayambhū* is the Lord (*īśvara*).
He made his own sense-faculties "turned away" (parāk), meaning he rendered them non-apprehenders of the Self;
for their destruction consists in their being created as apprehenders of unreal objects, because they were created by him in that manner.
The entire world perceives only the external object, not the inner Self.

However, a certain wise and intelligent person, whose vision is turned inward and whose senses are restrained, perceives the innermost Self within the pure mind by means of the scripture; this is the meaning of "seeking liberation.
Thereafter, with a mind purified by action, through the excellence of the quality of *sattva* known as knowledge, he meditates upon and beholds that partless [Self]; this is the meaning.
They are sleepless and free from darkness; the cause for this is their mastery over breath and their dedication to *prāṇāyāma*.
Those who are practicing meditation are *dhyāyins*; the Self attainable through yoga is the *yogātman*. //24//
[Objection: But surely, by accepting the relationship between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator, there would be a difference between the supreme Self and the individual self?
It is said: "And there is no distinction [of the Self], as in the case of light and so forth; and light [is perceived] in action through practice" (BBs 3.2.25).

Just as light, space, the sun, and so forth appear as if they possessed distinctions when associated with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as actions involving fingers, hands, water, and so on, [so it is with the Self].
Nor does it abandon its inherent nature as a non-differentiated self;
thus, this differentiation of the self is caused solely by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), while its true essence remains one with the Supreme Self.
For instance, in the Vedāntas, the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Lord (prājña) is established repeatedly through constant repetition. // 25 //

Just as light and other such phenomena appear to differ according to their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) but not by themselves, so too the conscious self (*cidātman*), though luminous, appears to differ according to the limiting adjuncts of activities such as meditation; yet in itself it is without distinction and of a single essence. This is established through the practice of "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*). Such is the application of the aphorism. //25//
Therefore, [the soul is] infinite; for thus is the mark [of its existence]. (BS 3.2.26)

And therefore, because non-difference is innate and difference is produced by ignorance, the individual soul, having dispelled ignorance through knowledge, attains oneness with the supreme, infinite, conscious Self.
For there is scriptural evidence to this effect: "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9);
"Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6), and so forth. // 26 //

The author of the Sūtras states that even from the indicative mark (liṅga) consisting of the scriptural declaration of the fruit—the identity of the individual soul with Brahman—it follows that difference is merely adventitious (aupādhika): "Therefore, [the soul is] with the Infinite" (Sūtra 2.3.26).
But on account of the designation of both [attributes], it is like a serpent and its coil. (BS 3.2.27)
Regarding this very relationship between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator, he presents another opinion for the sake of clarifying his own view: in some places,

a distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme conscious principle (*prājña*) is designated, as in "But by meditating upon Him, one beholds Him who is partless" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.1.8),
where they appear as the meditator and the object of meditation, and as the seer and the object seen.
"He attains the divine Person who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8),
thus [they are distinguished] by way of the goer and the goal;
yet in some places, the non-difference of those very two is designated, as in "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
"I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10);
"This is your Self, which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1);
"This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3).
In this case, when both designations are present, if non-difference alone were grasped as absolute, the designation of difference would be entirely without basis.
Therefore, because both designations are observed, the reality here must be like that of a snake and its coils.
Just as "snake" denotes non-difference while "coils," "expansion," and "length" denote difference, so it is here as well. // 27 //
Or, it is like light and its locus, because of its nature as luminosity.
Alternatively, this should be understood as being like light and its locus:
just as light and its locus, the sun, are not absolutely distinct from one another, since there is no difference between the two in their common nature as luminosity.
And yet, just as in those cases they are both subjects of distinct designations, so it is here as well. // 28 //
He states the connection between the two preceding sūtras concerning difference and non-difference with the words "In that very [state]": non-difference exists as the state of being a snake;
difference exists as the state of being a coil, which is a particular condition of the snake known as a "coil."
Likewise, there is non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman in its aspect as Brahman, and difference in its aspect as the individual soul;

or rather, just as there is both difference and non-difference between the sun and its light under the delimiting condition of the single attribute of luminosity, so too for the individual soul and the Supreme, both difference and non-difference must be accepted by virtue of the authority of scripture through the single attribute of selfhood—this is the meaning of the two sūtras.
"Being a bracelet" (kuṇḍalatvam) means having the form of a ring.

The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the state of being directed (*ābhogatva*), the state of being curved (*vakrākāratva*), the state of being tall (*prāṃśutva*), the state of having the form of a long staff (*dīrghadaṇḍākāratva*), and the state of having an upward-facing mouth (*udgatamukhatva*). // 27 // // 28 //
Or it is as before. (BBs 3.2.29)
Or rather, it must be exactly as previously proposed—that there is no distinction [between the two], like light and so forth.
For liberation through knowledge is logically possible only because bondage is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

If, however, some self were bound in an ultimate sense, existing as a particular configuration of the Supreme Self according to the analogy of a snake and its coils, [then liberation would be impossible].

Furthermore, if it were accepted as being a partial constituent according to the analogy of light and its substrate, then since ultimate bondage could not be set aside, the futility of the scriptures on liberation would follow;
moreover, the Śruti does not designate both difference and non-difference here as being equally real.

For it is non-difference alone that is pointed out as the subject to be established, whereas difference is merely restated as something already previously established for the purpose of intending to convey another meaning.
Therefore, this very point—that there is no distinction [between the Lord and the individual soul] like that between light and its source—is the final conclusion. // 29 //
And because of the prohibition [of another].
For this very reason, this alone is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Because the scripture prohibits a conscious being other than the supreme Self, stating: "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
And so forth.
"Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6) is the instruction from the Father;
"This Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).

And thus, because of the negation of the phenomenal world as distinct from Brahman and the resulting remainder of Brahman alone, it is understood that this indeed is the established conclusion (siddhānta). // 30 //
The *siddhāntasūtra* states: "As before.

This means that if one accepts both difference and non-difference through a distinction of attributes (*dharmabheda*) or by means of a single attribute (*ekadharma*), then because difference would be real, there could be no cessation [of duality], just as there is none for non-difference. Furthermore, it should be observed that if one accepts both difference and non-difference in one and the same thing, the very discourse on contradiction in the world would be destroyed.

Therefore, it is established that Brahman, which is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and consists of the single essence of consciousness (cidekarasa), is that which is indicated by the word "That" (tatpadalakṣya). // 29 // // 30 //
