Section on the Supreme (Parādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 31–37.
"Because of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction [the Brahman is not the highest].

(BS 3.2.31) Since there is a conflict of scriptural passages regarding whether this Brahman—which has been determined to be devoid of all phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*)—is itself the ultimate reality or whether there exists another reality beyond it, a doubt arises.
For certain statements, appearing at first glance, seem to establish that there is indeed another reality even beyond Brahman.
Indeed, this undertaking is made in order to state the refutation of those [objections].
From the perspective of the opponent, it must follow that there is a reality other than the supreme Brahman.
Why? Because of the designation of a "bridge," because of the designation of "measurement," because of the designation of "relation," and because of the designation of "difference."

First, regarding the designation as a "bridge" (*setu*): the passage, "Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1), proclaims the state of being a bridge for Brahman, who is denoted by the word "Self.
For in common worldly usage, the word "bridge" is well known to refer to a collection of earth, wood, and so forth, which serves to cut off the continuity of water.
But here, since the word "bridge" (*setu*) is applied to the Self, it implies the existence of something else distinct from the bridge of the Self, just as in the case of a worldly bridge;
this is also evident from the use of the verb "to cross over" in the phrase, "having crossed the bridge" (*setuṃ tīrtvā*, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.2).

Just as one who has crossed a worldly bridge reaches a desert region that is not a bridge, so it is understood that having crossed the Self, which is a bridge, one reaches the non-Self, which is not a bridge.
Furthermore, there is a designation of measurement: "This Brahman has four quarters, eight hooves, and sixteen parts.
And it is well known in the world that whatever is measured—such as a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin or the like, defined as "this much"—there exists something else beyond it.
Likewise, from the measurement of Brahman, it is understood that there must exist something other than it;
similarly, there is also the designation of a relationship, as in: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), and "the embodied self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.3.1).

And [the scripture says], "He is embraced by the intelligent Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21). Furthermore, a connection between measured things is observed through a measuring thing, as in the case of men with a city; and [the text] thus designates the connection of individual souls with Brahman during deep sleep.
Therefore, it is understood that there exists something else, immeasurable, beyond that;
and the designation of difference also leads to this very conclusion.
For instance: "Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6).

Having thus designated the Lord as having the sun as His locus, the text then designates the Lord as having the eye as His locus with the words: "Now, this person who is seen within the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).

Furthermore, it extends [the attributes of] that [solar Lord] to this [ocular Lord] regarding form and so forth: "The form of this one is the same as the form of that one; whatever the songs of that one are, these are his songs; whatever the name of that one is, this is his name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).
Moreover, it designates a limited sovereignty for both: "He rules over those worlds that are beyond this one and over the desires of the gods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8), referring to one;

and "He rules over those worlds that are below this one and over the desires of men" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.6), referring to the other—just as one says, "This is the kingdom of the Magadha king, and this is the kingdom of the Videha king. (Sūtra 31)
Note: A region abounding in wind is called *jāṅgala*.
As for the claim that the scriptural passages beginning with "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) negate any reality other than Brahman, that is incorrect.

He raises an objection with the words "paramata" (according to the opinion of others), on the grounds that the existence of other entities is indicated by scriptural passages concerning the bridge and so forth.

Although, in the section concerning heaven, earth, and so on (*dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa*), the word "bridge" was explained as being used figuratively in the sense of a supporter, this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is nonetheless raised by one who does not yet understand the resolution of the scriptural passages regarding measurement (*unmāna*) and the like; for in those cases, the passages concerning measurement and so forth are to be taken in their primary sense.

The distinction is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is that Brahman possesses duality; however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is the establishment of the non-dual reality signified by the term *tat* (That).
[An opponent argues: "Brahman possesses duality, because it is a bridge (*setu*)."
It is like a worldly bridge; and because of the scriptural statement regarding having "crossed over," he says, "having crossed the bridge.
According to the medical tradition's definition that "jāṅgala" is a region abounding in wind, *jāṅgala* is a place where wind is predominant.
But here, only the directions are to be grasped. The four directions are the digit (kalā) called "Possessing Light" (prakāśavat), which is one foot;
earth, atmosphere, heaven, and ocean are the digit called "Endless" (anantavat), which is the [other] foot.

"Agni, Sūrya, Candra, and Vidyut" is the quarter named "possessing light"; "the eye, the ear, speech, and the mind" is the quarter named "possessing abodes. Thus, Brahman is four-footed. Since its hooves are half of these quarters, it has eight hooves; and since there are four digits (kalās) in each of the four feet, the meaning is that it consists of sixteen digits (ṣoḍaśakala).
Sixteen paṇas measured in copper constitute what is known as a kārṣāpaṇa; likewise, Brahman is "dvayasa" (consisting of two), meaning it is limited.
And because of its being related [to the universe], it is like a city; thus he says: "tathā saṃbandhena" (likewise by way of relation).
"Immeasurable" (*amita*) means "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyāta*);
this should be understood because it is necessarily measured by its smallness when compared to other [sensations] such as touch (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, he says, "And because it is designated as distinct," just like a jar (*ghaṭa*), since it is mentioned separately.
The phrase "with that which resides in the sun" means "together with that which resides in this [eye].
Having stated the distinction based on the substratum (*ādhāra*) and by way of extension (*atideśa*), he states it also based on the limit (*avadhi*): "and it has a limit. //31//
Thus, when it has been argued on the basis of these designations such as "bridge" and so forth that there exists something higher than Brahman, the following is established:
"But on account of the commonality.
The word "but" (tu) precludes the attainment previously indicated;
for nothing other than Brahman can exist, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
For we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of anything else; indeed,
it has been established that for the entire class of born entities, their birth and so forth proceed from Brahman,
and that the effect is non-different from its cause.

Furthermore, nothing unborn other than Brahman is possible, because of the restrictive determination [in the scripture]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
Moreover, since there is the promise of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one, the existence of any entity distinct from Brahman cannot be conceived.
It was argued that the designations such as "bridge" and so forth indicate a reality distinct from Brahman;
to this, we reply: no.
First of all, the designation of a "bridge" is not capable of establishing the existence of something external to Brahman.
For it says, "The Self is the bridge," and "there is nothing beyond that.
Since there would be no "beyond" if that [Self] were not supreme, the status of being a "bridge" would not be tenable; thus, something else beyond it would have to be postulated.
But this is not logical.
Because it would contradict scriptural passages such as "unborn" (*ajātva*),
the application of the word "bridge" (*setu*) to the Self is justified by its commonality with a bridge;
for the Self possesses the common characteristic of a bridge in that it is the sustainer of the world and its boundaries.
Therefore, the Self under discussion is praised as being "like a bridge" (seturiva setuḥ).

Even in the expression "having crossed the bridge" (setuṃ tīrtvā), since it is impossible for one to cross over a bridge [in the sense of passing beyond it], the verb *tṛ* functions in the sense of "reaching" or "attaining. Just as when one says "he has crossed grammar," it means he has mastered it, not that he has passed beyond it; so it is here. // 32 //
He explains the *siddhāntasūtra* with the words beginning "by the word 'tu' (*but*)":
"As for that which is other [than Brahman], is it beginningless or with a beginning?

Not the first, because there is a lack of evidence and because an effect is non-different from Brahman and devoid of qualities. Having stated this, he says, "Nor is it the second, because of the determination of non-duality prior to creation," with the words: "And not something distinct from Brahman."
The sense is that the aforementioned inferences are sublated by scripture (*āgama*).
Having recalled what was stated, he declares the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reasons with the words beginning "nanu setu" (But [is it] by the scriptural mention of a 'bridge'?).
Does the establishment of the other [world] follow from the scriptural mention of a bridge, or by implication (*arthat*)?
Having stated "not this," he raises a second doubt with the words "therein, in the other.
He says "nor indeed" because it is improper to subvert the scriptural teaching of non-duality by means of the indicative mark (liṅga) of being a "bridge.
Furthermore, he states that the indicative mark is unestablished with the words "moreover."
The point is that the quality of being a support (vidhārakatva) is indeed logical even with respect to a second [element] that is merely imagined.
He states "having crossed the bridge" (setuṃ tīrtvā) to show that the reason [adduced for Brahman's non-duality], namely its having "crossed over," is also unestablished (asiddha). //32//
The purpose of the intellect is for the sake of cognition, like a foot. (BS 3.2.33)

As for what was stated—that there exists something beyond [the world] because of the designation of measurement—it is replied to this: even the designation of measurement is not for the purpose of establishing the existence of a reality distinct from Brahman.
For what purpose, then? It is for the sake of the intellect (*buddhy-artha*).
The meaning is: for the sake of meditation (*upāsanā*).

The thought—“How indeed might the intellect become stable regarding Brahman, which is four-footed, eight-hoofed, and sixteen-fold?”—leads precisely to the conceptualization of a measurement (*unmāna*) of Brahman by means of its modifications (*vikāra*).
For it is not possible for all persons, due to their being of inferior, middling, or superior intellect, to fix the intellect upon the changeless and infinite Brahman directly.
It is like the case of the feet.

Just as in the passages concerning the mind and space—which are taught as symbols of Brahman with respect to the internal self and the divine—four "feet" consisting of speech and so forth related to the mind are conceived, and four consisting of fire and so forth related to space, for the purpose of meditation; so it is here.

Alternatively, "like a quarter" (pādavat) means that just as a division into quarters is conceptually assigned to a *kārṣāpaṇa* coin for the sake of facilitating common transactions—for indeed, not all people are always able to transact using the entire *kārṣāpaṇa* due to the lack of fixed rules regarding the quantities used in buying and selling—it is the same in this case. [This is the meaning. // 33 // [Note:

The conceptualization of measurements for Brahman is for the purpose of the practice of meditation by those of dull intellect, just as the practice of dealing with quarters of a *kārṣāpaṇa* is employed.]
He states that its limited nature (*parimitatva*) is also unproven, saying "for the purpose of the intellect" (*buddhy-artha*).

The meaning is that speech, breath, sight, and hearing are the feet of the mind; fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters are the feet of space—all these being imagined for the sake of meditation—and likewise, this is the measurement (*unmāna*) of Brahman.
He provides a worldly illustration, saying "or else."
To the question, "Why should there not be worldly usage even without the postulation of quarters? he says: "Not so" (na hi).

Just as the quarter of a kārṣāpaṇa coin is postulated for the sake of worldly transaction, the measurement of Brahman is postulated for the sake of the practice of meditation by those of dull intellect; such is the meaning. //33//
[The difference in the Lord's powers] is due to the difference in location, as in the case of light and so forth. (BS 3.2.34)
In this sūtra, a refutation is provided for both the designation of relation and the designation of difference.
As for what was said—that because of the designation of relation and the designation of difference, there must be something other than the Supreme—that too is incorrect;
for even in the case of a single entity, these two designations are possible in relation to a particular location.

Regarding the designation of a "relation," this is the meaning: when the specific cognition that has arisen due to its connection with particular limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth ceases upon the cessation of those adjuncts, that cessation is figuratively described as a "relation" with the Supreme Self; this is expressed solely with reference to the adjuncts, not with reference to any limitation [of the Self].

Likewise, even the designation of difference regarding Brahman is applied figuratively with reference to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and not with reference to a distinction in its own nature (*svarūpa*), as indicated by the employment of the analogy "like light" and so forth. Just as in the case of a single light—whether solar or lunar—which acquires particularities through association with limiting adjuncts, there occurs a designation of relation upon the cessation of those adjuncts, and a designation of difference due to the distinction of the adjuncts; or just as in the cases of the space within a needle's eye, a water-pot, and so on, these two designations of relation and difference occur solely with reference to the adjuncts, so it is here. // 34 //
He states that the distinctions of relation and locus are merely imagined and do not establish the reality of a second [entity], beginning with the word "sthāna":

"The locus" refers to the intellect and so forth as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). When a single entity appears divided by its limiting adjuncts, the relation is figuratively attributed (*upacaryate*) once those adjuncts have ceased.

Just as the light of the sun and so forth, which appears divided by limiting adjuncts such as a finger, is figuratively attributed the relation of being a "great light" when separated from those adjuncts, so too, due to the difference between the two loci—the sun and the eye—the distinction of the Golden Person (*Hiraṇmayapuruṣa*) is imagined. This is the meaning.
And because it is logical. (BBs 3.2.35)

And here, only such a relationship is appropriate, and no other; for the text, "He becomes merged in his own Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), teaches this as a relationship of essential nature (*svarūpa*). And because essential nature is imperishable, a relationship based on the analogy of a man and a city does not hold.
However, because its own nature is concealed by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the statement "He goes to his own [Self]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1) is logically consistent;
likewise, no other kind of difference is possible.
This is because it would contradict the doctrine of the oneness of God, which is well-established by numerous scriptural passages.

Accordingly, scripture itself explains how even the single ether can be designated as distinct based on its location: "That which is the ether outside the person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.8), and "That which is the ether within the heart" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.9). // 35 //
To the question, "Why should not the two primary types of relationship themselves be the distinct [meanings]? there is the Sūtra: "And because it is logical" (upapatteśca) //35//.
Likewise, because there is a negation of others. (3.2.36)
Having thus refuted the arguments of the opposing side regarding designations such as "bridge" and so forth, he now concludes his own position with another reason:
likewise, from the negation of anything else, it is understood that there is no other entity beyond Brahman.
For it is said: "That indeed is below" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1).
"I alone am below" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1);
"The Self alone is below" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2);
"Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).
"Brahman alone is all this; the Self alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2);
"There is not the slightest diversity here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19);
"Than whom there is nothing higher, nor anything else" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9).

Furthermore, scriptural passages such as "This Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), which belong to their own respective contexts, cannot be interpreted as having any other meaning; they exclude the existence of any other entity distinct from Brahman.
Moreover, because of the scriptural teaching that [Brahman] is the innermost of all, it is determined that there is no inner self other than the Supreme Self. // 36 //

The connection of the individual soul with Brahman in its true nature consists in the cessation of duality; it is logical that this is so, and not a primary relation such as conjunction, because two distinct entities do not exist. Likewise, duality does not exist inherently, because of the scriptural teaching of oneness. This is the meaning.
By this [verse], "omnipresence" is established from the words "extent" (*āyāma*) and so forth (Brahmasūtra 3.2.37).
By this refutation of designations such as "bridge" and by resorting to the negation of anything else, the omnipresence of the Self is also established;
otherwise, it would not be established.
For if the designations of "bridge" and so forth were accepted in their primary sense, it would follow that the Self is limited, since the bridge and the like would constitute its very nature.
Likewise, even if there were no negation of other things, the fact that one object is distinguished from another object would still result in the consequence that the Self is limited.
Furthermore, its omnipresence is understood from such scriptural terms as "extent" (*āyāma*) and others.
The word *āyāma* signifies pervasion. This is evident from such scriptural passages as: "As far as this space extends, so far extends this space within the heart" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3);

"All-pervading and eternal like space" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6); "Greater than heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3); "Greater than space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3); and "Eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.24).
For such scriptural passages, traditional texts, and logical arguments as these demonstrate that the Self is omnipresent. // 37 //

[Objection: But surely, if there were no second [entity], there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning omnipresence. To this he says: "By this, omnipresence [is established]. If the second entity were real, Brahman would be limited, like a boat or similar objects, according to the scripture: "That wherein one sees another, that is limited. Furthermore, since it is impossible for the partless and unattached Brahman to have a connection with a real phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the contradiction with the scriptural texts on omnipresence would belong to you alone.

This is the intended meaning: the world, which is superimposed upon the substratum, is pervaded by it because of its being a superimposition, just as a snake pervaded by a rope; such is the logical principle (nyāya). //37//

Section 7: The Topic of the Fruit (Phalādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 38–41 START BsCom_3,2.8.38 7 phalādhikaraṇam / sū. 38-41 Now begins the section concerning the fruit [of the knowledge of Brahman]. Sūtra 38: But [the fruit of knowledge] is that which is heard [in scripture]; for that is what is seen [in the world]. The word "but" sets aside the previous view. It has been stated that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is liberation (*mokṣa*). Now, a doubt arises as to whether this fruit is something to be accomplished through human effort (*puruṣatantra*) or not. If it were dependent on human effort, then, like sacrifices and the like, it would be subject to gradations of excellence and deficiency; consequently, the claim that it is eternal and unchanging would be contradicted. Therefore, the opponent argues that since the fruit is something to be accomplished by human effort, it must be subject to gradations. To this, we reply: The fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is that which is heard in scripture—namely, liberation characterized by the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of supreme bliss. Why? Because that is what is seen. Just as in the world, when a person who is afflicted by disease and the like hears from a physician that their affliction will cease, they experience joy; so too, upon hearing from scripture that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of supreme bliss, there is joy. Furthermore, the cessation of suffering and the attainment of bliss are not things to be produced by human effort, such as cooking or weaving, but rather are merely states to be reached or manifested. Therefore, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is not subject to gradations. Sūtra 39: And because of the non-dependence [on other factors]. Furthermore, this fruit does not depend on anything else. For the scripture declares that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is independent of other means: "For one who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9); "He who knows the Self transcends sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3). Since it is heard that the fruit is attained solely through the knowledge of Brahman, it follows that it does not depend on other factors. Sūtra 40: And because of the absence of connection with the body and the senses. Moreover, the scripture teaches that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman exists where there is no connection with the body and the senses: "Where there is no darkness, there one sees the sun; beyond the sun is a higher light; beyond that light is the Supreme Light; attaining that Supreme Light, he becomes the Self of intelligence" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7). Since the state of being free from the body and the senses is impossible to achieve through human effort, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is not dependent on human action. Sūtra 41: And because of the denial of the other [means]. Finally, the scripture denies that any other means can produce the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman: "There is no path other than this" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8); "Knowing Him alone, one transcends death; there is no other path to the goal" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8). From this denial of other paths, it is understood that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is not dependent on human effort. Thus, it is established that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is liberation, which is eternal and unchanging. "From Him [proceeds] the fruit, because that is logical.
(BBs 3.2.38) Another nature of that very Brahman is described in its empirical state, characterized by the distinction between the ruler and the ruled.

Regarding this well-known threefold fruit of action—consisting of the desirable, the undesirable, and the mixed—which pertains to transmigratory existence for living beings, an inquiry arises as to whether it originates from karma or from the Lord.
In this regard, it is first established that the fruit must arise from that Lord.
Why? Because it is logically consistent (*upapatti*).

For He, as the sovereign supervisor of all, ordains the diverse processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; and because He possesses knowledge of the specific distinctions of place and time, it is logically consistent that He brings about the fruit for those who perform actions in accordance with their respective karma.
However, it is untenable that an action which perishes moment by moment can have a fruit occurring at a later time,
because from non-existence no entity arises.
This might be argued:
It is argued that karma perishes at its own time after having produced a fruit corresponding to itself, and that this fruit will be experienced by the agent at a later time.
This too is not tenable, because a thing cannot be established as a "fruit" prior to its connection with an experiencer.
For in the world, only that pleasure or pain which is actually experienced by the self at a given time is recognized as a "fruit."
For worldly people do not perceive that pleasure or pain which is unconnected to the self can be a fruit.
Now, it might be argued: "Let there not be the production of a fruit immediately after the action;
rather, the fruit will arise from the *apūrva* (unseen force), which is the effect of the action."
That too is not tenable;
for it is impossible for the *apūrva*—which is insentient, equal to wood or a clod of earth, and not impelled by a conscious agent—to engage in activity.
Furthermore, there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence.
If it is argued that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a means of valid cognition, we say no; for once God is established, the need for presumptive testimony ceases. (38) [Note:
*iṣṭa* refers to heaven.]
"Unpleasant" means fit for states such as the Avīci hell;
"mixed" refers to that which is experienced by humans.
It is that which has as its basis the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the continuous flow of birth and death.
Having thus clarified that which is indicated by the word (the *lakṣya*), he states the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*): "From Him [comes] the fruit, because it is logical.
Because He is devoid of distinctions, there exists another nature called the cause of fruits: the desired happiness of gods and others, and the undesired suffering of those in hell.

"Mixed" refers to that which has for its sphere (gocara) or basis (āśraya) the cycle of existence (saṃsāra)—the continuous flow of birth and death—of human beings; thus, it is "that which has the cycle of existence as its sphere.
Here, a doubt is raised—"What?"—because of the scriptural statements regarding both karma and the Lord being the cause of the fruit.

In this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the Lord who bestows the fruit—who is denoted by the word *tat*—is not established, the object of indication (*lakṣya*) is not established; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that [Lord] is established. This constitutes the difference in result.

As for the connection (*saṃgati*), it arises from the fact that the prima facie argument is raised on the grounds that, relying upon the previously mentioned quality of being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*), the Lord also lacks the status of being the bestower of fruits.

Although the bestowing of fruits, like omnipresence, is established during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāradaśā*), nevertheless, it is [the view of the opponent that] it is from action alone [that results arise].

Thinking that this section is commenced for the purpose of determining the expressed meaning—which sustains the intended meaning already stated—by dispelling the doubt regarding its being the giver of the fruit, [the author] first states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "In that regard, first...
Heaven and so forth have a giver who is cognizant of specific places, times, and actions.
The logical argument is that [the action] is the fruit of karma, just like the fruit of service.
To begin with, the action known as the performance of sacrifice and so forth is momentary; does it produce the fruit from its own destruction, or does it perish after having produced the fruit?
Or rather, is the accomplishment of the fruit from something unprecedented?
It is not the first case; thus he says, "because of non-existence.
He raises the second alternative with "it might be."

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "that too" (*tad api*) and so forth, on the grounds that there is no proof for the existence of heaven, pleasure, and the like, which remain unmanifest from the moment the karma perishes.
He raises a third objection with "now" (*atha*):
does the *apūrva* (unseen potency) act independently to bestow the fruit?
Or [is it] presided over by volition?
Regarding the first [alternative], he says "that too" (*tadapi*).

As for the second, the point is that since a soul (*jīva*) who is unperceived and lacks supernormal knowledge cannot possibly be a presiding agent, the existence of God as the presiding agent is established.
With a bold argument, he states that there is no such thing as *apūrva* (the unseen merit): "In its existence... [and so on].

If it is argued that the existence of a permanent *apūrva* is established because momentary acts such as sacrifices cannot logically be the causes for heaven and other results as taught in scripture, we say: no.
The meaning is that the attainment of the fruit occurs solely from the Lord (*Īśvara*), who is permanent, once He has been propitiated by those very actions.
The meaning is that the unprecedented (apūrva) is not established by mere reasoning alone. //38//
And because it is so stated in scripture. (BS 3.2.39)
We do not postulate God as the cause of the fruit solely on the basis of logical reasoning; rather, we consider God alone to be the cause of the fruit because He is so stated in scripture.

And there is a scriptural passage to this effect: "He, indeed, is that great unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.24), and other passages of a similar kind.
FN: He is called *annāda* because he gives food (*anna*) completely (*samantāt*) to all living beings;
he is *vasudāna*, the giver of wealth.

If it is argued that the existence of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is established by the scriptural and traditional texts cited under the sūtra "One who possesses residual karma (*anuśaya*) [returns] upon the exhaustion of [their] deeds" (*kṛtātyaye 'nuśayavān*), such as "Those whose conduct here has been pleasant," etc., then the Sūtrakāra states "And because it is heard [in scripture]" (*śrutatvācca*) to show that the Lord’s status as the bestower of fruits must likewise be accepted on the basis of those same texts.
He is called *annāda* because he gives food (*anna*) on all sides (*samantāt*) to living beings;
he is the giver of wealth (*vasudāna*), the bestower of riches.

Since action (*karman*) or the unseen merit (*apūrva*) is insentient and thus merely an instrument, it has been shown that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Lord (*īśvara*) alone is the independent bestower of results. //39//
Jaimini [holds that] dharma [is the purpose of the Veda], for this very reason. (BS 3.2.40)
The teacher Jaimini, however, considers dharma to be the giver of the fruit;
for this very reason, both because of scripture and because of logical consistency.
This meaning is indeed heard in such scriptural sentences as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and so forth.
And in that case, because the injunction (vidhi) enters into the sphere of its object, it is understood that the sacrifice is the producer of heaven;
otherwise, the sacrifice would result in being something never performed, and thus the instruction regarding it would be rendered purposeless.
[Objection: But since merit perishes moment by moment, a fruit [arising from it] is not possible; therefore, this position has been abandoned.
This is not a fault,
because the authority of the Śruti is supreme.
If the Śruti is authoritative, then this connection between action and its fruit, as it is heard in scripture, must be understood in such a way that it becomes logically consistent.
Furthermore, an action cannot perish after producing some unprecedented [result] and then bestow its fruit at a later time.
Therefore, it is inferred that there exists either some subtle subsequent state of the action or a prior state of the fruit called *avipraṇāśa* (non-perishing).
And this meaning is established by the manner already explained.
However, the claim that God bestows the fruit [of action] is untenable.

For it is impossible for a non-variegated cause to produce a variegated effect; otherwise, there would follow the charge of partiality and cruelty, as well as the consequence of rendering religious practice futile.
Therefore, the fruit arises from dharma alone. // 40 //
Now he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "dharma" and so forth.
The scriptural injunction (vidhi-śruti) has the injunction as its meaning;

the sacrifice is the object of that injunctive sense (liṅ-artha), which consists of an impulsion (preraṇā). From the comprehension of that [injunction's] existence, it is understood that the sacrifice is the means to heaven.
The meaning is that if the sacrifice lacked the status of being a means to achieve the desired end, then the instigation [to perform it] would be untenable.
Having stated that the fruit of the action is established by way of the *apūrva*, he refutes the established position (siddhānta) with the words "But the Lord" (*īśvarastu*).
Does the Lord bestow the fruit independently of the action, or dependent upon it?

The first [opponent] says, "Of that which is non-variegated," and so forth. Regarding the second [position], the sense is: since the fruit is established through the unseen merit (*apūrva*) alone—just as there is wrapping on a mat and such from the mere act of wrapping—what is the use of God? To this we reply: if pleasure and the like could arise simply from the perceived excellence of sandalwood, thorns, and so forth, then what would be the point of dharma and adharma? Since their necessity is established by the authority of Śruti and Smṛti, what offense has God committed against that requirement?
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the fruit [of action] comes from karma alone, independent of God. //40//
But Bādarāyaṇa holds the former view, because of the declaration of a reason. (BS 3.2.41)
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, considers the Lord mentioned previously alone to be the cause of the fruit.
The view that the fruit arises from action alone or from the *apūrva* (unseen potency) alone is set aside by the word "but" (*tu*).
Whether it be dependent on action or dependent on the *apūrva*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fruit comes from the Lord in whatever manner may be.
Why? Because of the designation of Him as the cause.

For even with respect to merit and demerit, God is designated as the cause by virtue of being their instigator, and with respect to the fruit, by virtue of being its giver, as it is said: "For He indeed causes him to perform good action whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds;
and He likewise causes him to perform evil action whom He wishes to lead down."
And this meaning is recorded in the Bhagavadgītā: "Whatever form of deity a devotee desires to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his unwavering."
"Endowed with that faith, he strives for His propitiation,
and from Him he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me for his welfare" (Gītā 7.21).
Furthermore, in all the Vedāntas, it is taught that creations have the Lord alone as their cause.
And that very fact—that the Lord creates offspring in accordance with their own past actions—is precisely what constitutes His status as the cause of their fruits.
Furthermore, defects such as the impossibility of diverse effects do not apply to the Lord, because He takes into account the efforts previously exerted by beings. // 41 //
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
He provides the final conclusion with the words "But previously... (pūrvaṃ tu).

Since it is impossible for insentient karma to act by itself, and because the scriptural texts following the analogies of service and so forth are more authoritative, as well as because all Vedānta texts declare that the Lord is the cause of the world, the general meaning is that the accomplishment of results included within the world proceeds from karma presided over by the Lord. //41//

Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the second chapter of the third [section], titled "The Purification of the Meanings of the Words *Tattvam*."
END BsCom_3.2.8.41 Third Chapter, Third Section:
I bow to Mārtaṇḍa for the destruction of darkness, and to Tilakasvāmin for my joy.
I bow down again and again to Vighneśa for the destruction of obstacles.
START BsCom_3,3.1.1 Third Chapter, Third Section / [In this section,
there is an exposition on the combination of qualities belonging to the knowledge of the higher and lower Brahman.]
1. The Section Concerning the Consistency of All Vedānta Teachings. Sūtra 1–4:
There is consistency of cognition regarding Brahman in all Vedānta texts, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.
The true nature of Brahman, the object to be known, has been explained.
Now, however, it is investigated whether the cognitions (*vijñāna*) differ from one Vedānta text to another or not.

But surely, Brahman—the object of cognition—has been determined to be devoid of distinctions such as before and after, to be of a single essence (*ekarasa*), like a mass of salt; so how can there be any introduction of an inquiry into the difference or non-difference of cognitions therein?
For it cannot be said that, like the multiplicity of ritual acts (*karman*), a multiplicity of Brahmans is intended to be taught in the Vedāntas.
Because Brahman is a single unity and possesses a single form,
and because in a single Brahman there cannot possibly exist cognitions of diverse forms;
for it is not the case that when the object is one way, the cognition is another way, and yet it be non-erroneous.

If, however, multiple cognitions of Brahman were intended to be taught in various Vedānta texts concerning a single Brahman, then one of them would be non-erroneous while the others would be erroneous; this would lead to a lack of confidence in the Vedāntas.

Therefore, it is not possible to suspect a difference in the cognition of Brahman for each respective Vedānta text. Nor can its non-difference be asserted on the grounds of the non-distinction of injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth.
Because the knowledge of Brahman is not characterized by injunction (*codanā*).

For the Teacher [Bādarāyaṇa] stated in the sūtra, "But that [is established] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (*brahma-sūtra* 1.1.4), that the knowledge of Brahman is produced by the statements concerning Brahman—which terminate in the reality of the thing itself (*vastu*)—and which have as their primary purport not injunctions.
How then does he undertake this investigation into difference and non-difference?

To this it is replied: there is no fault here, for this discussion regarding the difference or non-difference of cognitions concerns either the qualified Brahman or the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

For in this context, both difference and non-difference are possible for meditations just as they are for ritual acts (*karman*); and like ritual acts, these meditations are said to have either visible results, or some have the result of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) by way of the arising of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Regarding these [Upanishads], this reflection arises:
is there a difference in the consciousness (vijñāna) in each Vedānta, or is it not so?
In that regard, the arguments for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) are first set forth.
First of all, it is well known that a name serves as a cause for the cognition of difference, as seen in the case of "light" (*jyotis*) and other such terms.

Furthermore, in this context, there are various distinct names for the cognitions enjoined in different Vedānta texts, such as the *Taittirīyaka*, the *Vājasaneyaka*, the *Kauthumaka*, the *Śāṭyāyanaka*, and so forth.

Likewise, a difference in form (*rūpa*) is also well known to establish a difference in ritual action (*karma*), as in the case of "the curd for the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevyāmikṣā*) and "the whey for the Vājins" (*vājibhyo vājinam*), and so forth.
Moreover, there is a difference in form here;
for example, some followers of the Vedic branches (śākhins) designate a sixth additional fire in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, while others recite only five.
Likewise, in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃvāda) and so forth, some record speech and the other organs as fewer in number, while others record them as more.
Likewise, a specific feature of the ritual (*dharmaviśeṣa*) has been suspected as an indicator of a difference in action (*karmabheda*) in the case of the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others;
and such a specific feature exists here,
namely, the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*) of the followers of the Atharva Veda.
Furthermore, other grounds for differentiation, such as repetition and so forth, should likewise be applied to the various Vedānta texts as far as possible.
Therefore, it follows that there is a difference in the cognitions [of Brahman] according to each Vedānta text.
This being the position reached, we reply: the cognitions based on all the Vedānta texts must be one and the same in each respective Vedānta text.
Why? Because there is no difference in sensation and so forth.

By the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), the reasons for non-difference set forth in the sūtra concerning the conclusion of the section on other recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*) are drawn in here; the meaning is: because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, and name.

Just as in the case of a single Agnihotra sacrifice, even though there are differences in the Vedic branches (śākhā), the same human effort is enjoined by the injunction "one should offer oblations" (juhuyāt);

likewise, in the passages "He who knows the eldest and the best" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.1), the injunction is exactly the same for both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas.
The connection with the purpose is also indeed the same, as it is stated: "He becomes the eldest and the best among his own people" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1).
The form in both cases is also the very same for the knowledge—that is, the reality of Prāṇa endowed with the specific attributes of being the eldest, the best, and so forth.

And just as the substance and the deity constitute the form of a sacrifice, so should the object of knowledge be understood as the form of this knowledge, for by that [object] the knowledge is defined.
The designation is also the same, namely, "the science of breath" (prāṇavidyā).
Therefore, the cognitions [of Brahman] are based on all the Vedāntas.
In this same way, it should be applied to the knowledge of the five fires (pañcāgnividyā), the Vaiśvānara-knowledge, the Śāṇḍilya-knowledge, and so forth.

However, those apparent causes of differentiation such as name and form (*nāmarūpa*) have already been refuted in the very first section (the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā*), beginning with the statement: "There would be no [need for] a name, because it is not an injunction (*codanā*)," since an injunction refers to human effort—that is, human activity. Having determined the true nature of Brahman, [the author] now states the nature of the meditation (*upāsanā*) which is the means to its knowledge: "It is recognized in all Vedāntas, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. (Note: An injunction (*codanā*) is that by which one is impelled; it is human exertion, for it is an operation of the person.)
He states the connection between the chapters with the words "it has been explained.
In the previous chapter, the discrimination between the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* was performed;

here, the fruit thereof—the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—is determined by the sūtra "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal," through a synthesis of the referents denoted by the term *tat*, which were required and not yet repeated. Thus, there is a relationship of cause and effect (*phala-phalibhāva*).
Association (*saṅgati*).

It should be understood that the contemplation of the meaning of sentences concerning the qualities (*saguṇa*) is performed because it serves as a means to the knowledge of the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) through the gateway of one-pointedness of mind for those who possess such knowledge.
Concordance (*saṃprati*).

Thinking that the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-jñāna) has been described as the subject matter for investigating difference and non-difference, [the opponent] objects with the words "But surely" (nanu).

The meaning is this: an inquiry into the distinction between meditations (vidyā-bheda) would be appropriate if there were a distinction in the objects of knowledge; however, since Brahman—the object of knowledge—is one, there is no occasion for such an inquiry.
To the objection that even if Brahman is one, an inquiry may still occur due to a distinction in its attributes (dharma-bheda), he replies: "And because of its uniform nature" (ekarūpatvāt ca).
The meaning is "because of the absence of dharmas.
Since there is a suspicion of difference because various modes are possible even within Brahman, which is of a single nature, he says "nor... and so forth.

Having stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the suspicion of a difference in knowledge is untenable, he says "nor also of this... to show that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that there is no difference in knowledge because of the non-difference of the injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth—is also improper.
Having thus raised an objection regarding the commencement of the section, he provides the resolution: "That is being stated.

It should be said that the investigation into difference and non-difference is conducted only with respect to saguṇa-vidyās (meditations on the Lord with attributes), whereas in the case of nirguṇa-vidyā (meditation on the Lord without attributes), unity is already established; therefore, only the compendium of qualities in the form of the literal meaning of the words is performed for the sake of determining the sense of the entire passage.

That the vidyās such as the Pañcāgni, Prāṇa, Dahara, Śāṇḍilya, and Vaiśvānara are mutually distinct will be explained in the sūtra, "On account of the difference of words and so forth, they are manifold" (BS 3.3.58).

But here, since these [meditations] are mutually distinct, a doubt arises as to whether they differ according to each Vedic school (*śākhā*) or not, due to differences in name and so forth, and because there is no difference in the injunction (*codanā*) and other factors.

The distinction in results is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the meditations are different, there is no combination of qualities; in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because they are non-different, there is combination.

In the *Pūrvatantra*, the prima facie sūtra for the section on different schools states: "There is a difference of ritual action in another school because of difference in name, form, and specific duties, repetition, censure, incapacity, completion, scriptural statement, expiation, and the observation of another purpose."
It may be so.

In that regard, the reasons already mentioned—namely, name and the others—are stated here for the purpose of distinguishing between the Vidyās. For instance, in the passage, "Now this is the Jyotis; now this is the Sarvajyotis;

one should sacrifice with this [sacrifice] involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee," one might suspect that this is merely an injunction of the quality known as the "thousand-fold fee" with reference to the previously mentioned Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

Since it is possible for the word *jyotis* to be the name of a distinct ritual action, it cannot be taken as a mere indicator (*lakṣaka*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*; furthermore, because of the phrase "now" (*atha*), which marks a break in the context, a distinct ritual action with specific sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) is enjoined as different from the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Thus, it has been stated that a name serves as a differentiator of rituals.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the *Jyotis* and so forth," one should understand that a difference in ritual is established by the difference in designations, such as *ādhvaryavam* (the office of the Adhvaryu) and *hautram* (the office of the Hotṛ).
Heated milk that has become solidified by the addition of curds is *āmikṣā*;

therein, the liquid portion in the form of water is the *vājina*. This is the distinction [between them] in the context of the Vaiśvadeva-āmikṣā sacrifice, as stated in the passage: "One pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the *vājina* for the Vājins."

Having raised the objection that "vājibhyaḥ" is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) called *vājina* because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Viśvedevas, [the Siddhāntin] concludes that there is a difference between the two rites due to a difference in their essential form—namely, substance and deity. This is because it is impossible for "vājibhyaḥ" to be a restatement of the Viśvedevas who were already mentioned as being subordinate to the *āmikṣā*; furthermore, since the ritual action is already occupied by the *āmikṣā* prescribed at its origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), an injunction for the substance *vājina*, which was not required, would be illogical. Therefore, the sacrifice with *vājina* has a different deity, the Vājins, and thus it is established as a separate ritual action.
From the initial phrase, one should understand that a difference in sacrifice arises from the difference in substances, as in "curds for Indra" and "milk for Indra.
Similarly here too, there is a difference in the knowledge (vidyā) between the Vājasaneyins and the Chāndogyas due to the difference in form, namely five fires versus six fires.

Likewise, there is a difference in the knowledge of the vital breaths (prāṇavidyā), because in the Chāndogya the speech and other organs are deficient in semen, whereas among the Vājasaneyins they are accompanied by it.
In the study of the Kārīrī-vākya, the Taittirīyakas have the specific rule of eating on the ground, which does not apply to others;
in the study of the Agni, some have the duty of fetching water for the sake of the teacher, which does not apply to others;
and in the study of the Aśvamedha, some alone have the duty of bringing fodder for the horse, which does not apply to others.
Furthermore, it is not logical that those very same rituals, such as the Kārīrī sacrifice, should both depend upon and not depend upon specific qualities (dharma-viśeṣa);

therefore, just as a difference in ritual action (karma-bheda) was suspected in another recensional branch (śākhā) due to a specific quality, so too here, because of the study of the Muṇḍaka, there would be a difference in knowledge (vidyā-bheda), since the vow consisting of carrying a vessel of coals on the head is for some only and not for others.
Repetition (punarukti) refers to restatement (abhyāsa).

Just as the distinction between the *prayāja* offerings is stated through the repetition of the verb "he sacrifices" in the passage, "He sacrifices to the fuel-sticks; he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt," so too is there a distinction between meditations (*vidyā*) due to repetition in another recensional text.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), censure and other such factors are included, as in the case of the pre-dawn oblation: "In the morning, they speak untruth who offer the Agnihotra before sunrise."

Furthermore, there is a distinction [between the two views] because of the scriptural condemnation of the offering after sunrise: "If one were to offer in the morning when the sun has risen, it would be just as if they were to bring food to a guest who has arrived at an empty dwelling.
Since it is impossible for a single act to be performed both after sunrise and before sunrise, [the two must be distinct].

Likewise, even from the performance of expiation for the transgression of the *uditānuditahoma* (the fire-oblation performed either after sunrise or before), a division of the *Agnihotra* has been suspected.
These instances of censure and expiation do not exist in the case of the Vedāntic sciences, and thus they are not cited as examples.

Just as there is a division [of ritual action] due to the inability to know or perform a rite prescribed in all the Vedic branches (*śākhās*), so too there is a division of each specific Vedāntic science due to the inability to study or understand all the Vedāntas.

Just as it might be argued that the conclusion of all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*) is not stated to be uniform, but rather that the conclusion of a particular branch occurs at a particular point in a specific ritual act— and thus, due to this difference in the statement of conclusion, a difference in ritual acts (*karmabheda*) is suspected for each branch—

likewise, there might be a difference in knowledge (*vidyābheda*), since the conclusion regarding the universal nature of the syllable *Oṃ* occurs in one Vedānta text, while in another it occurs elsewhere.

The reasons stated in the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra—that "the perception of another purpose constitutes an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and that because of the difference therein, there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) just as there is a difference in ritual acts (*karman*)"—have been shown; some of these are employed here both in the *siddhānta* and in the *pūrvapakṣa*.

Likewise, differences in ritual acts are established by means of different words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*).
In that context, the triad of name, quality, and form has been explained.

Just as a difference in ritual action—specifically the *bhāvanā* delimited by the meaning of the verbal root—is stated through the distinction of verbal roots in the forms "one should sacrifice," "one should give," and "one should offer oblations" (*yajet*, *dadyāt*, *juhuyāt*), so too here, a difference between knowledges (*vidyā*) arises from the distinction of words such as "one knows" (*veda*) and "one meditates upon" (*upāste*).

Furthermore, just as a difference in ritual action is established by number—as in "one offers three oblations"—there would likewise be a difference in the Saṃvarga-vidyā due to the number two in the expression "Vāyu and Prāṇa."

In the section on the *nityāgnihotra*, it is heard in another context—that of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*—that "they offer the *agnihotra* for a month. Because it is situated in a different context, this *agnihotra* is considered a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Similarly, here, due to the difference in the contexts within the various Vedāntas, there is a difference between the two [teachings]; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "evam" (thus).

The term *sarvavedāntapratyayāni* means those which are recognized by all Vedānta texts; the meaning is that they are prescribed by them. Since a difference among rites such as the Agnihotra would appear to exist across various recensions (*śākhā*) due to the previously mentioned differences in name and so forth, there is the sūtra establishing the conclusion of the section on different recensions: "Or rather, it is one [rite], because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, and name. In this context, *codanā* refers either to the injunctive word or to the impelled effort.
He states the non-distinction between them with the words "just as in one [case]":
the meaning is that because there is a unity of effort delimited by the oblation for the sake of a single element (dhātu), there is a unity of the effort of meditation.

Just as the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa) characterized by qualities such as being the eldest is one and the same across all recensional branches (śākhā), so too the knowledge of the five fires (pañcāgni-vidyā) is one, due to the lack of distinction in its connection with the fruit and other such factors.
Likewise, he states that other knowledge is also distinct with the words "Thus, [the knowledge] of the five fires.
He refutes the reasons for the prima facie view with the words "But those who...
It is not logical that there is a difference in ritual action based on names such as "The Kaṭhaka" and so forth.

Why? Because words such as *Kāṭhaka* and others do not denote an injunction (*codanā*), but rather function as names of texts; thus, they lack the status of denoting the ritual action itself. Therefore, even though there are differences between the textual recensions (*śākhā*) that bear distinct names, the ritual action prescribed by them is one and the same. Even a minor difference in form does not contradict the unity of the ritual action. Furthermore, specific characteristics (*dharma-viśeṣa*) are auxiliary to the study (*adhyayana*) and not auxiliary to the ritual action; therefore, they do not cause a division of the ritual action. Consequently, the charge of redundancy (*punarukti*) regarding the different recensions is unestablished.

Even the presence of censure (*nindā*) or the mention of another purpose does not constitute a ground for differentiation, because they merely serve as praise for their respective injunctions. Furthermore, even when one lacks the capacity to study multiple recensions (*śākhās*), it is possible to obtain from elsewhere those specific details required by one's own recension that are not mentioned therein; thus, incapacity is not a differentiator. Since expiation is possible even for a single ritual act through the omission of an ancillary part (*aṅga*) and so forth, the difference in the statements regarding completion (*samāpti*) is likewise irrelevant. Thus, the meaning is that these grounds for differentiation have been refuted once the strength of the means of proof for the non-differentiation of the ritual act has been established. //1//
Here too, having raised a certain objection regarding a specific point, he provides a rebuttal: [text follows].
If it be argued that [the knowledge derived from different Upanishads] is not identical because of differences [in qualities], we say no, for this would apply even to a single [Upanishad].
It might be thought:
"The identity of the cognitions derived from all Vedānta texts is not tenable because of the difference in their qualities."

For instance, the Vājasaneyins, having introduced the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), mention a sixth fire as another [fire] in the passage beginning with, "For him, fire itself becomes the fire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.14).
The Chandogas, however, do not mention that [sixth fire], but conclude with the number five alone, saying, "Now, he who knows these five fires thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.10).
How can a single knowledge be possible for both groups when this quality exists for some and does not exist for others?
Furthermore, the combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) cannot be understood here, because it would contradict the number five.
Likewise, in the dialogue of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃvāda), the Chandogas mention four other breaths besides the chief one: speech, sight, hearing, and mind.
The Vājasaneyins, however, mention even a fifth [form]: "Prajāpati is indeed semen; he who knows this is procreated with offspring and cattle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.6).

If it is argued that there is a difference in the knowledge because of the difference in what is to be known—which arises from the difference in insertion and omission—and that there is consequently a difference in the meditative knowledge (vidyā), just as there is a difference in the sacrifice due to the difference in the substance and the deity, we reply:
this is not a fault.
Since such a difference in qualities is possible even within a single Vidyā—

despite the fact that the inclusion of a sixth fire is not possible— nevertheless, because the five fires beginning with heaven (dyu) are recognized as identical in both places, a difference between the two Vidyās cannot exist;
for the Atirātra sacrifice does not become different merely by the inclusion or exclusion of the Ṣoḍaśin cup.
Moreover, the Chāndogyas read of a sixth fire: "When he has departed from here, they carry him, as destined, to the fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9.2).

However, the Vājasaneyins, for the purpose of terminating the conceptualization of fuel, smoke, and so forth—which had been applied to the five fires that are merely constructed—state: "For him, fire itself becomes the fire; fuel becomes fuel" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.14).
Such passages as these are recorded; they are a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).
Even if this statement is for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), even so that quality can be combined by the Chandogas as well.
Nor should any contradiction with the number five be suspected here.
For this number five, intended to refer to the fires superimposed [upon the body], is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) and not an integral part of the injunction; thus there is no fault.
In the same way, in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the inclusion of an additional quality in another context is not contradictory.
Nor should one suspect that a difference in the object of knowledge (*vedya*) or a difference in the meditation (*vidyā*) arises from the variation of insertion and omission (*āvāpodvāpa*).
Because, even when certain portions of the objects of knowledge are added or subtracted, there is an understanding of the non-difference of the vast mass of objects of knowledge;
therefore, it is indeed a single science. [Note:
From this world, having departed—that is, having gone to another world as a deceased person—the kinsmen carry [the body] to the fire.]

If it is argued that, by the very logic of different recensions (*śākhāntara*), the unity of the meditation (*vidyaikya*) is established just as there is unity of action (*karmaikya*), and thus repetition [of the teaching] would be redundant, he says: "In this case also. The distinction lies in the fact that the form [of the meditation] is prescribed at the time of its origination (*utpattiśiṣṭatva*). There might be a difference in meditations due to the difference in forms—such as the five fires (*pañcāgni*) and so on—found in the originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*) for meditations like "one who knows the five fires," just as there is a difference in rituals due to the difference in forms such as *āmikṣā* and *vājina*. Since this is intended to dispel such an additional doubt, [the objection does not apply].
Thinking that this section might involve redundancy, he explains the doubt with the words beginning "It might be," and so forth.

It should be understood that because this is a separate treatise, and because the principles of ritual action (*karmanyāya*) are difficult to apply to mental meditations (*mānasavidyā*) without a formal Sūtra, there is not even a scent of redundancy.

Now, one might object: the fire belonging to the final oblation (*antyeṣṭi*), which is the sixth mentioned by the Vājasaneyins as being well-known for the purpose of cremating the deceased—that very fire is to be incorporated into the *Chāndogya*; thus, there is no difference in form (*rūpabheda*).
Regarding this, he says: "And not here.

Let it be that for the Vājasaneyins there is the insertion (*āvāpa*) of semen possessing the quality of procreation, and for the Chāndogyas its removal (*udvāpa*); what follows from that? To this he replies with the words beginning "āvāpa":

even if one admits the absence of the sixth fire in the Chāndogya, a minor difference in form does not contradict the identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*). He refutes [the objection] with the passage beginning "naiṣa" and so forth.
He abandons his initial position, saying: "It is also recited thus.
The meaning is that when a deceased person has gone from this world to another desired world, the kinsmen offer [the oblation] to Agni.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the Chāndogya only "Agni" is heard, whereas by the Vājasaneyins the specific details such as the *samit* and so forth are recited; thus, the difference in form remains as it was.
Regarding this, he says: "But the Vājasaneyins...

The meaning is that since the sixth fire and its specific details are merely restatements (anuvāda) and are not themselves objects of meditation, only the five fires are to be meditated upon in both [texts]; thus, there is no difference in form.
He further states, "Even though... to show that even if the sixth fire along with its specific details were an object of meditation, there would still be no difference in form.

The meaning is that the fivefold nature of the five fires—such as the heavenly world and so forth—which are established through the very injunction for their attainment as fires, is restated as an already established fact and is not enjoined as an object of meditation. Furthermore, having stated that the Chāndogyas should incorporate the "seed" (retas) found in the Vājasaneyaka branch, [the author] says "nor by addition," etc., to show that even if it is not incorporated, there is no difference in the knowledge (vidyā). //2//

Because of the nature of Vedic study, because of the qualification for the *Samācāra* [section], and because it is like the *Sava* sacrifice, there is a restriction regarding that [study]. (BBs 3.3.3)
As for the argument that there is a difference in the knowledge (vidyā) because the followers of the Atharva Veda require the "head-vow" (śirovrata) and others do not, that is answered as follows:
this is a rule pertaining to the private recitation of the text (svādhyāya), not to the knowledge itself.
How is this understood?

Because this is to be tasted as such— that is, as a dharma belonging to one's own practice— the followers of the Atharvaveda, in their text devoted to the instruction of Vedic vows, record that "this too" has been explained as a Vedic vow. Furthermore, from the word *ādi* (beginning) in the phrase "one who has not performed the vow does not study this" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.2.11), and from the word *adhyayana* (study), it is determined that this is indeed a duty pertaining to the study of one's own Upaniṣad.

But is it not the case that, because of the scriptural mention of a connection with the knowledge of Brahman in the passage, "One should impart this very knowledge of Brahman to those by whom the head-vow has been performed according to rule" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.10), this single knowledge of Brahman would be conflated everywhere and this duty [of the head-vow] would apply universally? No;
for even there, the word "this" (*etām*) refers back to the specific subject under discussion.

Furthermore, since the manifestation of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) depends upon specific texts, this duty is connected only with those specific texts. The phrase "and like the *sava* sacrifices" is an illustration of that restriction.

Just as the seven *sava* sacrifices, beginning with the *saurya* and ending with the *sauṛaudana*, belong exclusively to the followers of the Atharva Veda—because they are not connected to the three sacred fires mentioned in the other Vedas, but are connected to the single fire mentioned in the Atharva Veda.
Just as those [mantras] are restricted, so too this dharma is restricted to that very [context] due to its connection with a specific portion of the Vedic study (svādhyāya).
Therefore, the oneness of the knowledge (vidya) is also beyond reproach. // 3 //

Having stated thus that a difference in form does not constitute a difference in knowledge, he says "of the private recitation" (*svādhyāyasya*) to show that even a difference in ritual detail (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is not a differentiator.

The meaning is that, like the *godāna* ceremony, the *śirovrata* is prescribed in the *sūtra* of the Ātharvaṇikas as an auxiliary to the study of the Veda (*adhyayana*), and not as an auxiliary to the knowledge (*vidyā*).
He explains [the phrase] "and because of the context" (*adhikārāt*) with the words "not this... (*naitat*).

This is the subject at hand: the meaning is that the head-vow (*śirovrata*) is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the study of the *Muṇḍaka*, because of the scriptural statement, "A man who has not performed the head-vow does not study this [text].
Now, one might object: "But is it not the case that this vow is also heard as being an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*)? [The author replies:
If there were only one single knowledge of Brahman across all recensional branches (*śākhā*), then the vow connected to that knowledge would also apply everywhere.
The meaning is that there is no connection [between the two], and thus there is a difference between the two knowledges (*vidyābhedah*).

He refutes this, saying "No," on the grounds that the word "this" (*etac-chabda*) refers back to the subject matter of the current text; therefore, the term "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*) refers specifically to the section concerning the illumination of Brahman.
Regarding the rule that the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*) must be observed during the study of the *Muṇḍaka*, the mention of "like the *Soma* sacrifice" (*savavat*) serves as an illustrative example.
The meaning is that all oblations are to be performed in that single fire which is prescribed by the Atharvans in their own Sūtra as being well-known by the name "Ekarṣi. Thus it is restricted. //3//
And scripture also demonstrates this. BBs_3,3.4.

The Veda also demonstrates the unity of knowledge by teaching that the object of knowledge is one throughout all the Vedāntas, as in: "That supreme which all the Vedas proclaim" (Kaṭha 2.15). Likewise:
"For the Bahvṛcas meditate upon this very one in the Great Hymn; the Adhvaryus [meditate upon] this in the fire; the Chandogas [meditate upon] this in the Mahāvrata.
And similarly: "A great terror, a raised thunderbolt" (Kaṭha 6.2).

Thus, in the Taittirīyaka, there is seen a reference to that quality of the Lord characterized as the cause of fear, which was mentioned in the Kaṭhaka, for the purpose of censuring the perception of difference: "For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Self], then fear arises for him;
in that very [Self] there is fear for the one who knows but does not reflect" (Taitt. 2.7.1).

Likewise, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, there is the treatment as an established fact of the Vaiśvānara who was described as being the size of a span in the Vājasaneyaka: "But he who meditates on this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the measure of a span, the all-pervading" (Chā.

Similarly, because rites such as the Uktha, which are enjoined elsewhere, are taken up for the purpose of enjoining meditation upon them in another place, it follows by the principle of the observation of the majority that meditations also possess the status of being recognized across all Vedāntas.

Furthermore, the Sūtrakāra states, "And [the scripture] shows," meaning that the scripture demonstrates the identity of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahmavidyā) through the identity of the object of knowledge;

and because they are recited in proximity to that, he says "likewise" (tathā), meaning that it also shows the identity of the knowledges of the qualified Brahman (saguṇa-vidyā) across all Vedic branches (śākhās) through the identity of their object of knowledge in the three Vedas.

Furthermore, he states that the reference to a category of reality mentioned in one branch of scripture as if it were already established in another branch demonstrates the identity of the knowledge (*vidya*): "In the same way, [the passage] beginning with 'the great fear'...

When this person perceives even the slightest interval—that is, a difference—within this non-dual reality, then for him the fear of *saṃsāra* certainly arises; because for that wise person who perceives duality, that very Brahman becomes a source of fear.
The meaning is: for one who contemplates "I am indeed Brahman.
He says "tathā" (so it is), showing that the meditation on the "span-long" [self] is established as being identical with the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.

Furthermore, because the Uktha and other elements are perceived in all Vedānta texts, it is understood from this reason that those mentioned in one place are taken up in another for the purpose of meditation.
Therefore, he says "tathā" (likewise), meaning that because the meditations on those [elements] are also based on the authority of all the Vedāntas, their identity is established for the most part;
the sense is that, just as there is an identity among the knowledges of Brahman, there is likewise an identity among the knowledges of the Uktha and so forth. //4//

"Because there is no difference in the object, there is a combination [of qualities], as in the case of supplementary injunctions, when the [knowledge] is the same.
(BBs 3.3.5) This is a sūtra concerning the purpose.

Since it is thus established that all Vedānta texts have the same purport regarding all cognitions, there is a combination of the qualities of a cognition taught in one place within another cognition that is the same.
Because there is no difference in their meaning.
For that very same purpose served by those qualities in one instance—which is to assist in producing a specific cognition—is the same in the other instance as well.
Since in both cases it is that very same single cognition [that results], there is a transfer [of the qualities].
It is like the case of supplementary injunctions (*vidhiśeṣa*).

Just as there is a combination (*upasaṃhāra*) of the various subsidiary duties of the Agnihotra and other rites—because the object is non-different, namely that one and the same Agnihotra rite is everywhere—in the same way it is here as well.

For if there were a difference in the cognitions (*vijñāna*), then because the qualities would be bound to different cognitions and because there would be no relationship of original and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), there could be no such combination.
But this is not the case if consciousness is a single entity;
however, an elaboration of this very aphorism concerning its purpose will follow, beginning with the words "Because of the non-difference of all. // 5 //

He states the result of the inquiry into the unity of knowledge across all branches as "the combination" (upasaṃhāra). When there is a doubt— namely, whether the qualities heard in relation to an identical knowledge in different branches are restricted to their respective scriptural contexts, or whether those not heard in one place must be combined from other branches— the [author] maintains that even though the knowledge is one, the benefit of that knowledge is accomplished by the very qualities mentioned in each respective context.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the qualities are established according to the division of the Vedic branches (*śākhā*); in that case, the result would be the futility of investigating the unity of the knowledge under discussion.
He explains the aphorism as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "And when it is established," and so forth.
The meaning is that because qualities are inseparable from the possessor of those qualities, this knowledge located in one branch possesses the qualities of the knowledge mentioned in another branch,
since it is non-different from it— just like that [other] knowledge; thus, through this inference, the integration of qualities is established in the unity of the two knowledges.

Regarding the inclusion of various auxiliary members when the principal [act] is one and the same, he provides an illustration with the words "like the remainder of an injunction" (*vidhiśeṣavat*). He states the very same point by way of contrast with the words "for if" (*yadi hi*). Now, one might ask: if there is an extension of qualities restricted to the Āgneya sacrifice to the Saura sacrifice—which is not different from it—then why should there not be an extension of qualities belonging to one meditation (*vidyā*) to another meditation? To this, he replies: "In the archetype" (*prakṛtau*).

The meaning is that while the attainment [of qualities] is appropriate in the case of a modification of the *prakṛti* (primordial nature), there is no such attainment in the case of the *vidyās* (meditative knowledges) because the relationship between *prakṛti* and *vikṛti* is not established for them. "Not so" means that there is no non-inclusion of the qualities.
He avoids the redundancy of the subsequent sūtras with this sūtra by saying, "Of this very... [sūtra 6]. //5//
