The Section on Change (Anyathātvādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 6–8.
If it be argued that there is a difference [in the Udgītha] because of the word [“udgītha”], we say no, because there is no distinction.
In the Vājasaneyaka: “Those gods said, ‘Come, let us overcome the Asuras in the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha.

Having begun thus [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2], after censuring the vital breaths such as speech and the rest for being pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the acceptance of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is recorded: "Then they said to this breath in the mouth, 'Chant the Udgītha for us'; 'So be it,' he replied; and this breath chanted the Udgītha for them" (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.7).

Likewise, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as well, after beginning with, "Then the gods approached the Udgītha, thinking, 'By this we shall overcome them,'" and having censured the other vital breaths (*prāṇa*) as being pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the selection of the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is likewise recorded: "Then they meditated upon that which is this principal vital breath as the Udgītha" (Chā.

In both cases, by means of the praise of the vital breath (prāṇa), the injunction for the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā) is determined. Regarding this, there is a doubt: whether there should be a difference between the two knowledges here, or rather, whether they constitute a single knowledge.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That they constitute a single knowledge, according to the previously stated principle.

But is it not improper to maintain the identity of the knowledge because of the difference in introductory context? For the Vājasaneyins begin in one way and the Chandogas in another; the Vājasaneyins, for instance, enjoin the vital breath as the agent of the udgītha, saying, "Do thou sing out for us" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2).
But the Chandogas [regard it] as the Udgītha, according to the passage: "They meditated upon that as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.7).
If it is asked how there can be identity of knowledge in these cases, this is not a fault.
For the unity of the knowledge does not depart merely on account of this distinction, since a much greater degree of non-distinction is also perceived.

To explain: there is the introduction of the conflict between the gods and the asuras, the presentation of the *udgītha* with the intention of overcoming the asuras, and the mention of speech (*vāk*) and the other [organs].

Through that censure, the reliance upon the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) and the destruction of the Asuras by its power—illustrated by the example of the stone and the clod of earth—are understood as common to both [texts].
Furthermore, even in the Vājasaneyaka, the identity of the vital breath with the *udgītha* is heard in the scripture: "This, indeed, is the *udgītha*" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.23).
Therefore, even in the Chāndogya, agency must be understood as implied;
and from that, the identity of the knowledge [vidyā] follows. // 6 // [FN:
Āsanya means "situated in the mouth."]
The dialogue is intended for the destruction of the Asuras and is for the purpose of conquering them.

Previously, it was stated that knowledge is essentially one because there is no difference in the initial injunctions and so forth; now, in order to state an exception to that, he says, "Otherwise," etc.
Here, by the words beginning with "Vāja," he indicates the subject matter: the *Udgītha-brāhmaṇa* of the Vājasaneyins and the *Udgītha-adhyāya* of the Chandogas.

Those gods, whose functions are characterized by *sattva*, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), said to one another: "Come now, in this sacrifice, by means of the *udgītha*—the work of the *udgātṛ* priest—let us transcend the Asuras, who consist of the functions of *rajas* and *tamas*, and attain the state of divinity. Having thus reached an agreement to determine the faultless performer of the *udgītha* as their object of worship, they first examined speech (*vāk*), saying: "You [perform] the office of the *udgātṛ* for us."

Having reproached them, saying, "She has spoken falsely; likewise, the nose, the eye, the ear, and the mind have been seized by the evil of the Asuras through desire," they determined that the vital breath (prāṇa) residing in the mouth—the one situated within the oral cavity—is the object of worship.
The meaning is that when that battle consisting of mutual subjugation had commenced, the gods, as before, brought forth the Udgītha, thinking, "By means of this Udgītha, let us conquer these Asuras."
He states the doubt based on the measures of difference and non-difference with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

Here, according to the principle of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that because of the identity of the name—namely, "Udgītha-vidyā"—there is identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikyam*); the result of this view is the combination of qualities from one another.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, although the names are identical, there is no such combination because of the refutation of the identity of knowledge.

Thus, wherever there is a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) according to the previous method, it should be understood that the connection is one of exception (*apavādikī*). He explains the portion of the Sūtra containing the Siddhāntin’s objection with the words: "But this is not tenable.
For the Chāndogyas, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the performer of the entire Udgītha rite is the object of meditation.

Regarding the word "udgāyet" (one should chant), because it is a term denoting an agent, for the Chāndogas the syllable *oṃ*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*—is to be meditated upon as the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

This is because, having begun with "This syllable *oṃ* is the *udgītha*," the text uses the expression "the *udgītha* is the vital breath," which indicates its nature as an object of action (*karman*).
Thus, the meaning of the objection is that since there is a difference between the meditator as agent and the meditation as object, the two meditations (*vidyā*) are distinct.
"By way of being the *udgītha*" means "by way of being the syllable *oṃ*.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) refutes [the objection] by means of the principle already stated—that a minor difference in form does not contradict the identity of the knowledge—saying, "This is not so.
"The intention regarding the overcoming of the Asuras" means a dialogue for the purpose of conquering the Asuras.
The meaning is that it is heard in both places that just as a clod of earth is shattered upon hitting a stone, so too the Asuras who came to slay Prāṇa were themselves destroyed by his power.
Even having accepted a minor difference in form, the identity of the knowledge was stated; now he says "Vāk" to show that even this [difference] does not exist.
Since Prāṇa is heard in both places as being the agent of the Udgītha, the agency heard in one place is to be seen in both places as well. //6//
Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of the "higher than the high" (parovarīyas) and other such [meditations]. (BBs 3.3.7)
Nor is the identity of the knowledge alone reasonable; rather, a distinction between the knowledges is what is reasonable here.
Why?
Because of the difference in context.
The meaning is "due to a difference in the initial approach.
For instance, here a difference in the initial approach is observed.
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, for example: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" (Chā. 1.1.1).

Having thus introduced the fact that the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*, is to be meditated upon, and having provided an explanatory exposition of its qualities such as being the "most savory" (*rasatama*) and so forth, [the text] then says: "Now, indeed, there follows an explanatory exposition of this very syllable" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1).

Thus, returning once more to that very *oṃ* which is a constituent of the *udgītha*, it speaks by means of the narrative of the gods and the Asuras: "They meditated upon that breath as the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.2).

In this context, if the word *udgītha* were intended to mean the entire ritual section (*bhakti*), and if its performer—the *udgātṛ* priest—were meant, then both the introductory statement would be contradicted and the use of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would be necessitated.
Furthermore, there must be a conclusion in accordance with the beginning within a single passage;
therefore, in this context, the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the syllable *oṃ*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*—is being taught.
In the Vājasaneyaka, however, because there is no reason for the word *udgītha* to be taken as referring to a mere part, the entire liturgical portion (*bhakti*) is indicated.

In the passage, "Do thou sing for us" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.3.2), the agent of that [singing] is likewise determined to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgātṛ* priest; thus, this constitutes a different method of exposition.

Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the vital breath with the *udgītha* there is intended solely to demonstrate that the vital breath—which is sought to be shown as the *udgātṛ*—is the self of all; therefore, it does not bring about the identity of the two meditations (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, there is a difference [between the two cases] because in that instance as well, the word *udgītha* refers exclusively to the entire object of devotion (*sakalabhakti*).

Nor can the status of the *udgātṛ* (chanter) be discarded from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) on the grounds of impossibility; for just like its being the *udgītha*, its being the *udgātṛ* is taught as something intended for meditation (*upāsanārtha*).
And since the *udgātṛ* performs the office of the *udgātṛ* solely by means of the power of the vital breath, there is no such impossibility.
And thus it has been declared in that very same place: "With speech and with breath he sang the udgītha" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.24).
Moreover, when a difference in the intended meaning is clearly perceived, it is not proper to determine identity of meaning based merely on the imitation of the phrasing of the sentence.

For instance, in the *abhyudaya-vākya* and the *paśukāma-vākya*, [it is said]: "One should divide the rice-grains into three parts; those which are middling, one should offer to Agni... [and so forth].

Although there is similarity in the injunctions such as "one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Dātṛ," because of the difference in the introductory context (*upakrama*), it is determined that in the sentence concerning prosperity (*abhyudaya*), there is the removal of the deity,
whereas in the sentence concerning the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), there is the injunction of a sacrifice.

Likewise here also, there is a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*) due to a difference in the introductory passages (*upakrama*), as in the case of the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyas*) and so forth.

Just as, even though there is a commonality in the superimposition of the vision of the Supreme Self, [it is said]: "For space is indeed greater than these; space is the ultimate resort" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1).
"This very Udgītha is higher than the high, it is infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.2).

Thus, the meditation on the Udgītha characterized by the quality of being "higher than the high" is distinct from the meditation on the Udgītha characterized by qualities such as having golden hair and a golden beard located in the eye and the sun.
And just as there is no mutual combination of qualities even within a single recensional branch (śākhā), so too it is with meditations of this kind situated in other branches. // 7 //
FN: "Difference" (*vaiṣamya*) refers to the diversity of the sciences in both cases.
"Removal" (*apanaya*) means separation.
"Higher than the high" (*parovarīyān*) means more excellent than the most excellent.
He establishes the final conclusion—that there is no identity of knowledge due to the difference in many contradictory forms—with the words "Not so" (na vā).

He qualifies the Imperishable (akṣara) as "the Udgītha," meaning it is a constituent part of that [Udgītha]. It is the syllable Om, the most excellent essence among the essences such as the earth and others.

Having described the qualities as "attainment" and "prosperity," he introduces a narrative to enjoin the meditation on the syllable *oṃ* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within that which possesses those qualities; thus he says, "The most flavorful," and so forth. Now, one might object: for the sake of syntactic unity with the speech of Vājin, let the word *udgītha* found at the beginning of the Chāndogya refer to the entire division of the *sāman*, and let it be explained that in the passage "the vital breath is the *udgītha*," the vital breath is to be meditated upon as the performer of the *udgītha*. To this, he replies: "In that case, if [it were] the *udgītha*... and so forth.
The meaning is that there would be two defects: first, the introduction of the meditation on the syllable *oṃ*, and second, the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the agent in the word "udgītha.

Now, one might object: even in the Siddhānta view, a figurative indication of a part must be accepted in that word; therefore, it is better to accept the indication of the agent, as this is supported by another scriptural passage (*śruti*), and since the meditation on the agent-prāṇa is certain from the conclusion, it must also be certain from the introduction. To this, he says: "upakrama... [etc.].
For a commencement that is ambiguous is determined by the remainder of the passage;

as in the case of "The pebbles are smeared," where there is doubt regarding the substance for smearing, the determination is made from the remainder, "Clarified butter is light. But here, the fact that the Imperishable (akṣara) is the object of meditation is certain from the very commencement.

The meaning is that since the indication of a part (*avayava-lakṣaṇā*) for the word *udgītha*, which stands in grammatical apposition with that [breath], has been definitively established, the concluding statement "the breath is the *udgītha*" must be interpreted as having the same purpose as that [indication].

Thus, he states "Vāja" etc., meaning that because the object of meditation is different—the syllable *oṃ* being taught as the object of worship in the Chāndogya, whereas in the other [text] it is the breath—there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*).

He refutes the argument previously stated—that even in the Vājasaneyi-śruti there is identity of the object of worship because of the scriptural hearing of the breath's form as the *udgītha*—with the words "As for what was said... and so forth.

In this context, the meaning is that the *udgītha* is not mentioned as the object of meditation (*upāsya*), but rather as a quality (*guṇa*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is the object of meditation.

Furthermore, he states that there is a difference in the object of meditation—since the *udgītha* is the syllable *oṃ* in the *Chāndogya*, whereas here it is the *bhakti* (the portion of the chant)—by using the word "sakala" (entire).

Anticipating the objection that because the vital breath is insentient (*jaḍa*), it cannot be the *udgātṛ* (the chanter), but must be accepted by the Vājasaneyins as being merely the *udgītha* itself—and thus asserting their identity—he says "na ca" (and not).

The meaning is that it is not the case that [the identity of the meditations] is impossible on the grounds of the Śruti stating, "That Udgātṛ performed the office of the Udgātṛ with the breath distinguished by speech.
Regarding what was said—that the unity of the meditations follows from the non-difference of the greater number of elements—he says, "And not... (na ca).

The meaning is that since the distinction between the internal forms of worship is clear—namely, that in one case the *udgātṛ* (the breath) is to be meditated upon and in the other the syllable *oṃ*—it is not proper to assume the identity of the meditation merely on the basis of a similarity in external explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

To show that identity of meaning does not follow from mere similarity of wording, he provides an illustration with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). [The passage continues: "He indeed deprives of offspring and cattle him for whom the sacrificial offering has been set aside... and so forth.

"When the moon rises in the east, one should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size, from them he should make a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest, from them a pap of curdled milk for Indra Pradātṛ; and those that are the smallest, from them a pap of boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa"—this is the statement concerning the transgression [of the new-moon sacrifice].

The meaning of this is as follows: for that sacrificer who, on the fourteenth day itself, having mistaken it for the new moon (amāvāsyā), proceeds to perform the rites of the Darśa sacrifice, and for whom the oblation—consisting of rice, curds, and milk—is already set aside (*nirupta*) beforehand, intended for the deities of the Darśa such as Agni and others, and yet the moon rises from behind him; for that sacrificer, due to the fault of the transposition of time, that very same [oblation] which was set aside...
The oblation diminishes [the sacrificer's] progeny and so forth, separates him from his prosperity, and increases his enemy, because the sacrificer is subject to confusion regarding the proper time.

One should divide those rice-grains—which have been prepared in three ways as the middle portion and so on, and have been set aside together with curds and other ingredients—separating them from Agni and the other deities; and having separated them, one should offer them to Agni and the others, who possess qualities such as being givers and are non-different from the deities of the New Moon sacrifice, by means of the curds.
The meaning is that one should prepare a *caru* of the coarsest rice-grains in curd, and a *caru* of the finest grains in boiled milk.

Here, it might initially appear that because of the lapse in time, a different ritual—one distinct from the *darśa* sacrifice—is being prescribed as an expiation involving other deities. However, this is not the case; rather, by referring to the threefold division of the rice-grains and so forth through the injunction "one should divide," the text indicates that within that very same sacrifice, the oblation (*havis*) is to be separated from its original deities.

In the case of the *darśa* sacrifice, it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is merely an injunction regarding the connection with another deity, and not a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).

Similarly, in the *abhyudaya* passage, because the undertaking is due to a lapse in time, it is determined that within the *darśa* sacrifice itself, there is a removal or separation of the oblation from its previous deities.
However, in the passage concerning the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), although [it says] "one should offer those which are the largest as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Samanmat,"...

"The middling ones he should offer to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa as a cooked oblation (*caru*) of boiled milk; those that are the smallest, he should offer to Indra Pradātṛ as a *caru* of curd"—this injunction is identical to the statement regarding the *abhyudaya* (the moon rising after the new moon).
Nevertheless, the rule "he who desires cattle, having performed the New Moon sacrifice, should drive away the calves" refers to the obligatory (*nitya*) Darśa rite.

The meaning is as follows: having concluded [the previous discussion], it is shown that because the procedure for "driving away the calves" (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) begins for the sake of the body [of the sacrifice], there is indeed an injunction for a different sacrifice for one desiring cattle; thus, there is no identity of purpose with the *abhyudaya* passage. Likewise, in the present case as well, similarity of reference is not a cause for the identity of the knowledge (*vidya*). The phrase "one should drive away the calves" means that one should lead them from the mother's place to another location.
He explains the example mentioned in the Sūtra with the phrase "like *parovarīyastva* and so forth.

The word *para* ends in the letter *s*; [the compound] *parovarīyān* is a single term meaning "that which is higher than the high (*parasmāt paraḥ*) and more excellent than the excellent (*varāt varataraḥ*).
The meaning is that the *udgītha* is so called because it is the object for the contemplation (*ālambana*) of the infinite Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is known as space (*ākāśa*).

The meaning is that, although there is a similarity in the meditation on the *udgītha* as having the nature of space and the nature of the golden-bearded Person (*hiraṇyaśmaśru-puruṣa*), there is nevertheless a distinction here, just as there is a distinction between different meditations (*vidyā*). //7//
If it is argued that this has been stated by way of designation, we reply: even that exists. (BBs 3.3.8)
Now, it might be argued that because the name is the same, the unity of the knowledge (*vidyā*) is logical here, since the name "Udgītha-vidyā" is one and the same for both.
That too is not tenable;

for this has already been stated: "Or rather [there is no unity], because of the difference of context, as in the case of the 'higher than the high' (*parovarīyas*) and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.7).

And this alone is more reasonable here, for that identity of name follows the literal words of the scripture; however, the identity of name [between the *udgītha* and the *udgītha-vidyā*] is merely a figurative usage by worldly speakers based on the employment of the word "udgītha," as it lies outside the literal words of the scripture.

Moreover, this identity of name exists even among those things whose difference is well-established, such as the "Udgītha-vidyā" in relation to the meditations on the "Higher than the High" (*parovarīyastva*) and so forth.

Likewise, we observe that even for rites like the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa, whose differences are well-established, they are designated by the single name "Kāṭhaka" when they are recited in the single text of the Kaṭhas; so it will be in this case as well.
But where there is no such cause for difference, let there be unity of knowledge on account of the identity of the designation, as in the case of the Saṃvarga-vidyā and others. // 8 //
Having raised the identity of names as the seed of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he refutes it with the words "from the name" (saṃjñātaḥ).

The meaning is that the multiplicity of meditations (vidyā) based on the difference in the forms of the objects of worship—which was previously stated—is stronger because it follows the literal words of the scripture; whereas the name, being of human origin, is weak.
He states that identity of name is not invariably concomitant with identity of action, saying "And there is...
He asks: "Is identity of name entirely without authority everywhere? and answers: "But where...

In the absence of a subverting factor, even identity of name is a means of proof; for example, in the case of the "Saṃvarga-vidyā," because of the identity of the name, there is identity of that vidyā across all recensional branches (śākhās).
The meaning is that the identity of the Pañcāgni-vidyā and other such meditations has been demonstrated in the first sūtra. //8//

Section on Pervasion (Vyāptyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 9 END BsCom_3,3.3.8 START BsCom_3,3.4.9 4 Section on Pervasion / Sūtra 9: "Because of the impossibility of pervasion. (sū. 9) The opponent argues: Since the relationship between the probans (*liṅga*) and the probandum (*liṅgin*) is not established by perception, it must be established by inference. However, that inference would require another inference to establish its own pervasion, leading to an infinite regress. Furthermore, since the probans and the probandum are distinct entities, there can be no necessary connection between them; thus, pervasion is impossible. Therefore, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) cannot be established through inference. To this, we reply: This objection is not valid. Just as the relationship between fire and smoke is perceived through repeated observation, so too is the relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge perceived. Moreover, the relationship between the probans and the probandum is established by the very nature of things (*svabhāvataḥ*). For instance, the capacity to produce an effect is inherent in the cause; similarly, the fact that a certain cognition arises from a specific object is established by the nature of the thing itself. Thus, pervasion is possible, and the means of knowledge are indeed established through inference. Therefore, the objection regarding the impossibility of pervasion is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.4.9 START BsCom_3,3.5.10 5 Section on Non-Eternality (Anityatvādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 10 The opponent argues: If the means of knowledge are eternal, then they would be incapable of producing any new cognition, as an eternal entity cannot undergo change. Consequently, the objects of knowledge could never be known. To this, we reply: This is not so. Although the means of knowledge are eternal, they manifest their function through the conjunction with the sense organs and other auxiliary factors. Just as the sun, though eternally present, manifests light only when in conjunction with darkness, so too do the means of knowledge manifest their efficacy through the removal of ignorance. Thus, the means of knowledge are both eternal and capable of producing cognition. Therefore, the objection regarding non-eternality is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.5.10 START BsCom_3,3.6.11 6 Section on the Refutation of the Opponent's View (Pūrvapakṣanirākaraṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 11 The opponent argues: Since the means of knowledge are themselves objects of knowledge, they must be known by another means of knowledge, leading to an infinite regress. To this, we reply: This is not so. Just as a lamp illuminates both other objects and itself simultaneously, so too does the means of knowledge know both the external object and itself. There is no need for a second means of knowledge. Furthermore, the self (*ātman*), being the knower, perceives the means of knowledge directly. Thus, there is no infinite regress. Therefore, the objection regarding the infinite regress is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.6.11 START BsCom_3,3.7.12 7 Section on the Establishment of the Self (Ātmasthāpanādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 12 The opponent argues: Since the self is not perceived by the senses, it does not exist. To this, we reply: This is not so. The self is established by inference. We observe that cognitions such as "I see," "I hear," and "I know" possess a common substrate, which is the self. Furthermore, the body and the senses are material and insentient; therefore, they cannot be the locus of consciousness. The existence of the self is also inferred from the fact that the body is organized for a purpose, like a city or a chariot. Thus, the self exists as the conscious principle that experiences pleasure and pain and is the agent of actions. Therefore, the objection regarding the non-existence of the self is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.7.12 START BsCom_3,3.8.13 8 Section on the Refutation of the Theory that the Body is the Self (Śarīrātmavādanirākaraṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 13 The opponent argues: The body alone is the self, as it is the locus of consciousness and the performer of actions. To this, we reply: This is not so. The body is composed of the five elements and is subject to decay and death. Consciousness, however, is not found in the individual elements separately, nor in their combination. Furthermore, the body is insentient, while consciousness is sentient. If the body were the self, then upon death, when the body is reduced to ashes, consciousness would cease to exist, which contradicts the continuity of memory and experience. Therefore, the body is not the self. Therefore, the theory that the body is the self is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.8.13 START BsCom_3,3.9.14 9 Section on the Refutation of the Theory that the Sense Organs are the Self (Indriyātmavādanirākaraṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 14 The opponent argues: The sense organs are the self, as they are the instruments of perception and action. To this, we reply: This is not so. The sense organs are material and perishable. They are produced and destroyed, whereas the self is permanent. Furthermore, the sense organs are limited in their functions; for example, the eye sees but cannot hear. If the sense organs were the self, then upon the loss of one organ, the self would be destroyed, which is absurd. Therefore, the sense organs are not the self. Therefore, the theory that the sense organs are the self is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.9.14 START BsCom_3,3.10.15 10 Section on the Refutation of the Theory that the Mind is the Self (Mano'tmavādanirākaraṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 15 The opponent argues: The mind (*manas*) is the self, as it is the internal organ that coordinates the various perceptions and desires. To this, we reply: This is not so. The mind is an instrument, like the sense organs, and is subject to change and fluctuation. It cannot be the permanent witness of all experiences. Furthermore, the mind is atomic and cannot be the locus of the vast range of cognitions that arise simultaneously. Therefore, the mind is not the self. Therefore, the theory that the mind is the self is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.10.15 START BsCom_3,3.11.16 11 Section on the Refutation of the Theory that Pradhāna is the Self (Pradhānātmavādanirākaraṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 16 The opponent argues: Pradhāna, the primordial matter consisting of the three qualities (*guṇas*), is the self, as it is the source of all manifestation. To this, we reply: This is not so. Pradhāna is insentient (*jaḍa*) and lacks consciousness. It cannot be the enjoyer of pleasure and pain, nor the agent of actions. Furthermore, the scriptures declare that the self is pure and conscious. Therefore, Pradhāna cannot be the self. Therefore, the theory that Pradhāna is the self is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.11.16 START BsCom_3,3.12.17 12 Section on the Refutation of the Theory that the Void is the Self (Śūnyātmavādanirākaraṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 17 The opponent argues: The void (*śūnya*) is the self, as it is the ultimate reality beyond all attributes. To this, we reply: This is not so. The void is a mere negation and lacks any positive characteristics. It cannot account for the experience of consciousness or the continuity of the individual. Furthermore, the scriptures teach that the self is the substratum of all things, not a mere absence. Therefore, the void cannot be the self. Therefore, the theory that the void is the self is refuted. END BsCom_3,3.12.17 START BsCom_3,3.13.18 13 Section on the Refutation of the Theory that the Aggregate is the Self (Saṃghātātmavādanirākaraṇādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 18 The opponent argues: The aggregate (*saṃghāta*) of the body, senses, and mind is
"And because of pervasion, [the identity] is appropriate" (BBs 3.3.9). Regarding the passage,

"One should meditate on this syllable as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), since the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "syllable" (*akṣara*) and "Udgītha" is heard, there arises an inquiry as to which of the following positions— superimposition (*adhyāsa*), denial (*apavāda*), identity (*ekatva*), or qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*)— is the most reasonable here.
In this context, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is defined as follows: when the cognition of one of two things is not yet sublated, the cognition of the other is superimposed upon it;
and that upon which the other cognition is superimposed continues to persist even while the cognition of the superimposed object is present.
For example, even when the cognition of Brahman is superimposed upon a name, the cognition of the name continues to persist and is not sublated by the cognition of Brahman.
Just as there is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the notion of Viṣṇu and others upon images and the like,
so too here the notion of the syllable is superimposed upon the *udgītha*, and the notion of the *udgītha* upon the syllable.
Sublation (*apavāda*), on the other hand, occurs when a correct cognition arising later sublates a previously established false cognition regarding some object that has been firmly settled.
It occurs as follows:

just as the notion of a self regarding the aggregate of the body and the senses is removed by the subsequent correct cognition "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), which is directed toward the Self alone.

Just as the cognition of a directional error is sublated by the cognition of the true nature of direction, so too here the cognition of the *udgītha* is sublated by the cognition of the syllable, and the cognition of the syllable is sublated by the cognition of the *udgītha*.
Identity (*ekatva*) refers to the fact that the words *akṣara* and *udgītha* function with non-different meanings,

just as in the cases of "best of the twice-born," "Brāhmaṇa," and "god of the earth. Specification (*viśeṣaṇa*), on the other hand, serves to restrict the application of the syllable *om*, which pervades all the Vedas, to that specific portion belonging to the Udgātṛ priest.

"Just as one says, 'Bring that lotus which is blue,' so here too, one should meditate on the Udgītha, which is the syllable Om. When this sentence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is thus considered, these alternative views appear; and since there is no reason for determining any one of them, and thus a lack of determination would result, it is said: "And because of pervasion" (*vyāpteś ca*).

Regarding the term *samañjasam*: this word *ca* is placed in the position of the word *tu* (but), with the purpose of excluding three alternative positions. Thus, in this context, the positions [regarding] destruction (*kṣaya*) are set aside as being faulty (*sāvadya*).
Only the position that [the words] are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇapakṣa*) is accepted as being faultless.

In that regard, first concerning superimposition (*adhyāsa*): if the cognition of one thing were superimposed upon another, it would follow that the word for that [other] thing would have to function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and its fruit [as a result of such indication] would have to be postulated.
Yet the fruit is indeed heard in scripture: "He indeed becomes a fulfiller of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7).
If it is argued that this is so because of such passages [as those cited], we say no;
for that has a different result.
Indeed, that has as its fruit the attainment of the vision [of Brahman] and so forth, not the fruit of superimposing [the idea of Brahman] upon the *udgītha*.
Even in the case of negation (apavāda), the absence of a result is the same.
If it is argued that the cessation of false cognition is the result, we say no; for it is not understood how this serves the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha).
Furthermore, the notion of "Om" never ceases with respect to the syllable Om, nor does the notion of the "Udgītha" cease with respect to the Udgītha;
for this sentence is not intended to establish the ultimate reality of things,
as its purpose is the injunction of meditation (upāsanā).
Nor is the position of identity tenable, for in that case the utterance of two words would be purposeless,
since the intended meaning would be conveyed by one alone.
Furthermore, there is no established usage of the word *udgītha* for the syllable *oṃ* when it belongs to the domain of the Hotṛ priest or the domain of the Adhvaryu priest.
Nor is there any established usage of the word "udgītha" for the entire second section (bhakti) of the Sāman;

nor is there any established usage of the word "oṃkāra" for that which is denoted by the word "udgītha" as the entire second section of the Sāman, by virtue of which they would have identical meanings.
Therefore, by process of elimination, the view that [the terms] are qualifiers is accepted.

Because pervasion (vyāpti) is common to all Vedic branches, one might fear that the syllable (akṣara) being pervaded here [by the meditation] would be taken as referring to every syllable; therefore, the syllable is specified by the word "udgītha" so that the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the udgītha, may not be understood [in a general sense].
But surely, even on this view, the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is the same.
This is true because the word *udgītha* functions here as an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of its constituent part. Nevertheless,
even in the case of such indication, there remains a distinction between proximity and remoteness.

For in the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the cognition of one object is projected onto another object; thus, it would be a remote indication (*viprakṛṣṭā lakṣaṇā*). However, in the case of a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), words that function toward a whole are seen to function toward its parts as well—as in the cases of "cloth" or "village.
Therefore, because of this pervasion (*vyāpti*), the reasoning that "this syllable *oṃ*" is qualified by "the *udgītha*" is consistent; the meaning is that this is faultless. // 9 //
"And because of pervasion, [the identity] is consistent.

Having taken up the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as the subject, he states the doubt with the words "Om, this... and explains the meanings of the terms such as "superimposition" (*adhyāsa*) and so forth with the passage beginning "Therein, superimposition... and so on.
Superimposition (adhyāsa) is the attribution of non-difference preceded by the intellect; sublation (bādha) is negation (apavāda);
and unity (ekatva) is actual non-difference.

The distinction is that a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which differentiates. Previously, having taken for granted as established the fact that the syllable *oṃ*—the object of meditation—is a part of the *udgītha*, which consists of the duties of the *udgātṛ* priest, the conclusion was reached that there is a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*) due to the difference in the objects of meditation. [Now,] with the introduction of an objection—that this is not tenable—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented with the words "In that case" (*tatra*).

Considering that in this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) the previously stated final conclusion (*siddhānta*) fails to be established, whereas in the final conclusion it is established, he explains the sūtra of the final conclusion beginning with the words "The word *ca*," etc.

Having asserted the defectiveness of the three alternative positions, he states the flaw in the position of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) with the words "In that case, superimposition," etc. [He argues:

If the cognition of the *udgītha* were superimposed upon the syllable *oṃ*, then there would have to be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *udgītha*—which denotes that [sacrificial act]—in reference to the syllable *oṃ*, because [the word] would be intended to convey the quality of being the object of that cognition; furthermore, such a relationship is unestablished.
The meaning is that there would be the burden of having to postulate a fruit for the meditation on a mere symbol (*pratīkopāsti*).
He raises the objection that "the fruit need not be postulated" by saying, "It is heard," and so forth,
beginning with "attainment" (*āpti*).
The meaning is that the fruit mentioned in the scripture—namely, "Oṃkāra is attainment, Oṃkāra is prosperity; he who worships thus attains his desires"—does not belong to superimposition (adhyāsa).

Having previously accepted the sublation of the cognition of one thing by the cognition of another (such as the Udgītha or Oṃkāra) and stated the futility of such sublation of a false cognition, [the author] now says, "Nor ever at any time," because since the cognition of either one is not an error, there can be no sublation.
If it were an error, it would cease; but since it does not cease, the meaning is that it is non-erroneous (*abhrānti*).
Furthermore, the sublation of error occurs through a statement that reveals reality; he says "nor" (*na ca*) to show that this statement is not merely concerned with [conventional] reality.
He refutes the position that the words *oṃ* and *udgītha* are synonyms—like the words *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*—by saying "nor" (*nāpi*).
He states that even synonymy does not exist with the words "nor" (na ca).
Regarding the alternative view that [the term *udgītha*] is a qualifier for what remains, he applies the Sūtra with the word "because of pervasion" (*vyāpteḥ*).

The meaning is this: when it is said, "One should meditate on the syllable *Om*," it would follow that the syllable *Om*, which pervades all the Vedas, is intended here for meditation; therefore, the qualification of being a constituent part of the *udgītha* is appropriate in order to exclude that possibility.

In the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), a relationship consisting of the connection with the quality of being the object of that [Brahman] cognition would have to be postulated; thus, this would be a remote indication (*viprakṛṣṭā lakṣaṇā*). However, indication based on a part (*avayavalakṣaṇā*) is proximate, because the relationship between a whole and its parts is well-known in common usage—as in "the cloth is burnt" when a part of the cloth is burnt. As for the word "Brahman" applied to names and so forth, one must resort to an indication based on the quality of being graspable by the cognition of Brahman, as there is no other way, since the meditation on the symbol (*pratīkopāsana*) is intended therein.

In this context, however, if one were to assume that the passage prescribes a meditation on the *pratīka* (the symbol) and separately prescribes the viewing of *prāṇa* in the syllable *oṃ* as possessing qualities such as being the "attainer" (*āpti*), there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Therefore, it is established that—due to the parsimony of conceptualization—it is more appropriate to understand the qualification as intended solely for the purpose of prescribing the viewing of *prāṇa* in the syllable *oṃ*, rather than excluding the *oṃ* that pervades all the Vedas. //9//
END BsCom_3,3.4.9 START BsCom_3,3.5.10 5. Section on the Non-Difference of All (Sarvābhedādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 10.
Because there is no difference between all [the texts], these others [are also included].

In the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) among the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas, it is stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), endowed with the quality of preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*), is the object of meditation.

For even speech and the other organs are mentioned therein as being endowed with qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*); and these are again surrendered back into the vital breath: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), so are you the most excellent" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14).

By these and other such passages, the superiority of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is declared in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths among other Vedic schools as well—such as those of the Kauṣītakins and others—in texts like "Now, therefore, the attainment of the highest good; these deities, indeed, were disputing over who was superior" (KauṣU 2.14). However, even in those cases, these qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth are not mentioned.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should these qualities such as being Vasiṣṭha and so forth, which are mentioned in one place, be applied elsewhere as well, or should they not? On this point, the initial position is that they should not be applied. Why? Because of the connection with the word "thus" (evam).
Furthermore, in the passage, "But he who, knowing thus, having recognized the highest good in prāṇa," the object to be known is indicated by the word "thus" (evaṃ) in each instance.
And the word "thus" refers to what is proximate; it cannot indicate a collection of qualities of this kind that is recited in another branch of the Veda.
Therefore, the requirement for completeness is satisfied solely by the qualities situated within its own context.
This being the case, he replies: "In this rule, qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth, which are mentioned in one place, apply elsewhere as well.
Why? Because of non-difference in all cases;
for everywhere that same single knowledge of Prāṇa is recognized as undifferentiated."
This is because of the similarity [of the passages] such as the dialogue on the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*).
Furthermore, if there were no difference [between the Upanishads], how could these qualities mentioned in one place not be accepted elsewhere?
But was it not said that the word "thus" (*evam*) in various places, by means of distinction, offers up such a collection of qualities for the sake of being known?

To this it is replied: although the collection of qualities found in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa is not explicitly mentioned by the word "thus" (evam) in the Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa because it is not proximate, nevertheless, since that very same knowledge is referred to by the word "thus" in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa, the collection of qualities belonging to another recension— being encompassed within that identical knowledge— is not distinct from those belonging to one's own recension.
And this being the case, there is neither the abandonment of what is heard in scripture nor the assumption of what is not heard.
For even when qualities are heard in only one recensional branch (*śākhā*), they are indeed heard everywhere, because there is no difference in the possessor of those qualities.

Indeed, Devadatta, who is renowned in his own country for qualities such as valor, does not cease to possess those qualities upon going to another country simply because his valor and other attributes are not perceived by the inhabitants of that place.

And just as in that case, through a particular degree of familiarity, the qualities of Devadatta are perceived even in another location, so too, through a particular degree of application, the qualities to be meditated upon in one recensional branch (śākhā) should be extended to other branches as well.
Therefore, those attributes connected to a single primary subject, even when mentioned in only one place, must be integrated everywhere. // 10 //
FN: *Niḥśreyasa* means the attainment or determination of excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*). *Ahaṃśreyase* means for one's own excellence.
Because there is no difference between them, these [terms] are synonymous.
He states the intended meaning in order to explain the subject matter: "Of horses" (*vājinām*).
Being eloquent (*vāgmitva*) is the quality of speech, because one observes that those who possess speech dwell happily.
Having a firm footing (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the quality of the eye, because one observes that those who possess sight have a firm footing in their feet.

The ear possesses the quality of being the source of all attainments, because through hearing, there is the attainment of all objects. The mind possesses the quality of being the abode, because it is the substratum for all objects of enjoyment by means of its various functions.
And these qualities were offered to the Prāṇa by speech and the other organs after they had determined its preeminence; this is the meaning agreed upon by both recensions.
He states the subject matter with the words "of others," and so forth;
the meaning is that the taking up—that is, the determination—of *niḥśreyasa*, which is excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*), is being introduced.
Or, "the deities" refers to Speech and the rest; "for the sake of my own excellence" means for the sake of their own preeminence.
He states the doubt arising from the word "evam" (thus) and from the recognition of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as possessing the quality of excellence: "In that case.

The non-inclusion and inclusion of qualities constitute the results of the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions respectively. He presents the prima facie view by means of an analogy: just as the specific qualification of being the *udgītha* excludes the all-pervasive nature of the syllable *oṃ*, so too the word "evam," which grasps only the qualities mentioned in the present context, excludes the qualities of other recensional branches (*śākhā*). Thus he says: "In that case..."
"Attained" means:

just as the preeminence of the vital breath (prāṇa) over speech and the other organs is established, so too one who knows and meditates upon this quality of preeminence becomes preeminent himself by knowing the preeminence in the vital breath—this is the meaning of the Śruti. Since the qualities such as being the "best" (vasiṣṭhatva) and so forth are logically attained through the identity of the knowledge of this kind, the word "thus" (evam) does not include them, because it relies strictly on what is explicitly stated in the text. To this prima facie view, the author states the final conclusion: "They would be included."

In the Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa, the connection of the collection of qualities such as being the "best" (vasiṣṭhatva) with the knowledge of Prāṇa is established by the word "evam" (thus). That same knowledge is recognized in the Kauṣītaki-Śruti;

and thus, although the qualities are obtained by implication through their inseparable relation with the possessor of qualities, since there is no contradiction with the qualities explicitly mentioned [in the Kauṣītaki], both the qualities explicitly stated and those obtained by implication—being equal in their proximity through both direct statement and implication—are included by the word "evam" occurring in the Kauṣītaki.
He says "nevertheless" (tathāpi) to indicate that [the Prāṇa] is being referred to.
The Prāṇa residing in the Kauṣītaki Śruti possesses qualities such as being the most excellent (vasiṣṭhatva), because it is the pre-eminent Prāṇa.

It has been stated that when there is an inference of unmentioned qualities—as in the case of the prāṇa mentioned in the Vāji-śruti—there is no abandonment of what is explicitly heard (śruta-hāni), because there is no contradiction; this he clarifies with the words: "And this being so... and so forth.
He provides an illustration for the fact that even qualities that have not been specifically enumerated are indeed heard [in scripture]—namely, "nahi" (not indeed).
He states the conclusion—"tasmāt" (therefore)—as follows: //10//

Section on Bliss and Other Attributes (Ānandādyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 11–13.
Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal.

(BBs 3.3.11) In those scriptural passages dedicated to establishing the nature of Brahman, certain attributes of Brahman—such as being of the nature of bliss, being a mass of consciousness, being all-pervading, and being the self of all—are heard in some instances while others are not.
Regarding these, there arises a doubt: are the attributes such as bliss and the rest to be understood only where they are actually heard, or are they all to be understood everywhere?

In this regard, when the practice of the Dharma has been attained according to the specific divisions of the scriptural texts, the following is stated: the attributes of the primary Brahman, such as bliss and so forth, are to be understood everywhere.
Why?
Precisely because of the non-difference of all [the Upaniṣads].
For in all cases, that one and same primary object of qualification, Brahman, does not differ.
Therefore, the attributes of Brahman are universal, by virtue of that very example of Devadatta’s valor mentioned in the preceding section. 11.
But if this were so, would not the attributes such as "having joy as its head" also become confused across all [texts]?
For instance, in the Taittirīyaka, with reference to the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is taught: "Joy indeed is its head;
delight is its right wing."
"Bliss is the higher part;
bliss is the self;
Brahman is the tail, the support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).
"Bliss and so forth belong to the principal [Brahman].
Because the object of knowledge, Brahman, is one and devoid of distinctions, he states the doubt regarding them: "There is a doubt concerning them.
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because there is no synthesis of the terms such as "Truth" and so on, there is a failure to determine the meaning of the sentence.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the result is that there is indeed a restriction.

Since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses specific attributes, the inclusion of qualities such as "being the best" (*vasiṣṭhatva*) mentioned in another recensional branch (*śākhā*) is appropriate. But since Brahman is devoid of specific attributes, its realization is accomplished by the very words found in one's own recensional branch; therefore, the inclusion of other words is useless. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented by way of a counter-example.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "this" (*idam*).

The universals such as blissness (*ānandatva*), truthfulness (*satyatva*), and consciousnessness (*jñānatva*) are properties superimposed upon Brahman; their "synthesis" (*upasaṃhāra*) across all Vedic branches means the utterance of the words expressing them—such as "bliss," "truth," "consciousness," and "infinite"—as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), as in: "Brahman is bliss, truth, consciousness, and infinite."
"Purity, non-duality, and self"—these words in grammatical apposition, by abandoning contradictory attributes, denote a single, indivisible individuality that serves as the substrate of all.
Nor should it be argued that a subsequent word is redundant since the intended object is established by a single word alone; [for each word excludes a specific contrary].
Because there is no contradiction in a single word, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) does not apply;

even though figurative indication would apply to both words [if taken together], nevertheless, when it is said "Brahman is bliss" (ānando brahma), although the delusion regarding suffering and meagerness is dispelled, a misconception regarding non-existence, insentience, and so forth might still arise. Therefore, in order to dispel that, the words "Being," "Knowledge," and so forth must be employed.
Nor should it be argued that because delusion has no limit, the sentence would remain incomplete;

for when there is the specific realization—"I am Brahman, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, devoid of all attributes, non-dual, and free from conceptual construction"—all delusion is dispelled.
The sense is that as many words as are required to produce that specific realization, so many words must be employed. //11//
To this, the following [verse] is recited:

There is no attainment elsewhere of [the attributes] such as "having pleasure as its head," because increase and decrease exist only where there is difference. (BBs 3.3.12) There is no attainment elsewhere of those attributes—

pleasure, delight, extreme delight, and bliss— which are recorded in the *Taittirīyaka*, for the reason that these are perceived as having forms that increase and decrease relative to one another and relative to different experiencers.
Furthermore, increase and decrease are possible only when there is differentiation;
however, Brahman is without differentiation, according to such scriptural passages as, "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
Furthermore, these qualities such as "having joy as its head" are not attributes of Brahman;
rather, we have already taught in the sūtra *Ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt* (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.12) that these are attributes of the sheaths (*kośa*).
Moreover, these are conceived merely as means for directing the mind toward the supreme Brahman, and not as objects to be perceived [as Brahman itself].
Even so, there is even more clearly no application of the "having pleasure as its head" and so forth elsewhere.
However, having treated these as attributes of Brahman, the Teacher has merely demonstrated this logical principle—that there is no application of "having pleasure as its head" and so forth.

And that same logic must be applied to other well-established attributes of Brahman taught for the purpose of meditation, such as "the one in whom all blessings meet" (saṃyadvāma) and "whose desires are true" (satyakāma).

For even though the Brahman to be meditated upon is one in all those cases, since there is a difference in meditation due to the difference in the initial approach (*prakrama*), there is no transfer of the attributes of one to the other.

Just as two women may serve a single king—one with an umbrella and the other with a fly-whisk—even though the object of service is one, there is a difference in their service and a distinction in their respective duties; so it is here as well.

Indeed, the possession of more or fewer qualities is possible only in the case of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahman*) where conventional distinctions exist, but not in the case of the supreme, unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*).
Therefore, the meaning is that the qualities such as "having true desires" (satyakāmatva) and so forth, though heard in one context, are not to be applied everywhere. // 12 //

If, due to the oneness with Brahman, attributes such as bliss and so forth were to apply everywhere, then one might raise the objection that the attributes belonging to the knowledge of Saguna-Brahman would also apply [to the state of liberation]. To dispel this doubt, the author explains the Sūtra: "The [attributes] such as 'the dear'... The meaning is as follows:

the pleasure from seeing a son is "the dear" (*priya*); the joy derived from news of him is "delight" (*moda*); and when there is an excellence of such knowledge, there is "great delight" (*pramoda*).

Attributes characterized by such gradations do not apply to the non-dual object of knowledge, because those attributes—which are not the very nature of Brahman—are of no use for the realization of Brahman.
He states that their being Brahman and their nature as Dharma are unestablished with the words "And these are not...".
Anticipating the objection that they might still be attained even if they are merely means for directing the mind toward Brahman, he says "Even so...
The meaning is that because these [means] are themselves unknowable, there can be no attainment of them within Brahman, which is the object of knowledge.
To the question, "For what purpose then is the Sūtra? he says: "The qualities of Brahman" (*brahmadharmān*).
He states the result of this hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*) with the words "And if that" (*sa ceti*).

The meaning is that the Sūtra is to be explained as follows: since external objects are of no use regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), they are not attained; therefore, by the logic that [qualities] such as being the "abode of all blessings" (*saṃyadvāmatva*) and so forth are also not attained.

Anticipating the objection that even if knowledge (*jñāna*) is not employed, attainment might still occur in other forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) because those factors (*dharma*) are employed in meditation (*dhyāna*) due to the identity with the Brahman to be meditated upon, he says: "For in them...
The meaning is that there is a fixed arrangement of those factors subordinate to the injunctions for meditation according to the specific injunction. //12//
But the others [the organs] are [of the same nature] as the objects, because of the commonality of their purpose. (BS 3.1.13)

But the other attributes, such as bliss and so forth, being mentioned solely for the purpose of establishing the nature of Brahman, would be understood everywhere because the subject—the Brahman to be established—is one in its essential character; thus there is a difference, for those [attributes] have as their sole purpose the mere cognition [of Brahman]. // 13 //

He states that there is a difference between the attributes such as "the gathering of all desires" (*saṃyadvāma*) and those beginning with "bliss" (*ānanda*), because the latter serve the purpose of knowledge, and so forth: "But the others...
It is thus established that the five terms—*satya*, *jñāna*, *ānanda*, *ātman*, and *brahman*—are to be combined everywhere. //13//

Section 7: The Topic of Meditation (Ādhyāna-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 14–15 [The opponent argues: "Because meditation [is enjoined], [the fires are not to be meditated upon as Brahman]. (Sūtra 14) In the passage, "Let him meditate on the fire-altar as the mind" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*), and so forth, the fires are presented for the purpose of meditation. Therefore, they are not to be understood as having the nature of Brahman. This is because meditation is enjoined here; otherwise, the injunction would be meaningless. Furthermore, since the fires are well-known from the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) to be mere sacrificial implements, it is impossible for them to possess the nature of Brahman. Moreover, the word *brahman* is used here in its conventional sense of "greatness," just as in the case of the statement, "The earth is indeed the great *brahman*" (*pṛthivī vai mahad brahma*). Thus, the fires are merely objects of meditation. [The Siddhāntin replies: "But [it is] for the sake of the excellence of the meditation. (Sūtra 15) The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the objection. Because there is no purpose for [the mention of] meditation.
For it is recited in the *Kaṭhaka*: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind;
but higher than the mind is the intellect" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 3.10).
Beginning with this, it continues: "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.11).

Regarding this, a doubt arises: are all these things, beginning with the objects of sense, each taught as being superior to the one preceding it, or is it the Person alone who is taught as being superior to all of them?
On this point, the initial view is that each of these is indeed taught as being superior.

For it is heard thus: "This is superior to this; this is superior to that. But surely, if many objects were intended to be presented as being "superior," there would be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda).
This is not a fault,
because a plurality of sentences is established;
for these many sentences are indeed capable of establishing numerous objects endowed with various intended meanings.
Therefore, it might be argued that each of these is established as being supreme.
To this we reply: it is logical that the Puruṣa alone is to be established as supreme over all of these, rather than establishing each of them individually as supreme.
Why?
Because there is no purpose [in knowing them]. For when the others are understood as "the other" (para), no purpose whatsoever is seen; the purpose is the attainment of liberation (mokṣa).
And thus says the Śruti: "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15).

Furthermore, by means of the negation of others and by using the word "limit" (*kāṣṭhā*), [the author] shows that he pays respect to the Puruṣa as the subject matter, and thus demonstrates that the discourse regarding the preceding and succeeding [stages] is intended solely for the realization of the Puruṣa.
The phrase "for the sake of meditation" (*ādhyānāya*) means "for the sake of right vision preceded by meditation.
Indeed, it is for the sake of right vision alone that meditation is taught here, and not meditation itself as the primary goal. // 14 //
Regarding the phrase "In that case" (*tatra*), he states the doubt because it is not determined whether there is a difference or non-difference of sentences for the purpose of meditation.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), due to the difference of sentences, there is a difference of meditations; in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), due to the unity of the sentence, there is unity of the meditation—this is the result.

In the preceding section, it was stated that qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and others—which possess the nature of Brahman and are to be combined [in meditation]—serve as means to the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman.

Here, however, it is stated that even that which does not possess the nature of Brahman, namely the "devotion to wealth" (*arthaparatva*) and so forth—which are not to be combined [in all meditations]—serves as a means to that same fruit. Thus, the connection (*saṅgati*) lies in their having a single fruit.

Furthermore, because there is a distinction between the various objects such as wealth, which are to be understood as being qualified by devotion to those respective things and are thus presented as something new (*apūrva*), there is a division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

"There is no fault"—this is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Having proposed a conclusion not explicitly stated in the sūtra, he explains the reason based on the sūtra itself: "The person alone.

The meaning is this: since [the person] possesses fruitfulness and is something not previously established [as the primary object], the person alone is to be understood as the primary subject; whereas the fact that the purpose, the means, and so forth are subordinate is stated because they exist as subservient to him.

Furthermore, the Veda—by means of the indicative mark of the negation of what is beyond ("There is nothing higher than Puruṣa; that is the limit") and by the indicative mark of being the ultimate boundary for all sublation—demonstrates its intent (tātparya) regarding Puruṣa, showing that the statement of the superiority of each subsequent one over each preceding one is for that purpose. Thus he says: "Moreover" (apica).

The commentary connects the sūtra as follows: "For the purpose of meditation" (ādhyānāya). The mention of the objects and so forth here is solely for the sake of perceiving the Puruṣa, preceded by meditation on each of those [objects] as being directed toward Him; it has no independent purpose of its own. Thus, the sūtra is applied. //14//
And because of the word "Self" (ātman). (BS 3.3.15)

For this reason as well, this discourse on the series beginning with the senses is intended solely for the purpose of realizing the Person (puruṣa). For it is said: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.12).
Thus, he calls the Puruṣa under discussion "the Self" (ātman).
From this, it is understood that the non-selfhood (anātmatva) of all other things is intended.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that this very [Self] is difficult to know and that it is to be understood through refinement (saṃskṛta).
For the sake of that very knowledge, the scripture prescribes meditation in such passages as, "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind" (Kaṭha 3.13).
This has been explained under the sūtra, "Even that which is based on inference [is Brahman], for some [mention] even one [such]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.1).
Thus, such a manifold excellence of intention is observed in a person who has heard [the Veda], and not in others.

Furthermore, when it is said, "He reaches the end of the path; that is Viṣṇu’s supreme abode" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.9), upon the inquiry, "What is that end of the path, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu?", it is determined from the sequence beginning with the senses that this progression is indeed for the sake of attaining the supreme abode.
He states that by means of such marks as "selfhood" (ātmatva), it is the Puruṣa alone who is to be established, saying: "And because of the word 'Self'.

Furthermore, since there is consistency between the opening and the conclusion—namely, "That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu" and "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa"—and since it is certain that the entire passage constitutes a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva) directed toward the one Puruṣa as having a well-established fruit, any assumption of a split in the sentence (vākyabheda) or a plurality of fruits is [untenable].
It is not logical [to say it arises] from respect; thus he says: "Moreover" (api ca). //15//

Section 8: The Topic of the Grasping of the Self (Ātmagṛhītyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 16–17. [The opponent argues: "In the passage, 'That which is this subtle essence, in it all that exists has its self; it is the true, it is the Self; thou art that, O Śvetaketu' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), the word *ātman* (Self) is used in reference to the individual soul (*jīva*), because it is the individual soul that is understood from the context. [The author replies: This is not so. In this passage, the word *ātman* denotes Brahman. Why? Because of the connection with what precedes and follows. For in the preceding section, the nature of Brahman is set forth: "It is the True; it is the Self; thou art that, O Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7). Furthermore, in the subsequent section, the same Brahman is described as the cause of the world through the passage beginning, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). Therefore, since the word *ātman* is connected to both these contexts, it must refer to Brahman. Moreover, the word *ātman* is commonly used to denote the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), who is none other than Brahman. Thus, the word *ātman* here signifies Brahman. Furthermore, the word *ātman* is applied to Brahman in the sense of its being the inner self of all things, as seen in such passages as "He who dwells in the earth and is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22). Therefore, the word *ātman* in the passage under discussion refers to Brahman. Thus ends the Section on the Grasping of the Self.
