"The grasping of the Self [is taught] as in other cases, because of what follows" (BBs 3.3.16).

In the *Aitareyaka*, it is heard: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Shall I now create the worlds? (Ai. 1.1); and: "He created these worlds: Ambhas, Marīci, Mara, and Āpaḥ" (Ai. 1.2), and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is it the Supreme Self alone that is denoted by the word "Self," or is it some other [entity]? What, then, is the initial position? That the Supreme Self cannot possibly be denoted here by the word "Self.
Why?
Because the syntactical connection of the sentence is observed [with the Supreme Self].
But surely the syntactical connection is seen to pertain even more clearly to the Supreme Self, because it establishes the oneness of the Self prior to creation,
and because there is a statement regarding a creator preceded by reflection (*īkṣaṇa*).
This is not so, it is said, because of the mention of the creation of the world.
For if the Supreme Self were intended as the creator, the creation of the great elements would have to be mentioned first; however, here the creation of the world is mentioned at the outset.
And the worlds are specific arrangements of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Thus, [the scripture] explains water and the others as being worlds themselves, starting with: "That which is beyond the sky is water" (*Ai. 1.2*).
Furthermore, the creation of the worlds was performed by a certain other Lord presided over by the Supreme Lord, as seen in passages such as: "He became embodied" (*Bṛ. 1.4.1*).
The *Smṛti* also states: "He is indeed the first embodied one; he is called the Puruṣa;

the creator of beings, Brahmā, existed at the beginning. Furthermore, the followers of the *Aitareya* recension, in the preceding section of the passage beginning "Now, therefore, from the seed of Prajāpati; the gods are the seed," record a manifold creation having Prajāpati as its agent.
The word "ātman" is also seen used in reference to that [Brahman]: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1).
Furthermore, the determination of oneness prior to creation is appropriate with respect to its own effects.
And its "seeing" is also appropriate, since its nature as conscious is accepted.
Moreover, many such specific activities as "bring a cow for them," "bring a horse for them," and "bring a man for them"— which are well-known among worldly individuals possessing particularities—
are observed here [in the Vedic texts].
Therefore, the self (ātman) here must be some kind of particularized entity.
This being the case, we reply: "The Supreme Self alone is grasped here by the word 'Self,' as in other instances;
just as in other scriptural accounts of creation, such as 'From that very Self, space was produced' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), the Supreme Self is what is understood."

Just as in other instances of the use of the word "Self" (ātman) in common worldly parlance, the inner self alone is understood by the word "Self" in its primary sense, so too should it be here. However, where another qualification such as "of the form of a person" (puruṣavidhaḥ) is heard— as in passages beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad)— there the Self must be understood specifically [as the Supreme Self].
Furthermore, in this context, a subsequent qualification is found that is indeed consistent with the apprehension of the Supreme Self: "He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds? (Ai.
1.1), and "He created these worlds" (Ai. 1.2), and so forth.
Therefore, it is logical that only that [water] is what is being grasped. // 16 // [FN:
Water is heaven;
the rays are the atmospheric world.]
"Maru" is the mortal world;
"āpaḥ" is the netherworld (pātālaloka).
"Puruṣavidhaḥ" means having a human form;
"ātman" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha;
"retas" means the product of semen.
It is grasped as a self;
it blinks and moves;
people call it "water."
Ambhas is heaven,
Marīcis is the intermediate world (antarikṣaloka),
and Mara is the world of mortals (martyaloka).
"Water" means the world of Pātāla.
Since the word "Self" (ātman) is used for both Brahman and the Sūtrātman, he states the doubt with the words "In that regard.

Here, in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because the passage is intent upon the meditation on the Sūtra, there is no inclusion of the attributes of the Supreme Brahman, such as bliss and so forth, in the Aitareyaka.
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is that there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) because [the passage] has Brahman as its ultimate subject.

It was stated that, due to the consequence of being distinct from the "Puruṣa" statement, the passages concerning the object and so forth do not have the function of establishing the object and so forth; likewise here too, due to the consequence of being distinct from the preceding Prajāpati statement—namely, "The gods are the semen of Prajāpati"—there is the same status for the passage beginning with "The Self, verily... (*ātmā vā*).
He presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of the example that [the passage] does not have Brahman as its ultimate purport, using the words "not the Supreme Self" and so forth;
the meaning is that the intention of the sentence is seen to lie in Prajāpati.

Having thus raised the prima facie view, he refutes it with the words "But surely," etc., stating that because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of being the creator of the world, the syntactical connection of the sentence does not reside in Prajāpati.
Since it might be thought that the worlds themselves are the great elements, he says: "and the worlds.
Because the word "world" (loka) is not conventionally established (*arūḍhatvāt*) in the sense of the great elements, the worlds are indeed composed of derived matter (*bhautika*).
And because of its etymological derivation (*nirvacanāt*), he says: "and likewise."

Having stated in the Sūtra, "The waters are the rays, death is the water," the Śruti itself explains: that world which is beyond the sky, further than the sky, established in heaven, and pervaded by the water of the moon—that is "the water";
the intermediate space is "the rays";
and the earth is "death."
"That which is below is water.
[The opponent objects: "But surely even the creation of the worlds must proceed from the Lord alone? [The author replies: "No," he says, "in the world... "Man-like" means having a human form.
The meaning is that the Self, as Hiraṇyagarbha, created everything down to the ants;
"of beings" means of the worlds.
He states that Prajāpati is the creator of the world also on the basis of the context, saying "the Aitareyins also [state this]"; "retas" (seed) means the effect.
He applies the marks of Brahman to Prajāpati with the words beginning "the word 'Self' also," and so forth.
Furthermore, having created living beings, the Creator of the world brought a cow to them for their enjoyment, and likewise he brought a horse.
But they were not satisfied with the acquisition of the cow and the horse; therefore, when a human body was brought, they said, "We are satisfied.
He states that this worldly transaction is a mark (*liṅga*) of [the Lord's] status as Prajāpati by saying, "Moreover" (*api ca*).

The author establishes the final conclusion—that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is to be understood—on the grounds that the word "Self" (ātman) has its primary meaning in the conscious Self (cidātman), that there is no sublation in accepting this primary sense, and that it is consistent with the subsequent mention of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and so forth; thus he says, "Thus, [the prima facie view] having been reached.
The intention is that the scriptural passage stating "He created the worlds preceded by the creation of the great elements" is to be explained accordingly. //16//
If it is argued that [the self exists] because of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it would be so because of the restriction [of the term]. (BS 3.3.17)
Regarding what was stated previously—that the Supreme Self is not being grasped here because the syntactical connection of the sentence [points elsewhere]—that must now be refuted.
To this, it is said:
"It may be so, on account of the restriction."
The apprehension of the supreme self would be appropriate.
Why?
Because of the restrictive emphasis.

For in the case of grasping the Supreme Self, the determination of the oneness of the Self prior to creation is appropriately understood as direct; otherwise, it would have to be conceived as indirect. As for the mention of the creation of the world, I shall connect it with the creation of the great elements as established in other scriptural passages.
Just as you have connected the statement "That [Being] emitted heat" (Chāndogya 6.2.3) with the emission of ether and air well-known from another scriptural passage, so it should be here as well;
for a specific detail concerning the same subject, though established in one scriptural passage, must be integrated into other scriptural passages.

Furthermore, this sequence of specific activities, such as "bring the cow" and so forth, which follows from those [words], must also be understood solely as being conducive to the determination of the intended meaning.
For it cannot be said that this entire narrative sequence is what is intended to be expressed, because there is no human purpose in the comprehension of that [narrative] itself.
However, what is intended here is the identity with Brahman as the Self.

For, after teaching the creation of the worlds beginning with water and the world-protectors beginning with Agni, as well as the sense organs and the body which is the abode of those organs, that same Creator [asks]: "How indeed could this exist without me? (Ai. 3.11).
Having thus observed this body, he entered it; so it is shown: "He, having split open this very suture, entered by this door" (Ai.
3.12). And again: "Whether there is an utterance by speech, or whether there is an inhalation by breath" (Ai. 3.12).
Having thus discerned the operations of the instruments through such passages as these, and having reflected, "Now, who am I? (Ai.
3.11), he determines the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self in the words, "He saw this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman" (Ai. 3.13).

Likewise, later on, by the passage beginning with "This is Brahman, this is Indra" (Ai. 5.3), having sublated the entire collection of differentiated entities along with the great elements, [the text states]: "All that has consciousness as its leader, is established in consciousness; consciousness is the leader of the world, consciousness is the foundation;
consciousness is Brahman" (Ai. 5.3).
Thus, it confirms that the vision of Brahman as the Self alone is intended.
Therefore, the apprehension of the Self here is beyond reproach. There is another interpretation: "The apprehension of the Self [is established] because of what follows, as in other cases."

In the Vājasaneyaka, beginning with the word "Self" in the passage, "Which is the Self? He who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart, the person" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7), the text establishes that this very Self is Brahman by demonstrating its freedom from all attachments.
Thus, it concludes: "Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).
In the Chāndogya, however, beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chā.
6.2.1) without using the word "Self," the text teaches identity in the conclusion: "That is the Self; thou art That" (Chā. 6.8.7).
In this regard, there arises a doubt: do these two scriptural recensions (āmnāna) have the same meaning, or do they have different meanings?
For the time being, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they have different meanings, because the two recensions are dissimilar;
for when there is a discrepancy in the scriptural recension, it is not reasonable to assume identity of meaning, since the determination of meaning is dependent upon the scriptural recension itself.
In the Vājasaneyaka, because the discourse begins with the word "Self," it is understood that there is an instruction regarding the reality of the Self;
however, in the Chāndogya, due to the reversal of the opening statement, there is a reversal of the instruction.
But was it not already stated that even for the Chandogas, there is an instruction of identity in the concluding portion?
True, it has been said;
however, because the conclusion depends upon the introduction, it is thought that "attainment of identity" is what is meant.
This being the case, it is replied: "The grasping of the Self [is intended], in the passage: 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
In this case, it should apply to the Chandogas as well, just as in other instances;
for example, just as the term "Self" was understood [as the primary meaning] by the Vājasaneyins in the passage, "What is the Self? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7), so it should be here too.
Why?
Because of the subsequent teaching of identity (tādātmya).
If it is argued that [the relationship] is due to positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth, it is not so, because of the restrictive emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

If it is asked, "What is the rebuttal to the argument that because of the connection with the opening statement, and because the word 'Self' (ātman) is not heard in that opening, there is no grasping of the Self?"—that is now stated: "It may be so, on account of the restriction. It is indeed appropriate here that there is a grasping of the Self, because of the restriction.

For instance, having established that through the knowledge of one thing everything becomes known— in the words, "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1)— the text says, "Being alone," with the desire to bring this about; and that [realization] is accomplished only when the Self is grasped.
For otherwise, if this subtle self were not known, the realization of "the knowledge of all" would never be accomplished.

Likewise, the determination of oneness prior to creation, the reference to the individual soul by the word "Self," the description of its attainment of that very nature during the state of deep sleep, and the repeated instruction "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) following a series of inquiries— all these would be inconsistent.
The restriction expressed by "thus" and the entire context are appropriate only for establishing identity, not for producing identity.
Furthermore, it is not logical to introduce the argument that the opening statement is dependent on the ignorance of the seeker;
for in the opening statement, there is neither a mention of selfhood nor a mention of non-selfhood.

Furthermore, a general introduction is not contradicted by a specific detail found in the supplementary portion of the text, because the general requires specification. Moreover, when the meaning of the word "Sat" (Being) is carefully considered, nothing other than the primary Self can possibly be its referent; for all other categories of entities are established as unreal on account of their being mere "verbal handles" (*ārambhaṇa-śabda*) and so forth. Even a discrepancy in the scriptural recensions does not necessarily entail a discrepancy in the underlying meaning.

Because we observe such usage even when the meaning is identical—as in "Bring the bowl" and "The bowl, bring it"—it is established that in sentences of this kind, although there is a difference in the mode of presentation (*pratipādana-prakāra*), there is no difference in the object to be presented (*pratipādya-artha*). // 17 // *Note:
*Tatama* means most pervasive.*
The elision of the letter *ta* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). "Udarka" means conclusion.
Having stated the argument for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it with the word "anvayāt" (due to concomitance).

The sense is that, because the identity [of the Self and Brahman] is determined by the scriptural statements regarding the Self (*ātman*) and Brahman found in the opening and conclusion— namely, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" and "Brahman is consciousness"—

and because of the indicative marks such as "entering," which override marks such as being the creator of the world, the inner Self (*pratyag-brahman*) is what must be understood. That is the Supreme Lord.

The meaning is that he entered through this very opening called the *brahmarandhra*— having split it open and made a hole at the boundary of the head, which is the limit of the division of the hair— thereby becoming distinguished by the *liṅga*.
If speech and the other organs had performed their respective functions without me,

then [the seeker] would have reflected on the referent of the word "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*) by asking, "Then who am I?", and would have perceived for himself this very Self, purified as Brahman, the most pervasive (*tatamatama*).
The elision of the letter *ta* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

"Having wisdom as its guide" (*prajñānetram*) means that which has the conscious self (*cidātman*) as its guide—that is, that which is governed by the conscious self—since it is led (*nīyate*) by this [wisdom] as its regulator (*niyāmaka*).

Thinking that the previous explanation lacks clarity regarding the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) and thus does not properly fit the context of the section, he offers an alternative explanation, beginning with "others say" (*apare*).
*Udarka* means conclusion.
Since the word *sat* (Being) is common to both the Self and the non-Self, he states a doubt regarding it with the words "In that context" (*tatra*).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is the meditation on the attainment of the nature of Brahman as the Self upon the universal Being (*sattāsāmānya*) in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Because the two [texts] regarding Vājaśravas are distinct as being a knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇavidyā), there is no mutual combination of their attributes.

However, according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), because the knowledge of the attributeless is one and the same in both places, there is a combination; this constitutes the difference in result.

Since the capacity of words is grasped with respect to the universal (jāti), the word "sat" also denotes the universal of existence (sattājāti); thus, because the opening statement has a determined meaning, the teaching of identity—by virtue of the strength of the opening statement which has not yet encountered contradiction—is intended for the purpose of meditative identification (saṃpatti).
"Is to be led" (*neya*) is the summary of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the previous case, because of the unity of the sentence, it was stated that there is unity of knowledge after setting aside the fact that [the texts] were intent on different meanings and so forth; here, however, since there is a difference of sentences due to a difference in the introductory statements—by means of the two words "Being" (*sat*) and "Self" (*ātman*), which denote a genus and a self respectively—there is a difference of knowledge.
This is the connection as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
Furthermore, the word "Self" (ātman) is not a term denoting a genus (*jāti*), because there is no genus due to the identity of the individual Self; rather, it denotes the reality that is within all.

Even if one were to assume it denotes an imagined genus, the difference in the initial context (*upakrama*) would remain clear, as there is a distinction between pure existence (*sattā*) and the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*). This is how it should be understood.
He establishes the conclusion with the words "Thus," and so forth. "Because of the connection with the introduction" means that the conclusion is dependent upon the introduction.
And that restriction is appropriate only when the Self is understood by means of the word "Being" (sat); thus he says, "And that.
The restriction is that "Being is one alone";
by the phrase "by this living self," there is a reference to the living self by the word "Self" (ātman), with the divine Being as the agent.
The statement that "during deep sleep, the individual soul becomes merged with Being" (sat) is followed by the request for further instruction:
"Venerable Sir, please explain this to me again.
By the term "Being" (sat), that which is the substratum of existence is denoted, not merely a generic class-character (jāti).

Because [the word *sat*] ends with the suffix *śatṛ*, which denotes an agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, since the opening statement mentions a general locus of existence (*sattāśrayasāmānya*), when the expectation arises as to what that locus is, it is determined from the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) to be the Self (*ātman*). This is why he says "And not... (*na ca*). Having accepted that the word *sat* is common to both the Self and the non-Self, he states that even this is not the case; for like the word *ātman*, the word *sat* denotes a specific individual (*vyakti*), and that individual is none other than the conscious Self (*cidātman*), which is incapable of sublation. Therefore, there is no discrepancy between the Chāndogya and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka regarding the opening statements. This is why he says "The word *sat*... (*sacchabda...*).

Having addressed this discrepancy, he says: "By the scripture," etc. Although there is a difference in method—since in the Vājins' statement the referent of *tvaṃ* (the "you") is taught as culminating in the referent of *tat* (the "That"), whereas in the Chāndogya statement the referent of *tat* is taught as culminating in the referent of *tvaṃ*—there is oneness of knowledge because of the oneness of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc. //17//
Section 9: The Topic of the Manifestation of the Task (Kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 18.
"Because of the mention of an action, it is something new.
(BBs 3.3.18) The Chandogas and Vājasaneyins, in the dialogue of the Prāṇas, having recorded that the food of the Prāṇa extends from dogs down to dogs, further record that water is its clothing.
Immediately thereafter, the Chandogas record: "Therefore, when about to eat, one surrounds [the mouth] both before and after with water" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.2).

The Vājasaneyins, however, record this: "Knowing this, learned Śrotriyas sip water before eating and sip water after eating; they think that they are thereby making this very [breath] non-naked" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14);
"Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating; he thereby makes this very [breath] non-naked.

In this regard, it is deliberated whether both—the sipping of water and the contemplation of non-nakedness—are enjoined with respect to the breath, or whether only the sipping of water is enjoined, or only the contemplation of non-nakedness.
What, then, is the established position? Both of these [acts] are worthy of being enjoined because they are not previously established.
Alternatively, it is the act of sipping water (ācamana) alone that is enjoined.
For in that passage, the injunctive suffix is clearly expressed; therefore, for one who knows this, it is said: "One should sip water before eating and one should sip water after eating.
The mention of the state of being "not naked" (anagnatā) is merely for the purpose of praising that very injunction.
This being the position reached, we reply: the injunction of water-sipping is not tenable, because it is a description of an already established practice (kāryākhyāna).
For this sipping (ācamana), which is well-known in the Smṛtis as being for the purpose of purification, is merely restated here as something already established by its nature as a duty;
it is not that this Śruti serves as the source for that Smṛti.
This is denied.
Because their objects are different:
for recollection (*smṛti*) has a general object and thus enjoins sipping of water (*ācamana*) for the sake of purification as something connected to all persons;
whereas the *śruti*, being read within the context of the knowledge of the vital breaths (*prāṇavidyā*), would enjoin that very sipping of water only as having that [knowledge] as its object.
Moreover, the relationship of root and derivative cannot be established between a Śruti and a Smṛti that have different subjects.
Nor can it be maintained that this Śruti passage enjoins a previously unknown sipping of water (ācamana) connected with the knowledge of the vital breaths (prāṇavidyā);
for the very same sipping of water, which was already connected with human beings in general, is recognized here as well.
For this very reason, there is no injunction for both [the acts].
If both were enjoined, the sentence would be split.

Therefore, having merely restated the rinsing of the mouth before eating and after eating as something already established, [the text says]: "By doing so, they consider him alone to be made free from nakedness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14).

Thus, by this sentence, a previously unknown resolve to ensure the non-nakedness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is taught as being connected with the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) in relation to the water used for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
Nor is it logical to claim that this statement regarding non-nakedness is intended merely as a praise of the act of sipping;
for the act of sipping itself is not something to be enjoined here.

Furthermore, since the resolution (*saṃkalpa*) regarding nakedness itself is understood as that which is to be performed, it cannot be the case that a single act of sipping water (*ācamana*) is admitted to serve both purposes—namely, for the sake of purification (*prāyatya*) and for the sake of clothing.
This is because we admit it to be a different action; for what is called "sipping water" is admitted to be a distinct action performed by a person for the purpose of purification.

However, it is faultless [to maintain our position] because it is accepted that in the case of those waters, there is a distinct action called the "intentional resolve to wear" (*vāsasaṃkalpana*) for the purpose of clothing the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Furthermore, one cannot claim that in the passage, "Whatever here exists, down to the worms and down to the insects and moths— that is your food" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14), the consumption of all food is enjoined.

Because [the act] is neither expressed by words nor possible [to perform], this meditation on food—that "everything is the food of the vital breath"—is what is enjoined; and due to its association with that, even in the passage "water is the garment," it is not the sipping of water that is enjoined. Rather, it is more reasonable to hold that a meditation on wearing [a garment] is enjoined with respect to the very waters already well-known as being used for sipping.
For a partial destruction [of the injunction] is not possible.
Moreover, the word "ācāmanti" (they sip water) is a statement in the present tense, yet it is capable of being an injunction.
But is it not the case that the same applies to "manyante" (they think), as it too is a statement in the present tense?
This is indeed true.

However, since one of the two must necessarily be enjoined, it is the mental resolve regarding water as a garment that is enjoined as something new (*apūrva*)—on account of the mention of the function of a garment—and not the sipping of water (*ācamana*), for it has already been established that the latter is like the former.
As for what was said—that there is a clearly expressed injunctive suffix in the case of sipping—that too has been answered by the fact that sipping is merely a restatement of what is already known.

For this very reason, because the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) is not intended to be enjoined here, the Kāṇvas conclude at the point, "They think that by this they make him [the breath] clothed and not naked," and do not recite the passage beginning with "Therefore, one who knows thus...

Therefore, even in the text of the Mādhyandinas, it must be understood that, while the rinsing of the mouth is merely restated, the state of being "one who knows thus" is what is enjoined—namely, the knowledge of the garment of the aforementioned prāṇa.
Furthermore, the position that in some places the rinsing of the mouth is enjoined while in others the knowledge of the garment is enjoined is also not correct.

Since the application of the scriptural passage beginning with "Water is indeed clothing" is uniform in all cases, it is logical that here it is the cognition of clothing itself that is enjoined, not the act of sipping water. // 18 //
"Because it explains what is already known, it does not convey anything new.

Thus questioned by Prāṇa, "What is our food? What is our clothing?", Vāk and the others replied, "Whatever exists here, down to dogs and even worms—that is your food; water is your clothing. This refers to that which is consumed by all living beings.
The meaning is that the practitioner should contemplate as follows: "Whatever food is well-known, down to that of dogs and other such creatures, that is your food, O Prāṇa; water is your covering.
Having thus stated the common scriptural teaching found in both recensions, he speaks of the difference in their specific scriptural teachings with the words "And immediately after... and so forth.

Therefore, because water is the garment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), learned *śrotriyas* who are eating—that is, performing the act of eating—do this: they sip water both before and after the meal. This means that with water they "clothe" or cover the vital breath.

The sense is that one should perform the meditation on non-nakedness, consisting of the contemplation of water as the garment of the vital breath, in relation to the waters connected with the preceding and succeeding sips.

Therefore, for that reason—the meaning of which has already been explained—since the ancient sages, both before and after eating, sipped water (ācamana), they considered that very breath of theirs to have been made "anagna" (not naked, i.e., covered) by that sipping; therefore, a modern-day worshiper who knows this should also act in this same way. This is the meaning of the Vājin-śruti.
Here, because both [the sipping and the covering] are unprecedented (*apūrva*), he states a doubt: "What then? etc.

Just as there is a determination of a doubtful commencement through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), so too, when there is doubt regarding whether the word "they should sip water" (*ācāmanti*) is an injunction, its status as an injunction is determined by the remainder of the sentence "one should sip water" (*ācāmet*). With this analogy as the logical connection (*saṃgati*), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "What, then...

The connection with the chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*) should be understood as arising from the investigation into the injunctions for the subsidiary parts of meditation (*upāsana*), which is a means to knowledge.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is established that a previously unestablished act of sipping water (*ācamana*) enjoined as an auxiliary to the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) must be integrated elsewhere; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because that act is not something to be enjoined, there is no integration as an auxiliary—this is the distinction. Fearing that enjoining both would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), he states another position with the words "or rather" (*athavā*).
"This rinsing of the mouth is indeed praiseworthy, because by means of it they consider the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to be unclothed"—this is the praise.

He establishes the final conclusion according to the logical principle that "that which is not yet established is to be enjoined by way of restating what is already established," using the word "thus" (*evam*).
"Purity" (*prāyatya*) is the state of one who possesses effort (*prayatna*); the meaning is "for the sake of that [purity]."

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: since the act of rinsing the mouth (ācamana), which is prescribed as a subsidiary part of all ritual acts for the purpose of purification by means of Smṛti, is already established, this [Vedic] text merely restates it as a reference (anuvāda) and enjoins only the previously unknown meditation on non-nakedness. One might raise the objection: "But surely the Smṛti-based ācamana is not being restated by this Śruti; rather, it is the ācamana enjoined by this Śruti that is being restated by the Smṛti. The author refutes this with "No," because there is no relationship of source and derivative between these two—the Śruti and the Smṛti—due to their having different subject matters.

The Smṛti passage beginning with "A twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet)" has its status as a root-source refuted by accepting it as an injunction for a different act of ācamana;
now [the author] states that this injunction is unestablished: "And this is not a Śruti.
"For this very reason" means precisely because there is no injunction for ācamana.

He states with the words "Therefore" that the resolve known as meditation (adhyāna) upon water as the clothing of the vital breaths (prāṇa) is enjoined as an ancillary part of the knowledge of the vital breaths (prāṇavidyā).
By the phrase "and himself," he means that this is because it is something not previously established (apūrvatva).

Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory for the sipping of water (ācamana), which is prescribed for the purpose of purification, to serve the purpose of clothing the vital breaths, he says: "And this being so..."
The meaning is that it is unestablished that the sipping of water (ācamana) has clothing as its purpose.

Furthermore, just as in the preceding passage the meditation on food was prescribed as an ancillary to the vital breath (prāṇa), so here the meditation on clothing is prescribed in relation to the waters; otherwise, if this were merely a rule for sipping water, there would be a partial inconsistency—meditation being enjoined in the former case and a mere action in the latter—as he says with the words "Moreover" (api ca).

The meaning is that because the word "should eat" (*bhakṣayet*) is absent, and because it is impossible for a human householder to consume all food fit for dogs, there is no injunction of action in the preceding sentence.
Furthermore, he states "moreover" (*apica*) to show that the sipping of water (*ācamana*) is not to be enjoined here.

He raises an objection—beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*)—that even the mental visualization of clothing (*vāsastvadhyāna*) in the passage "they consider it as if not naked" (*anagnaṃ manyante*) should not be enjoined, since the defect [of redundancy] is the same.

Since both [the passages] would be redundant if they were merely restatements (*anuvāda*), one must necessarily be a restatement and the other a prescription (*vidhi*). And that which is to be prescribed is indeed the meditation on the garment, because it describes the effect of the garment—namely, the state of being unclothed—and because it is something not previously established (*apūrva*).
This is the sense of the resolution.
"As before" means that it is obtained through traditional scripture (*smṛti*).

The statement "one should sip water" (ācāmet) is not an injunction; rather, like the statement "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to with the Aṃśu vessel," it is a restatement (anuvāda). To this point, he provides the supporting evidence: "For this very reason.

This means that since the sentence, "Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating," is not an injunction, the fact that the Kāṇvas do not recite it serves as the evidence.

He then refutes the opinion of someone who claims that, by the force of the textual reading, there is an injunction for sipping water in the Mādhyandina recension and an injunction for meditation in the Kāṇva recension: "As for the one who... (yo 'pi) //18//
Co-ordination. Sūtra 19.
It is exactly the same because there is no difference [between the two texts].
In the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyi-śākhā, a knowledge (vidyā) marked by the name Śāṇḍilya is known;
and therein qualities are heard, such as: "One should meditate upon that Self as consisting of mind, having the vital breath as its body, and having light as its form," and so forth.
In that very same scripture, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, it is further recited: "This person consists of mind; he is light and truth within this heart.
As a grain of rice or a grain of barley, so is he. He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, who governs all this, whatever exists" (Bṛ. 5.6.1).

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is this a single meditation (vidyā) with a combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) in both the *Agnirahasya* and the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, or are these two meditations distinct with no combination of qualities? What, then, is the initial position?
That the meditations are different and the qualities are restricted to each.
Why? Because of the consequence of tautology (*paunaruktya*).

For in the case of different recensions (*śākhā*), having considered how to avoid tautology due to the difference in students, one determines the unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikatva*) and, concluding that it is one, the additional qualities found in one place are integrated into the other—as was stated regarding the dialogue with the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and so forth.
However, in the case of a single recension, since there is no difference in students or knowers, tautology cannot be avoided; therefore, a single knowledge cannot exist across distant locations.
Nor is it possible here to make a distinction such that one recitation is for the purpose of enjoining the meditation and the other is for the purpose of enjoining qualities;

for in that case, only additional qualities would be mentioned in one place and in the other, rather than the identical ones. However, qualities such as "consisting of mind" (manomayatva) and so forth are mentioned in both places.
Therefore, there is no mutual combination of qualities.
This being the case, we reply: just as there is unity of knowledge and a combination of qualities across different recensions (śākhās), so it must also be the case within a single recension.

Because the object of meditation is non-different, we recognize that very same Brahman—characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind (manomaya) and so forth—as the identical object of meditation in both places;
and the form of the object of meditation constitutes the identity of the knowledge.
Furthermore, when there is no difference in the nature of the object (*rūpa*), we are unable to determine a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*);
nor, when there is a difference in knowledge, can there be a fixed distribution of qualities (*guṇavyavasthāna*).
[Objection: But surely, a difference in knowledge is determined due to the consequence of redundancy (*paunaruktya*).
No, it is said;
for the distinction of meaning is logically consistent.
For one scriptural passage is intended for the prescription of knowledge and ignorance, while another is intended for the prescription of qualities—thus, nothing is inconsistent.
Now, if this is the case, then that which is recited in the *Agnirahasya*—namely, "He is the lord of all," and so forth—should have been recited in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.
As for what has already been recited there, such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so on, it should not have been recited.
This is not a fault.
This is because, by that very power, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the same knowledge (*vidyā*) recited in another location.
For, by the mention of qualities belonging to the *mānasagaṇa*, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā situated in a distant place is recognized, and within it, attributes such as lordship (*īśānatva*) are taught.
Otherwise, how could this injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) be said to apply to it?

Furthermore, since a sentence becomes meaningful by teaching what has not been previously established, and since the reference to what has already been established can be justified as a permanent restatement (nityānuvāda), it is not possible to establish recognition [of the same knowledge] on the strength of that [reference].
Therefore, even though the branch (śākhā) is the same, the unity of the knowledge and the combination of its qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) are both logically established. // 19 //
It is the same because there is no difference.
It was seen by Śāṇḍilya and is marked with his name;
the meaning is that it exists subtly within the heart, like a grain of rice or similar seed.
He states the doubt by means of repetition (*abhyāsa*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), using the word "therein" (*tatra*).
The non-inclusion and inclusion of qualities constitute the results of the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions, respectively.
In the preceding case, the injunction for meditating on the state of being unclad was stated as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the already established practice of sipping water (*ācamana*).

But here, within a single recension (*śākhā*), because there is no certainty as to which of two statements located in distant places is the injunction (*vidhi*) and which is the restatement (*anuvāda*), the opponent advances a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of a counter-example, stating: "What, then, [is the case]?
As for what was further stated:

Anticipating the objection that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) because the rule fails in the case of the Prāṇa-vidyā, the Pañcāgni-vidyā, and others, he states "in different [branches]" to show that the charge of tautology is unestablished when the Vedic branches differ.

Anticipating the objection that— just as the Agnihotra-sentence prescribes the rite while the sentence "he offers with curd" prescribes a quality— so too here there may be a prescription of qualities rather than a difference in the knowledge (vidyā), he says "and here there is not one [single thing]."

The repetition of qualities already mentioned would be useless; therefore, the sense is that there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) due to this repetition, just as there is a difference in the *prayāja* offerings.

[The opponent argues: "The mention of qualities already stated is not useless, because it serves to recognize the non-difference of the object of meditation (*upāsya*) as qualified by certain specific qualities; thus, because the form of the object of meditation is non-different, there is unity of knowledge even within the same recensional branch (*śākhā*), just as there is among different branches.
To this, he applies the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) with the words "Just as... (*yathā*).
The "ca" (and) in the Sūtra has been explained as having the sense of "also.

Since it is certain that where many qualities are heard, there is a primary injunction, whereas elsewhere there is a subsidiary injunction by way of restating that [primary act], the intention is that the Agnirahasya constitutes the primary injunction, while the subsequent [passages] constitute subsidiary injunctions. //19//
