In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, after stating "Brahman is Truth" (*Bṛ. 5.5.1*), it continues: "That which is Truth is this Āditya—the person who is in that orb, and the person who is here in the right eye" (*Bṛ. 5.5.2*).

Thus, having taught the specific abodes of that very same true Brahman—both with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*) and with respect to the self (*adhyātma*)—and having established its nature as having the *vyāhṛtis* for its body, two secret names (*upaniṣads*) are taught: "Its secret name is *hari*" with respect to the deities; "Its secret name is *ahaṃ*" with respect to the self.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should both secret doctrines (upaniṣads) be combined in both places without distinction, or should they be applied separately—one pertaining to the divine (adhidaiva) and one pertaining to the self (adhyātma)?
On this point, he begins with the Sūtra itself:

just as in the case of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, where it has been taught that even when [the doctrine] is studied separately, there is a combination of qualities, so it must be in other cases of a similar nature.

Because of the connection with a single knowledge; for this same knowledge of the Truth (satyavidyā) has been studied both with reference to the deities and with reference to the self, due to the non-difference of the opening statement and because of the intermingled recitation.
How could a practice enjoined for that [state] not also apply to that very same state?
For whatever conduct, such as following behind [the teacher], is enjoined for a certain teacher, it remains exactly the same whether he has gone to a village or has gone to the forest.
Therefore, both secret doctrines (upaniṣads) apply to both places. // 20 //
The same connection applies elsewhere as well:

having introduced the Brahman known as Hiraṇyagarbha, which consists of the three existent elements— namely earth, wind, and ether— and which consists of the true, the beyond-the-senses, and the elemental self;
That which was stated as the Truth—that which is yonder sun—is not merely the orb; rather, in that place there is a Person consisting of instruments (the senses).

Having taught that he is the very same one who resides within the body in the place of the eye, and having described his body in the form of the *vyāhṛtis*—namely, "Bhūḥ" for the head, "Bhuvaḥ" for the arms, and "Svaḥ" for the feet—two *upaniṣads*, that is, secret names of the deity, are then taught.
The name of that [Self] residing in the solar orb is "Ahar" (Day) because of its luminosity; the name of that residing in the eye is "Aham" (I) because of its inwardness.

Regarding these two names as the objects of inquiry, a doubt is raised—expressed by the word "tatra"—because the Brahman designated as "Satya" is one and the same, yet there is a mention of different locations.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is the performance of both names in each respective location; in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is the performance of each single name according to the scriptural text.
He explains the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra by means of an analogy with the word "yathā" (just as):

just as it was stated that there is a combination [of details] due to the unity of knowledge (*vidya*), so too in other cases there ought to be a combination of a single knowledge; this is the meaning.
There is indeed no difference in the opening statement, "Brahman is Truth," and these two—the person in the eye and the person in the sun—are established in one another.

Because the rays of the sun are established in the eye, and the eye is established in the sun—this reciprocal reading, which is a reading of mutual connection, establishes the identity of the two vidyās.
To the question, "Even if there is identity of the vidyās, what would follow?", he replies with the word "How?

He removes the doubt that even if the vidyās are identical, there might be no commingling of the two upaniṣads due to the difference in their locations, by means of an illustration: "For he who... (20).
This being the case, he provides the following rebuttal:
Or rather, it is not so, because of the distinction;
nor is there the application of both [rules] to both [cases].
Why?

"Because of the distinction"—the meaning is: because of the connection with a specific distinction in the mode of meditation (*upāsana*). How is there a connection with a specific location? It is said: "This person who is in this orb [of the sun]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3).

For thus, having introduced the person with reference to the divine (*ādhidevika*), the scripture declares: "His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is 'Ahar'"; and having introduced the person with reference to the corporeal (*ādhyātmika*)—in the passage, "This person who is in the right eye" (5.5.4)—it declares: "His secret name."
The pronoun "of that" (tasya) is a term that refers to what is proximate;
therefore, these two secret doctrines (upaniṣads) are taught specifically by depending upon particular bases (āyatana). How, then, could both apply to both?

But surely this is one and the same person, both with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*) and with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), since there is the presentation of two abodes for the single, true Brahman?
True indeed;
however, because specific secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*) are taught by taking up specific states of that very same [Brahman], that [doctrine] must belong to that particular state of it.

Furthermore, there is this illustrative example: even though the essential nature of the teacher remains unchanged, that which is prescribed as following the teacher when he is seated does not apply when he is standing;
and that which is prescribed for him when he is standing does not apply when he is seated.

However, because the essential nature of the teacher does not change between the village and the forest, and because there is no distinction in the Dharma realized through that very nature regardless of whether one is in the village or the forest, the rule applies equally in both places; thus, that [previous case] is not a valid illustration.
Therefore, [this applies] to the two systems of the Upaniṣads. // 21 //
Because the names are not identical, a confusion of names is not appropriate;

thus, it might be argued that the one residing in the eye possesses the name "Day" because it is the True Brahman, just like the one residing in the sun. To this, the author applies the sūtra of the established conclusion with the words "Not so.
The meaning is that the two names are distinguished by their connection to specific forms of meditation and locations.

The point is that the inference—based on the concluding passage consisting of the two sentences "His secret names are *ahar* and *aham*"—which intends to connect the names with the two persons referred to by the word "his" (tad-) as qualified by their respective proximate positions, must be set aside.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a confusion of names because the substrata (the persons) are one and the same, [the author] states the fixed allocation of names based on the distinction between the persons as qualified by their different positions, beginning with the words "But surely... (*nanu*).
He provides an example regarding a qualified relation with the word "asti" (it exists).

Since a counter-example possesses a relation by way of its own nature (*svarūpa-sambandhitva*), he states with the word "grāma" (village) that there is no example for the subject at hand, which is the qualified object of meditation. //21//
And scripture also demonstrates this: BBs_3,3.22.

Moreover, there is an observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) regarding the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of such qualities: "This very form belongs to him; whatever his songs were, those are his songs; whatever his name was, that is his name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).
How this serves as an indicative mark is now explained.

Seeing that the attributes distinguished by their different locations—such as the eyes and so forth—are not to be combined with one another, [the text] here applies, by way of extension, the qualities such as form belonging to the person in the sun to the person in the eye, through the passage beginning, "The form of this very one is the same as that" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5).
Therefore, the conclusion is that these two secret doctrines (upaniṣads) remain strictly restricted to their respective subjects. // 22 //
He states that "and it shows" [in the Sūtra] because the indicative mark (liṅga) is the extension (atideśa) [of qualities] when the determination of names has been stated.

For if the combination [of qualities] were established solely by the identity of the knowledge (vidyaikya), the extension would be redundant; therefore, it is established that even within a single knowledge, there is no combination of the qualities mentioned in different locations without an extension. //22//
Section on the Accumulation of Materials (Saṃbhṛtyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 23. 12. [The section concerning the accumulation of materials. Sūtra 23.
"And from this [passage], there is also the accumulation and pervasion of heaven.

In the *Khilas* of the Rāṇāyaṇīyas, the following manifestations of Brahman are recited: "The powers, with Brahman as the eldest, have been accumulated; Brahman, as the eldest, stretched out the sky at the beginning. Thus, the accumulation of power, the settling in heaven, and so forth are taught.
Furthermore, in their very Upanishads, Brahma-knowledges such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others are recited.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether those manifestations of Brahman should be combined within those Brahma-knowledges or not—since their combination would initially appear necessary due to their connection with Brahman—the author states the following: the manifestations such as "supporting" (saṃbhṛti) and "pervading heaven" (dyuvyāpti) are not to be combined within the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and other such meditations.
For this very reason, it is due to the connection with a particular abode.
To illustrate, in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, Brahman is described as having the heart as its abode: "This is my Self within the heart" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).
In exactly the same way, in the Dahara-vidyā as well, it is said: "In the small lotus-palace there is a small inner space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).
In the Upakośala-vidyā, however, the eye is mentioned as the abode: "This person who is seen in the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1).
Thus, in those various instances, an internal abode is recognized in these vidyās.
But how can there be an inclusion in these [vidyās] of those divine manifestations, such as the collection [of food], pervasion, and so forth?
But surely, even in these [passages], supermundane manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) are heard: "Greater than heaven, greater than these worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3);
"He indeed is the light-bearer, for he shines in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.4);
"As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3).
These and others such as these exist; and there are also other Brahma-vidyās here, such as that of the sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśakalā*), which are likewise devoid of specific sense-bases (*āyatana*).
This is true.
Nevertheless, there exists here a distinction that serves as the reason for the non-combination of the *saṃbhṛti* and other qualities.
For it is logical that when meditations located in distant places are brought to mind through the mention of identical qualities, the qualities belonging to those distant places may also be combined.

However, the qualities such as *saṃbhṛti* and others, as well as the qualities like "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) which fall within the scope of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and other passages, do not bring to mind the meditations existing in other locations, because their essential natures are mutually exclusive; this is what is being stated.
For that [multiplicity] is possible even when there is a difference in the specific knowledge (vidyā);
for it is an established principle that even the one Brahman is worshipped in many ways through various manifestations (vibhūti),
as seen in the case of the "Greater than the Great" (parovarīyas) and other such passages which show such distinctions.
Therefore, there is no inclusion of the accumulation of vigor and so forth in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and other meditations.
[Sūtra 23] *Note:* "Brahmajyeṣṭhā" (the plural form) is a Vedic archaism for "brahmajyeṣṭhāni," with the elision of the case-ending.
"Vīryā" (the plural form) refers to various types of heroic prowess or valor.
And because of the accumulation, the shining, and the pervading;
those for which Brahman is the eldest (the primary cause) are "brahmajyeṣṭhāni," with the elision of the suffix being Vedic.
The heroic deeds (*vīryāṇi*) are specific acts of prowess, such as the creation of space and so forth; and these heroic deeds were accumulated and brought to fulfillment without obstacle,
because there was no one to create obstacles for the work of the Universal Controller.
And that [Brahman] is the eldest; even before the emergence of the gods and others from the fire of Brahman, it pervaded the sky—that is, heaven—meaning it is eternally all-pervasive.
The qualities mentioned in the supplementary portion of the text, such as being the very first of all and being beyond rivalry, are to be understood through the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*).
The term "in the *khilas*" means in those passages that are devoid of injunctions or prohibitions.
He states the doubt arising from the connection with Brahman and the appearance of a difference in the meditations: "In those [meditations]...

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is that because the glories of Brahman, though taught as unconnected [to specific meditations], are recognized in all meditations on Brahman through their connection with Brahman, they should be combined.
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "The [glories] such as 'being collected'..."

The construction of the Sūtra is as follows: "Accumulation and pervasion of heaven" (*saṃbhṛtidyuvyāpti*)—even that [set of qualities] is not to be combined everywhere, because of the application of specific limiting factors, just as in the case of the two Upaniṣadic passages.

When it has been stated that there is no attainment [of these qualities] because there is no reason for the recognition of divine manifestations in those meditations associated with specific internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), the author raises an objection regarding the reason: "But in these...

The meaning of the objection is that there is attainment of "accumulation" and so forth in those respective meditations either due to the commonality of being "divine" (*ādhidaivika*) or due to the commonality of being devoid of internal bases.

The two reasons stated do not result in the acquisition of qualities, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of a mutual commingling of qualities between the Śāṇḍilya, Dahara, and other such meditations on the divine (ādhidaivika), as well as with the meditation on the "abode-less" (āyatanahīna).

Therefore, he provides the rebuttal beginning with "True" (*satyam*), stating that the cause for the acquisition of qualities is the identity of the object of meditation characterized by several common attributes, which brings about the unity of the meditations; since that [identity] is absent here, there is no acquisition.

This is like the fixed distinction between two names based on their specific locations; likewise, there is a distinction between Brahman as qualified by the qualities of the *saṃbhṛti* and other meditations, and Brahman as qualified by the qualities mentioned in the Śāṇḍilya and other meditations.

Because of the mutual difference in form, there is no synthesis of the *saṃbhṛti* and other meditations; since this [present case] is an extension of the logic already stated, it does not require [further discussion of] connection and so forth.

Just as in the case of a single *udgītha*, the meditation on qualities such as "higher than the high" differs from the meditation on [qualities like] "having golden hair," so too, even though the Brahman is one, the distinction between different meditations (*vidyā*) is possible. Therefore, he says, "as in the case of 'higher than the high' and so forth," meaning that the recognition of Brahman does not necessitate the inclusion of the qualities.
Therefore, it is established that this is an injunction for another knowledge distinguished by qualities such as the accumulation [of merit]. //23//
Section 13: The Topic Beginning with the Person (Puruṣa). Sūtra 24.
"And because the others are not mentioned as in the Puruṣavidyā. (BBs 3.3.24) There exists a Puruṣavidyā in the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇa* of the Tāṇḍins and the Paiṅgins;
therein, the person (*puruṣa*) is conceived as the sacrifice (*yajña*).

Having divided his lifespan into three parts, the three daily libations (savana) were established; furthermore, states such as hunger and thirst were conceived as the initiatory rites (dīkṣā) and so forth; and other attributes pertaining to that [state], such as the application of benedictory mantras, were likewise attained therein.

The followers of the Taittirīya school also construct a certain "sacrifice of the person" (*puruṣayajña*) by means of this section: "Of that sacrifice of one who knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife... (Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 80).

In this regard, a doubt arises: should those characteristics of the sacrifice of the person which have been mentioned elsewhere be combined with the Taittirīya version, or should they not be combined?

Since the specific characteristic of being a "sacrifice of the person" (puruṣayajña) might lead one to conclude that [the details] should be combined [from other sources], we say: they are not to be combined.
Why?
Because there is no recognition of their identity with that [original form].
Regarding this, the Teacher says: "As in the Puruṣavidyā.
Just as there is a scriptural mention in the Puruṣavidyā of certain reciters—the Tāṇḍins and the Paiṅginas—such a mention does not exist for the others, the Taittirīyas.

For in their case, the accomplishment of the sacrifice is seen to be entirely different, due to the sequential enumeration of the wife, the sacrificer, the Vedas, the altar, the sacrificial grass, the post, the clarified butter, the horse, the officiating priests, and so forth.

Even that which constitutes the performance of the *savana* rites is entirely distinct from others, as stated in the Nārāyaṇīya Upaniṣad (80): "Those [rites] which are performed in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.

Furthermore, whatever slight similarity there may be—such as death being the final bath (*avabhṛtha*)—is overwhelmed by the greater dissimilarities and is therefore incapable of producing recognition.
Moreover, the status of the person as a sacrifice is not heard of in the Taittirīyaka.
Regarding the phrase "of the sacrifice of the wise" (*viduṣo yajñasya*), these two genitives are not in apposition— meaning it does not mean "that which is the sacrifice, being itself the wise man"—
for a person cannot possess the primary status of being a sacrifice. Rather, these two genitives are in different cases (vyadhikaraṇa), meaning "of the sacrifice which belongs to the wise man."
For a person has a primary connection with sacrifice;
and when a primary meaning is possible, one must resort to that very meaning rather than a figurative one.

Furthermore, by explaining the person's status as a sacrificer through the statement "the Self is the sacrificer," [the text] shows his connection with sacrifice precisely through a grammatical coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya).

Moreover, since there is the scriptural statement "of him who knows thus" (*tasyaivaṃvidaḥ*), which is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) as if something were already established, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) for one who intends to understand the state of sacrifice belonging to the person and the state of the sacrificer and so forth belonging to the self and the rest.

Furthermore, having previously taught the knowledge of the Self together with renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), the subsequent sequence beginning with "of him who knows thus" is a recitation that forms a supplement to what precedes; it is not independent.
And thus we perceive a single fruit for both sections of the Anuvāka: "He attains the greatness of Brahman" (*brahmaṇo mahimānam āpnoti*).
But for the others, the recitation of the Puruṣa-vidyā is not subsidiary to anything else;
for its fruit is the increase of lifespan, as is evident from the statement: "He who knows this lives for a hundred and sixteen years" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.16.7).

Therefore, in the Taittirīyaka, there is no application of the mantras of benediction and other attributes of the "knowledge of the person" (puruṣavidyā) that are studied in other recensional branches.

He speaks of the Puruṣavidyā, the knowledge contained in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with the words "There is": "Man, indeed, is the sacrifice. His twenty-four years constitute the morning libation (prātaḥsavana); his forty-four years constitute the midday libation (mādhyandinasavana); and his forty-eight years constitute the third libation (tṛtīyasavana). This is for the purpose of establishing an analogy with the well-known ritual sacrifice.
The three pressings have been conceptualized:

"When he is hungry, when he thirsts, and when he does not find pleasure—these are the *dīkṣās*. Then, when he eats, when he drinks, and when he finds pleasure—these are the *upasads*. Then, when he laughs, when he eats solid food, and when he engages in sexual intercourse—these are the *stuta-śastras*. And then..."

Whatever austerity, charity, and so forth [are performed], that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); death itself is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). "My vital breaths, in the form of Vasu and others, extend these three pressings (*savana*) throughout the duration of my life"—this is the prayer. The application of the three mantras—"Thou art imperishable, thou art unshakable, thou art sharpened vital breath"—shows that the fruit is a lifespan of one hundred and sixteen years.
He states the Puruṣavidyā belonging to another recension for the sake of resolving this doubt, saying "the Taittirīyakas.

Here, because it is uncertain whether the two genitive cases in the phrase "of the wise one" (*viduṣaḥ*) and "of the sacrifice" (*yajñasya*) are in apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or not (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), he expresses the doubt with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
The result [of this analysis] is precisely the determination of whether there is a combination of details or not.

In the previous case, a difference between the two meditations was stated because there was no recognition of common, unique qualities in the "Accumulation" (saṃbhṛti) and other sections. Here, however, since there is a recognition of identity in the form of the "Person as Sacrifice" (puruṣayajña), which is characterized by the unique quality of death being the final bath (avabhṛtha), the prima facie view—arrived at by way of this counter-example—is that the meditations are one and the same. To this, the author states the final conclusion: "They are not to be combined."

For one who knows this, the sacrifice is as follows: the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife, the body is the fuel, the chest is the altar, the hair is the sacrificial grass (barhis), the Veda is the tuft of hair on the crown, the heart is the sacrificial post, desire is the clarified butter, anger is the victim, austerity is the fire, self-restraint is the pacifier, the sacrificial fee is speech, the Hotṛ priest is the out-breath, the Udgātṛ priest is the in-breath, the Adhvaryu priest is the eye, and the Brahman priest is the mind; [this is not the same as the other] because of the great difference in their respective characteristics.
The meaning is "recognition of identity" (rūpaikyapratyabhijñā).
The grammatical connection is: "the Veda is the handful of kuśa grass, self-restraint is the pacifier, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is [the means of] subduing.
Furthermore, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, there is the conceptualization of the three divisions of life as the three Soma-pressings (savana).

But here, he points out the dissimilarity by saying "yadapi" (even that which), namely, that [the ritual] occurs at evening and so forth. Since even a similarity appears in the Taittirīya Śruti—"That which is death is the avabhṛtha bath; that which one enjoys is the upasad"—he says "yadapi kiñcit" (whatever it may be).
The meaning is that this similarity, like the similarity between an elephant and a camel in their both having four legs, does not necessitate identity.

Furthermore, he states another point of dissimilarity with the words "And not... (na ca). While in the *Chāndogya* the identity of the person and the sacrifice is heard, here there is a distinction; thus, another difference is expressed.

Although, according to the principle of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (*niṣādasthapati*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two genitives is appropriate, nevertheless—due to the complexity of postulating an unestablished identity, because of the statement of their distinction as "the self of the sacrifice," and because of the contradiction of one and the same thing being both the sacrifice and the sacrificer—it refers to that well-known sacrifice which belongs to the knower of the Self.

Discrepancy in grammatical coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya) alone is logical. Furthermore, when there is a syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) perceived through the injunction of the perfection of the ritual accessories by means of the accessories belonging to the learned person—this being an explanatory reference (anuvāda) to the qualified object (viśeṣya) which is the sacrifice connected with the learned person—then, for you who maintain that there are separate injunctions for the qualified object and for the accessories, the fault of sentence-splitting (vākyabheda) would arise; such is the meaning.

Furthermore, after teaching renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) through the words "the laying down [of actions] beyond truth and the rest, and whatever else," and then teaching the knowledge of the Self to be accomplished by that renunciation in the preceding *Prājāpatya-anuvāka* with the words "having known this Self as 'all this world by means of all,' the wise man does not again undergo death," [the text] subsequently,
in the following *anuvāka*, refers back to that very same knowledge of the Self mentioned earlier for the purpose of its praise, saying, "for one who knows thus... and so forth.
Because of the scriptural statement regarding the unity of the fruit, the perfection of the sacrifice is accomplished as a subordinate element (śeṣa) [of that knowledge];

however, for the Chandogas, there is an injunction for independent knowledge. He states this with the words, "Moreover, together with renunciation" (sasaṃnyāsām). He states the result of this reflection with the words, "Therefore" (tasmāt). //24//
END BsCom_3,3.13.24 START BsCom_3,3.13.25 14.
Section on Piercing and so forth (Vedhādyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 25.

Because of the difference in meaning regarding piercing and so forth. At the beginning of the Upaniṣads of the Atharvaṇikas, there is a recitation of mantras: "Piercing all, piercing the heart, cutting open the vessels, cutting open the head—divided threefold," and so on.
For the Tāṇḍins, it begins with "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice" and so forth; for the Śāṭhyāyanins, it begins with "Thou art the white-horsed, green-and-blue one" and so forth;
for the Kaṭhas and Taittirīyas, it begins with "May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.1) and so forth.
In the case of the Vājasaneyins, at the beginning of their Upaniṣad, the Pravargya-Brāhmaṇa is recited: "The gods, indeed, sat down," and so forth.

Among the Kauṣītakins as well, there is the Agniṣṭoma-Brāhmaṇa: "The Agniṣṭoma is indeed Brahman; that day is Brahman; by means of Brahman they approach Brahman; those who approach this day attain immortality."

We now investigate whether all these mantras, beginning with the *pravidhya*, and the rituals, such as the *pravargya*, are to be combined with the meditations (*vidyā*), or whether they are not to be so combined. What first appears to us is that these are indeed to be combined with the meditations.
Why?
Because they are recited in proximity to the Upaniṣad texts, which have knowledge as their primary subject.
But do we not perceive any injunction for these [rites] as being for the sake of knowledge?
Certainly.
Even though we do not perceive [any specific power], we shall infer it from the force of their proximity;
for when the meaningfulness of proximity is possible, it is not right to assume it to be accidental.
But surely, we do not see any capacity of these mantras regarding the subject matter of knowledge (vidyā).
And how can we understand that rituals such as the Pravargya, which are enjoined for other purposes, also serve the purpose of knowledge?
This is not a fault;
for it is possible to conceive of some capacity of the mantras pertaining to knowledge as well, since they mention the heart and other parts of the body.

For the heart and other organs are generally taught in meditations as the abodes and so forth; and by means of them, the status of mantras such as "pierce the heart" as being auxiliary to meditation is established.
Moreover, the application of mantras in meditations is observed, for example, in "I take refuge in Bhūḥ with this one, that one, and that one" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.15.3).

Likewise, even for rites such as the Pravargya, which are employed elsewhere, their application to the meditations (vidyās) is not contradictory—just as the Bṛhaspatisava is [employed] in the Vājapeya.
This being the position reached, we reply:
there is no inclusion of these [rites] within the meditations.
Why?
Because of the difference in their purposes.

For the purposes of mantras of this kind, such as "Pierce the heart,"—namely, the piercing of the heart and so forth—are distinct and unrelated to the forms of knowledge (vidyās) proclaimed in the Upaniṣads.
They have no capacity to be joined with those [qualities].
But is it not the case that, because they are also employed in the meditations (*upāsana*) upon the heart, a connection with meditation was proposed by way of that [heart]?
No, it is said in reply.
For the utility of merely mentioning the "heart" might somehow be imagined in this way; however, the "heart alone" is not the meaning of the mantra here.
Indeed, a mantra such as "having pierced the heart, having cut the veins," and so forth, is not connected with the [knowledge of] sciences (vidyās).
For this meaning belongs to the domain of malevolent magic (ābhicārika); therefore, this entire mantra—"piercing everything"—is connected with a rite of malevolent magic.
However, the specific connection of those [mantras] must be pursued through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Thus, for other mantras as well— some by their indicative mark (*liṅga*), some by direct statement (*vacana*), and some by other means of knowledge— once they have been assigned to different purposes, it is not possible for them to be subordinate to a *vidyā* merely by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), even though they are recited in the secret section (*rahasya*).

For it has been stated in the first *Tantra* that "proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is weaker than direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest," in the sūtra: "When there is a conflict between direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker because of its remoteness from the purpose" (*Jaimini Sūtra* 3.3.13).
Likewise, it is not possible for rites such as the *Pravargya*, which are enjoined elsewhere, to be subordinate parts of the meditations (*vidyā*).
Indeed, there is no commonality of purpose whatsoever between these [rites] and the *vidyās*.
In the case of the *Vājapeya*, however, there is a clearly distinct application for the *Bṛhaspatisava*: "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava.
Moreover, this single *Pravargya* rite, having been produced once, is employed elsewhere by a stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); it cannot be employed elsewhere by a weaker means of knowledge.

For this [conclusion] would hold true only if there were no perceived distinction between the two means of knowledge; however, it is impossible for there to be no perceived distinction between two means of knowledge that possess the qualities of being stronger and weaker, precisely because of that distinction between strength and weakness.
Therefore, one should not suspect that such mantras or rituals constitute a subsidiary part of the meditative knowledge (vidyā) merely by virtue of being recited in proximity to it.
Rather, one should be content with the fact that they are recited in proximity due to common characteristics such as the requirement of recitation in the forest (araṇyānuvacana). // 25 //
Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth, the performer of the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) addresses the deity: "All this.
O deity, pierce—that is, tear apart—all the limbs of my enemy; specifically, split his heart, rend the *dhamanīs* (veins), crush the *śirās* (arteries), and destroy his head on all sides.
The meaning is: "O God Savitṛ, let my enemy be thus divided and separated in three ways. The meaning is: "Impel the sacrifice and its lord; that is, bring them to completion."
The meaning is: "You are blue like an emerald, like Indra who possesses the white horse Uccaiḥśravas.
The meaning is: "May you be *śam*, a bringer of happiness, for us (*naḥ*).
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed Brahman; that day on which it is performed is also Brahman. Therefore, that which is to be accomplished on this day [is Brahman].
The construction is as follows: those who perform the rites and carry them out reach Brahman by means of Brahman itself, and they attain immortality in due course.

He states the doubt—using the words "What [is it]?"—regarding whether the mantras and so forth constitute a supplement to the respective Upaniṣadic knowledge, based on the presence or absence of evidence.
The result [of the inquiry] is as before.
One might object: "But surely there is no inclusion [of these elements], because there is no evidence for their being subordinate parts (śeṣa) of those [vidyās]. He answers:

"Certainly. Mantras and so forth are subordinate parts of their respective vidyās because they are in proximity to the fruit-bearing vidyās, just like the Puruṣamedha sacrifice found in the Taittirīyaka;
thus, the consistency with the illustrative example is established.
Regarding the Siddhāntin’s position, he states the objection that the proximity [of the mantra] would otherwise be purposeless with the words "For not...

The purposefulness of the proximity consists in its making known that mantras and the like, which lack a fruit themselves, are subsidiary to that which possesses a fruit; since this is possible, it is not reasonable to resort to that proximity as being devoid of meaning without cause.
(In the reading with the negative particle *nañ*, the meaning is: it is not reasonable to resort to that [proximity] for such a purpose without cause—that is, without a reason.

One might object: "Since mantras lack the capacity to reveal a meaning inherent in the knowledge (vidyā), they cannot be subordinate to that knowledge. This is the doubt expressed by the word "nanu" (now, an objection). He states the counter-argument with "kathaṃ ca" (and how so?): by the sentence "They proceed with the Pravargya rite before the Upasads," the subordination of the Pravargya to the sacrifice is heard; and since rites such as the Agniṣṭoma have heaven and other results as their purpose through their respective scriptural injunctions, they do not have knowledge as their purpose. Thus he says: "And how?"
He states that "this is not so" because mantras possess the capacity to illuminate the heart, the channels (*nāḍī*), and other such elements associated with *vidyā*.
He says "and it is seen" because the employment of mantras in meditative adorations (*upāsti*) is not observed anywhere [else].
In the *Chāndogya*, for the sake of a son's long life, the meditation on the three worlds as hair is taught; in that context, this is the mantra of supplication by the father.

In this context, by saying "with this one," he utters the name of his son three times; the meaning is: "Together with this son, I attain this world and that world—may I not suffer separation from my son.

He provides an example for the fact that even rites enjoined elsewhere may be applied to the meditations (*vidyās*) through proximity (*saṃnidhi*), despite their specific application by other sentences: "In the case of the *vājapeya*... [referring to the rule]:
"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with the *bṛhaspatisava*. Although [the *bṛhaspatisava*] is enjoined as having spiritual luster as its fruit by this sentence...

The meaning is that there is no contradiction, just as in the case of the *bṛhaspatisava*, where the sentence situated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *vājapeya*—namely, "Having sacrificed with the *vājapeya*, one should sacrifice with the *bṛhaspatisava*"—enjoins it as a subsequent subsidiary (*uttarāṅga*) to the *vājapeya*.
Even though a single sentence effects both the recognition of the *bṛhaspatisava* located in another context and the injunction of its status as a subsidiary; [there is no conflict].

Furthermore, it is improper to treat [the Agnihotra] as the primary act because that would entail the fallacy of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); therefore, just as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra*, a distinct ritual act named the Bṛhaspatisava is enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*).
Thus, there is no "application of what has already been applied" (*viniyuktasya viniyoga*), as established in the two systems of the Bhaṭṭas and the Gurus.

This is just as, for example, the obligatory (*nitya*) Agnihotra is recognized by its name in the context of the Aśvamedha sacrifice through the statement: "Restraining his speech, he performs this Agnihotra for one night."

Just as in the case of a modified sacrifice (vikṛti) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, where in a single sentence— "he performs the two ājyabhāgas"— there is recognition of the two ājyabhāgas established in the archetype (prakṛti) by means of the word, and their injunction by means of the sentence, why should it not be the same here, where there is recognition by the term "Bṛhaspatisava" and the injunction of its status as an auxiliary (aṅga) by means of the sentence?

Nor should it be argued that a noun (*nāmapada*), being dependent on a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) which enjoins something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is incapable of recognizing an already established action (*siddha-karma*).

For even an established action can be treated as something to be accomplished again by virtue of its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*); thus, it is logical that the verbal suffix itself—whose meaning is otherwise established—can be dependent on a noun whose referent is well-known.

Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana* sacrifice would likewise enjoin the permanent *agnihotra* merely as a subsidiary; for such a conclusion is indeed acceptable.
Nor is there any contradiction with the earlier treatise (*pūrvatantra*), because the later treatise (*uttaratantra*) is more authoritative,
and because the earlier treatise is concerned with the distinction between independent and dependent meditations (*svatantra-paratantra-bhāvanā*).

Therefore, the intention of the venerable Bhagavatpāda is that there is an application of the very same verbal root-meaning named "Bṛhaspati"— which had already been applied toward spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)— as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice.

And there is a universally accepted example for that which is enjoined in one context being enjoined elsewhere: the quality of being made of *khadira* wood and so forth, since that which is enjoined for a sacrifice is also enjoined for results such as vigor (*vīrya*). Likewise, it might be argued that mantras and rituals already enjoined elsewhere become subordinate to knowledge (*vidyā*). Having reached this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "Not these" (*naiṣām*). Even though the mantras are connected to the heart and other parts in the context of knowledge, because their meanings—such as piercing (*vedha*) and so forth—are not connected [to knowledge], the entire meaning of the mantras is connected to rites like malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). This is because proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is weaker than the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which connects them to malevolent magic and the like. Thus, the mantras [belong] only to malevolent magic and so forth.
The meaning is *viniyoga* (application).
From the statement, "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," one sprinkles water around the fire from left to right; thus there is a connection with the sprinkling of water around the fire.
Furthermore, from the statement, "He offers the Sāvitra oblation before the ritual action, offering at each pressing," there is a connection with the specific ritual action in the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Regarding the phrase "of this mantra," he says "tadviśeṣa" (its specific [details]).
He extends the stated reasoning to passages such as "the white horse" (Śvetāśvataropaniṣad) and so forth by saying "evamanyeṣām" (so for others).
"Other means of knowledge" refers to context and the like.

Now, it was argued that even for those [mantras] already employed elsewhere by means of *liṅga* (indicative power) and so forth, there may also be an application within the meditations (*vidyā*) by means of *saṃnidhi* (proximity), since there is no contradiction;
to this, he replies: "For [the latter] is weak.
This refers to a conflict between two [means of proof] when they have the same object and are in conjunction (*samavāya*).
The weakness of the other [word] is due to remoteness from the meaning;
that is to say, in conveying its own meaning, the other word functions with an intervening step.
This is the intended meaning: since that which has been applied to one [purpose] is already free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), its application to another is indeed contradictory.

However, when the two means of proof (*pramāṇa*) effecting the application are of equal strength, it is impossible to abandon the application of either one; therefore, as a last resort, the application of what has already been applied is accepted by generating a new expectancy, as in the cases: "The sacrificial post is made of *khadira* wood" and "For one desiring vigor, the post is made of *khadira* wood."

By the two sentences "one should make a sacrificial post" and [the subsequent one], the quality of being made of *khadira* wood, which is already enjoined for the sacrifice, is further enjoined for the fruit of vigor (*vīrya*).

However, where there is an inequality between the two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such an application is not accepted, because the application by the weaker means of knowledge is sublated by the stronger one. For example, in the case of the verse "Never art thou barren," which is addressed to Indra (*aindrī*), the injunction "he worships the *gārhapatya* fire" is established by the direct statement of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti-śruti*), which is independent of anything else.

The status of being subsidiary to Indra—which is established by *liṅga* (indicative power) in the form of the capacity to manifest Indra—is set aside by the fact that [the mantra] is understood to be subsidiary to the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire.
For *liṅga* does not directly indicate subsidiarity; rather, it merely effects the manifestation of Indra.
By means of this *liṅga*, one must then postulate a *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) to the effect: "Indra is to be worshipped with this mantra."

Since the understanding of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) arises through that [syntactic connection], the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which indicates subsidiarity—being separated by the Vedic text—is immediately sublated by the direct statement (*śruti*) which conveys its own meaning.

Likewise, syntactic connection (*vākya*) is sublated by the indicative mark, as in the case of the two parts of the mantra: "I prepare this seat for thee; I fashion it with a stream of clarified butter," and "Sit upon it, O essence of rice, and take thy stand in this immortal [place], being well-disposed. Here, each part [of the mantra] individually...

When, through the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting in the capacity to manifest that [specific act], there occurs an application (*viniyoga*) by way of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding both the making of the seat and the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*),
the perceived syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is sublated;
for that [syntactic unity] exists even in the case of the entire mantra having the capacity to manifest the making of the seat and the capacity to manifest the placing of the sacrificial cake.

Furthermore, having postulated the indicative power (*liṅga*), there is a conceptualization of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*); thus, in both cases, when the application of the entire mantra is understood, there is an intervention by two factors—indicative power and scriptural injunction—which renders it weaker than the indicative power that is established with only one intervention by the scriptural injunction.
Nor should it be argued that the capacity (*sāmarthya*) need not be postulated.

Because that which lacks capacity cannot be employed [in a function], for this very reason it is postulated that the word *gaṅgā* possesses the capacity in the form of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the purpose of conveying the meaning "bank.

Likewise, context (*prakaraṇa*) is sublated by syntactical connection (*vākya*), just as the twelve *upasad* rites mentioned in the context of the *sāhna* sacrifice are displaced from their status as subsidiaries of the *sāhna*—which is obtained through context—by the syntactical statement "twelve [upasads] belong to the *ahīna*," which conveys their status as subsidiaries of the *ahīna*.

Context, which consists of the primary rite's requirement for its subsidiaries, is [sublated] by syntactical connection, capacity (*sāmarthya*), and direct assertion (*śruti*), which relate the subsidiary and the primary into a single unified sentence.

When there is a cognition of the application for its own purpose through what is being inferred, both the capacity of the subsidiary (aṅga) and the direct statement (śruti) are weaker than the inferring sentence because they are mediated by a gap;
likewise, proximity (saṃnidhi) is sublated by context (prakaraṇa).

For example, that which is obtained through the reading in proximity to the specific Soma sacrifice called the Abhiṣecanīya, which is included within the context of the Rājasūya—[is sublated by the context].

In the case of the narrative of Śunaḥśepa and others, their status as a subsidiary to the Abhiṣecanīya rite is set aside, and they are established as subsidiaries to the entire Rājasūya sacrifice; this is because proximity (saṃnidhi) is weaker than the context (prakaraṇa) that is already established [by other means], since proximity functions merely as a basis for inferring a context. In the same way, proximity overrides name (samākhyā). For instance, in the section titled *Pauroḍāśika*, mantras are recorded in sequence for rites such as the cake-offering to Agni (*āgneyapuroḍāśa*); therein—
The mantra "śundhadhvaṃ daivyāya karmaṇe" (be purified for the divine rite) is recited in proximity to both the curd and the milk used for the *sānnāyya* offering;

although by the force of its name (*samākhyā*) this mantra would initially be understood as a subsidiary element for the purification of the *puroḍāśa* vessels, that application is set aside by the principle of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), and it is thereby established as a subsidiary element for the purification of the *sānnāyya* vessels.

The section related to the *puroḍāśa* cake is called "Pauroḍāśika"; thus, although the human designation (*pauruṣasamākhyā*) indicates a general connection between the mantra contained within that section and the *puroḍāśa*, it is weaker because it depends on factors such as proximity (*saṃnidhi*) when it comes to indicating the specific application (*viniyoga*) in the form of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*).
Therefore, when there is such a conflict, direct statement (*śruti*) is indeed the sublater, while the designation is merely the sublated.

However, regarding the four intermediate [means of proof], the meaning of the *Śrutiliṅga* Sūtra is that the preceding one sublates the subsequent one and the subsequent one sublates the preceding one.

Therefore, it is established that mantras already employed elsewhere by means of *liṅga* (indicative power) and so forth cannot be employed in the *vidyās* by means of the weaker *saṃnidhi* (proximity). The same applies to ritual actions (*karmāṇi*).
The meaning is that there is no evidence whatsoever for [the view] that ritual actions assist knowledge (*vidyā*) or that they share a single fruit with them.
The phrase "apica" (furthermore) expresses this same point.
Now, one might ask: what then is the status of the recitation of passages such as those concerning "piercing" (*vedha*) alongside the Upaniṣads? To this he replies: "In the forest" (*araṇye*).
Therefore, it is established that rites involving mantras such as piercing (vedha) and so forth are not to be combined with the [meditative] knowledges (vidyās). //25//

Section on Loss (Hānyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 26.

"But in the case of falling away, because the word for 'approaching' (*upāyana*) is subordinate [to the act of falling], it is like the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the chanting; this has been stated.

(BBs 3.3.26) There is a scriptural passage among the Tāṇḍins: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, shaking off the body, with a perfected self, I attain the uncreated world of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1).
Likewise, the Atharvaṇikas [read]: "Thus the wise one, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.8).
Similarly, the Śāṭyāyanins recite: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds.
In the same way, the Kauṣītakins [state]: "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen take up his good deeds, and those not dear his evil deeds" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.4).

Thus, in some places the abandonment of good and evil deeds is heard; in others, the taking up of those very same deeds by means of loved ones and those who are not loved through their distribution; and in yet others, both abandonment and taking up are heard.
Regarding that case where both are heard, there is nothing at all that needs to be said.
Even in a place where only the taking up is heard and not the abandonment, abandonment follows as a matter of course.

Since the abandonment of one's own good and evil deeds by others is necessarily implied when those deeds are being taken over, there arises a doubt as to whether the taking over (upāyana) should be supplied where only the abandonment is heard and not the taking over. In such a case, because it is not explicitly heard, it should not be supplied; furthermore, this is because the scriptural mention in another recension pertains to a different branch of knowledge (vidyā).

Furthermore, since the abandonment (*hāna*) of good and evil deeds has the self as its agent, whereas the taking up (*upāyana*) of them has another as its agent, and since these two do not necessarily coexist, how could the taking up be implied by the abandonment? Therefore, there is no simultaneous occurrence of the taking up with the abandonment. To this position, the author of the Sūtra replies: "But in the case of abandonment... (*hānau tu*).
However, even when this [act of] abandonment is heard alone, the taking up (upāyana) must necessarily be included,
because it is supplementary to it; for it is understood from the Kauṣītaki-rahasya that the word "taking up" is supplementary to the word "abandonment."
Therefore, even when only the word "abandoning" (hāna) is heard elsewhere, the term "attaining" (upāyana) follows by implication.

As for the argument that there is no such inclusion because it is not explicitly mentioned, because it pertains to the scope of other meditations, and because it is not mandatory— that is now being addressed.
This stated distinction would hold if these two were proclaimed as things to be performed;
however, their mention here is for the purpose of praising knowledge.

Thus highly blessed is this knowledge, by whose power the good and evil deeds of this wise man—which constitute the cause of transmigratory existence—are shaken off, and they enter into his friends and enemies respectively.

Furthermore, since in this particular glorificatory passage it is heard in some places that the "attainment" (*upāyana*) occurs immediately after the "forsaking" (*hāna*), one infers that even where there is a scriptural mention of forsaking, the attainment follows as well, for the sake of achieving the excellence of the praise.

And it is well known that one glorificatory statement (*arthavāda*) proceeds by depending upon another glorificatory statement, as in such passages as: "This sun over there is indeed the twenty-first" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 2.10.5).

For how could the twenty-first [element] of the sun be designated here without regard for another explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), such as: "Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first"?

Likewise, in passages such as "There are two *triṣṭubh* verses for the sake of possessing the senses," one observes a dependence on other explanatory passages such as "The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the sense-organ.

Furthermore, since this statement regarding the taking up [of the fires] is for the purpose of praising knowledge, one should not be overly insistent on the question of how the good and evil deeds belonging to one person could be taken up by others.

By uttering the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "because of being supplementary to the word 'attainment' (*upāyana*"), [the author] indicates that the recurrence of "attainment" (*upāyana*) in the context of "relinquishment" (*hāni*) is solely for the purpose of praise.
For if he had intended to discuss the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*), he would have stated the recurrence of the meaning of "attainment" itself in the context of "relinquishment.
Therefore, this sūtra is intended to demonstrate the synthesis of praise as an incidental discussion following the inquiry into the synthesis of qualities.
The comparison is introduced as being "like the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the singing.

For example, among the Bhāllavins, in the Vedic text (Nigama) stating, "O *kuśa* grass, you are of the nature of trees; protect me," although the *kuśa* grass is heard of without distinction as having its origin in trees (*vanaspati-yoni*), the specific statement of the Śāṭyāyanins that "the *kuśa* grass is made of *udumbara* wood" leads one to conclude that the *kuśa* grass consists of *udumbara* wood.
Just as, when there is no distinction regarding the sequence of the *devacchandas* and *asuracchandas*, they are understood to be "the *devacchandas* come first" based on the *Paiṅgi* tradition;

and just as, when some obtain no specific time for the *ṣoḍaśistotra*, the specific time is established by the *Ṛgvedic* scripture stating, "when the sun has half-risen"; and just as some transmit the *upagāna* without distinction while the *Bhāllavins* transmit it with distinction.

The meaning is that just as in these cases of the *kuśa* grass and so forth, there is a connection with specific details found in other scriptural passages (*śruti*), so too in the case of "leaving behind" (*hāni*), there is a connection with "taking up" (*upāyana*).
For if one were not to accept the specific details established in one scriptural passage within another scriptural passage, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) in every instance;
and that is improper when a consistent interpretation is possible.

This has been stated in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇā*: "But rather, because it is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), there should be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the other; in the case of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*).
Alternatively, this very point should be considered by means of this Sūtra in relation to these very scriptural passages concerning "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*):
whether by this mention of "shaking off," the abandonment of good and evil deeds is expressed, or whether it signifies something else.

And in this regard, it should be understood as follows: "shaking" (vidhūnana) does not denote "destruction," because of the traditional rule that the root *dhū* with the suffix *adhañ* means "to shake" (*kampane*).
Furthermore, we observe the usage of the term in the expression "the tips of the banners are shaken" (*dodhūyante dhvajāgrāṇi*) when the banner-tips are being moved by the wind.
Therefore, "shaking off" (vidhūnana) is said to mean "moving.
However, having first established that moving consists in the temporary obstruction of the fruition of good and evil deeds for some time, one must reply as follows:
this term "shaking off" can properly apply only to abandonment.
Because the word "appropriation" (upāyana) is the remainder [of the syntactical context].
For it is not possible for others to appropriate good and evil deeds that belong to another and have not been relinquished.

Even though this appropriation by others of the good and evil deeds belonging to another is not directly conceivable, nevertheless, because of its connection with that [word], "shaking off" (vidhūnana) must be understood as "relinquishment" (hāna) itself, in accordance with its suitability.
It can be determined as follows:

since this "taking up" (upāyana) is heard in some instances in proximity to "shaking off" (vidhūnana), it—like the *kuśa* grass, meters, praise, and singing—requires the hearing of "shaking off" everywhere; thus, it becomes a universal cause for determination.
Moreover, a primary shaking away of good and evil deeds, like that of the tip of a banner, is not possible, because they are non-material (adravyatva).
And when a horse shakes its hair, it casts off dust along with it, and thereby sheds even its worn-out hairs—as in the text: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1).
And thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, because it is accepted that verbal roots have multiple meanings, there is no contradiction with traditional recollection (smṛti).
Thus, the phrase "it has been stated" has been explained.
But regarding the removal [of impurities], it has been said:
"Just as a horse becomes stainless by casting off old hairs mixed with dust, so too shall I,
having shaken off evil and being one who has perfected the self— that is, having purified the mind— become clear, like the moon released from the mouth of Rāhu."

In that same way, having shaken off and abandoned the body—being liberated from the identification with the body—he "comes toward" (abhi-sambhavāmi) the uncreated, immutable world whose essence is Brahman as his own inner self; this is the meaning.
Just as rivers, upon reaching the ocean, abandon their names and forms, so it is with the man of knowledge; such is the meaning.
The meaning is that, upon the death of that wise person, he abandons his inheritance— his wealth— as well as his good and evil deeds by means of that power of knowledge.

Acquisition (*upāyana*) is the taking [of something], because it is preceded by abandonment; since taking is impossible for two things that have not been abandoned, abandonment follows by implication.

However, where abandonment alone is explicitly stated in the scripture, a doubt arises as to whether the coexistence of abandonment and acquisition is necessary or not—this is what he expresses with the words "But where... (*yatra tu*).

In this context, the result is that the excellence of the praise is not established in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas it is established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Although in the *Tāṇḍya* and *Atharvaṇa* Śrutis—both of which concern knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇavidyā*)—only the "falling away" (*karmahāna*) is heard and not the "attainment" (*upāyana*), one might object that the attainment heard in the *Kauṣītaki* Śruti regarding the knowledge of the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahmavidyā*) situated on the couch should nevertheless be integrated here. Anticipating this objection:

He states that there is no synthesis [of attributes] due to the difference between the meditations (*vidyā*), saying "in another meditation" (*vidyāntara*). Furthermore, just as it was stated that there is no synthesis of mantras and ritual acts in the meditations because they are not mandatory, so too, since abandonment is possible even without the acquisition [of attributes], acquisition is not mandatory; thus, by way of analogy, it follows that there is no attainment [of those attributes].
He establishes the conclusion with the words beginning "But in the case of abandonment" (*hānau tu*).
The meaning of the Sūtra is that because the word "appropriation" (*upāyana*) is supplementary, it requires the word "abandonment" (*hāna*).
The underlying sense is that, by the analogy of horse's hair, since the merit and demerit shaken off require a location elsewhere, their appropriation by others must be stated.

He states—by the words "yaducyate" (as for what is said)—that the rule that qualities are not to be combined when there is a difference in the Vidyās pertains to the domain of ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), not the domain of praise (*stuti*).
This means that the author of the Sūtras holds this view.

Now, one might object: since praise is accomplished even by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the abandonment of what was previously heard, for what purpose is the explanatory passage concerning the "taking up" (*upāyana*) brought in?
Regarding this, he says: "for the sake of attaining the excellence of praise.
Now, one might object: "The connection of an *arthavāda* with an injunction (*vidhi*) is well-known, but not its connection with another *arthavāda*. To this he replies:
"And [this connection] is well-known," meaning from this world, the earth.
Since the *hemanta* and *śiśira* seasons are combined, there are five seasons.

Regarding the conceptualization of the sacrifice as having the form of a person, it is stated in the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* that "there are two *triṣṭubh* [verses] for the sake of [the sacrifice] possessing sense organs.

In this regard, the meaning is that since the *triṣṭubh* is merely a meter, when the question arises as to how it can be conceived of as a sense organ, the statement from the Yajurveda is brought forward as a corroboration.

[Objection: Since merit and demerit are formless, their material cause cannot exist; therefore, there can be no "ascent" (anupasaṃhāra). To this, he says: "And because it is for the purpose of praising knowledge. The meaning is that the word "they attain" (upayanti) expresses that others obtain the fruit of those two [merit and demerit] residing in the knower through the power of knowledge. [Objection: But how can the fruit of actions residing in one person be transferred elsewhere?
If it is argued that this is so by the force of the scriptural statement, we say no;
for there is no mention of them "attaining the fruit.
Nor should it be said that, as in the case of a śrāddha rite performed by a son which bears fruit for the ancestors, so it is here.

According to the maxim that "the fruit belongs to him for whose sake an action was performed," although an action performed with the intent of satisfying the ancestors has a fruit residing in a different locus (the ancestors), it is impossible for a wise person at the time of performing the rite to have a fruit in a different locus that was not intended. Furthermore, since the action ceases to exist upon the fall of the body of the wise person, the fruit would otherwise accrue to one who serves the wise person throughout their life or to one who hates them; therefore, he says: "one should not be overly attached."

The meaning is as follows: through service to or hatred of a wise person, merits and demerits equal to those residing in the wise person arise for the servant and the hater respectively; since the acceptance of these [merits and demerits] has already occurred by way of their fruit, there is no insistence on them being "received" (upāyana) [anew], as this would be easily established.
He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the "receiving" and so forth are merely figurative praise: "upāyana... and so on.

If the intention were to speak of the offering (*upāyana*), the author of the Sūtras would have mentioned only the offering in the concluding summary; therefore, by mentioning that [the Self] in the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he indicates praise—this is the meaning.
To the question, "What is the connection of an inquiry into praise within this chapter (*pāda*) which consists of an inquiry into knowledge (*vidyā*)?", he says: "Therefore.
He provides an illustration for the principle that a specific detail found in one Vedic branch (*śākhā*) should be adopted in another branch as well: "The *kuśa* grass," etc.
The *kuśās* are wooden sticks used by the *udgātṛ*s for counting the hymns (*stotra*).

"O *kuśās*, you are of the forest (*vānaspatyāḥ*); 'forest-lord' (*vanaspati*) refers to a great tree standing in the forest, and you originate from that. Being such as you are, protect me—i.e., guard me," this is the prayer of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

In this context, because of the feminine designation "tāḥ" (they) and because of the commentary stating "audumbaryaḥ" (the udumbara sticks), one should understand that the word *kuśa* has a feminine gender when referring to the splinters (*śalākā*), but it does not have a feminine gender when referring to *darbha* grass, according to the grammatical rule: "The word *kuśa* is not feminine. He explains the example from the Vedic meters with the words "yathā ca" (and just as).

The nine-syllabled meters are of the Asuras, while others are of the Devas; the meaning is that when there is a general possibility [of applying] any of these meters in the passage "they praise with the meters," a specific one is selected based on the statement of Paiṅgi.
He explains the praise by saying "just as":

in the Atirātra sacrifice, when the Chandogas and others have the expectation "When is the Stotra of the Ṣoḍaśin cup, which is an auxiliary of the Ṣoḍaśin draught?", the specific time is determined by the Ṛgvedic revelation (ārca-śruti): "The Stotra of the Ṣoḍaśin is when the sun has entered the time of rising."
This is the meaning.
Those who study the Ṛgveda are called *ārcikas*.
He analyzes the "singing along" (*upagāna*) with the words "just as... (*yathā*).

The meaning is that because of the general scriptural statement, "The officiating priests (ṛtvij) sing along," and because of another scriptural statement, "The Adhvaryu does not sing along," one concludes the specific point that the officiating priests other than the Adhvaryu are the ones who sing along.
[An objection is raised: Why is a syntactical unity with another specific scriptural statement accepted even for sentences such as those concerning the *kuśa* grass?
To this, he replies: "For that which is established by another scriptural statement... etc.

When there is a possibility of a single unified meaning consisting of a general rule and a specific exception, it is not proper to create a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and thereby assume an option (*vikalpa*)— such as that the Adhvaryu both sings along and does not sing along— based on the prohibition "the Adhvaryu [does not]" and the non-specific scriptural statement; the meaning is that an option is resorted to only as a last resort (*agatyā*), as in the case of *vrīhi* and *yava* grains.
The assumption of an alternative option is improper because it is vitiated by eight defects.

To explain: if one relies on the statement regarding rice (*vrīhi*), then there is the abandonment of the accepted authority of the statement regarding barley (*yava*), and the acceptance of its unaccepted lack of authority.

If one were to rely on the barley-injunction at some point, there would be four defects in that single barley-injunction: the abandonment of its established authority and the acceptance of its authority, as well as the acceptance of its lack of authority and the abandonment of that lack of authority.

Similarly, there are four defects in the rice-injunction as well. Thus, in order to avoid such faulty alternatives, Jaimini maintains that even two scriptural texts from different recensions (śākhās) form a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā); as it has been said: [tad uktam].

In the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard [in the scripture]: "One who is not initiated does not offer oblations," whereas elsewhere it is heard: "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives. In that case, if the sentence regarding the non-initiated were a prohibition of the oblation, then there would be an option: either the prohibition should be observed because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), or the oblation should be performed according to the injunction to perform it throughout one's life.
And that would be improper;

rather, since the sentence concerning the initiated (*nadīkṣita*) is supplementary to the sentence concerning "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), the negative particle (*na*) must serve to exclude other [acts], acting as an indicator of something other than the initiated,
and not as a prohibition of the *homa*.

Therefore, the meaning of the Siddhānta-sūtra of the *Nadīkṣitādhikaraṇa* is that there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) stating: "Therefore, one who is not initiated (*adīkṣita*) should offer oblations for as long as he lives.

Here, the venerable Bhagavatpāda recited the sūtra itself; however, the Miśras stated that the Siddhānta-sūtra of the *Paryudāsādhikaraṇa*, "But it should be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), because an option (*vikalpa*) is improper; it should be a part of the injunctions," was recited here by implication (*arthataḥ*).
That is to be considered:

for the meaning of the Sūtra is that it is heard [in scripture] that "the phrase *yeyajāmahe* should be employed in every sacrifice," and it is also heard that "one does not perform the *yeyajāmahe* in the *anuyāja*s."

In that case, even though the negative particle (*na*) functions as a prohibition, there would arise an option—namely, "it should be employed" versus "it should not be employed"—because there is no difference in their being sacrifices within the *anuyāja* offerings, just as there is regarding the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *atirātra* sacrifice.

Since such an option is improper, the sentence concerning the *anuyāja*s must be a part of the injunction for the *yeyajāmaha* formula itself; that is to say, through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it should be understood as a supplementary portion of the injunctive statement.
And thus, there is a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) to the effect that "the formula *yeyajāmahe* must be employed in sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*s.
He states another interpretation with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*).

In the previous [interpretation], it was stated that the gathering together of the *upāyana*s was established on the basis of taking the "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) as the abandonment of karma as a proven fact.
In this case, that very [meaning] is what is being established; thus there is a distinction.
Because the definition is the same in both instances, he raises a doubt with the words "What...?
For two results of shaking (vidhūnana) are observed in the case of horses' hair and the like: falling away from one's previous nature and transferring to another place.
In this regard, the meaning of the doubt is whether one should understand it as a "transference" (*saṃkrānti*) or a "diminution" (*rūpahāni*), or rather as a "falling away" (*cyuti*).
Among these, it is universally agreed that the primary meaning of the word *vidhūnana* is "shaking.
However, that [shaking] is not possible for merit and demerit, which are formless (*amūrta*).

Therefore, the "shaking" (*cālana*) of those two refers to their intrinsic nature—the capacity to yield fruit—and their displacement from that state through knowledge, which is a falling away (*cyuti*) due to obstruction; it does not mean "destruction" (*hāni*), because those two are formless and thus cannot migrate elsewhere, and because [knowledge] depends on something else.
This is the meaning of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "It is indeed destruction."
If mere falling away (*cyuti*) were the intended meaning, then the expression "they go toward" (*upayanti*) would be incoherent.

Nor should it be argued that where the word "going toward" (*upāyana*) is in proximity to the root *dhū* (to shake), there "falling away" (*hāni*) is indicated, whereas in other cases—such as with a learned man, a servant, or the like—the mere root *dhū* signifies the transfer of equal karma, and thus there is no impossibility [of the term being applied]. Why? Because:

The sense is that even for the root *dhū* (to shake off) alone, since its primary meaning is impossible [in this context], it is more appropriate for it to signify "loss" (*hāni*) through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as this is what presents itself to the mind. Having raised the objection that because "appropriation" (*upāyana*) is not the primary meaning, it cannot serve as the basis for the indication of "loss" anywhere, he refutes it with the words "Even though... and so on, showing that appropriation—consisting of the acceptance of merit and demerit by way of their results—is logically untenable without loss, and thus serves as the determinant for the indication of "loss."

Just as elsewhere the mention of *audumbara* wood and so forth serves to determine the use of *kuśa* grass and other materials, so too this "taking up" (*upāyana*) serves to determine that the "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) signifies abandonment; thus he says, "In some cases also.
Why is the shaking not said to be primary?
To this he replies, "And not..."

Nevertheless, raising the doubt as to how "abandonment" (hāna) is indicated [by implication], he says "and a horse" (*aśvaśca*), meaning that it is through the primary relationship (*mukhya-sambandha*).

Having stated the two bases for indication—namely, the impossibility (*anupapatti*) and the relationship (*sambandha*)—he points out the indicative word (*lakṣaka-pada*) with the words "like a horse" (*aśva iva*).

The meaning is that the word *vidhūya* (having shaken off), which in the example reaches the point of abandonment, indicates abandonment even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).

Alternatively, let it be that [the term *vidhūnana*] expresses only "abandoning" (*hāna*). Nor does this contradict the Dhātupāṭha’s entry "dhūñ, to shake," because that [meaning of shaking] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus he says, "aneka... (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.34). The meaning is that the Jaimini Sūtra, which was previously cited and explained, establishes that the "attainment" (*upāyana*) found in another recension serves to determine that "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) is indeed "abandoning. Thus, since it is established that "shaking off" means "abandoning," it is proven that the mention of "attainment" is to be combined with the mere act of "abandoning. //26//
