Because there is nothing further to be crossed in the hereafter, so it is with others;

for the Kauṣītakins record in the Paryaṅka-vidyā that for one who has set out toward Brahman seated on the couch by way of the path of the gods, there is a division of good and evil deeds midway along the journey: "Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni" (KauṣU 1.3).

Having begun thus, [the text] says: "He comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it by mind alone; there he shakes off his good and evil deeds" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.4). Now, a deliberation arises as to whether this statement regarding the separation from deeds is to be understood according to the literal text as occurring precisely on the path, or rather at the very beginning upon departing from the body. When the prima facie view suggests that one should accept it according to the literal text due to the authority of the scripture, [the author] recites the sūtra:
"At the time of departure."
He asserts that this abandonment of good and evil deeds occurs at the very moment of departing from the body for the sake of the hereafter;
and he states the reason: "because there is nothing left to be crossed.

For when the knower has passed away and is seeking to reach Brahman through knowledge, there is nothing whatsoever to be attained in the interval by means of good and evil deeds for which those two might be imagined to remain undestroyed for a few moments.

However, because they have results contrary to knowledge (*vidyā*), their destruction occurs through the power of that knowledge; and that destruction must take place precisely when the knowledge is about to manifest its fruit.
Therefore, although this destruction of good and evil deeds actually exists prior [to death], it is mentioned later [in the text].

For likewise, other schools—the Śikhins, the Tāṇḍins, and the Śāṭyāyanins—declare the casting off of good and evil deeds in the pre-mortem state itself: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1).
Thus [it is said]: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds. // 27 //
"In the next world" means in another state;
"on the way" means on the middle path.

Relying on the previously mentioned fact that "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) signifies abandonment (*hāna*), and considering the scriptural statement regarding the immediate sequence of abandonment following the crossing of a river—as well as the scriptural statement in passages such as "like the hairs of a horse" that [the shaking off] occurs prior to the casting off of the body—the author states the doubt with the words "Then what? (*tatkim iti*).

In the passage, "In the midst of the path to the world of Brahmā, he crosses a river named Virajā; by that, he shakes off his good and evil deeds," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the destruction of karma occurs at the halfway point. This is because the use of the pronoun *tat* (in the phrase *tena*) refers back to the immediately preceding act of crossing the river, thereby stating that the crossing itself is the cause of the abandonment of karma. However, in that prima facie view, it remains unestablished that knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of the destruction of karma.
Considering that this is established in the final doctrine (siddhānta), he establishes the conclusion: "In the state beyond" (sāṃparāya).

This means prior to death. The meaning is that destruction occurs at the very outset, because for one who has departed—that is, one who is dead—there is an absence of fruit while karma exists for some time, and because entry onto the path of the gods (devayāna) would otherwise be impossible.
He says "contrary to knowledge" because knowledge, which is the cause of exhaustion, does not exist in the middle of the path.
He says "therefore" to show that the reading immediately following the passage on crossing the river must be rejected, as it contradicts the meaning.
The meaning is that by the pronoun "that" (tat), the very knowledge under discussion is expressed. //27//
According to one's wish, because there is no contradiction with either [alternative]. (BBs 3.3.28)

Furthermore, if it were admitted that the destruction of good and evil deeds occurs halfway along the path of the gods for one who has departed from the body, then— once the body has fallen— that destruction of good and evil deeds caused by human effort (consisting of the practice of restraints, observances, and knowledge) would be impossible, because the performance of such effort according to one's will would no longer be possible; thus, the destruction of good and evil deeds resulting from that cause would indeed be unestablished.

Therefore, it should be understood that in the state of being a seeker (sādhaka), the performance [of rites] occurs first according to one's desire, and preceded by that is the casting off of good and evil deeds. In this way, the logical relationship between the cause and its effect is established, and the consistency with the *Tāṇḍi* and *Śāṭyāyani* Śrutis is maintained. // 28 //

Furthermore, since the practice of knowledge according to one's own will (*chanda*) is impossible for one who has died, the causal relationship between the two—namely, knowledge and the exhaustion of karma—which is heard in scripture, would be contradicted.

Moreover, according to the principle that "when the complete cause exists, there is no delay in the effect," you would incur a contradiction with scriptural texts such as the *Tāṇḍya*, whereas in our position there is no contradiction; thus he says, "according to one's will" (*chandataḥ*).

Therefore, since the abandonment of karma is the fruit of knowledge, it is established that the mention of the means of transition (*upāya*) in the case of mere abandonment is for the purpose of praising knowledge. //28//

The purposefulness of the departure is established in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
(BBŚ 3.3.29) In some places, the path of the gods is heard of in proximity to the casting off of merit and demerit, while in others it is not.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the path of the gods apply without distinction to all cases of casting off, or does it apply only in certain cases and not in others?

Just as it has been stated that the following along with the means of attainment occurs without distinction in the case of falling away, so too it might be argued that the following along the path of the gods (*devayāna*) should likewise occur. To this position, we reply: the purposefulness of the journey on the path of the gods must exist through a division into two ways—that is, the journey is purposeful in some cases and not in others, rather than being without distinction.
For otherwise, if this journey were accepted as occurring without any distinction, a contradiction would arise.

In this scriptural passage, "Having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, he attains the supreme state of equality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3), a movement leading to another location would be contradicted;
for how could one who is stainless be a traveler going to another place?
Furthermore, the supreme equality that is to be attained does not depend upon reaching another place; therefore, we consider that movement (gati) here is indeed purposeless. // 29 //

Regarding the purposefulness of the departure (*gati*): in some cases, such as in the knowledge with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*), the path (*mārga*) is heard of in scripture, whereas in the case of the knowledge without attributes (*nirguṇavidyā*), it is not heard of. Since the path is mentioned in proximity to the "leaving behind" (*hāna*) in that context, yet is not required [there], a doubt arises. With the connection provided by the analogy, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Just as...
The meaning is that, just like the "taking up" (*upāyana*), because the path is also heard of in some instances, it should be combined [and applied] everywhere.
In this context, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) holds that even those who know the attributeless Brahman require a path for the sake of liberation;
however, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is that no such requirement exists.

The established conclusion is that there can be no synthesis [of the paths], because it would contradict the scriptures supported by logic, which state that a path is required only for reaching an object obstructed by space and other factors.
Stainless and unattached, Brahman is equanimity. //29//
[The self] has been reborn, because there is perception of objects characterized by that [rebirth], as is seen in the world. (BS 3.3.30)
And this dual state—where in some cases the transition [to another realm] is purposeful and in others it is not—is established;

for the object characterized by that [transition] is perceived in the arts of magic (*paryaṅka-vidyā*) and in the meditations accompanied by qualities (*saguṇa-upāsana*). For the object that serves as the cause of transition is indeed perceived in those instances.

For where it is heard that there is the mounting of a celestial chariot (*paryaṅka*), conversation with that Brahman, the attainment of extraordinary fragrances and so forth— such manifold fruits dependent upon reaching another region—
in those cases, movement is purposeful;
for in the case of perfect realization (*samyagdarśana*), no such attainment of objects characterized by those [fruits] exists.

For those who have realized the oneness of the Self, whose desires are fulfilled, and for whom the seeds of all afflictions have been burnt away even here in this life, there remains nothing whatsoever to be expected other than the exhaustion of the residual karma that has already begun to bear fruit; therefore, the journey [to another world] is useless for them.

This distinction should be understood as being like the worldly usage: just as in the world a path leading to another country is required for reaching a village, but not for attaining health, so it is here as well.
Furthermore, we shall establish this distinction more precisely in the fourth chapter.

[Objection: "In that case, would not the path also be useless for the knowledge possessing qualities (saguṇavidyā)? To this he says: "It is appropriate. That which has that journey as its characteristic—that is, its cause—is "that which has that as its characteristic" (tallakṣaṇa). [Thus, the path serves as the means for attaining the fruit. //30//
Section 18: On Non-Restriction. Sūtra 31. *aniyamādhikaraṇam* (The section concerning non-restriction). Sūtra 31.
There is no restriction; there is no contradiction with all [the meditations] because of both scripture and inference.

(BBs 3.3.31) It has been stated that movement [to higher worlds] is purposeful in the case of meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vidyā*), but not in the case of the meditation on the supreme Self (*paramātma-vidyā*) which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
However, even among the meditations on the qualified Brahman, movement is heard of in some, such as in the Paryaṅka-vidyā, the Upakośala-vidyā, the Pañcāgni-vidyā, and the Dahara-vidyā.
It is not so in other cases, as in the case of the Madhu-vidyā, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Ṣoḍaśakala-vidyā, and the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is this path restricted only to those specific meditations in which it is heard, or is it connected without restriction to all such meditations of this kind?
What, then, is the initial position? That there is a restriction.
It must exist precisely where it is heard,
because the context is restrictive.

If a journey mentioned in one place were to apply to another meditation, the authority of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof would be undermined, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence that everything could serve every purpose.

Moreover, the single path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) is taught identically both in the Upakośala-vidyā and the Pañcāgni-vidyā; if it were intended for all [meditations], such a repeated mention would be purposeless.
Therefore, when the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is a restriction [to specific meditations], the author states: "There is no restriction.
This path known as the "way of the gods" (devayāna) ought to belong without distinction to all qualified meditations (saguṇa-vidyā) whose fruit is the attainment of exaltation (abhyudaya).
But surely, it was argued that if non-restriction is accepted, there is a contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*).
This contradiction does not exist; the meaning is that [the conclusion follows] from verbal testimony and inference, that is, from *śruti* and *smṛti*.
For instance, the *śruti* says: "Those who know thus... (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.1).

Thus, by introducing the path of the gods for those who possess the knowledge of the five fires, the text— through the passage, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1)— indicates that even those devoted to other forms of knowledge share the same path as the knowers of the five-fire doctrine.
But how is it understood that this destination belongs to those devoted to other forms of knowledge?
[Objection: But surely that [attainment] would belong only to those who are devoted to faith and austerity, since that much alone is heard [in the text].
[Reply: This is not a fault;
for this goal cannot be reached by faith and austerity alone without the power of knowledge (vidyā). By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where all desires have gone to rest.
For another Vedic text states: "Neither sacrificial gifts go there, nor do the ignorant ascetics.
Therefore, in this context, faith and austerity serve as indicators for other forms of knowledge.

However, the Vājasaneyins study this in the section on the knowledge of the five fires: "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, meditate upon truth with faith" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15).
In this context, it should be explained that those who possess even a "morsel of faith" (śraddhālavo) are those who worship Brahman as Truth (satyam),
because the word *satya* has been used repeatedly for Brahman.

Furthermore, since those who know the Pañcāgni-vidyā have already been included by virtue of their specific knowledge, it is logical that this inclusion refers specifically to those devoted to other forms of knowledge.
Furthermore, the Śruti passage, "But those who do not know these two paths become the crawling insects, namely, the biting ones" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.16),
which indicates a miserable downward destiny for those who have strayed from the two paths, includes them within the very scope of the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna paths.
Even so, due to their specific knowledge, they attain the Devayāna path.
Smṛti also states: "These two paths of the world, white and black, are considered eternal;
by one a man goes to non-return, by the other he returns again" (Bhagavad Gītā 8.26).
As for the twofold mention of the path of the gods in both the Upakośala-vidyā and the Pañcāgni-vidyā, that is for the purpose of meditation in both cases.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule. [Note:
They meditate upon Brahman characterized by faith and austerity.
*Daṇḍaśūka* means a snake.]
There is no fixed rule regarding all [meditations].

Here too, the subject matter is precisely the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*). Since there is doubt—arising from the context of specific meditations (*vidyā*) on one hand and the scriptural statement of non-distinction on the other—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "What, then, [is the case]?

Just as there is a settled distinction between the existence and non-existence of the path in meditations with attributes (*saguṇa-vidyā*) and those without attributes (*nirguṇa-vidyā*), it follows by way of this analogy that there is likewise a settled distinction even among the meditations with attributes. In response to this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) sets aside that restriction; thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the path.
The fruit [of the teaching] applies to both cases.
Having stated the context regarding the restriction (*niyama*), he states the reason for the repetition by means of the word "apica" (moreover).
The meaning is that if the mode of progression already stated in one place were to apply elsewhere as well, the repetition would be redundant.
He establishes the conclusion with the words "of all.
"Exaltation" refers to the world of Brahman.
He states that "this is not so," meaning that there is no fault in the sublation of the context by means of scriptural statements and other evidence that lack specific qualification.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: among those qualified for this path, those who know the five fires in this manner, and those who, in the forest, "worship with faith and austerity"—that is, they meditate upon Brahman characterized by faith and austerity—they "attain the light.

Now, one might object: "Since only faith and austerity are mentioned in the scripture, would it not follow that only those two lead to the journey via the light and so forth, and not those whose practice consists of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā and other such meditations? To this, he raises the doubt: "But how [is this so]? He resolves it: "This is no fault," because the departure of the ignorant is prohibited; therefore, by the words "faith" and "austerity," what is indicated is the knowledge of Brahman which is accomplished through them.
That is the station of the Brahma-world;
"gone beyond" means turned away,
insofar as the defects of desire and anger do not exist there.
The meaning is that those who perform mere ritual acts—even if they are ascetics—do not go [to the world of Brahmā] if they are ignorant.

To state a sentence free from the fault of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), he says: "But the Vājasaneyins... Furthermore, since scripture declares a downward path for those who have fallen away from both paths characterized by knowledge and action, he states that those who meditate on Vaiśvānara and others attain the path beginning with light (arcirādi): "Now, as for those two... and so forth.

The *daṇḍaśūka* is a snake. Furthermore, since the Smṛti—after stating without distinction that those who have attained [the Lord] proceed by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*) according to the passage, "Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice; departing there, the people who know Brahman go to Brahman"—concludes its teaching, it says "Smṛti" to indicate that they attain that [Brahman].
The bright path consists of the route beginning with light (arcis) and so forth; the dark path consists of the route beginning with smoke (dhūma) and so forth;
for the world that is subject to knowledge and action.
Regarding the two paths considered eternal and constant:
by one of them, the white path, one goes to Brahman from which there is no return; by the other, having gone to heaven, one returns again—this is the meaning.
He refutes the fault of tautology with the words "as for what was repeated."

In each of those cases, there is the daily hearing of the path for the purpose of reflecting upon the path, since it is understood through the context that meditative reflection on the path is an auxiliary limb of knowledge (*vidyā*).
And so the author of the Sūtras will state: "And because of the application of recollecting the course of rebirth remaining after that."
The meaning is that this repetition is for the purpose of making it known that those who have not heard of the path obtain the path through the power of knowledge even without meditating on the path.
Therefore, it is established that in all meditations (*upāsanā*) that differ from the symbol (*pratīka*), there is the attainment of the worlds beginning with light (*arcis*). //31//
The section concerning [the soul's state] as long as its office lasts. Sūtra 32.
"The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their office.
(BBs 3.3.32) It is now considered whether another body arises for the knower after the fall of the present body or not;
that is to say, upon the completion of the means of knowledge (*vidyā*), does the attainment of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) occur or not?
This reflection is not appropriate;
for it is not possible to reflect whether or not rice becomes cooked upon reaching the cooking vessel,
nor is it reflected upon whether or not one who is eating will be satiated.
However, this reflection arises even for some knowers of Brahman, because the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* show the production of another body;
for instance, they record that the ancient seer Apāntaratamas, a teacher of the Vedas, was born as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana at the junction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages by the command of Viṣṇu.
And Vasiṣṭha, though a mind-born son of Brahmā, having lost his former body due to the curse of Nimi, was born again from Mitra and Varuṇa by the direction of Brahmā.
It is heard in scripture that even Bhṛgu and the others, who were the mind-born sons of Brahmā, were born again at the sacrifice of Varuṇa.
Sanatkumāra also, though a mind-born son of Brahmā himself, manifested as Skanda through the granting of a boon to Rudra.
In this very manner, the repeated production of new bodies for Dakṣa, Nārada, and others is recounted in the Smṛti due to various causes.
This is also frequently observed in the *mantras* and *arthavādas* of the Śruti.

Among them, some assume another body after the previous one has fallen away, while others, by means of the power of yoga (*yogaiśvarya*), assume multiple bodies even while that [original] body remains, according to the principle of [simultaneous] assumption of many bodies.
And all of these are recorded in the Smṛti as having fully mastered the meaning of the entire Veda.
Since the arising of new bodies is observed for these [sages], it follows that the knowledge of Brahman might have the status of being either an occasional cause of liberation or not a cause at all.
To this, the following answer is given: No;

for in the case of those such as Apāntaratamas and others, their state remains dependent upon their office, as they have been appointed to offices such as the promulgation of the Vedas, which serve as causes for the maintenance of the world.

Just as that Blessed Sun, having performed his office for the world until the end of a thousand ages, experiences at its conclusion the absolute liberation (kaivalya) free from rising and setting—according to the Vedic scripture: "Then, having risen above that, he neither rises nor sets; he stands alone in the midst"—(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.1).

Just as the knowers of Brahman existing in the present world experience absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) upon the exhaustion of the fruits of their commenced karma—as stated in the Śruti: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall attain [Brahman]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2)—so too Āpāntaratamas and other such lords, having been appointed by the Supreme Lord to various offices, remain in those positions until the end of their term, even though they possess perfect realization which is the cause of liberation, because their karma has not yet been exhausted.
And at the conclusion of that [period], they are released; this is not contradictory.

For, while carrying forward the accumulation of karma (*karmāśaya*) that was set in motion once for the sake of yielding its fruit, they move from one body to another—just as from one house to another—independently, with their memory unimpaired, until the completion of their specific office.
Because they have mastery over the body, the senses, and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), they create bodies and preside over them either simultaneously or successively.
Yet these are not called "rememberers of former births" (*jātismara*), precisely because of the traditional usage of the term "these very ones" (*ata evaite*) in reference to memory.

For instance, it is recorded in tradition that the female proponent of Brahman named Sulabhā, desiring to debate with Janaka, cast off her own body, entered Janaka’s body, defeated him, and subsequently re-entered her own body.

For if, once the [present] karma has been exhausted and set in motion, another karma that causes the commencement of another body were to manifest, then other karmas whose seeds have not yet been burnt would likewise necessarily follow; consequently, one might suspect that the knowledge of Brahman is either a cause of liberation only occasionally or not a cause at all.
However, such a suspicion is not reasonable.
This is because the burning away of the seeds of karma through knowledge is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.
Thus says the Śruti: "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder, and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
And there are such passages as: "Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the complete liberation from all knots" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
Furthermore, the Smṛti also says: "As a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna..."
"The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.37),
and "Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again,
so the self is not joined again with afflictions once they have been burnt by knowledge"— such passages as these [establish this].

Furthermore, when the afflictions such as ignorance have been incinerated, it is not possible for there to be both the partial burning and the partial sprouting of the seed of the afflictions, which is the latent disposition (*karmāśaya*).

Indeed, one does not observe the partial sprouting of a rice seed that has been scorched by fire. However, the latent disposition of karma whose fruit has already begun to manifest ceases through the exhaustion of its momentum, like a released arrow.
Because of the statement, "For him, there is delay only so long [as he is not released]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2), which establishes that the duration ends with the falling away of the body;
therefore, it is logical that those who hold office remain in their positions for as long as their office lasts.
Nor is the fruit of knowledge uncertain;

for thus the Śruti shows that liberation results from knowledge for all without distinction: "Among the gods, whoever awakened to That, he indeed became That; likewise among the seers, and likewise among men" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
Furthermore, it is logical that the great sages might have been attached to other forms of knowledge whose fruits are powers such as sovereignty;

later, becoming disillusioned upon seeing the decay of those powers, they became firmly established in the knowledge of the Supreme Self and attained liberation (*kaivalya*). As it is said: "When the time of universal dissolution arrives, all of them, together with Brahmā..."
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "Those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of their lives.
Furthermore, because knowledge has a perceptible result, any suspicion regarding the absence of its fruit is untenable;
for regarding the fruit of ritual action, such as heaven, which is not yet ascended by direct experience, there might indeed be a doubt as to whether it exists or not.

But the fruit of knowledge is established in direct experience, according to the Śruti: "That Brahman which is immediate and direct" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1), and because of the instruction [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad] "That thou art" (6.8.7) as something already accomplished.
Indeed, the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" cannot be transformed into "You will become That after you have died";

for the text, "Seeing this very [Self], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and the Sun'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), shows that the fruit of universal selfhood is attained at the very time of perfect realization.
Therefore, for the wise one, the attainment of absolute liberation is certain. (32) [FN:
Having risen upwards, being of a distinct nature and in the form of Brahman, by that Janaka...]
Having cast aside and settled their dispute,
they became disillusioned and detached;
this is the withdrawal from idle chatter.
The established rule is that for the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-vidyā*), the journey [to the world of Brahmā] is purposeless because its fruit is liberation;
whereas for all the knowledges of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vidyā*), it is purposeful because its fruit is the world of Brahmā, lasting as long as one's office endures.
That [view] is not tenable;

for there is a connection [to the present discussion] by way of the objection that since even those who possess knowledge of reality (tattvajñānin) are seen to undergo rebirth in works such as the Itihāsas, knowledge does not have liberation as its fruit.
The observation of rebirth among those possessing knowledge is shown in the Bhāṣya to be a seed of doubt.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the scriptural texts concerning liberation through knowledge are merely praises of knowledge—and thus knowledge lacks liberation as its fruit—there is no distinction from [other meditations] that have the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) as their fruit; consequently, the result is the inclusion of the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*).
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the distinction is that the aforementioned systematic arrangement is established. This is also the case in the Śruti.
In the mantra "medhātither meṣa," the birth of Indra as a ram is perceived;
the meaning is that the *arthavāda* of the *Bahvṛca* [Ṛgveda] has the sense that Vasiṣṭha was born as the son of Urvaśī. The term "occasional" (*pākṣika*) is used in a superficial sense.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [knowledge] is indeed not a cause [of liberation]. He establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that knowledge is not non-causal for liberation—with the words "But those...
(*te ca*). In the established order of the world, "authority" (*adhikāra*) refers to ownership.
As long as there exists the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) that brings about that [liberation], for that duration those who hold office remain in the state of *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living);
upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha*, due to the absence of obstacles, there is *videhakaivalya* (bodiless liberation). Regarding this, he states the authoritative proof: "Now" (*atha*).
"Now" means immediately after the exhaustion of *prārabdha*.
Thereafter, being of a different nature, solitary, and of the very essence of Brahman, it rises—meaning it emerges and abandons the body;
it remains alone, without a second, in the intermediate state, abiding in its own indifferent (udāsīna) essential nature. This is the meaning.

Now, one might ask: "If even the wise possess another birth, how can there be liberation? To this he says: "Having once set forth... If the wise were subject to another birth dependent on karma other than that which has already begun (*prārabdha*), then there would be no liberation through knowledge;
but this is not the case.

However, they exhaust the *prārabdha* karma—which has arisen once but yields fruit over many births—and even while taking birth, they do not grieve due to the power of the yoga of knowledge; the meaning is that they are liberated upon the completion of the *prārabdha*.
The reason for the persistence of unimpaired memory in the case of the next birth of the knowers is its dependence on the *prārabdha* karma caused by their previous birth.
For there is a pervasion (vyāpti) such that whoever possesses another birth dependent on other karma while being endowed with the recollection of past lives is one whose memory has been lost; thus,
since the pervader is absent among the possessors of knowledge (jñānin), the absence of the qualified pervaded is established.

Now, one might object that their state of having unimpaired memory is otherwise established by the fact that they remember their past births (*jātismaratva*). To this, he says: "And these [are] not... The meaning is as follows: since they lack the qualifying attribute of remembering past births, the absence of the qualified entity (the state of unimpaired memory) is established simply through the absence of the qualifier.
Those who remember their past births are characterized by a lack of recognition of their previous bodies, being dependent on others and possessed of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*).
However, there is a distinction: those who hold office retain their former names, whereas these [liberated souls] are independent and free from egoism.
Thus, the meaning is that they have "disputed" (vyudya)—that is, engaged in debate—with Janaka.
For the wise man, there is no bondage because there is no karma remaining beyond what has already begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha*).

He establishes the point that the scriptural statements regarding liberation through knowledge—which are supported by the maxim "in the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect"—are not merely figurative praise, by means of the passage beginning with "yadi hyupayukte" (if indeed [the fuel] has been consumed).
He also provides a logical argument for the meaning stated in the Śruti and Smṛti, beginning with "na cāvidyā" (and ignorance is not...).

[An objection is raised: "If the destruction of karma, which is its effect, occurs because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are burnt away by knowledge (*vidyā*), then how can there be the continued existence of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma?"
Regarding this, he says: "of that whose fruit has already begun" (*pravṛttaphalasya*).

The sense is that, because scripture declares that for the knower [liberation] lasts until the fall of the body, and because of actual experience, it is established that knowledge—which removes certain portions of the ignorance that veils [the Self]—lacks the capacity to remove those portions of ignorance that are conducive to the persistence of the distractions of *prārabdha* karma; therefore, the exhaustion of *prārabdha* occurs through experience alone.

Anticipating the question of how those who possess knowledge can hold office, he says "And in other cases of knowledge," [meaning] that it is due to the power of worship and so forth performed prior to the attainment of knowledge.
"Pratisaṃcara" refers to the great dissolution (mahāpralaya),
and "of the other" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha.
The meaning is that at the conclusion of their qualification (*adhikāra*), those who have directly realized the Self are liberated.

Anticipating the doubt that even the fruit of becoming Brahman might be something yet to be produced (*bhāvya*), he states the contradiction with the scriptural text "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) by saying "Not so" (*na hi*).
Therefore, it is established that in the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa-vidyā*), there is no inclusion of a path (*mārga*). //32//
Topic 20:
The Section on the Twenty-Syllable [Mantra] Sūtra 33: "On account of the difference in number. (BS 3.3.33)

"But there is an inclusion of those [meditations] whose objects are syllables, on account of the commonality and the presence of that [object]; as in the case of the *aupasada* [offerings], so it has been stated.

(BS 3.3.33). In the *Vājasaneyaka*, it is heard: "This, O Gārgī, is indeed that syllable which the Brāhmaṇas declare to be neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8.8), and so forth.
Likewise, in the *Atharvaṇa*, it is heard: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that imperishable syllable is apprehended."
"That which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without color" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5), and so forth;
likewise, in other places as well, the supreme Brahman is heard of as the Imperishable (akṣara) by means of the negation of specific attributes.
And therein, in certain instances, some additional specific attributes are presented.

Regarding these cognitions of specific negations, when a doubt arises as to whether they apply everywhere or are restricted to specific contexts, it is stated that— given that a restriction might otherwise result from the division of the scriptural texts— all cognitions of specific negations concerning the Imperishable (akṣara) must be included everywhere,
on account of both their commonality and the presence of that [Imperishable] itself; for the form consisting in the rejection of specific attributes is the same everywhere.
This is the method for establishing Brahman;
and that very Brahman, which is to be established everywhere, is recognized as non-different [from itself].
In that case, why should cognitions produced in one place not apply to another?
And so it has been explained in the [Brahma-sūtra] passage, "Bliss and the rest belong to the Principal" (3.3.11).
The distinction here is that while in that [passage] the qualifying attributes were considered in their affirmative form, here they are considered in their negative form.
This distinction in reflection is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). The illustration is "like the *aupasada* [sacrifice].

Just as when the *puroḍāśa*-offerings are enjoined at the *upasads* in the *Jāmadagnya-ahīna* sacrifice, the mantras for offering the *puroḍāśa*—such as "O Agni, protect the sacrifice," "protect the rite," and so forth—which originate in the *Udgātṛ-veda*, are nevertheless connected with the *Adhvaryu* priests.
It occurs because the offering of that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) has the Adhvaryu as its agent, and because the subordinate elements (aṅga) depend upon the primary element (pradhāna).
Likewise here too, since the qualifiers depend upon the syllable (akṣara), the meaning is that they are connected everywhere with the syllable, regardless of where they may have originally arisen.

This has been stated in the first book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "In the case of a conflict between the subordinate and the principal, because the purpose belongs to that [principal], the Vedic connection is with the principal" (Jai. Sū. 3.3.8). // 33 //
Regarding the phrase "of those whose intellects are fixed on the syllable" (*akṣaradhiyām*):
here, the subject matter consists of the negative words that establish the Brahman as the Imperishable (*akṣara*).

Among these, a doubt is raised—expressed by the words "tāsām" (of them)—based on whether or not it is possible for all the negations heard in each respective passage to negate the entirety of duality.

Just as in the case of knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā), there is no synthesis because the path is not required, so too, since the prohibitions heard in one's own scripture can— by way of being indicative marks (upalakṣaṇa)— subsume the negation of all duality, the words of prohibition found in other recensions (śākhā) are not required; thus, by means of this analogy, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is established, wherein the result is simplicity (lāghava).
In the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, the result is the absence of these two defects.
To explain: if the negation of what is not heard is indicated by the words that are heard, then there is the defect of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*);

if it is not so indicated, then because the negation of all duality would remain unestablished, there would be the defect of the absence of the realization of the non-differentiated (*nirviśeṣa*). This is the distinction.

The construction of the sūtra is as follows: "akṣaradharmīṇi" means in the substrate that is the Imperishable; "akṣaradhiyaḥ" refers to the cognitions that negate duality; "taddhetavaḥ śabdāḥ" means that the words are the causes of those cognitions; "tāsām avarodhaḥ" means their inclusion or synthesis.

If it is argued that because the subordinate element, Brahman, exists in all Vedic branches and because the knowledge of Him is uniform, there should be a synthesis of the remaining [attributes], then—since the same logic applies—the problem of redundancy remains. To this, he says: "for the sake of detailed exposition."
Thus:

[one might raise] the objection regarding the scope [of the attributes], namely, that while there may be a synthesis of qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) because they constitute the essential nature [of Brahman], there can be no synthesis of negations because they are non-self (*anātman*) and infinite;

however, even though they are non-self, since their purpose is the realization of the undifferentiated Brahman, their inclusion is established by virtue of being negations of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its products.

The meaning is that it is logical to consider the subsumption (upasaṃhāra) of words expressing prohibitions— established by their state of being independent, neither gross nor subtle, and residing in sentences— into syntactic unity with other scriptural passages containing prohibitions.
He explains the illustrative example for the connection of supplements (śeṣa) heard elsewhere with a primary element (śeṣin) situated elsewhere, beginning with "yathā" (just as).

Having begun with the statement, "Jamadagni, desiring prosperity, performed the sacrifice with the four-night rite," the *Jāmadagnya*—the *ahīna* (non-soma) four-night sacrifice performed by Jamadagni—is established. Regarding that sacrifice, it is ordained in the *Taittirīyaka* that "the *upasads* consist of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*)," meaning there are offerings to be accomplished by means of sacrificial cakes.

Since these are to be performed by the *adhvaryu*, and because the mantras originating from the Sāmaveda are to be employed therein [by him], the point is that their performance is by the *adhvaryu* alone, not by the *udgātṛ*.
The meaning of the mantra for addressing Agni is that the *hotr* function and the ritual act (*adhvara*) belong to Agni through you alone.

The originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is subordinate because it depends on a result; the applicatory injunction (*viniyogavidhi*), however, is primary for what has already originated, as it possesses a fruit.
Likewise, since the mantras originate in the *Udgātṛ-veda*, their performance is by the *Udgātṛ*.

The meaning of Jaimini’s sūtra is as follows: "In the case of a conflict between a subordinate and a primary element regarding application (*viniyoga*), the primary—being more powerful—determines the application; thus, the *mantra*-constituted Veda is to be employed by the *adhvaryu* priest, because the origin [of the mantra] is for the purpose of application. Although, according to the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, because the *vāravantīya* and other *sāmans* originate in the *Sāmaveda* which is characterized by the loud (*uccaiḥ*) accent, they are to be recited loudly as subsidiaries to the fire-installation (*ādhāna*).

Regarding the application of accents, in the passage "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya, sings the Yajñāyajñīya, or sings the Vāmadevya," their application is governed by the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) belonging to the Yajurveda; thus, the *upāṃśu* (whispered) accent of the Yajurvedic [mantras] is employed.

When there is a conflict between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and the primary factor (*mukhya*), because the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) exists for the sake of the application, the Sāmans are connected with the accent of the Yajurveda by virtue of the strength of that primary application.

Thus the Sūtra has been explained; nevertheless, because the logic is the same, the mantras of the Aupasadahomas are cited as being within the scope of the Sūtra, and thus there is no contradiction. //33//
END BsCom_3,3.20.33 START BsCom_3,3.21.34 21.
This much is the section. Sūtra 34.
Because of this constant teaching: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree;
one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
Thus, in the section concerning the internal self, the followers of the Atharva-veda and the Śvetāśvataras recite [this mantra].

Likewise, the Kaṭhas read: "Drinking the Truth (ṛta) in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest supreme realm, those who know Brahman call them Shadow and Light—the knowers of the five fires and those who have thrice performed the Nāciketa rite" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.1).
In this matter, there arises the doubt: is there unity of the knowledge (vidyā), or is there plurality of the knowledges?
What, then, is the prima facie view?
That there is plurality of the knowledges.
Why?
Because a distinction is observed;
for in the verse "Two birds," the state of being an enjoyer is seen to belong to one of them.
Furthermore, in one case [the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*], the state of being a non-enjoyer is observed;

however, in the passage "The two who drink the Truth" (*Ṛtaṃ pibantau*), the state of being enjoyers is observed for both. Thus, when it is argued that the difference in the form of the object of knowledge (*vedyarūpa*) should differentiate the two meditations (*vidyā*), the author replies: "There is oneness of meditation. Why? Because in both these mantras, they teach an identical form of the object of knowledge, characterized by the number two and limited to this specific extent.
Is it not the case that a difference in form has been shown?
No, it is said;
both of these mantras establish the Lord with the individual soul as His companion, and there is no other meaning.

In the verse "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), the Supreme Self, who transcends hunger and other such states, is established by the words "the other looks on without eating" (*anaśnan anyo abhicākaśīti*).

Furthermore, in the remainder of that passage, it is seen that He alone is the subject to be established: "When he sees the other, the Lord, as the beloved one, and His greatness... (*juṣṭaṃ yadā paśyatyanyamīśamasya mahimānam*, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.7).

In the verse "The two drinking the *ṛta*," however, while the individual soul (*jīva*) is actually drinking, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), though transcending hunger and thirst, is metaphorically said to drink by virtue of association, according to the maxim of the "umbrella-bearer.
For this is a context concerning the Supreme Self, as indicated by the opening statement: "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.14).
And in this case as well, the remainder of the passage has that very same subject matter: "The bridge for those who sacrifice, the imperishable Brahman which is supreme" (KaU 3.2).
This has also been elaborated upon in the sūtra: "For the two selves have entered the cave" (BSū 1.2.11).
Therefore, there is no difference in the object of knowledge (*vedya*), and consequently, there is oneness of knowledge (*vidyaikatva*).

Furthermore, upon examining the preceding and succeeding passages in all three of these Vedānta texts, it is understood that it is indeed the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātmavidyā*) that is being conveyed; the mention of the individual soul (*jīva*) is intended solely to express its identity [with the Supreme Self], not to suggest any other meaning.
Moreover, it has already been stated that in the knowledge of the Supreme Self, there is no room for an investigation into difference or non-difference.
Therefore, this yoga is for the purpose of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) alone;
and from that, there is the addition of further qualities. // 34 //

Because of this repeated instruction, and because there is a difference in the manner of presentation in both mantras despite the appearance that the object of knowledge is one and the same, he states the doubt: "What is it here?
In the passage concerning the drinking of the *ṛta*, qualities are heard [stated] such as, "The Imperishable is the Brahman which is supreme."

In the case of the *Suparṇa* passage, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that attributes such as "not eating" and so forth are not to be combined with one another; however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because the meaning of the sentences regarding the nature of Brahman is one, there is a combination.
Let it be granted, then, that there is a combination of the cognitions of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) due to the unity of the object of knowledge.
But here, because of the difference in the objects to be known (*vedya*), there is no synthesis; this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of a counter-example.
If it is objected that "this has already been refuted in the section concerning qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*)," we reply: true.

However, in order to maintain the primary sense of the word "drinking," the two who drink— the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*)— must be understood as the substrates of the act of drinking, both by their own nature and through metaphorical attribution. As for the "two birds" (*suparṇau*), since there is no sublation of the recognition of two identical entities characterized by an innate duality— due to the commonality of the dual number in both mantras— and because this is supported by the context and other factors, [the passage] refers back to the individual soul (*jīva*) to describe the non-transmigrating Brahman.
The intention is that this aphorism is for the purpose of explaining the purport of the two mantras. //34//
END BsCom_3,3.21.34 START BsCom_3,3.22.35 22.
The Section on the Immediate [Succession] (Anantarādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 35–36.

The Vājasaneyins record [this] twice in immediate succession in response to the questions of Uṣasta and Kahola: "That Brahman which is direct and immediate, that Self which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1–3.5.1), just as [one speaks of] the multitude of beings being within oneself.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is there identity of the knowledge (vidya), or is there a plurality of knowledges? For the moment, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is a plurality of knowledges, on account of the force of repetition.
Otherwise, if the meaning were neither deficient nor redundant, the double recitation would indeed be purposeless.

Therefore, just as the repetition [of a ritual act] implies a difference in the ritual (*karmabheda*), so too the repetition [of the teaching] implies a difference in the knowledge (*vidyābheda*). To this position, the author replies: "On account of the lack of distinction in the intermediate recitation, there is oneness of the knowledge regarding one’s own Self. For one’s own Self, which is the innermost of all, is without distinction in both places; it is questioned and answered in both instances.
For two selves cannot both exist as the innermost of all within a single body;
for in that case, the status of being the innermost of all could only be attributed to one [of them].
But for the other, there would be no status as the innermost of all, just like [the individual] members of the aggregate of elements.

The meaning is that just as in the body, which is a collection of the five elements, although there is a relative "interiority" such that water is interior to earth and fire is interior to water, yet this does not constitute the primary state of being the interior of all; so it is here as well.
Alternatively, the phrase "like the group of elements" points to another scriptural passage as an illustration:
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
6.11) Thus, in this mantra, the one and only Self that is within all is taught as being inside all the collections of beings;
the meaning is that it is likewise so in these two Brāhmaṇa passages.
Therefore, because the object of knowledge is one, the knowledge is one. // 35 //
Just as in the case of the multitude of living beings within,
objects such as a jar are immediate through being objects of consciousness, whereas Brahman is immediate by virtue of not being an object at all.
The ablative case is used in the sense of the nominative.
Here, in the Śruti, the attribute of the Self— immediacy— is predicated of Brahman,
and the attribute of Brahman— being the innermost of all— is predicated of the Self.
Therefore, it should be understood that their identity has been firmly established;

thus, in response to Uṣasta’s question, "Explain that to me," Yājñavalkya set forth the witness of seeing and so forth as the impeller of the vital breaths and other functions. Likewise, in response to Kahola’s question, "Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all," he set forth the one who transcends hunger and the rest.

In that regard, although there was a doubt concerning both Brāhmaṇas because of the question, the repetition, and the recognition of the innermost Self, let it be granted that the knowledge is one in those two cases due to the identity of the object to be known;
however, here, even though the object to be known is identical in the two Brāhmaṇas, the knowledge is distinct because of the repetition,
just as the *prayāja* offerings are distinct due to the repetition of the act of sacrificing— this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by way of a counter-example.

In this regard, the distinction is that there is no mutual application of attributes (*dharmopasaṃhāra*) [in the case of the two Upaniṣadic passages], whereas in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) there is such an application.
First of all, it is established that the two Brahman passages have a single referent, because it is impossible for both to be the innermost of all.
And thus, since the object of knowledge is one, there is no dispute regarding the unity of the Nirguṇa-vidyā. //35//
If it be argued that otherwise the distinction [between the two states] would be untenable, we say no; for it is like other [various kinds of] instructions. (BBs 3.3.36)
Now, as for what was stated—that if a difference in knowledge is not admitted, the difference in scriptural transmission (āmnāna) would be untenable—that must be refuted.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault, because it is as tenable as other instances of instruction.

Just as in the sixth chapter of the *Tāṇḍinām Upaniṣad*, despite the instruction being given nine times in the passage, "That is the Self; thou art That, Śvetaketu" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7), there is no difference in the knowledge [conveyed], so it will be here as well.
How is it that even with an instruction given nine times, there is no difference in the knowledge?
Because the identity of the subject matter is understood from both the introduction and the conclusion;

and because, in the passage "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4), there is the presentation of the very same single subject as that which is to be explained again and again.
Furthermore, since repeated instruction is justified by the removal of various doubts,

so too here, because there is no difference in the form of the question and because there is no distinction in the conclusion with the words "other than this is perishable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2–3.5.1), it is evident that the introduction and the conclusion both have a single subject matter.

By employing the particle *eva* in the second question— "That which is Brahman, directly and not indirectly" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1)— the text shows that the very same subject matter contained in the preceding question is being carried over into the subsequent one.
And in the preceding Brāhmaṇa, the existence of the Self as distinct from the body and the organs was stated.
In the subsequent [passage], however, the very same [Self] is described as transcending the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as hunger and so forth.
Thus, the identity of meaning is established;
therefore, knowledge is one. // 36 //

If it is objected that otherwise the unity of knowledge would be undermined by the impossibility of repetition (*abhyāsa*), it is replied: that repetition alone differentiates ritual actions which is purposeless; however, in this case, since the repetition serves the purpose of stating specific qualities—namely, the transcendence of hunger and so forth—of the very Self described in the *Uṣasta-Brāhmaṇa*, the repetition is established for another reason and does not differentiate the knowledge. This is the collective meaning. //36//

There is an exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [the two] as in other cases.
Likewise, with reference to the person in the sun, the followers of the Aitareya recension record: "He who is I, he is that; he who is that, he is I.
Similarly, the Jābālas record: "Verily, O Venerable One, I am you, O Divinity; indeed, you are I."
In this regard, there is a doubt: whether here, through the exchange [of attributes], the meditation is to be performed in both forms, or in only one form.
For now, he says it is in only one form;
for here, apart from the oneness of the self with the Lord, there is nothing else to be meditated upon.

If such a distinction were to be conceived as follows—that the transmigrating being possesses the nature of the Lord, while the Lord possesses the nature of the transmigrating being—then in the case of the transmigrating being having the nature of the Lord, there would be an elevation; but if the Lord had the nature of the transmigrating being, how could there be any degradation?
Therefore, the form of the cognition must be one and the same.
"But the traditional teaching of the exchange [of attributes] is for the purpose of strengthening the realization of oneness.
This being the position reached, he replies: "This exchange is taught for the sake of meditative reflection (*ādhyāna*), just like the others.
Just as other qualities, such as being the self of all and so forth, are taught for the sake of meditative reflection, so it is with this.
For indeed, the reciters distinguish [the two] by uttering both: "Thou art I" and "I am thou.
And that becomes meaningful when a cognition of a dual form is to be produced;
otherwise, this specific recitation of both would be purposeless.
Because it is established by one [text] alone.
Now, it was argued that if a specific meaning is postulated for the mention of both [texts], it would follow that the deity suffers degradation by becoming identical with a transmigrating soul;
however, this is not a fault.
Because it is precisely the single self (aikātmya) that is being contemplated in this manner. [Objection:
But if that is the case, would it not result in the very same reinforcement of the notion of oneness? [Reply:
We do not deny the reinforcement of oneness.
What then? We establish only this much: that here, by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, a cognition of two forms must be formed through mutual exchange, and not a single form;
yet as a result, even oneness becomes firmly established.
Just as when qualities such as "having true desires" are taught for the purpose of meditation, the Lord is nevertheless established as possessing those very qualities, so it is here.
Therefore, this reciprocal exchange (*vyatihāra*) must be meditated upon, and it should be integrated when the subject matter is the same. (37) [FN:
*Vyatihāra* is the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).]

The mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is an exchange; for this is what is heard in scripture, and because of the maxim that "the vision of the superior applied to the inferior becomes fruitful," when a doubt arises, one must indeed effect the attribution of lordship to the individual soul, according to the stated principle.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that the scriptural mention of the exchange (*vyatihāra*) is established as being otherwise explained—as a mere repetition for the purpose of strengthening that very [notion of identity], just like other repetitions.
The distinction here is that in the prima facie view, the result is simplicity (*lāghava*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the result is the meaningfulness of the scripture.
The meaning is that since the cognition of oneness is accomplished by the single utterance "I am thou," the statement "thou art I" would be redundant.
He recalls the previously stated objection with the words "nanu" (but surely).
Reasoning has scope only regarding a matter that is doubtful;
here, however, there is mutual identity because it is so stated in scripture.

He offers a rebuttal, stating "This is not a fault," on the grounds that even if the nature of being the individual self (*jīvātmatva*) is superimposed upon Brahman for the sake of meditation— just as its being composed of mind (*manomayatva*) and so forth is— the consequence of any degradation [of Brahman] does not arise. He then raises an objection, saying "But if this is so," suggesting that by discarding the degradation in Brahman and meditating on identity with the individual self, one arrives at exactly what he himself has stated.

"But the twofold nature of the mother has not been mentioned by you; we state that this sentence is primarily concerned with meditation, while oneness is established because it does not contradict other means of knowledge. To this he replies: "Not we... He says: "Therefore... [37], meaning that this exchange (vyatihāra) is to be combined in the meditations involving the assumption of the self (ahaṅgrahopāstis).
