For that very [Brahman] is indeed [the subject of] the "Satya" and other [vidyās].

In the Vājasaneyaka, after prescribing the knowledge of Satya and the meditation on its names and syllables through the passage beginning, "He who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.4.1), the following is subsequently recorded: "That which is Satya is... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2).
"That Āditya who is this person in this orb, and he who is this person in the right eye" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2), and so forth.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: "Are these two instances of the knowledge of Truth (satyavidyā), or is it only one?
For the moment, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they are two.
For there is a connection with the fruit through distinction, as stated earlier: "He conquers these worlds" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.4.12),
and "He slays evil and leaves it behind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3, 4).
This will be explained further below.
As for the reference back to the subject matter [of the previous section], it is because the object of worship is one and the same.
This being the case, we reply: this is indeed one single "knowledge of Truth" (satyavidyā).
Why? Because of the reference back to the subject matter in the passage, "That which is that Truth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2).
But was it not argued that even when there is a difference in knowledge, a reference back to the subject matter is justified because the object of meditation is one and the same?
This is not so.
However, where a distinction between knowledges (*vidyā*) is understood from a clearly evident other cause, there this [distinction] would indeed apply.

But here, since such a possibility does not exist, because of the attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) of the subject matter under discussion by the words "That which is the Truth" (*tadyattatsatyam*), the very same Truth connected with the preceding knowledge is attracted into what follows; thus, there is the certainty that it is a single knowledge.

As for the argument that because a different fruit is heard mentioned, it must be a different knowledge (*vidyā*), we reply: this hearing of a different fruit is merely a commendation (*stāvaka*) of the instruction regarding another auxiliary (*aṅga*), namely, "His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is *aharaham*"; thus there is no fault.

Moreover, since a fruit must be inferred from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) alone, when the unity of the knowledge is established, even many fruits heard in relation to the parts must be subsumed within the knowledge as a whole.

Therefore, this very same single knowledge of Truth (satyavidyā) is taught with various specific attributes; consequently, all the qualities beginning with "Truth" must be combined within a single performance [of meditation].

However, some [commentators] maintain that in this sūtra, this passage from the Vājasaneyaka—which concerns the Person within the eye and the sun—and the Chāndogya passage—"Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun" (Chānd. 1.6.6)—[refer to the same thing].

Having cited the passage, "Now, this person who is seen in the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1), some maintain that because this very same knowledge concerning the person in the eye and the person in the sun is one and the same in both places, the qualities such as truthfulness and so forth must be combined by the Chāndogyas from the Vājasaneyins.
This, however, does not appear correct.

For in the Chāndogya, this knowledge based on the udgītha is understood to be connected with the jyotiṣṭoma ritual; for there, at the beginning, middle, and end, there are signs of connection with the ritual, such as at the commencement: "This [earth] is indeed the ṛc, fire is the sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1).

In the middle [of the section], it says: "The *ṛk* and the *sāman* are its two shoulders; therefore, it is the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8); and in the conclusion: "He who, knowing thus, sings the *sāman*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.9).
In the Vājasaneyaka, however, there is no such mark connected with the ritual action.

Since there is a difference in the introductory passages (*prakrama*), resulting in a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*), it is logical that the attributes (*guṇa*) should remain distinct. (38) [FN:
*Geṣṇau* means "two singers."]
Therefore, because it is the essence (*geṣṇa*) of the Ṛg and Sāman,
it is indeed that which consists of *satya* and so forth.

Whosoever among those qualified for spiritual practice meditates upon this Brahman called Hiraṇyagarbha— which is the Great Pervasive One, the worshipful one, the first-born among elemental beings, and which is "truth" (*sattya*) because it is both *sat* (being) and *tyat* (that)— for him...
The meaning is that the conquest of the world is the fruit. Regarding the name "Satyam," which consists of three syllables— *sa*, *ti*, and *yam*—
the first and the last syllables are "truth" (*satyam*).

The middle syllable is false, yet because it is enclosed on both sides by truth, it becomes essentially true; thus, the meditation on the syllables of the name is stated as a subsidiary part of the knowledge of Truth (Satyavidyā). That which was previously introduced under the name of the "Heart" and now possesses the qualities such as being the Yakṣa and so forth—that very Person in the solar orb and in the eye—yields the fruit of the destruction of evil through the knowledge of His two names, "Ahaḥ" and "Aham. This is the meaning.

Regarding this, he states the doubt— using the word "therein" (tatra)— because a difference in results is heard between the preceding and following sentences, and because there is a reference back to the subject matter under discussion.

The result is that, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the qualities are to be performed according to their specific distribution, whereas according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), there is a single unified performance.

Just as a twofold understanding was stated regarding the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) due to differences in scriptural passages concerning their mutual identity, so too here, due to differences in the scriptural statements regarding the fruits [of the teachings], there is a difference in the meditations (vidyā); thus he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of this analogy with the words "two.
It is improper to draw [the conclusion] based solely on the attraction of the qualified object, Brahman alone.

By employing the pronouns "that" and "this," the Brahman characterized by the previously mentioned qualities is drawn forward for the purpose of prescribing its attributes, such as having the sun and the eye as its locus;
thus, he establishes the final conclusion that the unity of the knowledge is proven from the sentence itself by stating, "It is one alone.
He says, "Not so," to show that this case is not like the mere recognition of the identity of Brahman found in the Dahara and Śāṇḍilya meditations.
"Other causes" refers to differences in context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth.

Thus, even when there is a difference in the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*), this knowledge of the identity of the object of worship may occur; however, since both possibilities exist here, and when a doubt arises as to whether the meditative knowledge is one or many, the literal meaning is that because of the knowledge of the identity of the form of the object of worship—as in "the Truth" (*satyam*)—there is a determination of the oneness of the meditative knowledge.

Furthermore, in the absence of a cause for sublation, the general rule (*utsarga*) that the meditative knowledge is one due to the identity of form is established, and the sublation of this rule does not occur merely because of a difference in results.

He states that because the mention of a fruit in relation to an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is based on mere scriptural statement, no distinct fruit is established for it—beginning with the words "But as for...

Furthermore, where a fruit such as "desiring this" is heard in the primary injunction itself, there the expectation of a fruit for the auxiliaries is satisfied by the fruit of the primary alone; thus, the mention of a fruit in relation to the auxiliary is merely for the sake of praise (*stuti*).

In this case, however, we have stated that the mention of the fruit for the subordinate members (aṅga), such as name and form, is merely a eulogy (stuti), because it occurs within the injunction for the primary knowledge (*pradhāna-vidhi*)— namely, "One should know that the first-born is truly Brahman"— and because its fruit is the conquest of the worlds. But in reality,

since even in the primary injunction there is no word expressing a specific desire (*evam-kāma*), and a fruit must therefore be inferred according to the principle of the *Rātri-satra*, any fruit whatsoever that is heard— whether in the primary rite or in its subordinate parts— being equally "heard" (scriptural), should be understood according to the principle of the fruit of the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice.
He states that the distinction regarding the result being a single primary fruit obtained through accumulation is unestablished with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
He applies the Sūtra with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Having set forth the interpretation of a certain partial school (*ekadeśin*), he refutes it with the words beginning "Some people" (*kecit*).

Regarding the view that the golden person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*) is to be meditated upon within the *udgītha*—which is an auxiliary part of ritual action—in the *Chāndogya*, he states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) therein: "In that context, the *ṛc* and *sāman* are seen as the two feet, having the nature of earth and fire; therefore, because they have the *ṛc* and *sāman* as their feet..."
The meaning of the scripture is that a priest who knows "the Puruṣa is the Udgītha" is capable of the successful attainment of the fruits of the ritual action.
However, the knowledge of Truth (satyavidyā) does not depend on being a subsidiary part of a ritual; thus he says, "not so.
The meaning is that because the independent Hiraṇyagarbha-vidyā is distinct from the knowledge of the ritual subsidiaries (aṅgavidyā), there is no combination of their attributes. //38//
Section 25: The Topic Concerning the Authority of Desire and Other Factors. Sūtra 39.
[The attributes such as] desire and so forth [belong] elsewhere, and not to those bases and so on.

Now, having introduced the subject with the words, "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1), the Chāndogyas study the passage beginning: "This is the Self, free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5).

Likewise, the Vājasaneyins [state]: "This indeed is that great unborn Self, who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths; he rests in that space which is within the heart; he is the ruler of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

Regarding this, when a doubt arises as to whether there is identity of knowledge and a mutual connection of qualities [in these two passages], or not—the conclusion being that there is identity of knowledge—it is said in response:
"Because of desire and so forth."
The meaning is "Satyakāma" (one whose desires are true). Just as Devadatta is called Datta and Satyabhāmā is called Bhāmā;

so too, that collection of qualities such as having true desires which is found in the Chāndogya with respect to the space within the heart is found elsewhere in the Vājasaneyaka as mastery and so forth, and that [mastery] is also found elsewhere in the Chāndogya in the passage: "This Self is free from evil... (Eṣa ātmāpahatapāpmā).
This is connected here [in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5].
Why? Because of the commonality of the abode and so forth.

For indeed, much that is common is seen here as well: the heart is the same expanse in both cases, the Lord to be known is the same, and His nature as a bridge with the purpose of preventing the confusion of worlds is the same; thus, many such similarities are observed.

But surely some differences are also observed: in the Chāndogya, there is an association of qualities with the space within the heart, whereas in the Vājasaneyaka, these belong to Brahman who has space as His support? No.

Since it was established in the *Chāndogya* under the sūtra "The small one [is Brahman], on account of the subsequent [arguments]" (*bra.sū.* 1.3.14) that even there the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) refers to Brahman alone,
this is the distinction found here.
For the knowledge of Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahmavidyā*) is taught in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "Now, those who depart from here having understood the Self and these true desires... (Chā.
8.1.6), because the desires, like the Self, are heard to be objects of knowledge.
In the *Vājasaneyaka*, however, only the supreme Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa*) is seen being taught: "Speak further for the sake of liberation" (Bṛ. 4.3.14).
For this is established by the harmony of questions and answers beginning with, "For this person is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15);
whereas the collection of qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth is mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka solely for the purpose of praising that [state].
And likewise, later on, [the text] concludes that Brahman is indeed devoid of qualities with the passage beginning, "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).

It should be understood, however, that this compendium of qualities is formulated in the Sūtra for the purpose of demonstrating the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the qualified Brahman due to its unity, and not for the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*). // 39 //

Regarding the question of whether the qualities such as "having true desires" and "mastery," which are heard in the texts concerning knowledge with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*) and knowledge without attributes (*nirguṇavidyā*), should be combined with one another or not—
given the doubt arising from the presence or absence of a fruit for such combination— the qualities would be intermingled because of the oneness of the knowledge (*vidyā*).

Even here, since there is a distinction between the two knowledges (*vidyā*) based on the difference between their qualified (*saguṇa*) and unqualified (*nirguṇa*) forms, and because there is no fruit for the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) in the unqualified knowledge, it follows—having reached this preliminary conclusion—that there is no such combination. To this, the author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) with the words "In that regard, this... and so forth. [Objection: Since the difference between the knowledges is thus manifest, how can there be a combination of qualities?
Regarding this, he says: "But [the qualities] of those possessing qualities.

Even though the qualities belong to different instances of ignorance (*avidyā*), their combination for the sake of praise is appropriate when they reside in the intellect (*buddhi*) within a locus devoid of qualities (*nirguṇasthala*), due to the equality of their substrates (*āyatana*) and so forth;
for there is a desire for the excellence of the praise of knowledge (*jñāna*).

Because it is appropriate to perform praise by means of qualities perceived anywhere [in the scriptures]. Although the qualities residing in the Nirguṇa are indeed included within those such as Satyakāma who reside in the Saguṇa, nevertheless, the statement regarding their inclusion (upasaṃhāra) is not redundant; for by dispelling the doubt that qualities heard in one place might be meditated upon elsewhere merely as a means of praising the Nirguṇa, it serves to strengthen the fact of their inclusion. Thus, there is no fault. //39//

Section 26: The Topic of Reverence (Ādara-adhikaraṇa) Sūtras 40–41 [The Sūtra: "Because of reverence [for the teacher], there is no contradiction. (Sūtra 40) [Commentary: Since reverence for the teacher is enjoined as a duty, there is no contradiction in the fact that the teacher is not to be saluted by one who has already performed the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Furthermore, because reverence is required, it is understood that the teacher must be honored even by one who has completed his studies. Therefore, the scriptural injunction regarding the teacher’s honor is not contradicted. [The Sūtra: "And because of the Smṛti. (Sūtra 41) [Commentary: Moreover, this is established by the *Smṛti* texts, which state: "One should always show respect to the teacher, even if he is younger than oneself. Thus, the conclusion is that the teacher must be honored at all times. END BsCom_3,3.26.41 START BsCom_3,3.27.42 27 Samāvartanādhikaraṇam / sū. 42–43 Section 27: The Topic of the Return Home (Samāvartana-adhikaraṇa) Sūtras 42–43 [The Sūtra: "But the return home is for the sake of the purpose [of study]. (Sūtra 42) [Commentary: Regarding the ritual of returning home (*samāvartana*) after completing the Vedic studies, some hold the view that it is merely a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the student. However, the correct view is that it is performed for the sake of the specific purpose of concluding the study. This is because the scripture prescribes it immediately following the completion of the study. [The Sūtra: "And because of the Smṛti. (Sūtra 43) [Commentary: Furthermore, this is supported by the *Smṛti*: "Having completed the Veda, having bathed, and having become a householder... Since the Smṛti explicitly links the "bath" (*snāna*) with the completion of the Veda and the commencement of the life of a householder, it follows that the return home is intended for the purpose of entering the next stage of life. Therefore, it is not a mere purificatory rite. END BsCom_3,3.27.43 START BsCom_3,3.28.44 28 Gṛhasthāśramādhikaraṇam / sū. 44–50 Section 28: The Topic of the Householder Stage (Gṛhasthāśrama-adhikaraṇa) Sūtras 44–50 [The Sūtra: "But the householder stage is prescribed for all, because of the scriptural statement. (Sūtra 44) [Commentary: It is argued that the stage of the householder (*gṛhastha-āśrama*) is mandatory for everyone. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "A Brahmin should desire to dwell in his own house until old age. Since this text prescribes the householder's life as a duty for all, it is concluded that the other stages of life are not independently mandatory. [The Sūtra: "And because of the Smṛti. (Sūtra 45) [Commentary: Furthermore, the *Smṛti* states: "All these stages of life are ordained for the Brahmin; however, the householder is the source of them all. This confirms that the householder's life is the foundation for all others. [The Sūtra: "And because of the absence of scriptural injunction for others. (Sūtra 46) [Commentary: Moreover, there is no independent scriptural injunction for the other stages of life apart from the householder's life. Therefore, the householder's life alone is the primary duty. [The Sūtra: "But [the others] are also prescribed, on account of the Smṛti and the practice of those who know the Veda. (Sūtra 47) [Commentary: However, the other stages of life are also indeed prescribed. This is known from the *Smṛti* texts and from the conduct of those who are learned in the Vedas (*śiṣṭa*). For instance, the *Smṛti* says: "Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, let him bathe," which refers to the stage of the religious student (*brahmacarya*). And: "Having offered sacrifices according to his ability, let him enter the forest," which refers to the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Furthermore, the practice of the wise supports this. [The Sūtra: "And because of the connection with the purpose. (Sūtra 48) [Commentary: Moreover, the various stages of life are connected to their respective purposes. For example, the stage of the student is for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, while the stage of the householder is for the purpose of performing sacrifices. Since each serves its own end, they are all equally valid. [The Sūtra: "And because of the non-perception [of a specific result for others]. (Sūtra 49) [Commentary: Furthermore, we do not perceive any specific superior result for the other stages of life that would exclude the householder's life. Therefore, all stages are equally enjoined. [The Sūtra: "And because of the Smṛti regarding the alternative. (Sūtra 50) [Commentary: Finally, the *Smṛti* mentions an alternative: "Or, having lived the life of a student for the full term, let him become a householder; or, having lived the life of a student for the full term, let him enter the forest; or, having lived the life of a student for the full term, let him renounce the world. Since this presents options, it is clear that all stages are equally prescribed. Thus, the householder's life is not the sole mandatory stage for everyone. (Sūtra 54) [Commentary: Regarding the sin of failing to perform the daily fire-sacrifice
There is no omission [of the offering] due to reverence.

In the Chāndogya, concerning the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, it is heard: "Therefore, whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice; whatever first oblation he may offer, let him offer it with the words, 'To Prāṇa, svāhā! (Chā. 5.19.1), and so forth.

In that context, five oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) are prescribed; and regarding them, the term *agnihotra* is employed further on in the passage: "He who, knowing this thus, offers the *agnihotra*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.2), as well as: "Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.4).
And likewise: "In this way, all beings perform the Agnihotra" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.5).
Regarding this, the following is considered: upon the omission of eating, is there an omission of the Prāṇāgnihotra, or is there no omission?

In this regard, because of the scriptural mention of its connection with the arrival of food, and because the arrival of food is for the purpose of eating, [the opponent argues that] upon the omission of eating, there is an omission of the Prāṇāgnihotra.
This being the case, he says that [the suffix] should not be elided;
why?
Because of respect.

For instance, in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā itself, the Jābāla Śruti states: "One should eat before the guests; for that would be as if one were to offer the Agnihotra for another without having offered it oneself. By thus censuring the priority of the guests' meal and establishing the master's meal as first, this passage shows its regard for the Prāṇāgnihotra.

For it is thought that while one [the *vaiśvadeva* offering] cannot tolerate the omission of its first performance, the other [the *agnihotra*] certainly can tolerate the omission of the *agnihotra* which possesses that priority.
But surely, because of the connection with the arrival of the rice-gruel intended for eating, its omission when eating is omitted is well known? No;
for that is for the purpose of prescribing a specific substance.

Since in the ordinary Agnihotra the substances such as milk and so forth are fixed, here too, by the word "Agnihotra," there is an extension of those properties—just as in the case of the Kauṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice. Thus, this sentence, "That which is rice-gruel," is intended for the purpose of enjoining a specific quality, namely the single substance of rice-gruel. Therefore, it follows that when a subordinate element is omitted, the primary act remains. This is the prima facie position.
Even in the absence of food, the Prāṇāgnihotra is to be performed by means of water or any other non-conflicting substance, according to the principle of substitution. // 40 //
"There is no omission [of the rite] due to respect.
Here, the author states the doubt by means of the words "yat" (which) and "agnihotra": "In this regard, the following is investigated.

The connection with the chapter (*pāda*) is established because the investigation of the Prāṇāgnihotra—which is a subsidiary part of the knowledge (*vidyā*)—is to be performed as a duty prior to the feeding of guests by one who meditates on Vaiśvānara.

The distinction is this: in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), even when the meal is omitted, the Prāṇāgnihotra is to be performed with another substance; whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta), it is omitted.

Now, an objection is raised: by the word "whatever" (*yat*) in the phrase "whatever food" (*yad-bhaktam*), the food implied by the act of eating is restated, and then by the injunction of connection with the oblation in the phrase "that which is to be offered" (*yad-dhomīyam*), if the implied eating is omitted, then the oblation dependent upon that implied food must also be omitted.

Thus the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) raises an objection with the words "tadyat" (Now, as for that...). He refutes this by means of an illustrative example in the sūtra of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), beginning with "evam prāpte" (this being the case), arguing that just as there is no lapse in the stability of qualities intended for praise even when the meditation on the qualityless (nirguṇa) is omitted, so too there is no lapse in the Prāṇāgnihotra out of respect, even when the actual eating is omitted, for the sake of accomplishing the praise.

"Thus that" means that, having not performed the Prāṇāgnihotra oneself, one performs it for the guests. Having recalled what was stated, he provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "But surely" (nanu).

Just as in the case of the Māsāgnihotra occurring within the Kuṇḍapāyinām Satra, because of the word "Agnihotra"—which denotes the obligatory Agnihotra in a figurative sense—the duties of the obligatory Agnihotra [are extended].

Just as there is the acquisition of milk and other substances [in the Agnihotra], so too here, in the case of the breath-oblations (*prāṇāhuti*), although milk and other substances are acquired by default due to the application of the term "Agnihotra," an exception is made by the rule prescribing food (*bhakta*) for the purpose of eating.
Therefore, since the rule regarding food serves as an exception, even when eating is omitted and the subordinate quality known as "food" is lost, there is no loss of the primary Agnihotra itself.

The meaning is that [the conclusion] is reached because its accomplishment is possible through milk and so forth, which are obtained by the general rule (*utsarga*) in the absence of an exception (*apavāda*).
"When a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, the primary element (*mukhya*) is not [omitted]" is a sūtra of Jaimini.
In the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), there are the *pavamāneṣṭi* offerings; therein it is said: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Agni Pavamāna."

The meaning is as follows: "offering" (nirvāpa) is heard [in scripture] as a subordinate part [of the ritual], such that it is established in the primary rite known as the New and Full Moon sacrifices by the rule, "one should offer the oblations in the *agnihotrahavaṇī* [ladle].

This [use of the ladle] is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the *agnihotrahavaṇī* prescribed in that context. Since there is no *agnihotra* at the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), the secondary [ladle] is indeed omitted;
however, even with its omission, there is no omission of the primary act of offering itself.

Since rites such as those that have been commenced must necessarily be performed, when the prescribed substance is unavailable, the rite must be carried out even with a substitute substance; this is the principle of substitution (pratinidhi-nyāya). //40//
To this, he recites the following:
Because of the scriptural statement regarding what is available.
When food is present, the *prāṇāgnihotra* must be performed from that very substance of food which first comes to hand. Why? Because of the scriptural statement to that effect.

Because of that statement; for it says, "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.19.1). By referring to the arrival of food as an established fact, this text enjoins that the oblations to the vital breaths are to be accomplished by means of a substance intended for another's use.
Since these [acts] have acquired the characteristic of being non-obligatory, how could they—when the food is omitted—cause another substance to be substituted?
Furthermore, there is no extension here of the properties (*dharma*) belonging to the archetypal *agnihotra*.

For in the case of the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*, where it is enjoined that "one performs the monthly *agnihotra*," the word *agnihotra* occurring within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) would cause the status of being like that [archetype] to be known; thus, the extension of its properties is logical. But this is not the case here.
Furthermore, in this case, the word *agnihotra*, being used figuratively, cannot enjoin the state of being that [original rite];
and if the transfer of its properties were admitted, then even the extraction of the fires (*agnyuddharaṇa*) and other such details would have to be performed,
which is impossible.
The extraction of the fire is for the purpose of providing a locus for the oblation;
furthermore, this is not an oblation into the [ordinary] fire, because that would entail a contradiction with its being for the purpose of eating.
Moreover, because it is connected with substances brought forward for the sake of eating, this is indeed an oblation belonging to that very act of eating.
And thus the Jābāla Śruti, stating "one should eat before the guests," shows that this very body is the substratum for the performance of the oblation.

For this very reason, it also shows here that the parts of the Agnihotra are merely metaphorical: "The chest is the altar, the hair the sacrificial grass, the heart the Gārhapatya fire, the mind the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and the mouth the Āhavanīya fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2).
In this context, the mention of the *vedi* (altar) should be understood as an indication for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) alone,
because there is no altar in the primary Agnihotra,
and because it is here intended to accomplish its constituent parts.
Furthermore, because the time for eating is fixed, there can be no conflict with the time for the Agnihotra sacrifice.
In this same way, other duties such as the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) and so forth may also be somewhat incompatible.
Therefore, these five oblations (*homāḥ*), through their connection with specific mantras, substances, and deities, must be performed only during the meal.
As for the statement regarding respect and the manner of looking, that is intended to prescribe priority in the case of eating;
for there is no such thing as an excessive burden for a scriptural injunction.
However, by this [statement], its obligatory nature cannot be demonstrated.
Therefore, the Prāṇāgnihotra occurs only when there is an omission of food. // 41 //
He establishes the conclusion: "Because that [word] is used when it is present" (Upasthite tadvacanāt).

The meaning is that the injunction for the oblation (*homa*) is based on the rice-grains (*bhakta*) already prepared for the purpose of eating, as indicated by the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "that belongs to the oblation" (*taddhomīyam*). The "arrival of the rice-grains as something already established" refers to the bringing in of the rice-grains under discussion.
The meaning is: by means of the reference to that [original substance] through that word.
When the substratum of the oblations prescribed as dependent [on a specific substance] is lost, there is simply a cessation [of the rite], and no implication of another substance;

just as, for example, when the sacrifice is omitted, the *godohana* vessel—which is dependent on the *praṇayana* rite performed for the sake of the sacrifice—is also omitted, and it does not necessitate another substratum. He states the resulting conclusion: "Those [oblations]"—referring to what was said regarding the attainment of another substance from the word *agnihotra*.
Regarding this, he says: "And not here.

The meaning is that the state of being like that—the similarity to the obligatory *agnihotra*—is appropriate for the word situated in the *arthavāda* because it serves as a praise (*stuti*). He states the fault in [the view that it] brings about the dharma: "And if there were the attainment of those properties," and so forth.

The phrase "ava eva" means precisely because there is an absence of the attainment of those properties; the sense is that if [those properties] were already attained, their ritual accomplishment would be redundant. If the primary auxiliary elements (aṅgas) of the Agnihotra are being accomplished, how can the altar (vedī), which is not an auxiliary of it, be accomplished here? To this, he says: "And because of the scriptural mention of the altar."
Since there is no application of even the two times—morning and evening—for the primary Agnihotra, just as there is no extraction of the fire [in that case], [the author says] "by means of eating.
He states "thus" because rites such as the standing worship (*upasthāna*) and the strewing around (*paristaraṇa*) do not apply due to the absence of the sacred fire.

Therefore, the conclusion is that the oblation (*homa*) is performed with the very substance used for eating, precisely because there is an absence of the application of those [primary] ritual properties.

The mantras beginning with "prāṇāya svāhā" [are intended here]. Now, an objection is raised: since the rule that the master’s meal occurs at a later time is prescribed by direct Vedic statement (śruti) and other authorities, how can it be set aside by the statement "one should eat before the guests"? To this he replies: "For there is not...
The meaning is that the injunction regarding the later timing applies specifically to a master who is other than a seeker of liberation (upāsaka).
"But not" means "not merely by way of priority.

Since the respect shown toward one who eats first by a practitioner of the *prāṇa* meditation can be accounted for otherwise (as being due to mere priority), he states the established conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). //41//
Section 27: The Topic on Determination of That [The Self] (Sūtra 42) 27.
The Topic on Determination of That (tannirdhāraṇādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 42.
There is no fixed rule regarding the determination of that [result], because it is seen [in scripture]; for the fruit is independent [of the ritual action], being distinct from it.
There are cognitions based upon the constituent parts of ritual actions, such as: "One should meditate on this syllable *oṃ* as the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), and so forth.

We shall now investigate whether these [subsidiary acts] are indeed permanent, like the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood in sacrificial rites, or whether they are non-permanent, like the *godohana* vessel and similar items.
What, then, is the prima facie position? They are permanent. Why? Because they are encompassed by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).

For even though these [meditations] are taught as unattached to any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), they are nonetheless connected to the sacrifice by way of the *udgītha* and other such elements; thus, they are touched upon by the very injunction for the performance of the sacrifice, just like other subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).

As for the mention of fruits in their own respective passages—such as "he indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7)—that is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) because it takes the form of a statement of present fact, like the hearing of blameless verses, and does not constitute the actual bestowal of a fruit.

Therefore, just as in the case of such statements as, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report," which—though not read within a specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇapaṭhita*)—are nevertheless obligatory because they enter into the sacrifice by means of the *juhū* and other implements, so too it must be with the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth.
This being the position reached, we reply: "The rule regarding that determination."

These determinations regarding the true nature of the qualities of ritual acts, such as the *udgītha*—namely, that it is the "most savory," its attainment, its prosperity, the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), the sun, and so forth—are not to be restricted as permanent requirements for the rituals.
Why? Because of the observation of that [in the scripture].
For the Śruti shows the non-restriction of things of this kind: "Therefore both perform it—the one who knows this thus, and the one who does not know" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).
This is because action is permitted even for one who lacks knowledge;

for we observe that the *prastotṛ* and other priests, though devoid of knowledge regarding the deities associated with the *prastāva* and so forth, nevertheless persist in their determination to officiate, as in: "O *prastotṛ*, if you shall chant the *prastāva* without knowing the deity that is inherent in the *prastāva*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.9).
"If you chant the udgītha not knowing that" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.10),
and "If you respond with the pratihāra not knowing that" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.11).
Moreover, the fruit of such knowledge, which relies upon ritual action, is perceived as being distinct from the ritual action itself.

The obstruction to the accomplishment of the fruit of action is its non-fulfillment; its fulfillment is a certain specific excellence. As it is said: "Both perform [the rite], he who knows this thus and he who does not know it.
But knowledge and ignorance are different; whatever one performs with knowledge, faith, and the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).

In this regard, because of the separate treatment of the practices of the learned and the unlearned through the phrase "there is a difference," and because of the use of the comparative suffix *tarap* in the expression "more powerful" (*vīryavattaram*), it is understood that even ritual action devoid of knowledge is powerful.
And this is possible only if knowledge is impermanent;
for if it were permanent, how could it be admitted that action devoid of it could be powerful?
For it is an established principle that an action must involve the employment of all its constituent parts to be considered "possessing vigor" (*vīryavat*).

Likewise, in the case of the *loka-sāman* and other such meditations, specific fruits are taught for each individual meditation, as in: "The worlds, both ascending and descending, are fit for him" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 2.2.3), and so forth.
It is not reasonable to understand this hearing of the fruit as being merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*);
for in that case, it would result in a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*).
However, when there is an instruction regarding the fruit, the occurrence of a primary (literal) statement is justified.

In the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, however, because the sacrifice—which stands in need of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—is already under discussion (*prakṛta*), it is appropriate that the mention of a fruit be an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), since [the *prayājas*] serve that purpose.
The same applies to qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood, which are taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*).
For qualities like being made of *parṇa*-wood, which are not themselves actions, a connection with a fruit is not possible without a substratum.
For in the case of the *godohana* vessel and the like, a prescription of a result is appropriate because they obtain a basis in the primary *praṇayana* (water-carrying) rite and so forth.
Likewise, for the *bailva* wood and the like, a prescription of a result is appropriate because they obtain a basis in the primary *yūpa* (sacrificial post) and so forth.
However, in the case of being made of *parṇa* wood and the like, no such basis exists within the context of the primary sacrifice.

However, if one intended to specify that the juhū and other implements are the substrata by means of the sentence itself, while also intending to enjoin them with respect to a fruit, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).

But since meditations (upāsanās) are of the nature of action, it is possible to enjoin them as qualified [by their substrata]; therefore, there is no contradiction in enjoining those meditations based on the udgītha and so forth with respect to a fruit.

Consequently, it should be understood that just as the godohana vessel and others—though based on a sacrifice—are non-permanent because they are connected to a specific fruit, so too are the meditations on the udgītha and so forth.
For this very reason, the authors of the Kalpasūtras did not prescribe such meditations within the sacrificial rites.
That is the determination.
He states a doubt—asking "what are those?"—because examples are seen in both ways:

just as the quality of being made of parṇa-wood, though not mentioned in connection with a specific rite, is invariably employed in rituals as an auxiliary part of the sacrifice by way of the *juhū* ladle.

The meaning of the doubt is as follows: Are meditations based on the constituent parts (*aṅga*)—such as those concerning the *udgītha* and so forth—obligatory by virtue of being subordinate to those parts, like the act of fetching water which depends on the ritual part of the *praṇayana*? Or are they non-obligatory, like the use of the *godohana* vessel for the sake of the fruit of cattle (which is thus non-obligatory), or like the use of *bilva* wood for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for the sake of the fruit of food (which is thus non-obligatory)? Likewise, because these meditations have fruits such as the success of rituals, they are non-obligatory and not subordinate parts of the rite. This is the sense of the doubt.

The difference in the results is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a necessity for the performance of meditations, whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is no such necessity.

He states the prima facie view by means of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa-dṛṣṭānta*)— namely, "What then?"— just as the *prāṇāgnihotra* (the fire-sacrifice to the vital breath) is non-obligatory because it depends on the non-obligatory act of eating, so too the meditations on the members of obligatory rites would be obligatory.

The meditations (*upāsanās*) are auxiliary parts of ritual acts, because, while they lack independent fruit, they are dependent upon ritual acts, just like the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood [which is an auxiliary of the sacrificial ladle].

Thus, since they are auxiliaries, they are employed by the obligatory injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*). Having reached this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he explains the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "those which," and so forth.

The meaning is that the *udgītha* and other such qualities—which are the subordinate members (*aṅga*) of ritual acts—and the meditations (*upāsana*) upon their true nature, such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*), are not restricted to those acts, just like the rule regarding the sacrificial ladle being made of *parṇa*-wood.
If these were essential parts of the ritual, then for one who lacks that knowledge, the ritual act would not be valid due to the omission of a constituent part;

therefore, he says "because they are seen [in the case of the ignorant]" to refute the inference of their being subordinate parts based on the scriptural indications that even the ignorant perform ritual acts.
The meaning is: "because that lack of restriction is observed.

Furthermore, since Cākrāyaṇa rebuked the officiating priests by saying, "If you chant the Prastāva while ignorant of it, your head will shatter," he states "the Prastāva, etc. to show that there is indeed the performance of ritual action even for those who do not practice meditation.
He says "moreover" (api ca) to show that meditations do not constitute auxiliary parts of the ritual, because a separate fruit is heard for them apart from the fruit of the ritual action.

Both he who knows this syllable *Om* in this manner—as having the nature of being the most flavorful (*rasatama*) and so forth—and he who does not know it, both indeed perform ritual action; yet there is a distinction between knowledge and ignorance, as they yield different results.
For it is observed that in the sale of a jewel, there is a disparity in the results for the merchant and the forest-dweller (*śabara*) due to their respective knowledge and ignorance.

Therefore, the meaning is that whatever action one performs with knowledge—such as the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth—with faith, which is the conviction of its efficacy, and with the *upaniṣad*, which is the meditation on the secret deity, that very action possesses an excellence of fruit.

The point is this: the "potency" (*vīryavattva*) of an action, understood as its fruitfulness even for one devoid of [formal] knowledge, is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that knowledge is not a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of the ritual.

Furthermore, he states "likewise" (*tathā*) because, in meditations such as viewing the worlds and so forth within the *sāman*, there is the scriptural teaching of fruits like the worlds which are distinct from the success of the ritual; therefore, [knowledge] is not a subordinate member.
The meaning is that for this wise person, the worlds above the earth and those below, which are turned toward him, become fit—that is, capable—of providing enjoyment.
For it is said, "it is a statement of quality" (*guṇavāda*);
if the mention of the fruit were merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it would result in the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise.
That [interpretation] is not tenable,
because it is possible for [the text] to have as its primary meaning the attainment of the fruit.

However, in the case of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* rites, since their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the *darśa* and other sacrifices is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the scriptural mention of the fruit of "overpowering rivals" has no other recourse but to be understood as a figurative praise (*stuti*).

Although there is no *prakaraṇa* (context) indicating that qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood are subsidiary (*aṅga*) elements, nevertheless, the mention of results (*phala-śruti*) regarding them must be understood as mere praise (*stuti*). This is because, since these qualities are non-active (*akriyātva*), they cannot logically be causes of a result without a connection to an action; thus, they require an action for the sake of the result, and the sacrifice (*kratu*) requires a material substance for the *juhū* ladle. Therefore, by the very sentence "The *juhū* is made of *parṇa*-wood," etc., [the connection is established].

The point is that since the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice—which is proximate—established through the *juhū* ladle by means of the offering of the raw material (*prakṛtidravya*), it is appropriate that the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

[Objection: Even for non-act-like things such as the *godohana* vessel, the mention of a fruit would have to be an explanatory passage; therefore, he says: "For in the case of the *godohana*, etc. [Response:

The statement, "If one were to bring water, that should be done with the *godohana* for one desiring cattle, and with a bronze vessel (*kaṃsya*) for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," is indeed an injunction regarding a fruit and not an explanatory passage. This is because the *godohana* and so forth are not required by the sacrifice and thus lack the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
Because the *camasa* (cup) can serve as the means to achieve its own result by being connected to an action that is already devoid of further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*).

Similarly, having relied upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—which is a subsidiary of the sacrifice and is itself devoid of expectancy through its quality of being made of *khadira* wood—the injunctions "one desiring food should use *bilva* wood" and "one desiring vigor should use *khadira* wood" have as their meaning only an injunction for a specific result.
[Objection: Why could there not be an injunction for a result in cases such as "made of *parṇa* wood"? To this, he says: "But not... (*na tu*).
The meaning is that such [an injunction] is independent, like the sacrificial post (yūpa) and so forth.
Since the *juhū* ladle itself is the substratum, he says "by means of the sentence" (*vākyena*).

Because the *juhū* requires a material substance as its source (*prakṛtidravya*), the connection between the *juhū* and its source material is established by this very sentence as a constituent part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*).

The meaning is that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*): first, the ladle (*juhū*) must be enjoined as something independent of expectation, and then the connection of that very material substance with a fruit must be enjoined.
He states the distinction of meditations (*upāsanā*) from [qualities] such as being made of *parṇa*-wood by saying, "But of the meditations... and so forth.
The meaning is that, because it is itself an action, its prescription as qualified by a result is possible, just like sacrifices and the like.
The phrase "therefore" means because there is no means of knowledge (pramāṇa) indicating that it is a subsidiary (aṅga).
The phrase "for this very reason" means precisely because it is not a subsidiary.
Therefore, it is established that there is eligibility for ritual action even in the absence of the worship of the ancillary limbs (aṅga). //42//

Section 28: On the Giving [of the Soul]. Sūtra 43. The soul is not given away, because it is not something that can be given. Just as a person does not give away his own self to another, so too the soul cannot be given away by the sacrificer to the priests. Furthermore, since the soul is the very nature of the agent, it cannot be transferred like an external object. Therefore, there is no such thing as the "giving" of the soul. End of Section 28. Sūtra 43.
That has been stated as being like the giving away [of the senses].

In the Vājasaneyaka, at the passage "I shall indeed speak; thus did Speech hold fast" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21), it is determined that among the internal organs, Speech and the others have Breath as their superior, and among the deities, Fire and the others have Air as their superior. Likewise, in the Chāndogya: "Air, verily, is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1).

Thus, in the passage concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*), Vāyu has been determined as the absorber (*saṃvarga*) of fire and the others; and in the passage concerning the self (*adhyātma*), "Breath indeed is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.2), Prāṇa [is determined] as the absorber of speech and the others.
In this regard, a doubt arises: should these two, Vāyu and Prāṇa, be meditated upon separately, or not separately?
First, it is established that [the deities] are indeed not separate, because their essential nature (*tattva*) is identical;
for it is not logical to contemplate what is non-different in its essence as being separate.
And scripture demonstrates the identity of essence between the internal (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaivata*): "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth" (Ai. 2.4).
Beginning thus, [the text] shows that the divine manifestations are the very self of the internal worlds, stating: "Therefore, all these are alike; all are infinite" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.13).
Likewise, in other places as well, there are various presentations of the distinction between principles regarding the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata).
And in some instances, it makes the wind and the vital breath clearly one and the same, stating, "That which is the vital breath is the wind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22).
Similarly, even in the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa cited above, it says, "From whence the sun rises" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23).
In this concluding verse, by concluding with "Verily, he rises from breath alone and sets in breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23), [the text] shows that [the observance] is through breath alone.
Therefore, one should observe only a single vow: "one should breathe in and breathe out" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23).
And thus, by means of this single vow regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he confirms this very point.

Likewise, in the *Chāndogya* as well, later on, the text leads one to understand only a single absorber (*saṃvarga*) in the passage: "The one God, the great-souled, who alone is awake—the guardian of the world" (Chā. 4.3.6); it does not state that the absorber of some four [elements] is one, while the absorber of others is another.
"Therefore, the approach [to the breath] is not separate.
This being the position reached, we reply: "The wind and the breath are indeed to be approached as distinct.
Why?
Because of the separate instruction.

For this instruction concerning the division between the internal (ādhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva) is for the purpose of meditation; it would be entirely meaningless if there were no distinctness in meditation.
But was it not said that there is no separate contemplation because of the non-difference of reality?
This is not a fault;

for even though there is no difference in reality (*tattva*), a distinction in contemplation is established by virtue of the distinction in states (*avasthā*) through the power of the different instructions.

Furthermore, the citation of the verse, while being consistent with the intention that there is no difference in reality, lacks the capacity to refute the previously mentioned distinctions among the objects of meditation (*dhyeya*).

And because of the employment of comparison and the object compared in the passage, "As the middle vital breath among these vital breaths, so is Vāyu among these deities" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22),
by this the instruction regarding the observance (*vrata*) is also explained.

Furthermore, in the passage "There is only one vow" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23), the particle *eva* is intended to establish the vow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by excluding the vows of speech and the other organs;
for it has been stated that speech and the others have broken their vows, according to the Vedic text: "Death, having become fatigue, seized them" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21).
For, having introduced the subject with "Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into the vow" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.5.21),
it is determined that the vows of Vāyu and Prāṇa are equally unbroken; thus [the text says],
"One should observe only one single vow" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.5.23).

Having stated this, the text— by declaring the fruit to be the attainment of Vāyu in the passage, "Thereby he wins union with and residence in the same world as that deity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23)— shows that the vow of Vāyu is not to be abandoned.
Here, "that" (*tat*) must refer to Vāyu, because it is the state of having an unlimited self (*aparicchinna-ātmakatva*) that is desired to be attained.
And prior to the formal application [of the meditation], it is said: "This deity that never sets is Vāyu" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22).

Likewise, it designates them separately: "These two, indeed, are the two absorbers—Vāyu among the deities and Prāṇa among the vital breaths" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.4); and further: "These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the Kṛta" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.8).
And thus he concludes by means of a distinction:
"Therefore, the approach is indeed separate,
just like the offering."

In the case of this sacrifice consisting of three *puroḍāśa* cakes— namely, "to King Indra a *puroḍāśa* on eleven potsherds, to Indra the Overlord, [and] to Indra the Self-Ruler"— there arises a doubt that the offerings should be made together because of the scriptural injunction, "He cuts off [the portions], making them reach all [deities] so as not to cause a failure," and because there is no distinction between the Indras. However, due to the difference in qualities such as "King" and so forth, and because of the prescription for the transposition of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, there is a distinctness of offering (*pradāna-pṛthaktva*) just as there is a distinctness of deities (*devatā-pṛthaktva*), since they are different.

Thus, the meaning is that even though the reality (*tattva*) is non-different, there is a distinction in meditation (*ādhyāna*) due to the distinctness of the portions to be meditated upon (*ādhyeyāṃśa*).

This has been stated in the *Saṃkarṣa*: "Or rather, the deity is not manifold, because it is known as one. In that case, however, a distinction of sacrifices exists due to the difference between the material (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*); here, such a distinction of knowledge (*vidyābhedo*) does not exist.

Because, through the opening and the conclusion, there is the perception that a single instruction regarding knowledge is being enjoined in the teachings concerning the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva);

yet, even when the knowledge is situated in one place, a difference in application arises due to the distinction between the internal and the divine, just as in the case of the Agnihotra sacrifice due to the distinction between the evening and morning times—it is with this very intention that it was stated, "as in the case of the offering" (pradānavat). // 43 //
That has been stated as being like the case of giving.
He states the doubt regarding the difference and non-difference between Vāyu and Prāṇa by means of two scriptural passages with the word "tatra.

Let it be that there is a distinction in performance consisting of the nature of being obligatory or non-obligatory, due to the difference in results between the auxiliary parts of the ritual and the meditations connected to them.

But here, because there is no difference between the essential nature of Vāyu and Prāṇa, and because the fruit characterized by attaining that essential nature is one and the same, the opponent maintains the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that the application of meditation is identical; this is expressed by the word "apṛthak" (not separate).
The meaning is that the passage beginning with "Fire, having become speech... and ending with "Vāyu, having become breath, entered the nostrils," demonstrates their non-difference.

Furthermore, regarding the question, "Tell me that from which the sun rises," the term "Vāyu" refers to the Sūtrātman (the thread-self); thus, by speaking of Prāṇa in the place of Vāyu, he shows their identity—this is what is meant by "tathā" (likewise).

Furthermore, if there were a separate meditation on air and vital breath (prāṇa), then there would also be a distinction between the meditative limbs and the vows; however, because of the scriptural teaching here of the unity of the vow consisting in the restraint of prāṇa and apāna, there is unity of meditation. He says "therefore," meaning because of the excellence of the unity of the vow. Moreover, having introduced air and vital breath as the two "absorbers" (saṃvarga) separately, the subsequent remainder of the passage teaches the identity of the absorber with the Deity; thus he says "likewise," meaning there is unity of practice.
"Of the great-souled ones" (*mahātmanām*) is the accusative plural.

A single God—Who is He? Prajāpati—has swallowed (*jagāra*), that is to say, has consumed or withdrawn, four—that is, four in number—namely fire, sun, water, and moon, as well as others in the form of speech, sight, hearing, and mind;
the ellipsis is "he does not speak of their difference."

Just as in the case of the Agnihotra sacrifice— where, although there is only one Agnihotra established by the injunction "He offers the Agnihotra," there is a difference in performance due to the difference in qualities such as curd and rice, and due to the difference in time such as evening and morning— likewise, although the Saṃvarga-vidyā is one, established by the injunction "He who knows thus becomes an eater of food," there is a difference in performance due to the difference in qualities taught therein, namely Vāyu and Prāṇa; thus [the sūtra] is set aside.
He establishes the conclusion: "They are indeed distinct.

The meaning is that because the scriptural statement regarding the difference between the objects of meditation—namely, "These two, indeed, are the two absorbers"—is intended to teach a difference in application, the distinction is established from the text itself.
Having restated the argument of the opponent, he replies with the words beginning "But has it not been said," and so forth.

The two [statements] regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) have been cited because they constitute distinct sentences concerning the object of meditation, characterized by the preeminent quality of being the "absorber" (*saṃvarga*).

Consequently, he says "the verse," meaning that the verse beginning with "whence it rises" lacks the power to refute the distinction between the objects of meditation as presented through the divisions of the internal (*adhyātma*) and external (*adhidaiva*) states.
He provides the indicative mark for this incapacity with the words "just as that."

He says, "By this," [meaning] that the presentation of the unity of the vows (*vrataikyopanyāsa*), like the presentation of the verses (*ślokopanyāsa*), is also intended to show the non-difference of their essential nature (*tattvābhedābhiprāya*).
Now, one might object: because of the restrictive particle *eva*, it appears that only Prāṇa alone is to be meditated upon after the withdrawal of the vow of Vāyu; to this he says, "only one.

Having stated that the vows of speech, sight, and so forth—namely those of the voice, the eyes, and the other senses—are broken by death in the form of exhaustion, it is determined that the vow of Prāṇa alone remains unbroken.

Likewise, having stated that the vows of fire, the sun, and so forth—consisting of blazing, heating, and the like—are broken, the fact that the vow of Vāyu is unbroken is determined by the scripture: "Just as among these vital breaths (prāṇas) the middle breath has a steady vow, even so among these deities Vāyu [has a steady vow]; for the other deities set, but not Vāyu; this deity, namely Vāyu, is one that never sets."
Therefore, the meaning is that the particle *eva* is intended solely to exclude the broken vow, not to indicate the cessation of the wind-vow (*vāyu-vrata*).
Regarding this very point, he states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as "one" (*ekam*);
the syllable *u* has the sense of "and" (*ca*).
The meaning is that by means of that vow, one conquers union with Vāyu—that is, identity of body—and residence in the same world.
To the objection that the attainment of Vāyu is not explicitly heard here, he says: "the deity.
Therefore, it is established that there is a unity of vows through the vision of the non-difference of their essential nature.
Now he explains the previously mentioned separate instruction with the words "tathā tau vā" (so too those two).
He expounds the scriptural illustration with the word "pradānavat" (like the offering).

Regarding the *tripuroḍāśinī* sacrifice—which is so called because it contains three *puroḍāśa* cakes—there arises a doubt: is there a simultaneous offering (*sahapradāna*) of all, or are they offered separately? To this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "sarveṣām" (of all).
Facing all the gods, he cuts and takes the oblation;
"acchaṃvaṭkāram" means the portion of the deity called *vaṣaṭkāra*.
Alternatively, the reason why the cutting must be performed simultaneously for the sake of all the gods is expressed by "acchaṃvaṭkāram," meaning so that it may not be in vain.
The sense is that once a portion of the oblation has been cut off for a single deity, the remainder would be useless because it is no longer fit for sacrifice.

Thus, since the scriptural injunction prescribes cutting off [the portions] together and there is only one deity, it might follow that the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*) should be offered together; however, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that they are to be offered separately—with the word "King" (*rājā*).
This means that because there is a distinction among the deities qualified by the attributes of King (*rāja*), Overlord (*adhirāja*), and Sovereign (*svarāja*), [the offerings must be separate].

Furthermore, there is a distinction between the two: that mantra which is recited by the Hotṛ when the Adhvaryu has issued the command "yajā" (sacrifice) is the *yājyā*, whereas the mantra recited after the command "anubrūhi" (recite after) is the *puronuvākyā*. In this sacrifice, the *yājyā* prescribed for the offering of the first cake (*puroḍāśa*) serves as the *puronuvākyā* for the second offering.
Since the Śruti prescribes that what was previously the *anuvākyā* is later the *yājyā*, thus enjoining an inversion,
he says "the *yājyā*" to indicate that there is a distinctness of the offering (*prakṣepa*) according to the scriptural injunction.
The *Saṃkarṣa* is the section concerning the deities (*devatākāṇḍa*).
The word "or" (*vā*) is used for emphasis;
the meaning of the sūtra is that there is indeed a distinction [among the deities], because they are understood to be distinct through differences in qualities such as being a king and so forth.

One might argue that, as in the illustrative example, there must be a difference in knowledge (vidyā) due to the difference in deities; to this he says: "But in that case... The difference in deities mentioned in the originative injunctions of ritual acts is a cause for a difference in those acts. However, here, in the case of the knowledge whose unity is known from the originative statement, "He who knows thus becomes an eater of food," the subsequent mention of a difference between Vāyu and Prāṇa does not constitute a differentiator.
The meaning is that it is like the difference in substances such as curd and so forth in the Agnihotra sacrifice.
If one asks, "In what respect, then, does the act of offering serve as an illustration? he says: "Even though the knowledge is one" (vidyaikye 'pi).
The meaning is that this is an illustration in the sense that there is a difference in deities and a difference in ritual application due to the difference in states (avasthābheda). //43//
