"Because of the abundance of indicatory marks, that indeed is stronger; for that [is stated] also.

In the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyins, in this Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "In the beginning, this was not existent," the mind (*manas*) is introduced as the subject of discourse, and it is taught: "He beheld thirty-six thousand fires of his own self, consisting of the *arka* and made of mind, built of mind," and so forth.

In the same way, they mention various fires to be meditated upon as substitutes (*sāṃpādika*), namely: "the fire built of speech, the fire built of breath, the fire built of sight, the fire built of hearing, the fire built of action, and the fire built of the sacrificial fire.

Regarding these, a doubt arises: are these fires, such as the one built of mind (*manaścit*) and the others, subordinate to ritual action and enter into it as its remnants, or are they independent, consisting solely of knowledge (*vidyā*)?
In this regard, although their entry into ritual action might be suggested by the context, the author first asserts their independence on the grounds of the force of the indicative marks (*liṅga*).

In this Brāhmaṇa passage, numerous indicative marks (liṅgas) are seen which support the view that these [fires] consist solely of knowledge (vidyā). Such passages include: "Whatever these beings conceive with the mind, that is indeed their work," and "All beings always pile these very fires for one who knows thus, even while he sleeps. Indeed, an indicative mark is more powerful than the context (prakaraṇa).

This has also been stated in the previous section (the *Pūrvakāṇḍa*): "When there is a conflict between direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the intended meaning" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.13). [The answer is: "On account of the abundance of indicative marks. Having begun with the statement that prior to creation all this was neither existent nor non-existent, and having described the creation of the mind, [the text] says, regarding the mind: "That mind looked upon itself," and thus saw the fires preceded by such an act of looking. Thus, it refers to the mind.
The meaning is "they recite.

Within the span of a human life—calculated as one hundred years—there are thirty-six thousand days and nights; by means of these, even though mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti*) are innumerable, they are reduced to thirty-six thousand.

With these [fluctuations], conceived as bricks, he perceived with his own mind the fires constructed by the mind (*manaścit*), namely the venerable suns (*arka*) produced within his own mental states, as belonging to himself. He beheld them through his mind.
Likewise, he says "so too" (tathā) to indicate that speech, the vital breaths, and so forth, also perceived fires consisting of their own respective functions.

The vital breath is the sense of smell; "built by action" (karmacita) refers to the fire built by the hand and other organs of action; and the skin is the fire, because the previous section concerned the construction of the fire-altar (agnicayana).

He states the doubt regarding these fires with the words "among them" (teṣu): whether these fires are for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha), or rather for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha) on account of the abundance of indicative marks (liṅga) and other factors that signal their primary importance.
The meaning is that they consist solely of knowledge (*vidyā*) and are composed of meditative realization (*bhāvanā*), being devoid of being auxiliary parts of ritual action (*kriyā*).

While there may be a difference in the application of meditation for Vāyu and Prāṇa due to the impossibility of a single performance (*ekaprayoga*), here, however, since the fires such as the *manaścits* are part of the context of ritual action, they constitute a single performance. Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he begins the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is accepted that the fires (*agni*) are subsidiary elements of the ritual (*kratvaṅga*); whether they are subsidiary to the action itself, or whether there be an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*), the result in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Thus, when there is firmness in meditation (*dhyāna*)—namely, "my fires are always being piled by all the mental functions of every living being"—then whatever all beings intend with their minds, that [result] belongs to those very fires.

"Making" (*kṛti*) and "instrumentality" (*karaṇa*) are one and the same sign (*liṅga*), because it is observed that whatever serves as an instrument for a constituent part of an action accomplishes its purpose; thus he says, "That which... Furthermore, another sign is that for one who knows this, even while sleeping or waking, living beings always pile up his fires.

The meaning is that it is impossible for a subsidiary of an action (*kriyāṅga*), which is to be performed at a prescribed time, to be performed by everyone at all times. Furthermore, the number thirty-six thousand is stated by means of such a word as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for its not being a subsidiary. //44//
The previous alternative [of the mental sacrifice] would apply because of the context, as in the case of the *kriyāmānasa* (mental rite). (BBs 3.3.45)
It is not stated that these fires are independent and not subsidiary to anything else;

because of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the preceding fire consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya*), this instruction regarding a specific alternative (*vikalpa-viśeṣa*) must refer to that very subject and cannot be independent.
[Objection: But surely indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than context.
This is true;
however, even an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of this kind does not possess greater force than the context (*prakaraṇa*),
for this is merely an observation of something intended for another purpose.

Because this [passage] has the form of a praise for the fires as superimpositions (*sāṃpādika*), and because the observation of another purpose— even when no other application exists— is compatible with being a figurative description (*guṇavāda*), it is not able to subvert the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore,
even these fires as superimpositions must enter into the ritual action by virtue of the context.

It is like the *mānasa* [rite]. Just as for the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), on the tenth day, the *Avivākya*, the taking up, placing, offering, bringing back, invitation, and consumption of the Soma— which is being offered to Prajāpati as the deity, with the earth as the vessel and the ocean as the Soma—
are prescribed as being purely mental (*mānasa*).

And that mental conceptualization of grasping, because it occurs within the context of ritual action, is indeed a supplement to that action; thus, the meaning is that this [mental fire] is also like a [real] fire. [Note:
*Avivākyam* is the name of the tenth day.
Having thus introduced the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he now sets forth the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding the statement, "One should pile the fire-altar with bricks in the east," this is an instruction on a specific alternative for that very fire-altar which is present at hand;

it is an instruction on a distinction of mode known as being composed of volition (*saṃkalpa*). The meaning is that, just like the ritual fire, these fires consisting of volition are also auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
Is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in an injunctive sentence more powerful than the context (*prakaraṇa*)?
Or [it may be] situated in an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
He accepts the first case, saying "True";
he states that the second is not so, saying "The indicative mark (liṅga)."

The meaning is that the indicative marks (*liṅga*) found in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning the mental fires (*mānasāgni*) are weak because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing their own [independent] purpose. He explains the verb in the Sūtra with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

An objection is raised: "But how can these fires, which are not of the nature of action and consist of meditation (*dhyāna*), be auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of an action? To this he replies: "Like the mental [sacrifice]" (*mānasavat*).

Excluding the first and last days of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is precisely the middle ten-night period that serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for sacrifices such as the two-night rite (*dvirātra*), because the properties of that middle ten-night period alone are extended (*atideśa*) to them. Regarding that middle ten-night period, the *mānasa-graha* (mental cup) is heard of on the tenth day—which effectively means the eleventh day—as follows: "With this vessel, the *rasā*, he draws the *mānasa-graha* belonging to Prajāpati."

With this juice as the liquid and the earth as the vessel, you—the ocean, having Prajāpati as its deity—are drawn as a *manograha* (mind-cup); thus it is called a *graha*, meaning the Soma-juice is drawn by the Adhvaryu priest while contemplating it as being of the nature of essence (*rasa*) through the mind.

For this very reason, because the priests are in a state of meditation and there is an absence of the utterance of various formulas, the day receives the designation *Avivākya* (the day without dispute).

The meaning is that these mental [acts] alone constitute: *grahaṇa*, which is the taking up of the Soma vessel; *āsādana*, the placing of what has been taken in its proper place; *havana*, the offering of the Soma into the fire; *āharaṇa*, the taking of the remainder of the offering; and *upahvāna*, the mutual invitation of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) for the consumption of the remainder, after which follows the consumption itself.

Anticipating the objection that this mental conception (*mānasa-graha*) might be an independent day distinct from the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "And that" (*sa ca*): it is not a separate day because that would contradict its designation as the "twelve-day sacrifice," but rather, by virtue of the context, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *Avivākya* day. "Kalpa" refers to the manner of conceptualization.

However, some say that in this commentary, the term "ten-night rite" (daśarātra) refers to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because even there, on the tenth day known as the Avivākya, the Mānasa cup is an auxiliary element since it is obtained through extended application (atideśa). //45//
And because of the extension [of the rule]. (BBs 3.3.46)

Furthermore, this extended application (*atideśa*) of these fires reinforces their entry into the ritual action: "There are thirty-six thousand fires; each one of them is as large as that former one. For an extended application proceeds only when there is a commonality [of nature]. Therefore, by extending the fires—which are composed of bricks and enter into the ritual action—to these fires that are merely to be produced, it demonstrates that these too indeed enter into the ritual action. // 46 //

Having stated that the *prakaraṇa* (context) establishes that the mind-made fires (*manaścidityādi*) are auxiliary to the ritual action, he states the *liṅga* (indicative mark): "And because of extension" (*atideśāt*).
The meaning is that there is an extension [of the ritual details] due to the similarity in their being auxiliary to the ritual action. //46//
But it is knowledge alone [that leads to the state of Brahman], because of the definitive determination. (BS 3.3.47)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
These fires, such as the mind-made fire (*manascit*) and others, must consist of knowledge alone and be independent, not being subordinate to ritual action.
For thus the text determines: "These, indeed, are built of knowledge alone."
And: "By knowledge alone, these [fires] become built for one who knows thus. (47)
He states the established conclusion: "Knowledge" (vidyā). //47//
And because it is seen [in scripture]. (BBs 3.3.48)
Furthermore, an indicative mark for their independence is observed;
this was demonstrated previously in the commentary on Brahma Sūtra 3.3.44, under the aphorism "On account of the abundance of indicative marks. // 48 //
The meaning of the three sūtras is that the context (prakaraṇa) is not to be set aside by direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), or syntactical connection (vākya). //48//

[Objection: But surely, even a *liṅga* (indicative mark) is not a means of establishing any meaning when another [means of proof] is absent; therefore, having set that aside, it was determined through the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*) that [the *liṅga*] is subordinate to the ritual action (*kriyā*). To this, he recites the following reply:
And because of the superior strength of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof, there is no sublation.
It is not the case that, having determined through the power of context (*prakaraṇa*) that [the Upanishads] are subordinate to ritual action, the position of their independence should be sublated;
for direct scriptural statement and the rest are more powerful.
For it is established in the *Śrutiliṅgasūtra* that direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) are stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*).
And these [three] are seen here to support the position of independence (*svātantryapakṣa*).
How so?

First, there is the Śruti: "These [fires] are indeed built of knowledge alone. Likewise, there is the indicative mark (liṅga): "Even while he sleeps, all beings build them at all times. Similarly, there is also the syntactical connection (vākya): "By knowledge alone do these [fires] become resorted to by one who knows thus."
For this scriptural statement, "It is piled by knowledge alone," being emphatic, would be contradicted if their entry into ritual action were admitted.
[Objection: But perhaps this emphasis intends to show that they have no external means [other than knowledge].
[Reply: No, it is said.

For if [the term "knowledge"] were intended to mean that [the means] are merely suitable for knowledge, then the restriction (avadhāraṇa) would be purposeless, since this would already be established by the mere mention of their essential nature—that their very nature is such that they require no external means. However, even though they require no external means, there might still be a suspicion that they enter into the performance of ritual action, as in the case of the mental cups (mānasagraha); therefore, the restriction will be meaningful as having the result of excluding that suspicion.

Likewise, the observation of continuity in the passage, "For one who knows thus, all beings always pile these fires for him, whether he is sleeping or waking" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.17.10), is possible only if they possess independence.

This is just as in the case of the preparatory Agnihotra consisting of speech and breath, where, after stating, "Then he offers the breath into speech; then he offers speech into breath" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5), it is further said, "These two endless oblations he offers continuously, both while waking and while sleeping" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5).
It is the same in this case.

However, if they were to enter into activity, their application would not be continuous because the performance of an action occupies only a short duration; and it is not logical to regard this as a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
For where a clear injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) or the like is perceived, it is appropriate that the mere mention [of an action] functions as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Here, however, since no other injunction is clearly perceived, the injunction for the knowledge of these [deities] must be inferred from the mention itself.

And since that [injunction] can only be inferred in accordance with the manner of the mention, it is inferred to be exactly of that nature, because of the observation of continuity (*sātatyadarśana*).
Consequently, by implication, their independence is established.
By this, such passages as "Whatever these beings conceive with the mind, that is indeed their own creation" are explained.
Likewise, the scriptural statement "to one who knows thus" (evaṃvide) indicates a connection with a specific person and does not tolerate a connection with a ritual sacrifice.
Therefore, the position of independence alone is superior. // 49 //
In this regard, he raises the objection that the restrictive hearing (*avadhāraṇa-śruti*) might be established otherwise: "But [it is said] 'not external' (*nanvabāhya*). He replies:
"No," because the fact that the means are not external is already obtained by the very phrase "built of knowledge" (*vidyācita*); thus, the restriction would be redundant.
To the question, "In that case, how does it have purposeful meaning? he says: "Not external... (*abāhya*).
He clarifies the indicative mark [of this] with the word "tathā" (so).
He states another example for the fact that the fires do not constitute a constituent part [of the sacrifice] because they pervade all times, with the word "tathā";
the meaning is "at that time," namely, at the time of meditation.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as "constancy" (*sātatyam*) is prescribed regarding the home, so too there is the observation of constancy regarding the fires.
As for the claim that an indicative mark (*liṅga*) situated in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is weak, that is not so;
for one must assume an injunction based on a novel purpose (*apūrvārthatā*), namely: "One should meditate [thinking], 'All beings always pile the fires for my sake.'"
And thus, because it resides within an injunctive sentence, the indicative mark (liṅga) is stronger than the context (prakaraṇa); this is what he states with the words "na cedam" and so forth.
By the word "etena," the meaning is "by way of being an injunction. He explains the sentence [of the opponent] with the word "tathā. //49//
On account of the connection and other factors, [the meditations] are distinct, just as the difference between various forms of knowledge is observed; this has already been stated. (BS 3.3.50)

Moreover, setting aside the context, the independence of the "mind-altars" (manaścita) and so forth must be understood; for the text connects the constituent parts of the ritual action with the operations of the mind and other faculties, stating: "They were studied by the mind alone, they were piled by the mind alone, the cups were taken by the mind alone, they praised with the mind, they recited with the mind—whatever rite is performed at the sacrifice, whatever is sacrificial..."
"By the mind alone, among those [elements] which consist of mind, within the consciousnesses that consist of mind, that which consists of mind is performed," and so forth.
For this sequence of meditations has the attainment [of identity with the object] as its fruit;
and the constituent parts of the ritual action, being perceptible, cannot be sought after through such identification.

Nor should it be suspected here that these [meditations] enter into the constituent parts of ritual action, as is the case with the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, because of the difference in the nature of the scriptural injunctions.
For this text does not say that one should take some part of a ritual action and then superimpose the name "Agni" upon it;

rather, taking the thirty-six thousand varieties of mental modifications, it conceives of them as the fires, the cups (*graha*), and so forth, just as in the case of the "Man-Personified-Sacrifice" (*puruṣayajña*).
It should be understood that this number, being observed in the days of a person's lifespan, is superimposed upon the mental functions associated with them.
Thus, through such connection (*anubandha*), the fire-altars consisting of mind (*manaścit*) and so forth possess independence.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other grounds such as extended application (*atideśa*) are also to be applied as appropriate.

For instance, by stating, "Each one of these [subsequent fires] is as great as that former fire which consists of action," the text attributes the greatness of the fire made of action to each of those consisting of knowledge, thereby demonstrating a disregard for mere ritual action.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that there is an option between the former and the subsequent fires while their connection to ritual action remains identical;
for the subsequent fires are not able to assist in the performance of the rite through the same function—such as carrying the sacrificial ladle—that the former assists in.

As for the argument stated in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the extended application (*atideśa*) serves as a supporting factor— on the grounds that an extended application proceeds only when there is a commonality— that has been refuted by our position, because the possibility of extended application exists here through the commonality of "fire-ness" (*agnitva*),
since even the fires that are merely meditative constructs (*sāṃpādika*) possess fire-ness.
Furthermore, the scriptural authority (*śruti*) and other reasons have already been demonstrated.
Thus, due to reasons such as the connection [with other rites] and so forth, the manas-cit and others possess independence,
just like the distinct meditations (*prajñā*).

Just as distinct meditations, such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, being connected with their own respective [elements], become independent from ritual acts and from other meditations, so it is in this case.

Furthermore, it is observed that the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice—which is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *rājasūya*—is extracted from that context because it is connected to the three social classes (*varṇas*) and because the *rājasūya* is a sacrifice performed by a king (*rājñaḥ sūyaḥ*).

This was stated in the first book (*kāṇḍa*): "If it is argued that [the rule] applies to what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthā*), it is not so, because of the connection with the three social classes" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.7). (Note:
*Aveṣṭi* is the name of this specific sacrifice.)

For the sake of perfecting the worship, the scripture establishes the application of the constituent parts (*kriyāṅga*) within the mental functions; this is the "connection" (*anubandha*). Furthermore, because that [application] would otherwise be impossible, the fires (*agni*) must serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), for if they served the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*), their status as established entities would make their "accomplishment" (*saṃpādana*) impossible. Thus he says, beginning with "And for this reason," etc. "Those fires" means that one should perform their installation (*ādhāna*) by means of the mind alone.
Because there is no fixed rule regarding the time or the meter (*chandas*).
"Bricks were piled" (*acīyanta*) means they were to be piled;
"cups" (*grahāḥ*) refers to the ritual vessels.
The Udgātṛ priests praised; they sang the hymns of praise. The Hotṛ priests recited; they performed the recitations.

What is the point of saying more? The meaning of the scriptural passage is that whatever sacrificial act in a sacrifice is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), is sacrificial (*yajñiya*), and produces the very nature of the sacrifice—all that one should make *manomaya* (consisting of mind).

Regarding the meditation on the fires (*agnidhyāna*), although it is not a constituent part of the ritual action (*kriyānaṅga*), one might think it could nonetheless be based upon a constituent of the action (*kriyāṅgāśritatva*), like the meditation on the *udgītha*. To this he says: "And here, not as the *udgītha...
He clarifies the difference between this scriptural statement and the scriptural statement concerning those tied to the constituent parts (*aṅgāvabaddha*) by saying: "For not..."

The meaning is that the accomplishment of the ritual with its constituent parts (*sāṅgakratu*) within the activities of the bodiless [deities] is an independent act for the person, like the meditation on [the fire-altars] as a sacrifice.
It is not an extended application (*atideśa*) intended to show disregard, but rather one intended to provide an option; therefore, he says "and not" (*na ca*).

An option (*vikalpa*) occurs between two independent means toward a single goal, such as in the case of rice and barley; however, here there is no option because the goals to be accomplished differ—the sacrificial fire (*kriyāgni*) and the meditative fires (*dhyānāgni*).
For this very reason, even the theory of combination (*samuccaya*) is refuted.
Regarding the claim that there is an extension (*atideśa*) based on the commonality of being auxiliary to the ritual action, he says "no"—namely, "as for what was said...
He states the meaning of the plural number in the Sūtra with the words "and [the means] such as direct statement (*śruti*), etc."
The meaning is: "from continuity, extended application, direct statement, indicative mark, and syntactical connection.

Regarding the word "thus" (*evam*), the word "meaning" (*artha*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Having raised the objection that if the Mind-altar (*manaścit*) and others were independent, they would have to be removed from the context of ritual action (*kriyā-prakaraṇa*), he says "it is seen" (*dṛṣṭaśca*) to show that such removal is indeed desired.

In the eleventh [book], it is considered: "A king desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. Having introduced this, a certain sacrifice named Āveṣṭi is recorded: "An offering to Agni on eight potsherds, gold is the sacrificial fee;
an oblation (caru) to Bṛhaspati, a white-backed animal is the sacrificial fee;
an offering to Indra on eleven potsherds, a bull is the sacrificial fee."

In that context, there is a difference in application based on the distinction of caste, as it is heard [in scripture]: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed the oblation for Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should pour the libation after each offering; if a Vaiśya, he should place the *caru* for the Viśvedevas in the middle; if a Rājanya, then [he should place] that for Indra.
The meaning is: having placed the *caru* for Bṛhaspati between the *puroḍāśa* for Agni and the one for Indra.

In that regard, the performance of the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) in the *caru* offerings dedicated to Agni and the other deities occurs by way of a single performance (*tantra*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of placing [the offering] in the center; for if there were a difference in performance, placing it in the center would be impossible. Furthermore, this is indicated by the singular number in the injunction, "One desiring food should sacrifice with this.

Moreover, that single performance of the auxiliaries is to be understood as applying only to the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice performed outside the *Rājasūya* ritual complex, which has as its performers members of the three higher castes desiring food, and not to the *Aveṣṭi* included within the *Rājasūya* itself.

If it is asked: "What is the restrictive factor here? Why could there not be a single performance of the auxiliaries even for the *Aveṣṭi* intended for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthā*)? The answer is: No.

Since the indicative marks such as the word "middle" (madhye) exist within the context of the *kāmyā* sacrifice— which belongs to those associated with the three castes and serves to establish the unity of the subsidiary ritual procedure (*aṅgatantra*)— therefore, due to the singular number and the indicative mark, when there is unity of the ritual procedure (*tantra*), the sacrificial fee consisting of gold and so forth must be given as a single combined unit;
otherwise, the unity of the performance (*prayoga*) would be impossible.

However, in the case of an *iṣṭi* included within a sacrifice performed by a mere king (*rājamātra*), because there is an absence of association with the three castes, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) such as "placing in the middle" does not exist; consequently,

due to the lack of any means to establish a unity of ritual procedure (*tantra*), there is a difference in procedure (*tantrabheda*) because of the difference in sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and thus there is indeed a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) in the case of the *caru* offerings— this is the meaning of the Sūtra.

And by this sūtra, which states that the mark of a single performance (*ekaprayoga*) is impossible in the case of rites for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha-iṣṭi*) but possible in the case of optional rites for specific desires (*kāmyeṣṭi*), it is indicated that because the optional rite for a desire is distinct from the rite for the sake of the sacrifice, it must be displaced from the context of the sacrifice (*kratu-prakaraṇāt*).
And that displacement is indeed logical.

It is established that, because a sacrifice such as the Rājasūya—which has only a king as its performer—cannot be included within a sacrifice such as the Iṣṭi—which has members of the three [higher] castes as its performers;
likewise, the intention is that there is an "exaltation" (utkarṣa) of the fire-altars consisting of mind and so forth. //50//
Nor [is it so] because of perception through similarity, for there is no attainment of the world as in the case of death. (BBs 3.3.51)
As for what was said—that [these fires] are like the mental [sacrifices]—that is replied to as follows:
Even on the basis of their commonality with mental grasping (*mānasagraha*), one should not assume that the fire-altars built of mind (*manaścit*) and so forth are subordinate to ritual action;
for, from the previously mentioned reasons such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), it is observed that they serve solely the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
For it is not the case that no similarity whatsoever exists between anything and anyone;
yet, by that much alone, the disparity of their respective natures does not cease,
just as in the case of death.

Just as, although the term "death" is applied equally to the person in that solar orb and to fire—according to the passages, "This very one is indeed death, who is this person in that orb" and "Fire, indeed, is death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.10)—there is no attainment of absolute identity between them;
and just as [in the passage], "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; the sun is its fuel" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1).
In this case, just as there is no attainment of the state of fire by the world due to the commonality of the *samidh* and other [sacrificial fuels], so it is here. // 51 //
Thus he refutes the analogy with the words "not because of a commonality.

The meaning is that even though there is a disparity between being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), the commonality of being mental (*mānasatva*) is not contradicted, since similarity is observed even between dissimilar things. //51//
And the nature of the word [as denoting the universal] is established by what follows; however, because of their multiplicity, they are merely adjuncts. (BS 3.3.52)

Furthermore, in the immediately following Brāhmaṇa passage, "This world indeed is this Agni Citta," the purpose of the text is observed to be the injunction of pure knowledge (*vidyā*) alone, and not the injunction of mere subsidiary elements of ritual action (*karmāṅga*).

For therein, by means of the verse: "By knowledge they ascend to that place where desires have gone to rest; neither those who perform sacrifices nor the ascetics who lack knowledge go there," it indicates this by censuring mere action and praising knowledge.

Likewise, even in the preceding section, in this Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "That orb which shines yonder," it is clearly observed that knowledge alone is primary; for the conclusion is made solely by means of the fruit of knowledge, stating, "He becomes immortal, for death becomes his very self. Since there is no emphasis on ritual action there, the same principle applies here as well due to the similarity between the two cases.

However, because a greater number of components of the fire-altar must be realized within the knowledge (*vidyā*), for this reason the knowledge is connected with the fire-altar, and not because it is a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karma*).
Therefore, it is established that the mind-altars (*manascid*) and others consist solely of knowledge.

Furthermore, since independent injunctions for knowledge are found in both the preceding and following Brāhmaṇas, he states—by the words "And by what follows"—that the Brāhmaṇa situated between them must also have as its purpose the injunction of independent knowledge.

For in the subsequent section, the injunction of viewing the worlds as the fire-altar (*agni*) is understood to be independent; whereas in the preceding section, there is the meditation on the Person within the orb (*maṇḍala*). By virtue of their proximity, the mental fires (*mānasāgnayaḥ*) in the middle are also independent; this is the meaning. [An objection: If that is so, for what purpose is their recitation together with the ritual fire-altar? To this, he replies: "But they are more numerous," etc. (Sūtra 52).

Section 30: On the Unity of Self (Aikātmyādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 53–54. START BsCom_3,3.30.53 30 aikātmyādhikaraṇam / sū. 53-54 END BsCom_3,3.29.52 START BsCom_3,3.30.53 30 aikātmyādhikaraṇam / sū. 53-54 30 aikātmyādhikaraṇam / sū. 53-54The section concerning the unity of self (aikātmyādhikaraṇa), sūtras 53–54. [The opponent argues: Since the individual soul (jīva) is of atomic size (aṇu), it cannot simultaneously experience the pleasures and pains occurring in all its various bodies; therefore, the scriptural teaching regarding the soul's omnipresence must be interpreted as figurative. [The author replies: This is not so. For the scripture declares that the soul is of the nature of consciousness (caitanya-rūpa). Just as fire, though existing in minute particles, manifests its own nature as heat and light when in contact with fuel such as grass and wood, so too the soul, though atomic in size, manifests its own nature as consciousness throughout the entire body by means of its connection with the sense organs. Furthermore, the soul is taught to be all-pervading because it possesses the quality of consciousness, which is itself all-pervading. Moreover, since the soul is the enjoyer of the fruits of karma, it must necessarily be omnipresent, for otherwise, the fruition of actions performed in one place would not occur in another. Therefore, the soul is indeed omnipresent. [The opponent asks: But how can there be a plurality of souls if they are all-pervading? [The author replies: There is no fault here, for their plurality is established by their distinct attributes such as knowledge, memory, and so forth. Furthermore, the scripture teaches that the soul is atomic in size in order to account for the fact that it experiences the results of its own specific karma. Thus, both the omnipresence and the atomicity of the soul are established by scripture. [The opponent asks: But if the soul is omnipresent, how can it be said to transmigrate? [The author replies: Transmigration consists merely in the soul’s conjunction with a new body and its departure from the old one; it does not imply movement from one location to another. Consequently, the soul’s omnipresence is not contradicted by the doctrine of transmigration. Moreover, the scripture teaches that the soul is "atomic" (aṇu) in the sense that it is difficult to perceive, or because it is subtle (sūkṣma), or because it is a part (aṃśa) of the Supreme Self. Thus, the two attributes are reconciled. Therefore, the soul is both omnipresent and atomic. This concludes the section on the unity of self.
