[The existence of] the Self is established because it exists in the body. (BBs 3.3.53) Here, the real existence of a Self distinct from the body is demonstrated for the purpose of establishing the qualification for bondage and liberation.
For if there were no Self distinct from the body, the injunctions regarding the next world would not be possible, nor could the identity of Brahman and the Self be taught to anyone.
But was it not already stated at the very beginning of the treatise, in the first quarter (pāda), that the Self—which is the enjoyer of the fruit of the treatise—is distinct from the body?
True, it was so stated by the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakāra); however, there was no sūtra regarding the existence of the Self there.
Here, on the other hand, the author of the sūtras himself establishes its existence by means of an objection.
It is precisely from this [work] that the teacher Śabarasvāmin has drawn [the discussion] and described it in his *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*.

For this very reason, the venerable Upavarṣa, when the occasion arose for stating the existence of the self (*ātman*) in the first book (*tantra*) of the *Śārīraka*, made a reference [to this work], saying, "it will be explained [there].

And here, while meditations characterized by injunctions (*codanālakṣaṇa*) are being investigated, the existence of the self is investigated in order to demonstrate that [this topic] is supplementary to the entire treatise.
Furthermore, in the preceding section, by accepting the displacement of the context, it was described that the "mind-altars" (manaścit) and so forth serve the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha).
Now, when the question arises—"Who is this person for whose sake these mind-altars exist?"—the existence of a self distinct from the body is stated here.
And this first Sūtra is intended to raise that very question regarding its existence.

For a refutation preceded by an objection produces a firm understanding regarding the intended meaning, according to the maxim of driving in a pillar. In this regard, some Lokāyatikas, who hold the view that the self is merely the body and who believe there is no self distinct from the body,

maintain that consciousness— though not observed in external elements such as earth, etc., whether taken collectively or individually— is present in the elements transformed into the form of the body.
Thinking "it might be so," they postulate consciousness from those [elements], like the power of intoxication, and assert that the person (*puruṣa*) is the body characterized by consciousness.
They maintain that there is no self (*ātman*) distinct from the body capable of going to heaven or attaining liberation (*apavarga*).
And they state the reason for this: "because [consciousness] exists only when the body exists."

For when something exists, another thing exists, and when it does not exist, that other thing does not exist, then the latter is determined to have the nature of a property (dharma) of the former, just as heat and light are properties of fire.

Furthermore, those things—vital breath, movement, consciousness, and memory—which are accepted by proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) as being properties of the self, must be properties of the body alone; since they are perceived only within the body and not outside of it, they cannot belong to a substratum (dharmin) distinct from the body, the existence of which remains unproven.

Therefore, the self is not distinct from the body. [This concludes the section. [The commentary states: "Uddhāra" means cessation. It has been stated that the mental fires (*manas-cit* etc. serve the purpose of the person; this is challenged as being untenable because there is no person distinct from the body—[the sūtra says]: "Because [cognition] exists when the self is present in the body. (1.1.53)
He states the fruit of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "bandha" (bondage).

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, he states the result by way of its negative counterpart (*vyatireka*)—namely, the lack of engagement in actions for the sake of the next world and in the knowledge intended for liberation—with the words "for [if it were] non-existent" (*na hyasati*). Anticipating the objection that there is redundancy because the investigation of a distinct self was already performed in the *Pūrvatantra* (the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras), he replies: "But surely... [stating that] this very sūtra is the source even for that prior investigation, as there is no such sūtra in Jaimini’s work; therefore, where is the redundancy? He says: "nanu... (but surely...).

By the words "In the Śāstra," etc., [the author] states the evidence from the Vṛttikāra’s statement: "For this very reason. This refers to the fact that when the lack of authority for statements such as "The sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes to the heavenly world" would follow due to the absence of an enjoyer, the investigation into the enjoyer was undertaken by drawing [the discussion] from this very point. Thus he says "for this very reason."
The meaning is that it is simply because there is no such Sūtra there.
"Uddhāra" means cessation.
He states "and here" to show that the connection of this topic (*adhikaraṇa*) with this section (*pāda*) is one of incidental relevance (*prasaṅga-saṃgati*).
The meaning is that, in the context of determining the meditation on the fruit pertaining to the next world, the existence of the self required for that [meditation] is now stated.

Taking this as an established fact, the first sūtra considered the qualified seeker by means of the word "atha" (then); therefore, he states the connection with the entire scripture (*śāstrasangati*) by saying "kṛtsna" (entire), indicating that this section is an auxiliary to the whole scripture.
He then states the intermediate connection characterized by an objection by saying "api ca" (moreover).

Regarding the doubt arising from the disagreement among disputants as to whether or not there exists a self distinct from the body, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "here some [say]":
although consciousness is not observed in all the elements when combined—since a heated water-pot lacks cognition—it is certainly absent in them when separated;
nevertheless, it might exist in the elements that constitute the body, and thus they postulate that consciousness arises from those very elements.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "Consciousness is like the power of intoxication; they say that the Self is a specific aggregate produced from an aggregate. The meaning is this: just as the power of intoxication—which is not observed in individual ingredients such as betel leaves within intoxicating substances—is nevertheless produced from their combination, so it is here. Now, one might object: "The body itself is not conscious, because, like a jar, it is composed of material elements (bhautika); rather, there exists some conscious being who experiences heaven and so forth, and due to its proximity, the body appears to possess consciousness. To this, he says: "No..."
"Heaven," [he said]. //53//
This being the case, we reply:
The distinction [of the self from the body] exists because [the self] exists when that [body] exists, but not as in the case of perception.
It is not the case that what was stated—that there is no distinction between the self and the body—is true;
rather, its distinction from the body must indeed exist, because it exists when that [body] exists.

If one were to think that the attributes of the self possess the nature of the body because they exist when the body exists, then why would one not likewise consider them not to be its attributes because they do not exist even when the body exists?
This is because they differ from the attributes of the body;
for those which are the attributes of the body, such as form and so forth, persist only as long as the body exists.
However, vital functions such as breathing do not occur during the state of death even though the body is present;
furthermore, while bodily attributes such as form and so forth are perceived by others, mental attributes such as consciousness and memory are not.

Moreover, while it is possible to determine the existence of these [mental attributes] during the living state when the body exists, their non-existence when the body is absent cannot be so determined.
Even if this body should perish, it might be argued that the attributes of the self would continue by migrating into another body;
yet, even on the basis of mere doubt, the opponent's position is refuted.
Furthermore, the opponent must be questioned as to what the nature of this consciousness is, which he desires to originate from the elements.
For the Lokāyatika does not perceive any reality whatsoever apart from the four primary elements.

If it is argued that consciousness is simply the experience of the primary elements and their derivatives, then, because they are its objects, it cannot possess them as its own attribute; for there is a contradiction in an action being directed toward itself.
For fire, being hot, does not burn itself;
nor will an actor, though highly trained, ever mount his own shoulders;
nor can the elements and their derivatives be made objects by consciousness, which itself consists of the elements and their derivatives.
For neither its own nature nor the nature of another is made an object by form and the other [sensory qualities];
rather, external and internal elements and their derivatives are made objects by consciousness.
Therefore, just as this apprehension which has the elements and their derivatives as its objects must be admitted to exist, so too must its existence be accepted.
Furthermore, the self is not of the very nature of perception; thus, the self is distinct from the body.
Its permanence is established by the uniformity of perception, and because there is recognition as the perceiver even when associated with different states, as in the thought, "I saw this."
Furthermore, because memory and so forth are possible [only for a conscious self],

as for what was said— that perception is a property of the body because it exists when the body exists— that has been refuted by the manner already described. Moreover, perception occurs when instruments such as lamps are present, and does not occur when they are absent.
Nor does perception become a property of the lamp and so forth merely by this much.
This being the case, since perception occurs when the body is present and does not occur when it is absent, it cannot be a property of the body;
for the utility of the body can be accounted for simply as an instrument, just like a lamp and such things.
Furthermore, the body is not even seen to be absolutely necessary for perception, since various kinds of perceptions are observed in dreams even while this body is motionless.
Therefore, the existence of a self distinct from the body is beyond reproach. 54.

Since the cognition "I am a human being" is a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the body's status as a knower, and since there is an experience of the presence and absence of those qualities well-known as attributes of the Self within the body, and because no such direct perception exists for a Self other than that, and because what is not perceived lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇika*), it follows that the body alone is the Self. To this prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "but not" (*na tv etat*) found in the Sūtra: "But this is not so."
The validity of inference must be accepted, even if one does not wish to do so, for otherwise worldly activity would be impossible.
Indeed, activity toward future cooking and the like is not possible without inferring that it is a means to a desired end.

Likewise, [the opponent argues] that cognition and other qualities have a substratum distinct from the body because they are absent even when the body is present—just as the form and other qualities of the body are absent in its absence; thus he says: "Its very absence [is the proof]."
Nor is there a deviation [in the pervasion] because the body was dark-complexioned at first and later assumes another form;

for what is intended is non-existence as delimited by a genus directly pervaded by the property of being a quality (guṇatva). While that which is delimited by the nature of color (rūpatva) certainly exists as long as the body persists, that which is delimited by the nature of cognition (jñānatva) does not; thus, cognition is not a property of the body.
Furthermore, he states that these are not qualities of the body because they are not perceived by others, saying: "And the properties of the body...
Moreover, since their non-existence in something distinct from the body is doubtful, there is no certainty that they are properties of the body; thus he says: "And also...
Nor can their non-existence be ascertained through non-perception, because for you, non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
The meaning is that its non-perception is established even through the attainment of another body, because it has that [body] as its substrate (*dharmī*).
He begins to explain the term *upalabdhivat* found in the Sūtra by asking: "Of what nature is it?
Does it refer to a reality distinct from the elements (*bhūta*), or is it a property of the elements (*bhūtadharma*) like color and so forth?

The first [alternative] is not tenable because it would constitute an abandonment of one's own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*); having stated this, he anticipates the second alternative and refutes it with the words "that which is experience," and so forth.

Since the elements that constitute the body are objects with respect to consciousness, and since it is impossible for an object to be the agent due to the contradiction between agent and object, consciousness cannot have the elements as its agent—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, if knowledge were a property of the elements, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*), just like color and other such qualities; therefore, it cannot have them as its property. He states this with the words "for not... (*na hi*).
He states the meaning of the scriptural passage that has been established with the words "Therefore" (*ataśca*).

If that which is distinct from the body and is of the nature of existence—the apprehension (*upalabdhi*)—were the Self, then it would be impermanent because apprehension is impermanent; therefore, he says "And as for permanence" (*nityatvaṃ ca*).

The meaning is that since there is no difference in the manifestation (*sphūrti*) everywhere—in such cases as "the jar manifests" and "the cloth manifests"—it is permanent; however, when the coloring by objects (*viṣayoparāga*) perishes, there is merely the delusion of its destruction.
Thus it has been stated that the self is distinct from the body because its nature is that of perception, just like perception itself.

Furthermore, since there is recognition of the oneness of the self despite the difference between the bodies in the waking and dreaming states, and since memory and desire would be impossible for one person regarding what was experienced by another if the selves were distinct, the self—which possesses dream-memory and so forth—is distinct from the body;
thus he says: "I."
He restates what was already refuted with the intention of explaining further: "As for what was said...

[The opponent argues that] the positive and negative concomitance of perception with the body does not prove that it is a property of the body, because that is otherwise established as being caused by it; to this he says further: "Moreover...
[And he states that] even the status of the body as a mere instrumental cause for perception is unestablished: "Nor is it absolutely... etc.
The perception in a dream is not produced by the body, because it occurs even without bodily activity, just like [the perception of] a tree;
for this very reason, the author of the Sūtras will state that yogis experience enjoyment even in the absence of a body, as in a dream.
It has been stated definitively that waking perception possesses the quality of being born from the body.

Therefore, he concludes—using the words "tasmāt" (therefore)—that the cognition of non-difference, such as "I am a human," is an error, because it is contradicted by the experience of difference expressed as "this is my body," which is supported by the aforementioned inference. //54//
Section 31: The Topic of That Which is Bound to the Body (aṅgāvabaddha-adhikaraṇam) / Sūtras 55–56. 31. [The topic concerning those things bound to the body. Sūtras 55–56.
"But those [meditations] connected with the limbs are not [restricted] to the branches of each Veda. The incidental discussion is now concluded;
we shall now return to the subject at hand: "One should meditate upon this syllable *oṃ* as the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1).
"One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.1.1);
"People say, 'The hymn, the hymn'; this very earth is that hymn. "This [earth] indeed is the Pṛthivī."

Regarding the meditative reflections (pratyayas) prescribed in various Vedic branches— such as "This world indeed is this piled fire-altar" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1), which are bound to the constituent parts of rituals like the Udgītha— the doubt arises whether they should apply only to the Udgītha and so forth belonging to their own respective branches, or to those found in all branches.
The meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth should not be enjoined for each individual branch [of the Veda] based on differences in accent and the like;
why? Because of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). [As it says:
"One should meditate upon the *udgītha*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1).
For thus, when general injunctions require a specific detail, that requirement is satisfied by the proximate specification found within one's own Vedic branch (śākhā) alone;
there is no reason to bypass that and adopt a specific detail enjoined in another branch. Therefore, the rule is determined according to each respective branch.
This being the case, [the author] says: "But those connected with the constituent parts. The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
These [rites] do not remain restricted solely to their own branches within each Veda.
Moreover, they should apply to all branches. Why? Because there is no distinction in the scriptural mention of the *udgītha* and so forth.

For if the meditation on the *udgītha* were restricted to one's own branch, then the general scriptural injunction "one should meditate on the *udgītha*"—which is set forth without qualification—would be strained if it were restricted to a particular instance merely by virtue of proximity.
And this is not logical;
for proximity is weaker than direct scriptural statement (śruti).
Nor is it the case that a cognition based on a general rule is untenable.

Therefore, even though there are differences such as the accent and so forth, because there is no distinction in their being the *udgītha* and so on, meditations of this kind should apply to the *udgītha* and other elements found in all the Vedic branches.
The "limb-bound" meditations:
the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*;
[furthermore]: "Earth is the *hiṅkāra*, fire is the *prastāva*, the intermediate space is the *udgītha*, the sun is the *pratihāra*, and the sky is the *nidhana*."

Thus, there exist meditations based on the constituent parts of ritual action, such as the meditation on the worlds upon the fivefold Sāman beginning with the *hiṅkāra*, the meditation on the earth upon the *uktha* litany, and the meditation on the worlds upon the fire-altar constructed of bricks.

Regarding these [passages], a doubt arises due to the common scriptural mention of the *udgītha* and so forth, as well as their specific proximity [to particular contexts]. Now, one might object: since the *udgītha* and other elements are identical across all recensional branches (*śākhā*), and because the objects of knowledge are one and the same, it is certain that the meditations apply everywhere; how then can there be a doubt? To this, he says: "And with respect to each recensional branch... Just as the attributes of the Self cannot belong to the body because of the difference between the body and the Self, so too, the *udgītha* and other elements [differ] according to each Veda.

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of an illustration: "In one's own branch" (*svaśākhā*). The meaning is that because the generality of "udgītha" found in the injunctive sentence "One should meditate on the udgītha" depends upon an individual instance, one must grasp the instance present in one's own Vedic branch; thus, meditations enjoined upon the udgītha and so forth in one Veda cannot apply to the udgītha and so forth located in another Veda, since those Vedas are distinct.

A restriction must be applied to a general term (*sāmānyaśruti*)—namely, the grasping of a proximate individual (*saṃnihitavyaktigraha*)—only where the grasping of the individual alone would otherwise be untenable;
for example, in the case of "Bring the white cow," the term "cow" is restricted to refer to the proximate white individual.

However, since there is no such untenability here, he establishes the conclusion that the universal connected with the individual as a whole is what is to be meditated upon, by means of the passage beginning with "Thus" (*evam*). //55//
Or rather, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of mantras and so forth. (BS 3.3.56)

Alternatively, no contradiction should be suspected here as to how meditative reflections (*pratyaya*) enjoined in one Vedic branch could apply to the *udgītha* and other elements found in another branch;
for there is no contradiction, as is established in the case of mantras and similar elements.
For instance, it is observed that mantras, ritual acts, and qualities originating even in one Vedic branch are incorporated into another branch.

Indeed, for those followers of a Vedic branch who do not have the mantra "kuṭarur asi" prescribed for the taking up of the stone, its application is still seen; likewise, for those who do not have the mantra "kukkuṭo 'si" prescribed, its application is seen, as they take up the stone with either "kukkuṭo 'si" or "kuṭarur asi."

Even for those [schools] where the *prayāja* offerings such as *samit* and so forth are not explicitly mentioned by name, an injunction regarding their qualities is recorded: "The *prayājas* are indeed the seasons; they are to be offered together.

Likewise, even for those for whom there is no instruction regarding a specific genus—such as "the *agnīṣomīya* animal is a goat"—a corresponding mantra-text is found: "Recite the invitatory verse for the omentum and fat of the goat.
Similarly, the adoption of mantras produced in another Veda, such as "O Agni, protect the sacrifice, protect the rite," is observed in other Vedas.

Likewise, the inclusion of the hymn recited by the Bahvṛcas—specifically the verse "He who, as soon as born, was the first wise one" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.6.7)—is observed in the context of the Adhvaryu priest's ritual, where it is stated that "the Sajanīya hymn is to be recited.

Therefore, just as there is a universal application of the ritual acts which serve as the substrata, so too is there an application of the meditative realizations (pratyayas) which depend upon them; thus, there is no contradiction. // 56 //

Previously, the connection between meditations enjoined in one recension (*śākhā*) and the constituent parts (*aṅga*) situated in another recension was stated by accepting the apparent contradiction that arose;

however, now it is said— starting with "Or rather" (*athavā*)— that there is no contradiction at all, because the stated connection is established just like the connection between constituent parts enjoined in one recension and the principal rite (*aṅgin*) situated in another recension.

The meaning is as follows: among the followers of the Yajurveda, there exists the mantra "kukkuṭo 'si" (you are a cock), but the mantra "kuṭarur asi" (you are a woodpecker) does not exist; nevertheless, since both mantras are applied optionally for the purpose of taking up the stone for grinding rice, that [second mantra] also becomes applicable.
He provides an example of the rites included under the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the Sūtra with the words "of those who... (*yeṣām iti*).
This means "of the Maitrāyaṇīyas."

Because the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons are combined, there are five seasons; likewise, there are five *prayāja* offerings. In a context where the ritual action is identical, they are to be offered in the same location. Thus, by the injunction of the quality of "fiveness," the substrata (the *prayājas*) prescribed in other recensions (*śākhā*) become connected. He illustrates this quality with the words: "In the same way, for those who... and so forth.

For the followers of the Yajurveda, the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma is heard in scripture as "an aja" (goat), yet despite this being a specific species, the meaning is that the specific species is included by virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *praiṣa* mantra.
He states another example of such mantras with the word "tathā":
the meaning is that those [mantras] residing in the Sāmaveda are incorporated into the Yajurveda.

"So be it. The meaning is that the *sūktam* characterized by the verse "O people, that Indra" (tatheti 'sa janāsa indra') is the *sajanīyam*; its recitation (*śaṃsana*) is observed in the performance conducted by the *yājuṣa-ādhvaryu*. The meaning of the Vedic text is: "He who, as soon as born, was the first among qualities, the most excellent, and possessed of mind—that is, discernment—he is indeed Indra; such is he, O people (*he janāsaḥ*). //56//
Topic 32: The Superiority of the Infinite (Bhūman). Sūtra 57.
"The greater importance belongs to the whole, like a sacrifice; for thus the scripture shows.
In the narrative beginning with "Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.1), the meditation upon Vaiśvānara both as divided and as undivided is heard.

First, there is meditation on the parts individually, as in: "O Aupamanyava, whom do you meditate upon as the Self? "The deity alone, O Venerable King," he replied. [The teacher said: "This indeed is the Self Vaiśvānara, the One of Excellent Splendor (sutejas), whom you meditate upon as the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.1), and so forth.
Likewise, there is also meditation on the whole: "Of this very Self Vaiśvānara, the head is indeed the One of Excellent Splendor, the eye is the All-formed (viśvarūpa)... and so on.
"Prāṇa is the self with diverse paths, the chest is the manifold, the bladder is wealth, and the feet are the earth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2), and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: should there be meditation here in both ways—on the parts individually as well as on the whole—or only on the whole?
What, then, is the prima facie view?

Since the verb "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) is heard with respect to each individual limb, beginning with Sutejas, and since a distinction of fruits is heard in such passages as, "Therefore, in your family, the *suta*, *prasuta*, and *āsuta* [soma-pressings] are seen" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.1), the prima facie view is that there should be separate meditations for each part. To this, it is replied: In this passage, the intention must be to convey the superiority—that is, the primacy—of the meditation on Vaiśvānara as a whole, which consists of the accumulation of all the constituent parts; [the separate meditations] are not intended.
This applies even to the meditations on individual parts; it is like a sacrificial rite (*kratu*).

Just as in rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the performance of the primary act together with all its auxiliary members (*aṅga*) as a whole is intended, and not the separate performance of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
Nor is it the case that the primary [meditation] endowed with only one part [of its members] is like that;
for why should the "Full" (bhūman) alone be superior?
For scripture demonstrates the superiority of the Full, since it is understood as forming a single syntactical unit.
Indeed, upon considering the preceding and following passages, this single statement is understood to concern the Vaiśvānara-vidyā;

for thus it begins: "Six sages, beginning with Prācīnaśāla and ending with Uddālaka, not attaining full perfection in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, approached King Aśvapati Kaikeya," and then proceeds by assigning to each sage one of the objects of worship, beginning with the sky.
Having caused them to hear this, [the teacher] ordains their status as the head and so forth, saying, "This is indeed the head of the self," and so on; [he further says],
"Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.2).
By such statements, [the text] refutes meditating on [the Self] in its separate parts;

and again, having set aside meditation on the separate parts and continued with meditation on the whole alone, it shows that the fruit rests solely upon the "Full" (bhūman), stating: "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1).

As for the fact that a distinction of fruits is heard in each individual case, such as Sutejas and the rest, this should be understood as follows: since this is so, the fruits of the auxiliary parts are actually accepted as belonging to the principal [meditation] itself. Likewise, the hearing of the verb "he meditates" (upāste) with respect to each member is intended merely to restate the opponent's view, not to enjoin separate meditations on each part.
Therefore, the position that meditation is upon the whole alone is superior.

However, some here, having established that the position of meditating on [the Self] as a whole is superior, claim that the author of the Sūtras must also approve of the position of meditating on it part by part, precisely because of the statement regarding its superiority. This is incorrect;
for when the unity of the sentence is understood, it is improper to assume a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). [Otherwise, one would have to face such consequences as:
"Your head would have fallen off" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.2).

This is because it would contradict such censuring statements as the above; furthermore, since the conclusion [of the Upaniṣads] clearly indicates that all meditations are to be combined, it would be impossible to maintain the absence of such combination in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa); and the statement in the Sūtra regarding "being greater" can also be understood as intending to mean that [the combined view] possesses greater authority. // 57 //
As in the case of the sacrifice (*kratu*) of the Whole (*bhūman*):

the meditation on Vaiśvānara in each of the heavenly worlds and so forth is "meditation on the parts" (*vyastopāsti*), while the meditation on him as a whole is "meditation on the aggregate" (*samastopāsti*); this is the distinction.
The narrative has already been explained previously.

Since both the injunction and the fruit are heard here, and since it is logical that they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), he states the doubt with the word "therein" (*tatra*). In the previous case [of the section beginning] "That same [Brahman] is indeed the True, etc.," the unity of the meditation was stated because of the reference back to the subject matter in the words "That which is the True. Thinking that the present case is not covered by that [previous discussion] due to the absence of such a reason for unity, [the author argues] that just as the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth—despite the proximity (*saṃnidhi*) being set aside by the direct scriptural mention (*śruti*) of the *udgītha* and so forth—are to be combined across all recensions, so too should the separate meditations [be combined].

He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "pratyavayavam" (with respect to each part), asserting that because of the hearing of an injunction and the hearing of a result, the status of being for the sake of praise— which would otherwise apply by virtue of proximity to the entire set of meditations— is set aside, and instead these [meditations] are themselves to be enjoined. When no specific result is mentioned, it should be understood that the very establishment of the prima facie and final positions constitutes the result.

"Suta" means that which has been extracted; "khaṇḍita" refers to the Soma substance itself; "prastuti" means its state as being pressed on all sides, which is a specific stage [of the ritual]. The meaning is that the perfection of the Soma sacrifice is seen in your family.
By the words "The head of Vaiśvānara, indeed, is sutejas" and by the context of the section, it is shown that the meditations on the parts are included within the meditation on the whole.

The intention of the Siddhāntin is as follows: since it has been established that there is a single performance—just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśa* sacrifice—the various fruits of the primary rites and their subsidiaries, which appear in the *arthavādas*, are subsumed under the single fruit of the primary rite; therefore, a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not appropriate.
He refutes the explanation of the "partialist" (*ekadeśin*) by restating it with the words "some [say]... (*kecit*).
If meditation in both ways is the established conclusion (siddhānta), then the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) must be stated as being only meditation on the separate [parts];
yet that is not possible, as he says: "And because it is clear...
How then is the superiority mentioned in the Sūtra? To this he says: "Of what is in the Sūtra..."
The intention is that this statement is made in order to demonstrate that meditations on [the parts] taken individually lack scriptural authority. //57//
Section 33: On the Distinction of Sound and Other Qualities. Sūtra 58.
"Because of the difference in various [attributes] such as sound and so forth.

(BBs 3.3.58) In the preceding section, it was stated that even though there is scriptural mention of different fruits for those beginning with Sutejas, the meditation on them collectively is superior.
Therefore, the notion arises that other meditations mentioned in different scriptural passages might likewise be combined and meditated upon together.
Moreover, a difference in knowledge cannot be discerned when there is no difference in the object of knowledge;
for the object of knowledge is the very form of the knowledge, just as the material substance and the deity are for a sacrifice.
And it is understood that the Lord is one and the same, even though there are various scriptural passages, as in: "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2).
In such passages as "Brahman is Ka, Brahman is Kha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5) and "He whose desires are true and whose resolve is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5), and so forth.

Likewise, there is only one vital breath (prāṇa): "The vital breath, indeed, is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.3); "The vital breath, indeed, is the eldest and the best" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.1);
"The vital breath is the father; the vital breath is the mother" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.1).
In such passages as these,
because the science is one, the knowledge is one;
and even the multiplicity of scriptural texts, under this view, does not have different meanings, since they are intended to convey other attributes.

Therefore, the collection of qualities prescribed in one's own and other Vedic branches, which depend upon a single object [of knowledge], must be combined for the sake of the completeness of the knowledge (*vidyā*). This being the position reached, the author of the Sūtras replies: "They are manifold. Even though the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is non-different, meditations (*vidyā*) of this kind must indeed be distinct.
Why? Because of the difference in words and so forth;
for there is indeed a difference in words such as "one should know" (*veda*), "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*), and "he forms a resolve" (*sa kratuṃ kurute*) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1), and so on.

It has been established previously that a difference in words is a cause for a difference in ritual action, as it was stated: "In the case of a different word, there is a difference in action because of the connection with a distinct [verbal] form.
By the inclusion of the term "etcetera" (*ādi*), other factors such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth should also be applied as causes of difference according to their respective possibilities.

Now, an objection is raised: in cases such as *veda* (he knows) and so forth, only a difference in the word itself is perceived, not a difference in the meaning as in the case of *yajati* (he sacrifices) and others; for all these [words] have no difference in their objective—the activity of the mind—and no other possible meaning exists.
How then can there be a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) due to a difference in words?
This is not a fault;

for even though there is no difference in the object of the mental activity (*manovṛtti*), since there is a difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) resulting from a difference in the adjuncts (*anubandha*), a difference in knowledge is logically established.

Even though the one Lord is the object of worship, distinct qualities are taught for each respective section. Likewise, although the Prāṇa is the single object of worship in various places, because of the difference in its adjuncts— such that in one place it is to be worshipped with one kind of quality and in another with a different kind of quality— a difference in the knowledge (vidyā) is understood when there is a difference in the object of knowledge (vedya).
Nor can it be said here that one [passage] is an injunction for knowledge while the others are injunctions for qualities; for there is no reason for such a distinction in their application,
and because the qualities differ in each context, it is untenable to enjoin them as restatements of a knowledge already established.
Furthermore, on this view, the identical qualities such as *satyakāmatva* (having true desires) and so forth need not be repeated more than once;

nor does there arise a single unified statement (*ekavākyatā*) because each section conveys its own self-sufficiency through the understanding that "this is to be meditated upon by one desiring this," and "that by one desiring that.

Moreover, unlike in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, there is no overarching injunction here by whose force the meditations on the individual parts occurring in each respective section would attain unity as a single statement.

And if the unity of the knowledge were established on the basis of the unity of the knowledge itself—whereby an unrestricted unity of knowledge were asserted everywhere—then the combination of all qualities would be asserted as impossible.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "They are different because of the difference of words and so forth.
Once this section (adhikaraṇa) is settled, the rule "the cognition [of Brahman] is the same in all Vedāntas" and so on is to be understood. // 58 //

Because of the difference in various sounds and so forth, there arises a doubt based on the presence or absence of identity of form as to whether the Brahmavidyā of Śāṇḍilya and others is one or many, and likewise whether the Prāṇavidyā of Saṃvarga and others is one or many. Having established the connection with the example, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "In the previous [case]"...
and because of the identity of form, he says "Moreover" (apica) to state that the Vidyās are one.

If it is argued that if there is identity of knowledge (vidyaikya), then the mention of a knowledge described in one scripture in another scripture would be redundant, he says: "Even the multiplicity of scriptures.
He states the result of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words: "Therefore.

However, considering that in the established conclusion (siddhānta) there is no synthesis of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra), he applies the Sūtra as follows: "Even though there is non-difference of the object of knowledge (vedyābheda)."

Now, an objection is raised: surely a word that denotes a distinct action is a different word, as in "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations. When there is such a difference in words, it is logical that there is a difference in the actions denoted by the injunctive suffixes, because those actions possess specific adjuncts (*anubandha*), because they have accepted distinct objects, and—what this amounts to—because the meanings of the verbal roots (the *bhāvārtha*) are distinct. But in the present case, regarding the practice of meditation (*upāsti*) through words such as "one should know" (*veda*) and "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*), there is no inherent difference as there is between sacrifice, giving, and offering. Furthermore, since the object is the single Brahman characterized by established qualities, there is no difference even from the perspective of the object. How, then, can there be a difference in meditation?
Thus he raises an objection with "nanu" (now, but).
In this sūtra, the difference in words is mentioned merely as a supplementary argument;
rather, it is the qualities and so forth, conveyed by the words "samyak" (perfectly), "hetu" (cause), and "ādi" (and so on), that constitute the actual reasons for the plurality of the vidyās.
For even an established quality possesses the nature of being an effect (kāryatva) by virtue of its connection with an action.

Just as qualities such as "redness" possess the nature of being an effect through their connection with the mental process (*bhāvanā*) of purchasing, so too, in their respective contexts, because the forms of the objects of meditation (*upāsya*) are non-different when qualified by those various qualities—which are themselves to be accomplished through their connection with the mental process of meditation (*upāstibhāvanā*) as enjoined at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*)—there is a difference in the meditations (*upāsanā*).
This is just as there is a difference in the meditations on a king based on the difference in qualities such as the parasol and the fly-whisk.
Just as there is a difference in sacrifices due to the difference between the qualities of *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) and *vājina* (whey), so too,

[the author] resolves the objection by stating "this is not a fault" and so forth, that there is a difference [between meditations] because of the difference in the connection with fruits for each respective *vidyā*, and because of the difference in designations such as "the small" (*dahara*) and "Śāṇḍilya.
He says "and here it is not one" to refute the claim that the multiplicity of scriptural texts is merely for the purpose of enjoining other qualities.

Furthermore, he states "and because of multiplicity" (*anekatvācca*) to show that if one were to refer back to the knowledge already established (*prāptavidyānuvāda*) while enjoining multiple unestablished qualities (*aprāptānekaguṇavidhāna*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Moreover, on the view that the knowledge is one, the repeated mention of the qualities would be redundant;
nor is it for the sake of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), since that is already established by the oneness of Brahman itself.

Regarding the position that the meditations (vidyās) are distinct, [the author] states "And not in this case" to show that since the qualities (guṇas) are not obtained [in one place], that meditation must be undertaken for the sake of obtaining them. He states "In each section," etc., to show that the meditations are distinct because there is no unity of injunction due to the difference in results, and because it is impossible to meditate on all the qualities [simultaneously]. The meaning is that there is a difference in results: for the meditator on the *dahara* (the small ether), there is "unrestricted movement in all worlds," while for the meditator on *vaiśvānara*, there is "eating food everywhere," and so forth.

[Objection: "Surely, once the plurality of meditations (vidyā-nānātva) has been established, it is appropriate to consider afterwards whether the Dahara-vidyā and others are one or many in each Vedānta; why then is that considered at the outset? To this he says: "And when [the difference] is established" (sthite ca). The meaning is that the section on the plurality of meditations is properly connected at the very beginning of the Pāda, whereas its treatment here is incidental (prāsaṅgika). //58//
Section 34: The Topic of Alternatives (Vikalpa-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 59.
There is an option because the fruit is not differentiated.

(BBs 3.3.59) Since the distinction between the knowledges (*vidyā*) has been established, it is now considered whether there should be a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*) according to one's wish,
or whether there is necessarily only an option.
Since the distinction between the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) is established therein, there is no reason whatsoever for a rule of their mandatory combination (*samuccaya*).
[Objection: But is it not observed that even distinct rites such as the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are subject to a rule of mandatory combination?
[Response: This is not a fault.
For in that case, the scriptural statement regarding eternality is the reason; however, there is no such scriptural statement regarding the eternality of the knowledges.
Therefore, there is neither a rule of combination nor a rule of option.
Since there is no prohibition against one who is engaged in one knowledge undertaking another knowledge,
it follows by the method of exhaustion that one may proceed according to one's desire.
But surely, because their fruits are indistinguishable, it is logical that they should be treated as alternatives.
For instance: "consisting of mind, having the vital breath as its body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2);
"Bliss is Brahman, space is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5);
"whose desires are true, whose resolves are true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5).
Thus, these and other [paths] are observed to have the attainment of the Lord as their equal fruit.
This is not a fault,

because even among ritual acts that are means for attaining heaven and so forth— which share the same type of fruit— it is seen that there is a distinction between those performed with desire and those performed without desire.
Therefore, when there is the possibility of obtaining [the result] according to one's preference, it must be that these [means] are optional (vikalpa) and not to be combined (samuccaya).
Why?
Because their fruit is not distinguished [in quality].
For the fruit of these meditations is indistinguishable, namely, the direct realization of the object of meditation.
Once the object of meditation, such as the Lord, has been realized through one meditation, a second meditation would be purposeless.
Moreover, it is impossible.
Because, according to the view that [knowledge] must be combined with direct realization, such realization would be a cause for mental distraction;
moreover, the Śrutis demonstrate that the fruit of knowledge consists in the attainment of direct realization: "He for whom there is this certainty, and no doubt... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4).
Thus, there are such passages as "Having become a god, he goes to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2).

Therefore, having selected any one of the meditations that yield indistinguishable fruits, one should be devoted to it until that fruit is attained through the direct realization of the object of meditation. // 59 //
[This is] the section on "Mental Construction" (vikalpa).

Having stated the essential nature of the vidyās, he states the word "established" (sthita) to indicate the logical connection based on their being the foundation for what follows, namely that the method of practice is now being determined here.
There are three kinds of vidyās: those involving identification with the Self (ahaṅgraha), those standing apart from it (taṭastha), and those dependent on auxiliary members (aṅgāśrita).

Regarding that, since there is equality in the multiplicity of the meditations (vidyās) with respect to both acting according to one's desire (*yathākāmya*) and optionality (*vikalpa*), he states a doubt:

"What [is the case]? The difference in results is as follows: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no fixed rule (*aniyama*) because performance may be according to one's wish; in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is a fixed rule because performance is by way of option. Therein, he establishes the absence of a fixed rule with the words beginning "because it is situated therein" (*tatra sthitatvāt*):

just as there is an option between rice and barley because they have the same result—a single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—so too it is logical that for these meditations there should be a fixed rule of option.
This is because their fruits are equal.
Nor should it be argued that even for one desiring an abundance of fruit, the combination of optional (kāmya) rites is not observed;

for although there may be a difference in fruit subsequent to the direct realization of the Lord, these meditations on the "I-am-Brahman" (ahaṅgraha-upāsti) are equal insofar as their fruit consists in the nature of direct realization itself.

And since one [moment of cognition] cannot be produced by another, and because there would be no further function for the second [moment], as well as because it would obstruct it by causing distraction of the mind—this is the meaning of the Siddhāntabhāṣya.
To the objection that "let there be no direct realization," he says: "and that which is to be accomplished through direct realization. Of which person...
The meaning is that there arises the direct realization "I am indeed the Lord," and there is no doubt as to whether he is the Lord or not; for him alone is the attainment of the Lord.
The meaning of another Vedic text is that, having realized divinity through meditative cultivation even while living, one attains the gods after the fall of the body.
He concludes the method of performing the *ahaṃgrahas* with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). //59//
Section 35: The Topic of Optional Rites (Kāmyādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 60.
But the optional rites may be combined according to one's desire, or they may not, because the reason for the previous [rule] is absent;
this is a counter-example to the argument that "the fruit is undifferentiated.
Furthermore, regarding those optional meditations [vidyās], it is said: "He who knows this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters does not weep over the death of a son" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.15.2).

And in such passages as, "He who meditates on Name as Brahman— so far as Name extends, so far he has unlimited freedom" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5), there is no requirement for direct realization, because these [meditations] accomplish their own fruit by means of an unseen self (adṛṣṭa) inherent in the action.
Therefore, they may or may not be combined according to one's desire, since the aforementioned reason [for non-combination] is absent.
Because there is no reason for an alternative [view], as the previous [position] possesses an undifferentiated fruit. // 60 //

36. *Yathāśrayabhāvādhikaraṇam* (Sūtras 61–66). Regarding the optional meditations (*kāmyopāsanās*): here, the subject matter consists of those meditations that are "subsidiary" (*taṭastha*). Since there is a doubt as before—whether there is an option (*vikalpa*) among them or whether they may be performed according to one's desire—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because they are equally meditations (*upāsti*), there is an option just as in the case of the "I-grasping" (*ahaṅgraha*) meditation. To this, the refutation (*apavāda*) is stated:
He establishes the conclusion with the words "aviśiṣṭa" (not distinct):

whoever knows this very Vāyu as the calf of the quarters thus conceived as cows, he does not weep—that is, he does not experience the weeping caused by the death of a son; the meaning is that he always has a living son.
The intended meaning is that, in the illustration of the "I-grasping" (ahaṅgraha) view, the state of being a means to direct realization (sākṣātkāra) is the limiting condition (upādhi). //60//
Just as there is a state of dependence upon their respective bases in the case of the limbs. (BBs 3.3.61)

Regarding the doubt as to whether the meditative realizations (*pratyaya*) prescribed in the three Vedas that are based on the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), such as the *udgītha* and so forth, should be combined or may be performed according to one's preference—the Sūtra states: "As is the nature of their bases.

For just as their bases, such as the hymns of praise (*stotra*) and so forth, exist collectively, so too do the meditative realizations, because meditative realizations are dependent upon their bases. (61)

Now, in order to state the sequence of performance for the meditations (*upāsanā*) connected with the constituent parts (*aṅga*) [of the sacrifice], he first raises an objection with the words "In the constituent parts" (*aṅgeṣu*).
He states the doubt because these meditations are dependent on the constituent parts and yet possess their own fruits: "Is it...?

The meaning of the sūtra is this: just as there is a rule of mandatory collective performance for the constituent parts when the sacrifice itself is being performed, so too there is that same rule regarding the meditations dependent on those parts when the constituent parts themselves are being performed.

[Objection: But was it not stated in the sūtra *tannirdhāraṇāniyamaḥ* that those [meditations] which depend on the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are non-subsidiaries (*anaṅga*), like the *godohana* vessel? How then can there be a suspicion of their being combined like the subsidiaries, since they are non-subsidiaries? [Response: The meaning is this: the intention behind the objection is that the one who thinks that if the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), while causing the subsidiaries to be performed, were not to cause the meditations to be performed as well, then their status of depending on those subsidiaries would be useless—such a person might harbor this doubt. //61//
And [the authority of the Veda is established] by the fact that it was taught by the learned. 3.3.62.
Just as the bases, such as the *stotra* and so forth, are included within the three [services], so too are the dependent conditions (*pratyaya*).
The meaning is that there is no distinction whatsoever created by the instruction between the auxiliary members (*aṅga*) and the conditions that depend upon them. // 62 //
In that case, there would also be a combination of the *godohana* vessel; to this he says: "And because it is taught.
"Teaching" (*śiṣṭi*) means instruction or injunction.
The meaning is that because there is no difference in being enjoined, there is a combination due to its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

However, there is no rule for the mandatory performance of the *godohana* vessel, because it is prescribed as a substitute for the *camasa* cup; if it were mandatory, the injunction for the *camasa* would be rendered useless.

But since the meditations (*upāsanās*) are not prescribed as substitutes for any specific subsidiary (*aṅga*), the rule of their combined performance (*samuccaya*) is not contradicted—this is the intended meaning. //62//
Because of their combination. (BBs 3.3.63)
Furthermore, the passage, "Indeed, from the Hotṛ's seat he repairs even a defective Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.5),

by stating that through the greatness of the knowledge of the identity of the Praṇava and the Udgītha, the Udgātṛ priest repairs the injury arising in his own ritual act from the act of the Hotṛ, indicates the inclusion of a meditative practice taught in one Veda within another Veda, on the basis of the commonality of the connection with the ritual elements taught in that other Veda.
The observation of an indicative mark. // 63 //
The indicative mark for the combination [of meditations] is the phrase "from the aggregate" (*samāhārāt*).

In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, there is an injunction for the meditation on the identity of the *praṇava* and the *udgītha* in the passage, "That which is the *praṇava* of the Ṛgvedins is the *udgītha* of the Sāmavedins.
The explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) regarding its fruit begins with, "From the Hotṛ's seat," and so forth.

By the term *hotṛṣadana*, which denotes the place where the Hotṛ recites, the act of recitation itself is indicated. The meaning is as follows: even if the Udgātṛ has performed the *udgītha* poorly due to errors in tone (*svara*) and so forth, he indeed makes it flawless by means of "reconciling" it with the Hotṛ’s well-performed recitation, through the power of meditating on the identity of his own *udgītha* with the *praṇava* being recited by the Hotṛ.
To this he says: "Speaking thus.

The very connection observed between the meditation on the *udgītha* found in the Sāmaveda and the *praṇava* mentioned in the Ṛgveda serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the combination of meditations enjoined across all Vedāntas; for there is a similarity in that the objects of meditation in the form of the *praṇava*, as well as the meditations themselves, are mentioned in other Vedas, and thus the connection with the ancillaries (*aṅgas*) mentioned in other Vedas is likewise established.
The meaning is "because of their equality. //63//
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of the qualities. (BS 3.3.64)

And with respect to the Vidyā, it makes known the syllable Om, which is the substratum of that Vidyā and common to the three Vedas, in the passage: "By that [Om], this triple knowledge proceeds; one intones 'Om', one recites 'Om', one chants the Udgītha 'Om'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.9).
Therefore, because the substratum is common, the supported [Vidyā] is also common; this is indeed a perception of an indicative mark (liṅga).
Alternatively, it is because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of the qualities (*guṇa*).
If these ritual qualities, such as the *udgītha* and so forth, were not common to all performances, then there would be no coexistence of the meditative realizations (*pratyaya*) based upon them.
However, those *udgītha* elements and others are declared by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), which encompasses all constituent parts, to be common to all performances.
And thus, because the basis coexists [with it], the conditions also coexist. // 64 //

He states another indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "guṇa"—to show that because the object of meditation, the syllable *Oṃ*, is common [to all three Vedas], the performance of the meditations based upon it is understood as being to be practiced collectively.

The meaning is that by means of that *Oṃ* syllable, the ritual action (*karman*) prescribed in the three Vedas proceeds. Having explained this very point through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he explains it again through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "or else" (*athavā*). //64//
Or rather, it is not so, because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture]. (BBs 3.3.65)
The phrase "or not" serves to exclude that alternative.
It is not the case that the existence of the meditations (*upāsanā*) which depend [on something] must necessarily follow the existence of their substratum.
Why? Because there is no scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding their coexistence with it.

For instance, the coexistence of the subsidiary elements—such as the *stotra* hymns and so forth—prescribed in the three Vedas is heard in scripture: "Having taken up the cup (*graha*), or having drawn out the goblet (*camasa*), he begins the *stotra*; he recites the *stotra* after [the *prastāva*]; O *Prastotṛ*, sing the *Sāman*; O *Hotṛ*, recite this *yajyā*," and so on.
But there is no such scriptural statement regarding the coexistence of meditations (*upāsanā*).

Objection: But would not the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) bring about the simultaneous occurrence of these [meditations]? We say: no; because meditations have the person as their purpose.
For the injunction of performance would bring about the simultaneous occurrence of the *udgītha* and other such elements that are subservient to the ritual (*ṛtvartha*).

We have already stated under the sūtra "For the fruit is separate, because there is no obstruction" (BS 3.3.42) that meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, although resting upon elements that serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*), lead to the goal of the person (*puruṣārtha*), just like the *godohana* vessel and other such things.

This very distinction based on scriptural instruction—that some auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) serve the purpose of the sacrifice while others, such as the meditations resting upon them, serve the purpose of the person—is the difference between them.

Furthermore, the two [other] indicative marks (*liṅga*) are not grounds for the coexistence of the meditations, because there is an absence of both scripture (*śruti*) and logical reasoning (*nyāya*) to support it.

Nor can it be understood that because the substratum is withdrawn in its entirety for each individual performance, those things dependent upon it must likewise be so; for meditations are not subject to that rule.

Indeed, although meditations are dependent on their substrata, they may well cease to exist in the absence of a substratum, yet they do not require a rule of coexistence with the substratum by virtue of being necessarily concomitant with it, precisely because there is no scriptural statement regarding such coexistence.
Therefore, meditations should be performed according to one's own desire. // 65 //

Since there is no fixed rule regarding the desire for the fruit, it is logical that there is likewise no fixed rule regarding its worship; because there is no evidence for a mandatory combination of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), he establishes the final conclusion with the words "Or rather not.

Indeed, the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) regulates the execution of the primary rite together with its auxiliaries, but it does not include those things which are not auxiliaries; thus he says, "We say: No."
The meaning is that various meditations (upāsanās) performed with different intentions should not be practiced in combination within a single sacrifice,
because they have distinct results, just like the *godohana* vessel;
this refutes what was stated [by the opponent] regarding "the teaching" (*śiṣṭeḥ*) by saying "this very [one]."

He states "and because of the commonality of qualities" (*guṇasādhāraṇya*)—referring to the two indicative marks (*liṅga*) previously mentioned—which merely indicate what is already established by other means of knowledge and do not themselves prove it, since they reside within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). He says "and further" (*paraṃ ca*). He refutes the second interpretation of the *guṇasādhāraṇya* sūtra with "nor" (*na ca*).
To the question, "If there is no being prompted by that [the primary act], how can there be dependence upon it? he replies with "dependence" (*āśraya*).
This alone is their dependence on the factors (aṅga): that they do not exist when the factors are absent; it does not mean, however, that they pervade the factors—this is the meaning. //65//
And because of [the Buddha’s] appearance. (BBs 3.3.66)

And scripture demonstrates the coexistence of all cognitions: "Thus indeed does the Brahmā, knowing this, protect the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.17.10).
For if all cognitions were withdrawn, everyone would be omniscient, and thus the fact that the others are to be protected by the Brahmā who possesses such knowledge could not have been proclaimed.
Therefore, according to one's desire, there may be either a combination or an optionality of the meditations. // 66 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.

Furthermore, because it is stated that the learned Brahman priest is to be protected by the other officiating priests (ṛtvij), there is no simultaneous performance of all meditations; thus he says, "And because it is seen.

The meaning is that the Brahman's "knowledge of such" (*evaṃvittva*) consists in his possessing the knowledge of the expiatory rites, such as the *vyāhṛti* oblations, for the omission of auxiliary elements prescribed in the Ṛgveda and other Vedas. //66//
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīraka* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter, titled "The Consolidation of Qualities in the Knowledge of the Higher and Lower Brahman."
Herein is the investigation into the internal and external means for the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman.

Third Chapter, Fourth Section / Section on the Goal of Human Life (Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 1–17 1. *sarvāpekṣā* sūtra 1: "There is a need for all [auxiliaries]. 2. *śamadamādi* sūtra 2: "[The means] such as tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth. 3. *sarvānnānumati* sūtra 3: "There is permission to eat all food [in times of distress]. 4. *achodanā* sūtra 4: "[That passage is] not an injunction. 5. *prāṇātyaye* sūtra 5: "[This applies] when life is at stake. 6. *abādhāt* sūtra 6: "Because there is no contradiction. 7. *api smaryate* sūtra 7: "It is also recorded in Smṛti. 8. *vidhūnana* sūtra 8: "[The passage concerning] 'shaking off' refers to the body. 9. *sāmparāya* sūtra 9: "[The passage concerning] the journey after death. 10. *gati* sūtra 10: "[The passage concerning] the destination. 11. *aniyamah* sūtra 11: "There is no fixed rule. 12. *yāvadadhikāram* sūtra 12: "As long as the qualification lasts. 13. *akṣaradhiyām* sūtra 13: "Regarding the meditations on the Imperishable (*akṣara*). 14. *iyadāmananāt* sūtra 14: "On account of the mention of this much [in both texts]. 15. *antarā bhūtagrāmavat* sūtra 15: "In between, like the group of beings. 16. *mānasvat* sūtra 16: "Like Mānasa. 17. *pratyayādhikaraṇam* sūtra 17: "The section on the mental [meditation]. [End of Third Chapter, Fourth Section]
"From this [knowledge] follows the human goal, according to Śabda; thus says Bādarāyaṇa.

Now, investigating whether the knowledge of the Self derived from the Upaniṣads enters into ritual action solely by way of a qualified person, or whether it is an independent means for accomplishing the human goal, he begins with the final conclusion: "From this follows the human goal."
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the human goal is accomplished through the knowledge of the Self prescribed in our Vedānta, which is independent [of ritual action].
From what is this understood? He says: "From the Word" (śabdāt).
For instance: "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3).
"He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9);
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1);
"The man who has a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad).
Thus [it is said]:

"Having begun with 'That Self which is free from evil' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), [the text continues] 'He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1)."

Beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6) and concluding with "This much, indeed, my dear, is immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), scripture of this kind proclaims that knowledge alone is the cause of the supreme human goal. // 1 //

In connection with the discussion of the branches of ritual action (*karmāṅga-vidyā*), a doubt arises as to whether the knowledge of Brahman might also be a branch of ritual action; to address this, [the Sūtra] states: "The human goal [arises] from that [knowledge], according to the Word—so says Bādarāyaṇa. In the preceding section (*pāda*), the nature of the higher and lower knowledges was determined through the discussion on the integration of their attributes (*guṇopasaṃhāra*). In this section, it is established that these knowledges are not branches of ritual action but are causes for the human goal. Consequently, when there is a requirement for auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), external auxiliaries such as sacrifice and internal auxiliaries such as tranquility (*śama*) are described; thus, they share the same subject matter of knowledge.

Regarding the connection between the two [sections], first, having taken the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) as the subject, he states the doubt arising from the conflicting views of the disputants with the words "Now" (*atha*).
In the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a combination of knowledge and action through the relationship of principal and subordinate;
in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), liberation results from knowledge alone—this is the difference in the result.

It should be understood that in the Brahmavidyā taught by Prajāpati beginning with "That which is the Self," the mention of the worlds and so forth as the fruit of saguṇa-vidyā is stated with the intention that they are included within the bliss of liberation (mokṣānanda). //1//

"Because it is a supplement [to ritual action], it is a commendatory statement (arthavāda) regarding human goals, as in the case of other [acts]; thus says Jaimini.

Since the self's agency is a supplement to ritual action, its knowledge—like the sprinkling of rice (*vrīhi-prokṣaṇa*) and so forth—is connected to ritual action precisely through its object; therefore, Master Jaimini considers that the scriptural mention of a fruit in regard to the knowledge of the self, whose purpose is already understood [from its connection to action], is merely a commendatory statement, just as it is with other acts concerning substances, purificatory rites, and rituals.
"Whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood, he hears no evil report;
in that [he uses it], he surely takes away the very eye of his rival.

Since the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are performed, this armor is indeed made for the sacrifice, as an act for the sacrificer's overcoming of his rival"—such scriptural declarations of results (*phalaśruti*) are merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
It is just like that.

But how can it be suspected that this knowledge of the Self, which is taught outside of any ritual context (*anārabhyādhīta*), enters into the ritual even in the absence of any reason such as *prakaraṇa* (context) and so forth?
If it is argued that its connection with the ritual is established through the sentence (*vākya*) by way of the agent (*kartṛ*), we say no.
Because it is impossible for that [connection] to be established through syntactical connection (*vākya*).
For even in the case of those [injunctions] studied as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*), a connection with a sacrifice based on syntactical connection is possible only through some non-deviating medium.
The agent, however, is a deviating medium, because he is common to both worldly and Vedic actions.

Therefore, it is not established that knowledge of the Self is connected to ritual action by means of that [knowledge of the body's distinctness]. No; for the cognition of the Self as distinct from the body has no application other than in Vedic rituals. Indeed, the knowledge of a Self distinct from the body is not of use in worldly activities.
For in every respect, engagement with objects perceived through the senses is possible [without such knowledge].

However, regarding Vedic injunctions whose fruits are realized only after the fall of the body, engagement is not possible without the knowledge of a self distinct from the body; thus, the cognition of this distinction is required.

Now, one might object that the Upanishadic vision, which concerns a non-transmigrating self characterized by attributes such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), could not be an auxiliary to engagement [with ritual action]. This is not so.
Because it is the transmigrating self alone, as indicated by terms such as "dear" (*priya*), that is taught as the object to be seen;
the attributes such as "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) will serve merely for the purpose of praise.

But has this not been established in various places: that Brahman, the cause of the world, which is non-transmigrating, is indeed taught in the Upaniṣads as the ultimate essential nature of the transmigrating self?
Truth has indeed been established; however, for the sake of strengthening it, an objection and its resolution are presented by way of the result, like the driving in of a pillar. // 2 //
Having thus introduced the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "because of being a subsidiary" (*śeṣatvāt*).
In the sūtra, the term *arthavāda* is to be repeated;
the meaning is that it is an *arthavāda* because it is a statement concerning the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) resulting from knowledge.

The meaning is that knowledge is an auxiliary to ritual action because, while it does not itself constitute a fruit, it serves as a substratum for the remainder of the ritual, just like the sprinkling of water or the quality of being made of parṇa-wood.
The mention of Jaimini is intended to indicate that this is a formal discussion (kathāvāda) between a teacher and a student for the purpose of determining the truth.

When the self, which is a constituent part [of the ritual], has its purpose understood through the fruit of the whole, then the scriptural mention of a fruit regarding the knowledge that is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) based upon that [self] is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). In this regard, there is the following illustration: "Just as..."—where the *parṇa*-wood is a substance (*dravya*), and the anointing of the sacrificer is a refinement (*saṃskāra*).
The meaning is "in those [rites]," namely the prayāja and other such rituals.
"Varman" means armor.
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) raises an objection: "How so?"—on the grounds that self-knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action, as there is no evidence for it.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says: "As the agent" (*kartriti*).

For it is logical that the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, which is taught as unconnected to any specific rite (*anārabhyādhīta*), becomes an auxiliary to the sacrifice through the medium of the *juhū* ladle, because the *juhū*—by virtue of pervading the sacrifice—serves to bring the sacrifice to mind.
However, such a connection with the sacrifice for the knowledge of the Self is not tenable on the basis of the statement, "The Self is to be seen."
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) refutes [the opponent] by stating, "No," because the self lacks pervasion by the sacrifice.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) replies, "Not so, because of non-distinction," meaning that for the self known as distinct from the body, there is indeed pervasion by the sacrifice.
[The siddhāntin replies: "In no way."
The meaning is: "even as the self of the body.

He raises an objection, saying "But [the text says] 'one whose sins are destroyed,'" suggesting that even if knowledge of the agent distinct from the body is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*), knowledge of Brahman as the non-agent self is not a subsidiary element.

The purpose of the reply is this: there is no nature of a non-agent distinct from the enjoyer, which is indicated by the mark of the object of enjoyment through the statement, "That Self for whose sake wife and so forth are dear—that Self should be seen. Thus, the non-agent is not separate from the enjoyer.
He raises the doubt, "But how can that which has been established starting from the *janmādi-sūtra* not exist? with the words "nanu" (but).

He replies, "True," meaning that the fruit of the Vedāntas is the knowledge of the true nature [of Brahman], and its firmness is brought about by investigating whether that knowledge serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*) or the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). //2//
Because we observe their conduct. (BBs 3.4.3)
"There was Janaka, the King of Videha, who performed a sacrifice with many gifts" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1);
"I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice, O venerable sirs" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.5)—
such passages, even concerning those who know Brahman, show their connection to ritual action within texts that have other primary purposes.
Likewise, from the observation of the instruction of his sons and other such acts by Uddālaka and others, their connection with the householder's life (gārhasthya) is understood.

If the goal of human existence were accomplished through knowledge alone, why would they perform rituals involving manifold exertions? This is according to the maxim: "If one should find honey on an arka tree, why should he go to the mountain? // 3 //

He states that the observation of the ritual conduct of those who know Brahman is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the fact that the knowledge of Brahman has ritual action as its auxiliary: "Ācāra... etc.
The meaning is that he performed a sacrifice (*īje*).

Addressing the Brāhmaṇas with the words "O Venerable Ones," the King of Kekaya, a knower of Brahman, says: "I am about to sacrifice—I shall perform a sacrifice; may the venerable ones dwell here. This is the meaning.
The phrase "in those concerned with other matters" means in those concerned with the injunctions for knowledge (*vidyā*).

Having obtained knowledge, which is the means to liberation involving little effort, they should not perform ritual action, which involves great effort; regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "nearby" (*akva*), meaning in close proximity.
Even if the reading is "arka," the meaning is exactly this. //3//
Because of that scriptural statement. (BBs 3.4.4)

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement that knowledge is subordinate to ritual action— namely, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad, that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10)— knowledge by itself is not the cause of the supreme human goal.

He states that there is also a scriptural mention in the instrumental case to show that the knowledge of Brahman is an auxiliary part of ritual action: "Because of the scriptural mention of that" (tacchruteḥ). //4//
Because of simultaneous undertaking. (BBs 3.4.5)
