Furthermore, because the passage "Knowledge and action both take hold of him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2) shows that knowledge and action act as concurrent causes in the commencement of the fruit, knowledge does not possess independence. // 5 //
He states another indicative mark with the word "samit":
the meaning is that knowledge and action follow him as he goes to the other world. //5//
Because [the meditation] is prescribed for one who possesses that [knowledge]. (BS 3.4.6)

And scriptural texts of this kind, such as, "Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the rules, and having returned home at the conclusion of the service to the teacher, let him dwell in his household, studying his own sacred recitation in a clean place" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1), show that one who possesses knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda is qualified for ritual action; therefore, even for this reason, knowledge does not have the status of being a cause of results through its own independence.
But surely, here [in the cited text], only the mere study of the Veda is heard, not the knowledge of its meaning?
This is not a fault;
for it is established that the study of the Veda, being for a visible purpose, extends as far as the comprehension of its meaning. (6)

Performing service to the guru as his duty, having studied the Veda according to the prescribed rules with the remaining time after [other obligations], and immediately thereafter having performed the *abhisamāvartana* (the rite of returning home) from the teacher’s household— that is, from the state of studenthood (*brahmacarya*)— and being established in the household life (*gārhasthya*), he dwells in the family; performing daily the study of his own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) in a pure place, and practicing other obligatory duties such as the daily rites, he [attains] the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
The meaning of the Vedic text is that [one] attains [the result].
Just as threshing extends only until the removal of the husks, so too does study extend until the comprehension of the meaning.
This is established in the Pūrvatantra (Mīmāṃsā) that since the visible result known as the comprehension of meaning is possible, it is improper for study to have an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose.
And therefore, since even the Brahman is the meaning of the Veda, the injunction of ritual action pertains to one who possesses the knowledge of it; such is the sense. //6//
And because of the rule. BBs_3,4.7.
"Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years;
thus it is for you, and not otherwise than this—action does not cling to a man" (Īśa Upaniṣad 2).

Likewise, from such injunctions as "This Agnihotra is indeed a lifelong sacrificial session; for one is released from it either by old age or by death," it follows that knowledge is a mere supplement to ritual action.
He states that even the lifelong observance of ritual action (*karmaniyama*) is a sign here, saying "and because of the observance" (*niyamācca*).
While performing actions in this body, one may wish to live for a hundred years; thus, while you live as a performer of action, O man, evil action does not cling to you.
There is no way other than through action [to achieve this].
The meaning is that there is no higher good (śreya) without action (karma).
"Ending with old age and death" means having old age and death as its limit. //7//
This being the position reached, the author provides the following rebuttal:
"But because of the additional instruction, Bādarāyaṇa holds this view, for that is seen [in scripture].
The word "but" (tu) reverses the previous position.
As it was stated: "Because it is a subordinate element, it is a statement of human purpose" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.2).
Thus, that is not tenable.
Why?
Because of the teaching of something additional.

If the transmigrating self alone—the embodied agent and enjoyer—were taught in the Vedāntas as being distinct from the body alone, then, in the manner described, the mention of results would be a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda).

However, in the Vedāntas, that which is superior to the body—the non-transmigrating Lord, the Supreme Self—is taught as the object of knowledge; He is devoid of the attributes of transmigratory existence such as agency and so forth, and is characterized by qualities such as being "free from sin" (apahatapāpmā).

Furthermore, that knowledge does not become an instigator of actions; on the contrary, as he will state in the sūtra "And [it brings about] the destruction" (Brahmasūtra 3.4.16), it rather cuts off actions.

Therefore, the view of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa—that "the human goal [arises] from this [knowledge], because of the scriptural word" (Brahmasūtra 3.4.1)—stands exactly as it is, and cannot be shaken by fallacious arguments such as its being a subordinate element (śeṣatva).
For indeed, the Śrutis show that Supreme Self, who is distinct from the embodied self and so forth, as follows: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9);
"From fear of Him the wind blows" (Taittirīya 2.8.1);
"A great terror, a raised thunderbolt" (Kaṭha 6.2).
"Under the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9);
"It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3)—such passages as these [are the evidence].

As for the reference to the transmigrating self alone—indicated by [the mention of] "dear things" and so forth—as the object of knowledge, as in: "But it is for the sake of the self that everything becomes dear;
the self, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), and "He who breathes with the breath, he is your self, which is within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1).
Beginning with "This person who is seen in the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.4) and continuing with "I shall explain this very same one to you further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3),
and so forth— that too [is consistent] with the statement: "The Ṛgveda is the breath of this great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10).
"There is he who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1);
"Having attained the highest light, he emerges in his own true form; he is the Supreme Person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
Through such supplementary statements, when there is indeed a desire to teach a higher [truth], the intention is one of absolute non-difference, and thus there is no contradiction.
For the supreme Lord alone is the ultimate, real nature of the embodied self;

its state as an embodied being, however, is produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), as evidenced by such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) and "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
This is established by such scriptural passages as these.
Furthermore, all of this has been described by us in detail previously in various places. // 8 //

He establishes the final conclusion—that knowledge of reality is not an auxiliary part of ritual action—on the grounds that there is no remaining ritual duty for the agent who is the transcendent, non-transmigrating Self; this is indicated by the word "transcendent" (*adhika*).
Because of the supplementary statement, "of this great [Self]," the Self to be seen, which is indicated by what is dear, must be understood as the Supreme Self alone.
Furthermore, he who impels the vital breaths and so forth is also the Supreme Self alone, because of the supplementary statement regarding the transcendence of hunger and other such needs.

Likewise, the person within the eye (*akṣipuruṣa*) is also the Supreme (*para*), because of the supplementary statement that he is the "supreme light" (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*). Thus, the distinction [between the two] is established. If it is accepted that the reference back to the individual soul (*jīva-anukarṣaṇa*) is intended to express non-difference (*abheda-abhiprāya*), how can there be no contradiction? [One might argue: "Because non-difference contradicts the state of being an individual soul. To this, he says: "The supreme state of the Lord" (*pārameśvaram*).

The reason previously stated—that knowledge is a subordinate part of ritual action (*karma-aṅga*) because, while not itself a fruit, it is the locus for the remainder of the ritual—is unestablished (*asiddha*); this is the sense. //8//
But the perception [of the object] is equal. (BBs 3.4.9)

As for what was said—that knowledge is a supplement to ritual action because we observe [the learned] following certain practices—we reply: the observation of such practices is equally applicable even if knowledge is not a supplement to action.
For there is a scriptural passage: "Knowing this, indeed, the Ṛṣis of the Kāvaṣeya clan said: 'For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices?'"
"Indeed, knowing this very thing, the ancients did not perform the Agnihotra sacrifice. Having known that Self,
Brāhmaṇas rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of mendicancy" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1).
Such instances are of this nature;

even among those who know Brahman, such as Yājñavalkya and others, steadfastness in the Self is observed from scriptural passages such as: "Having said, 'O dear one, this much indeed is immortality,' Yājñavalkya departed" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
Furthermore, the observation of the indicative mark in the passage, "I am indeed about to sacrifice, O venerable sirs" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.5), pertains specifically to the Vaiśvānara-vidyā;
and it is possible for a knowledge of Brahman that possesses limiting adjuncts to be seen as being associated with ritual action.
But even here, there is no status as an auxiliary to the ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*), because of the absence of context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such factors. // 9 //
Furthermore, regarding what was stated [in Brahma-sūtra 3.4.4], "Because of that scriptural statement," we reply here:
it is not universal.
The scriptural passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10), does not refer to all forms of knowledge,
because it is connected to the specific knowledge under discussion.
And the Udgītha-vidyā under discussion is that found in the passage: "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1). // 10 //

Since renunciation is also seen among those who know Brahman just as action is, he says "But it is the same" (tulyaṃ tu) to show that their outward mark consisting of the performance of action is established otherwise—as being for the sake of the welfare of the world (lokasaṃgraha).
Furthermore, he says "Moreover" (api ca) to show that he who possesses action is not a knower of Brahman.
Then, lest it be argued that the Vaiśvānara-vidyā might be a subsidiary part of ritual action, he says "But not" (na tu).

The sense is that even for those who know Brahman, action performed for the sake of maintaining the world does not constitute [binding] action, because they lack the sense of ego-identification and thus possess no [karmic] qualification [for its fruits]. // 9 // // 10 //
Division is like [the division of] a hundred. BBs 3.4.11.

As for what was said— that the statement "knowledge and action follow after him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2), which speaks of their simultaneous following, is an indicative mark of the non-independence of knowledge—
that is now answered: here a distinction must be understood, namely that knowledge follows after one person, while action follows after another.
It is like "a hundredfold.

Just as when it is said, "Let a hundred be given to these two," it is given by dividing it—fifty to one and fifty to the other—in the same way. Furthermore, this statement regarding "conjoint undertaking" (*samanvārambha*) does not concern those seeking liberation, as seen in the passage: "Thus, indeed, he who desires... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
This is because of the conclusion that [the former] has the transmigrating being as its object,
and because there is a separate introduction for the seeker of liberation in the passage, "Now, he who does not desire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
In that context, regarding the domain of transmigratory existence, both prescribed and prohibited knowledge is included, as there is no distinction made;
likewise, both prescribed and prohibited action is included, because it is merely restating what has already occurred.
This being so, this statement concerning the simultaneous undertaking [of the sacrifice] is also intelligible even without such a distinction. // 11 //

Having accepted that the statement regarding "taking hold together" (*samanvārambha*) refers to one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), the author of the Sūtras stated the distinction that knowledge takes hold of another seeker of liberation as one already liberated. However, in reality, that is not the case; thus he says:
"And this statement regarding taking hold together...

In that context, regarding the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), he explains the meaning of the terms "knowledge" and so forth in the sentence beginning with "That [knowledge] takes hold of him," which is a restatement of what is already established. Thus: "In that context..."
The knowledge of the *udgītha* and so forth is prescribed, while that consisting of meditating on a naked woman and the like is prohibited. //11//
And as for this [argument], "Because of the injunction regarding that which possesses it" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.6).
To this, he reads the following reply: "Of one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]," as in:
"Having studied the Veda from the family of a teacher" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1).
Thus, from hearing that there is instruction regarding study alone, we conclude that the injunction for ritual action applies only to one who possesses mere study.
But if this were so, would it not follow that those lacking knowledge (*avidya*) would be ineligible for rituals?
This is not a fault.

We do not deny that the understanding of ritual action arising from Vedic study is a cause for qualification [for rites]; rather, we establish this much: that the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*) resulting from the *niṣada* (Upanishads), being perceived as purposeful in its own right, does not function as a cause for qualification for ritual action.
And just as the knowledge of one sacrifice is not required for qualification for another sacrifice, so too should this be understood. // 12 //
Regarding what was also stated in [Brahma Sūtra] 3.4.7, "And because of the restrictive rule," it is here replied:
"Not so, because there is no distinction."
In such scriptural injunctions as "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live" (Īśā Upaniṣad 2), there is no specific qualification that they apply only to the knower;
for these restrictive rules are prescribed without distinction. 13.
"And this which..."—the word "stated" is to be supplied as the remainder; the meaning is "because of ignorance," that is, because of being devoid of knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
He says, "This is not a fault," to show that the word "only" (mātra) excludes the knowledge of the Self, but does not exclude the knowledge of ritual action. // 12 // // 13 //
Or rather, it is for the purpose of praise, or it is an approval. (BsCom_3,4.1.14)

Regarding the passage "Even while performing actions here" (Īśā Upaniṣad 2), another specific point is explained: although, by the force of the context, the word "performing" is connected specifically with the knower, nevertheless, this permission for action should be understood as being for the purpose of praising knowledge,
as expressed in "action does not cling to the man" (Īśā Upaniṣad 2).
For he will say this; the following is what is meant:
even though a wise person performs actions throughout his entire life, he will indeed say [this].
This is what is meant:
even while performing actions throughout his entire life, no action results in defilement for the wise man because of the power of knowledge; thus, in this way, knowledge is praised. 14.

It has been stated that the injunction regarding observances (*niyamavākya*) is intended for the ignorant, or else it is for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the wise; thus he says, "The praises.

Even when it is said, "Perform action in this manner," it means that for you, O man, there is no transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) through action other than this state of Brahmanhood obtained through knowledge—that is to say, there is none—because action does not taint [the knower].
The meaning is that it does not lead to the application of a new form; this is the intention of the Śruti. //14//
And some [hold] that it is by one's own will. (BBs 3.4.15)
Moreover, some wise men, having directly realized the fruit of knowledge, rely upon that and reflect on the absence of any purpose in offspring and other means for attaining further results.

There is a scriptural text of the Vājasaneyins stating: "Indeed, the ancient knowers did not desire offspring, saying, 'What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Thus, we have stated more than once that the fruit of knowledge is indeed established in immediate experience and does not occur at a later time like the fruit of ritual action;
for this reason as well, it is impossible to maintain either that knowledge is a subsidiary part of ritual action, or that the scriptural declarations of its fruit are untrue.

He states that knowledge (*vidyā*) has independent fruit because of the renunciation of progeny and so forth—which are the means for accomplishing ritual action (*karma*) according to one's own will—as well as because of its characteristic mark. He says "kāma" [etc.]:

the meaning is that those of us for whom this very Brahman is the immediate Self (*aparokṣa-ātman*), and for whom this very [Self] is the world and the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), have reflected, "What shall we do with progeny and the rest? and have thus abandoned ritual action. Now, an objection: is it not improper to say that the fruit of knowledge is perceptible by saying "this world," since, like the fruit of ritual action, it is invisible? To this he replies: "anubhava" [etc. //15//
And [the teaching on] the crushing [of the self]. BBs 3.4.16.

Moreover, they teach that through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), the entire phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)—consisting of action, agent, fruit, and characteristics, which is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*)—is utterly destroyed in its very nature, as stated in such passages as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he smell? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

But if the attainment of eligibility for ritual action were preceded by the knowledge of the Self taught in the Vedānta, it would follow as a consequence that the very eligibility for ritual action is abolished for one who holds such a view.
Therefore, for this reason also, knowledge is independent. // 16 //
Knowledge is not only not a constituent part of ritual action because it serves no useful purpose for it, but also because it destroys ritual action; thus he says: "And [because of] sublation" (16).
And [the rule applies] to those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), for there is a scriptural statement (*śabda*) to that effect. (BBs 3.4.17)
Furthermore, knowledge is heard of in the stages of life (āśrama) characterized by the upward flow of vital energy (ūrdhvaretas),
and in those cases, it is not possible for knowledge to be subordinate to ritual action,
because of the absence of such action.

For those [ascetics], Vedic rituals such as the Agnihotra do not exist. It might be argued that the stages of life (āśrama) for those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas) are not mentioned in the Veda; but even that is not the case.
For these are also understood from Vedic words: "There are three branches of dharma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1);
"And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1);
and "Those who dwell in the forest, practicing austerity and faith" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11).
"In this very [path], mendicants go forth, desiring this world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22),
and "One should go forth from the stage of studentship itself" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4)—
in such passages as these.

The state of being an *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose vital energy is drawn upward) is well known from the Śruti and Smṛti for both householders who have entered [the life-stages] and those who have not, as well as for those who have discharged the three debts and those who have not;
therefore, knowledge is independent. // 17 //

Furthermore, he states—beginning with "ūrdhva"—that the knowledge of the reality of action (*karmatattvajñāna*) and [action] itself do not stand in a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhūta*), because they reside in different classes of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), just as in the case of the Rājasūya and the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifices.

The meaning is that there are three divisions of dharma consisting primarily of ritual action corresponding to the [first three] stages of life (*āśrama*), while the fourth is "one who is firmly established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*).
This is based on the Vedic scripture: "By means of studentship one pays the debt to the sages, by sacrifice to the gods, and by progeny to the ancestors; thus one becomes free from debt."

Nor should one entertain the doubt that renunciation belongs only to one who has attained the householder stage and has discharged the three debts, based on the Smṛti: "Having paid off the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation; but he who pursues liberation without having paid them off goes downwards. For this would contradict the scriptural injunctions and Smṛtis such as "One may renounce even from the stage of studentship" and "He who desires the second stage of life should dwell in it," since it is understood that the explanatory passages (arthavādas) in the Śruti and Smṛti regarding the three debts apply only to those who lack dispassion. Thus he says: "pratipanna... (having entered...).
"Therefore" means because of being established in renunciation (saṃnyāsa). //17//
END BsCom_3,4.1.17 START BsCom_3,4.2.18 2.
Section on the Consideration of the Subsequent Reflection (Parāmarśādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 18–20.
Jaimini [holds that] there is no injunction for the life-stages of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), and he refutes them because they are not enjoined;

for the scriptural passages such as "There are three branches of dharma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1), which were cited to establish the existence of those stages of life for those who have sublimated their sexual energy, are not capable of proving that.
For the teacher Jaimini considers that there is only a reference (*parāmarśa*) to these words regarding other stages of life (*āśrama*), and not an injunction (*vidhi*).
Why? Because here there is no word of injunction such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) or others;
moreover, each of these is observed to have a different purpose.

Regarding the passage "There are three branches of dharma": first, sacrifice, study, and charity; second, austerity alone; and third, the student who dwells in the teacher's house, exhausting himself completely in the teacher's house—all these attain worlds of merit.
Having thus proclaimed, by way of a preliminary reflection, that the stages of life (āśramas) have non-eternal fruits, [the text proceeds] with the view of their having eternal fruits.
The state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) is praised: "One who is established in Brahman attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1).
[Objection: But even in the case of the reference (*parāmarśa*), the stages of life (*āśrama*) are indeed understood. [Reply:
True, they are understood.
However, their authority is established through tradition and custom, not through direct Vedic revelation;
therefore, when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation,
they will either be disregarded or restricted to subjects for which one is not qualified.

[Objection: But is it not the case that the householder’s life (*gārhasthya*) is also mentioned alongside those whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*), in the passage: "Sacrifice, study, and giving—this is the first"?

[Reply: True, it is so; nevertheless, because the rites such as the *agnihotra* are prescribed specifically for the householder, its existence is indeed well-established by the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Therefore, this reference is solely for the purpose of praise (*stuty-artha*) and is not intended as an injunction (*codanā-artha*).
Moreover, direct Vedic revelation indeed censures other stages of life, as in: "He who lets the sacred fire go out is a slayer of the heroes of the gods";
"Having brought dear wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the thread of progeny" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.11.1);
and "There is no world for one who has no son—this all animals know," and so forth.

Likewise, the passages, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1) and "Those who in the forest worship austerity and faith" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11), are instructions regarding the path of the gods (devayāna), not instructions regarding other stages of life (āśrama).
Furthermore, the designation of "other stages of life" (*āśramāntara*) is ambiguous in such passages as, "Austerity alone is the second [stage]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1),
and likewise, "Seeking this very world, mendicants go forth into homelessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Thus, this is merely worldly praise; it is not an injunction for wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*).
But surely, among the Jābālas, there is this very clear and perceptible injunction for wandering mendicancy: "One should go forth from the stage of studentship itself.
This is true.
However, it should be understood that this inquiry is independent of this scriptural statement. // 18 //

He raises the objection that "there is no renunciation" with the words, "Jaimini [says] there is a reference [to it]. Regarding whether the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya), designated by the term *ūrdhvaretas*, is to be practiced or not, a doubt arises based on whether its source is a valid means of knowledge (*māna*) or an error (*bhrānti*). He states that it is not to be practiced because its source is an error, using the words, "The three.
The plural number is used in view of the internal subdivisions of the stages of life (*āśrama*).
Accordingly, the *Kāṇvāyana-smṛti* is cited here according to its meaning:
"The *gāyatra*, the *brāhma*, the *prājāpatya*, and the *bṛhat*—thus the religious student (*brahmacārī*) is of four kinds.
Among these, he who, after the initiation (*upanayana*), for three nights eats neither pungent nor salty food and studies the *Gāyatrī*, is the *gāyatra*.
He who practices celibacy until the completion of his Vedic studies is a Brāhma.
He who always approaches only his own wife during her fertile period and avoids the wives of others is a Prājāpatya;
likewise, a student (brahmacārī) who performs the Vedic vows for one year is a Prājāpatya.
One who dwells in the teacher’s house until death is called a *naiṣṭhika* or *bṛhat*.
The householder (*gṛhastha*) is also of four kinds: the *vārtāka*, the *yāyāvara*, the *śālīna*, and the *ghorasaṃnyāsika*.

Among these, the *vārtāka-vṛtti* is one who lives by the occupations of Vaiśyas and others, such as agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth, and is devoted to the regular rites beginning with [the five great sacrifices].
The *yāyāvara* is one who subsists on what is unasked for, being averse to officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts;
the *śālīna*, however, is devoted to the six duties and subsists by officiating at sacrifices and the like, and is a hoarder.
One who performs his daily duties with water that has been drawn and purified, who subsists by the practice of *uñcha* (gleaning), and who lives in a village, is called a *ghorasaṃnyāsika*.

Because he is averse to violence, the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is also of four kinds: the *vaikhānasa*, the *audumbara*, the *vālakhilya*, and the *phenapa*. Among these, one who performs the *agnihotra* and other rites using uncultivated plants that ripen spontaneously and grow outside the village is called a *vaikhānasa*.
He who, rising early in the morning, looks toward whatever direction and, being devoted to ritual action, subsists there upon *audumbara*, *badarī*, *nīvāra*, and *śyāmāka* grains, is an *Audumbara*.

He who wears matted hair and bark garments, having gathered enough for his livelihood by eight mornings, eats sparingly during the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*), and renounces all flowers and fruits on the full moon of Kārttika, is a *Vālakhilya*.
As for the *Phenapas*, they subsist on withered leaves and fruits, dwelling anywhere at all while remaining devoted to ritual action.

Likewise, there are four kinds of wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*): the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*. Among them, the *kuṭīcakas* are those who carry three staffs (*tridaṇḍin*) and wander for alms within the houses of their own sons. The *bahūdakas*, however, are also carriers of the triple staff; they wear a water-strainer (*śikya*), a water-purifier (*jala-pavitra*), sandals, a seat, a topknot, a sacred thread, a loincloth, and saffron-colored robes. Wandering among sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) and subsisting on alms, they seek the Self.

The *haṃsas*, however, carry a single staff, wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) except for the topknot, hold a sling and a water-pot in their hands, dwell in a village for only one night, and are devoted to the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
The *paramahaṃsas*, on the other hand, carry a single staff, have shaven heads, do not wear the sacred thread, have abandoned all ritual actions, and are established in the Self (*ātman*).

In this regard, the difference in the result is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is absent, it is not established that knowledge has independent fruit; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because that [renunciation] exists, its establishment follows.

The meaning is that the "stages of life" (āśramas) refer to the self—that is, the body—wasting away in the family home of the teacher; thus, he is a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). It might be objected: "In the *skandha-śruti*, the stages of life are not enjoined, but rather the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) is restated as the fourth. To this, he replies by acknowledging the understanding derived from the preceding injunction required for the restatement: "True."

One might argue that the direct perception of the scriptural text regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) itself should be the original injunction (*purovāda*), and not a restatement (*anuvāda*); to this, he says: "Smṛti" [referring to the Smṛti texts].
Let this very scriptural text be the source for those two as well, because there is parsimony in postulating only the injunction when the scripture is already established.

If this [text] were merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), there would be the cumbersome assumption of two things: first, the scriptural injunction regarding the stages of life (*āśrama*) for those with and without the sacred fires (*sāgnika* and *anagnika*) as its source (*mūla*), and second, that very injunction itself; therefore, he says "And hence" (*ataśca*).
Because they are based on the Smṛti, the stages of life should be accepted provided they are not contradicted by the direct Vedic injunctions concerning lifelong duties (*karma*).

However, those stages of life involving no sacred fires (*anagnika*) which are contradictory should be disregarded, or else they are to be practiced by those such as the blind who are not entitled to perform [Vedic] rites—this is the meaning.
The sense is that because it would contradict the scriptural injunction [to remain a householder] for as long as one lives, the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) must be abandoned.

Having raised the objection that—since there is no difference in their being merely restated (*anuvādya*) in the *skandha-śruti*—the other stages of life (*āśrama*) should likewise be practiced just like the householder stage, he replies with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely), stating that while its practice follows from its being based on scripture (*śrautatva*), the others do not because they lack a scriptural basis; therefore, this statement regarding the "aggregates" (*skandha*) is intended solely as praise for being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthatā*).

The meaning is that the phrase "and likewise those who... is a completion of the sentence [beginning with] "they go toward the flame" (*arciṣam abhisaṃbhavanti*). Thus, it refers to the continuity of the thread.

He states, "And because it is doubtful," [meaning] that since the word *skandha* is not conventionally established (*arūḍha*) in reference to the stages of life (*āśrama*), there is no injunction regarding the stages of life here.
Then, [the opponent might argue] that in the phrase "those who go forth" (*pravrajanti*), there is an injunction for the stages of life; to this he replies, "In the same way, this...

The meaning is that this is a statement of praise (*stuti*) based on a description of the present state, implying: "The light of the Self (*ātmaloka*) is so great that for its sake they even undertake the difficult task of renunciation (*pravrajyā*)."

Now, having set aside the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he states that this scripture is considered under the assumption that it does not exist, beginning with the words "nanu" and so forth. //18//
Bādarāyaṇa maintains that [the meditations] are to be performed, because of the scriptural teaching of their equality. (BS 3.4.19)
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that another stage of life (āśrama) is to be practiced, because it is heard in the Veda.

He refutes the view that—since the Agnihotra and other rites must necessarily be performed—another stage of life is to be practiced only by those not qualified for them, [and thus would conflict with those duties]; rather, he holds that another stage of life is to be practiced just like the householder's stage, even by one who does not desire it.
Thinking that it must be practiced [as a separate stage], why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding equality;
for a scriptural reference to another stage of life as being equal to the householder's stage is seen in such passages as, "There are three branches of duty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1).
Just as here the householder's stage (gārhasthya), which is enjoined by another scriptural text, is referred to, so too it must be understood that the other stages of life are likewise referred to.

And just as in a sentence intended to enjoin the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (upavīta), there is a reference to the *nivīta* and *prācīnāvīta* postures already established by other scriptures;
therefore, the other stage of life is equal to the householder's stage in its status as something to be practiced.

Likewise, there is the mention [of renunciation] in connection with the study of the Vedas and other such acts in the passage: "Seeking this very world, mendicants go forth from their homes" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22);
and also in: "And those who here in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1).
And this [is established] by means of the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).
As for what was said— that the mention of other stages of life (*āśrama*) in passages such as "Austerity alone is the second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1) is ambiguous— [that objection is refuted].
This is not a fault,
because there exists a cause for certainty:
"There are three aggregates of dharma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1).

Thus, indeed, the threefold nature of the *dharmaskandhas* has been asserted. And since sacrificial rites (*yajña*) and other such numerous duties, being distinct in their origin, cannot be subsumed under anything other than the threefold connection with the stages of life (*āśrama*), it follows that the householder’s stage, characterized by sacrifices and the like, is indicated as one *dharmaskandha*; "the student" (*brahmacārī*) is a clear indication of a specific stage of life; and as for "austerity" (*tapas*), what other *dharmaskandha* could there be besides the stage of life in which austerity is predominant?
And by the indicative mark of the "forest" in the passage, "And those who [dwell] in the forest" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1), the stages of life are understood through faith and austerity.
Therefore, even in the case of reflection (upon the scriptures), another stage of life must be undertaken.

The author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*) that the other stages of life (*āśrama*), though prescribed in other Vedic texts, are merely restated (*anūdyante*) in this passage—just as the householder’s stage is—because they are subject to restatement by this very statement; thus he concludes: "It is to be performed.
To provide an example where a restatement is preceded by an injunction, he says: "And just as...

In the sentence, "The *nivīta* [wearing of the sacred thread] is for men, the *prācīnāvīta* for the ancestors, and the *upavīta* for the gods," the *upavīta* is enjoined for rites dedicated to the gods.
Two things are restated for its praise:

because the *nivīta* (the mode of wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder) is already established in human activities due to its practical convenience, and because the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing it over the left shoulder) is also already established by another injunction for ancestral rites (*pitrya-karma*).

Furthermore, he states that the injunction for wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is found directly in another passage, because it is mentioned in conjunction with the prescribed duties: "In the same way, this very [Self]... and so forth.
The phrase "of this" refers to the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*).
The meaning is that because it is mentioned together with enjoined acts such as the study and recitation of the Vedas, the state of wandering mendicancy itself is also enjoined.
He states that there is a similar scriptural declaration even in another passage: "And he who... and so forth.

The phrase "of this" refers to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). The meaning is that because the forest-dweller is mentioned together with the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) which is itself enjoined, that [knowledge] must also be enjoined. He states, beginning with "As for what was said," etc., that the word *skandha* is determined to refer to the stages of life (*āśrama*) because the number three mentioned in the scripture would otherwise be inexplicable.
"Distinct in their origin" means that they have arisen separately, such as "one should sacrifice," "one should study," and "one should give. //19//
Or rather, it is an injunction, like the rule regarding the wearing [of the sacred thread]. (BBs 3.4.20)

"This is not merely a reference to another stage of life (āśrama), but rather an injunction; for if it were accepted as an injunction, the perception of syntactic unity would be obstructed. [The opponent replies: "But indeed, syntactic unity is perceived here, in that 'the three branches of dharma have the worlds of merit as their fruit, whereas being established in Brahman has immortality as its fruit'—this is true."
However, even though there is a perception of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), one must accept it as an injunction (*vidhi*) because it conveys something not previously known (*apūrvatva*),

and because no other injunction is observed; furthermore, since there is a clear cognition of a different stage of life (*āśrama*), it is impossible to establish syntactic unity by resorting to the assumption that it is merely a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*).
It is like the case of *dhāraṇa* (holding).

For instance, in the passage, "Holding the fuel-stick below, he should run after [the fire]; for he holds it above for the gods," although there is no contradiction and the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is perceived through the act of holding, the "holding above" is indeed enjoined because it is something not previously established (*apūrvatvāt*).
Thus it has been stated in the section on the definition of subsidiary elements (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*): "But it is an injunction regarding holding, because it is something new."
Similarly, here too, the scriptural passage concerning the reference to the stages of life (āśrama) is to be understood as an injunction, even if it appears as a mere reference.

Even when this is indeed a reference to other stages of life, nevertheless, "being established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā) must necessarily be accepted as something enjoined by virtue of its being praised.
Furthermore, it must be discerned whether this applies to anyone among the four stages of life, or only to the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka).

If, when the stages of life beginning with that of the student (brahmacārin) are being considered, the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) is also included therein, then— since there would be no distinction in all four stages of life being considered and since it is impossible for anyone to remain without a stage of life— it follows that whoever among those in the four stages of life is "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃstha) [is meant]. On the other hand, if he is not included, then by process of elimination, the wandering mendicant alone will be established as the one "established in Brahman."

Regarding this, some maintain that the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) is also included by the term "asceticism" (tapaḥ), which refers to the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa). But that too has been refuted;
for when another way is possible, it is not appropriate to include the wandering mendicant by means of a qualification specific to the forest-dweller.

Just as here the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhamedhin*) are distinguished by their own respective specific characteristics which are not common to both, so too it is logical that the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) and the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) are likewise distinguished.
Furthermore, austerity (*tapas*) is the non-common duty of forest-dwellers because it consists primarily of physical mortification;
for the word "austerity" is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in that sense.
Furthermore, the duty of a monk, characterized by restraint of the senses and so forth, is certainly not denoted by the word "austerity" (*tapas*).
Moreover, it is improper that the stages of life (*āśrama*), which are well-known to be four, should be referred to as three.
Furthermore, there is a distinction made here: "These three partake of the worlds of merit; one partakes of immortality."
Furthermore, this designation of distinction is intelligible only if there is indeed a difference [between them].

For it does not happen that one says, "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted, but another among these two is highly intelligent. Rather, it happens thus: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted, but Viṣṇumitra is highly intelligent."
Therefore, the first three types of ascetics partake of the worlds of merit, while the remaining one—the wandering mendicant alone—partakes of immortality.
But how can the term *brahmasaṃstha*, which applies to everyone through its etymological derivation (*yoga*), be restricted to the wandering mendicant alone?
Furthermore, if its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) were accepted, it would follow that immortality is attained merely by belonging to that stage of life, which would render knowledge useless.

To this it is replied: By the term "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*), that state of being fixed in Brahman which consists in being completely absorbed in it and having no other activity is denoted. And that is not possible for the first three stages of life (*āśrama*s), because of the scriptural teaching of transgression resulting from the non-performance of the duties prescribed for one's own stage of life.
For the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), however, no transgression arises from the non-performance of rituals due to his renunciation of all actions.
His own duties, such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), serve to strengthen his state of being grounded in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) rather than contradicting it;
for his very foundation in Brahman, augmented by tranquility and self-control, constitutes the duty prescribed for his own stage of life, including sacrifices and other rites.

And for others, there is transgression if they violate it; thus: "Renunciation (nyāsa)—Brahmā is renunciation, for Brahmā is the Supreme, and the Supreme is Brahman. These other austerities are indeed inferior; renunciation alone surpasses them" (Nārāyaṇīya Upaniṣad 78). And: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6; Nārāyaṇīya Upaniṣad 1.2.3; Kaivalya Upaniṣad 3).

Such are the Śruti texts. And the Smṛti texts— such as "Those whose intellect is fixed on That, whose self is That, who are established in That, and for whom That is the supreme goal" (Gītā 5.17)— demonstrate the absence of ritual action for one who is established in Brahman.

Therefore, the objection that knowledge would become useless because the state of immortality is attained merely by entering the stage of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) does not apply here either.
Thus, even through this reference (*parāmarśa*), the state of being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) is indeed obtained for the wandering mendicancy among the other stages of life.
This investigation was undertaken by the Teacher without even taking into account the *Jābāla* Śruti, which prescribes the other stages of life.
Indeed, there exists a direct scriptural injunction regarding the rule for other stages of life:
"Having completed the stage of studenthood, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce.
Or otherwise, one may renounce directly from studenthood, or from the home, or from the forest" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).
Nor can it be said that this scriptural statement has as its subject those who are not qualified [for Vedic study],

because it is heard without qualification and because there is a separate mention of those who are unqualified, starting with: "Now, whether he be one who observes vows or one who does not, whether he be a Snātaka or one who is not a Snātaka, whether his sacred fires have been extinguished or he is without fires" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).

Furthermore, because the life of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is a constituent part of the maturation resulting from the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*), it does not have as its object those who are ineligible [for Vedic study].

This is shown by the text: "Now, the wandering mendicant, wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, without possessions, pure, non-injurious, subsisting on alms, becomes one with Brahman" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 5).
Therefore, the stages of life for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*) are established.
And since it is established among those of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) that knowledge possesses independence through its own inherent power, [it is not dependent on action]. // 20 //
Having accepted that the mention of the "stages of life" (*skandha*) is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), it was stated that the stages of life must be practiced by postulating another injunction.
Now, he says "or rather, [it is] an injunction" (*vidhir vā*), because it is simpler to postulate that this very [mention] possesses injunctive force.

The implication is that the scriptural texts such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) concern those who lack dispassion, and therefore they do not invalidate the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).

This single passage appears to be intended solely for the praise of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) by means of disparaging the other three stages of life (*āśrama*) due to their yielding meager fruits. To this, the opponent raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), suggesting that it is improper to enjoin the four stages of life here, because since they are not obtained through any other injunction, they cannot be the subject of a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

And because of the fault of [interpreting the text as] praise by implication (*stutilakṣaṇā*), it is better to assume a distinction between the injunctions (*vidhi*) due to their being previously unknown (*apūrvatvāt*); thus he says, beginning with "It is true" (*satyam*).
He provides an illustration for assuming such a distinction by breaking the perceived unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*) with the phrase "like the *dhāraṇa*.
When, in the *Mahāpitṛyajña* and the *Pretāgnihotra*, the oblation (*havis*) placed in the *sruc* ladle is being carried toward the *āhavanīya* fire—

The meaning is that, although the phrase "for above" (*upari hi*) appears to form a single syntactical unit with the statement enjoining the holding of the fuel-stick below the oblation— "one should run after [the butter] while holding a fuel-stick below that oblation"— nevertheless, because this is a previously unknown injunction regarding the holding of the fuel-stick above the ladle-handle (*srugdaṇḍa*) in a divine *homa*,
it constitutes a distinct injunction (*vidhi*); thus, a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) was declared by the teacher Jaimini in the third chapter.

Thus, the position that four stages of life (āśramas) are prescribed has been stated. Now, by way of restating the three stages of life, he states another position—that only wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is prescribed—beginning with the words "yadāpi" (even when). Anticipating the objection as to how wandering mendicancy is prescribed when the injunction concerns being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā), he investigates this with the words "sā ca" (and that).

One might object: "Since the sentence 'There are three' does not include the four stages of life (āśrama), this inquiry is groundless. Anticipating this doubt, one wonders whether the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) is referred to in that sentence or not. Regarding the first possibility—that he is not referred to—the proponent states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "If [the mendicant] were not mentioned... One might ask: "Why could one who is not in any stage of life (*anāśramin*) not be 'established in Brahman' (*brahmasaṃstha*)? To this, he replies: "Because of the state of being without an āśrama," meaning that there is a prohibition stating, "One who is without an āśrama should not remain [so]. This is the intended sense.
In the second [verse], he states the attainment of the perfected ones (siddhas), beginning with "atha.
Having thus expressed doubt through the presence or absence of such reflection, he presents the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with "tatra":
for it is well known that for one dwelling in the forest, asceticism such as the *kṛcchra* penance is unique [to that state].
Therefore, it is improper to include both [asceticism and learning] by means of that single word "tapas" (asceticism), because a mendicant is not commonly known to possess asceticism.

And thus, just as the three stages of life beginning with the householder are understood through their respective specific duties such as sacrifice, the fourth stage—characterized primarily by steadfastness in Brahman—is grasped by the very term *brahmasaṃstha*.

And he establishes the final conclusion—that this [fourth stage] is enjoined along with the state of being established in Brahman on the strength of its being a praise—by the words "That is incorrect," and so forth.

Furthermore, because of the separate designation, he states that the one established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*) is distinct from the previously mentioned practitioners of the stages of life, using the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Nor should it be said that those very same persons could attain "abiding in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthā*) through a difference in their stages of life;

for even with a difference in time, if they possess dull intellect, it is impossible for those distracted-minded individuals—despite possessing an abundance of wisdom—to abide in Brahman while remaining engaged in ritual action (*karmitva*).
Furthermore, since it is established that only the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) who has renounced action abides in Brahman, our desired conclusion is proven; this is the intended meaning.

To clarify this very point, he raises an objection with the words, "But how? Although the term *brahmasaṃstha* is not conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsāśrama*), it nevertheless brings that very stage to mind through its etymological connection (*yoga*). He states, "To this it is replied," because the etymological meaning is not applicable in the other stages of life.

Regarding the point that for one who has renounced all actions, there is nothing further to be performed beyond being firmly established in Brahman as the meaning of the Praṇava, he states the authoritative proof with the words "And so" (tathā ca).
He provides the reason for praising renunciation (nyāsa) as Brahman with the words "For Brahman... (brahmā hi).

Since Hiraṇyagarbha is well known to be the Supreme (para), renunciation is praised as being the Supreme by virtue of its identity with Brahman; having thus praised it, he censures those ritual acts with the words "those... (tāni).
Therefore, the meaning is that *nyāsa* alone is superior because it is the liberator through the gateway of knowledge.

For the sake of that [knowledge], those whose minds are fixed on Brahman, who have become one with It, whose nature is Brahman, who are established in It, who are intent on hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, who are devoted to That, and who seek Brahman—meaning, those who are free from desire—are the ones concerned.

Thus, since the word *brahmasaṃstha* denotes an order of life (*āśrama*) in which knowledge is predominant, the injunction is transformed into: "One who desires immortality should practice that very order of life."

Therefore, he concludes that there is no fault of the knowledge being purposeless with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). Now, he sets aside the hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*) with the words "anapekṣya" (without regard for).
The intention is that this inquiry was conducted by taking up the scriptural mention of the aggregates (*skandha*) for the sake of clarifying the student's intellect.
"Or otherwise" (yadivetarathā) means:

if, while remaining in the state of a religious student (brahmacarya), detachment should arise due to the ripening of previously performed merit. Regarding the claim that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is intended for those such as the blind who are ineligible for ritual action—that is not so; he says "nor... (na ca).
The meaning is that there is no reason for the restriction of a general scriptural statement. The word "separately" implies "of renunciation" as the ellipsis.
The sequence of the construction is as follows: one who has taken vows (*vratī*), meaning one who has performed Vedic vows such as the *godāna* and others;

a *snātaka*, meaning one who has returned from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*) but has not yet entered the householder stage and continues to serve his teacher; a *vidhura*, meaning one whose sacred fires have been extinguished; and an *anagnika*, meaning one who has not yet taken up the sacred fires—such a person may renounce (*pravrajed*). He states "Brahma... [in the verse] to explain that renunciation is appropriate for those who are somehow disqualified from ritual action due to being deficient in all their limbs, whereas those with deficient limbs, such as the blind and so forth, do not possess the qualification for the renunciation that is centered on knowledge (*jñānapradhāna-saṃnyāsa*).

The meaning is that there is no eligibility for the blind, the lame, the mute, the deaf, and others, because knowledge does not arise without such things as moving about purified by right views and hearing [the teachings], and because of the indicative mark of the prayer for the integrity of the limbs: "May my body be most excellent; may my tongue be most sweet; may I hear much with my two ears."
"And that" means that renunciation is a constituent part of the knowledge of Brahman; "for the sake of becoming Brahman" means, in short, for the sake of the direct realization of Brahman. //20//
END BsCom_3,4.2.20 START BsCom_3,4.3.21 Section on Merely Laudatory Statements (stutimātrādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 21–22.
If it be argued that this is merely a figurative praise because of the mention [of the syllable], we say no, because of its being something new (*apūrvatvāt*). For instance:
"This Udgītha is the essence of essences, the highest, the best, the eighth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.3), and "Thus, fire is the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1).

"This world indeed is this piled fire-altar; this [earth] is the Uktha, this very earth," and other such scriptural passages— regarding the doubt as to whether these are for the purpose of praising the Udgītha and so forth, or for the purpose of enjoining meditative knowledge (upāsana)— it is reasonable that they are for the purpose of praise,
because they are heard in connection with the Udgītha and other such constituent parts of ritual action.

If it is argued that these [passages] are for the purpose of praising the *juhū* and other items—just as in the case of such texts as "This *juhū* is indeed Āditya; the tortoise is the heavenly world; the *āhavanīya* fire is the heavenly world"—we say:
no.
For it is not appropriate that the sole purpose of these scriptural passages (*śruti*) is mere praise, because they convey something previously unknown (*apūrva*).
For if it were intended as an injunction (*vidhi*), an unprecedented matter (*apūrva*) would be enjoined; however, if it were intended as a praise (*stuti*), it would result in mere meaninglessness.

It has been stated that "praise is useful only when it attains the status of a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) to an injunctive word" (as in *JS 1.2.7*: "But because they form a single sentence with the injunction, the [passages] are for the purpose of praising the injunctions"). However, in the case of the *udgītha* and other elements enjoined in one location, this praise recited in another location—which does not attain the status of a supplementary part—would indeed be meaningless.
However, passages such as "This indeed is the Juhū ladle" are recorded only in proximity to an injunction; thus there is a disparity.
Therefore, scriptural texts of this kind have the injunction as their sole purpose. // 21 //
This is merely a praise:
among the seven essences—earth, water, herbs, man, speech, Ṛg-veda, and Sāman-veda—the eighth essence is the syllable *oṃ*, which is the supreme part of the *udgītha*.
Because it is a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self, it is the "supreme half" (*parārdhya*), meaning it is worthy of the place of the Supreme Brahman.
Regarding these scriptural passages, he states a doubt because they mention specific limbs (*aṅga*) and because their meaning is not something previously established: "What [is the case]?

Just as renunciation (*pārivrājya*) is to be practiced based on the scriptural statement of its similarity to the stage of the householder (*gārhasthya*) which is to be practiced, so too, since these scriptural passages are similar to the scriptural statements praising the *juhū* ladle and other implements, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they serve the purpose of praise; thus he says: "They are for the purpose of praise."
This very earth is praised as the *juhū* ladle;
the tortoise situated upon the altar is praised as the sun;
and the *āhavanīya* fire is praised as the heavenly world.
The meaning is that there is praise of the *udgītha* and so forth by means of qualities such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*).

The author establishes the final position (*siddhānta*)—that it is better to assume an injunction (*vidhi*) rather than a mere praise (*stuti*)—because of the attainment of the fruit through performance; thus he says, "For [it is] not [mere] praise.
It should be understood that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is non-performance, whereas in the final position, the result is performance.
To the question, "Why should [the passages] not have purposefulness by way of being laudatory (stāvakatva)? he says: "Of the injunctive [passage].

The sense is this: it is appropriate that passages such as "This indeed is the juhū-ladle" have purposefulness by way of being laudatory, because they reside within the context of injunctions regarding the juhū and other implements which possess fruit; however, since passages such as "The most flavorful" (rasatama) do not reside within the context of injunctions for the constituent parts of a sacrifice, it is more appropriate that they enjoin a meditation on the unprecedented (apūrva) which possesses fruit, just like the scriptural texts concerning other sacrifices. //21//
And because it is a word denoting a state of being (bhāva). (BBs 3.4.22)

Expressions such as "One should meditate on the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), "One should meditate on the Sāman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.1), and "One should know: 'I am the hymn'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.1) are clearly heard as injunctive words; and these would be contradicted if their purpose were merely for the sake of praise.

And thus there is the traditional teaching of those who know the Nyāya: "One should do (*kuryāt*), one should be done (*kriyeta*), it is to be done (*kartavyam*), it would be (*bhavet*), and the fifth is *syāt*; this is the fixed definition of an injunction (*vidhi*) in all the Vedas. Thinking that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is the injunction, they remember it in this way.
Furthermore, in each section, the fruits [of the practice] are proclaimed: "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7).
"For he alone has power over the singing of desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.9), "For him the worlds, both ascending and returning, become fit" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3), and so forth.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the scriptural passages concerning the *udgītha* and other such elements are intended to enjoin meditative worship (*upāsanā*). // 22 //

Furthermore, as for the statement "what is to be enjoined here?"—this was said by way of a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical consideration); in reality, however, it is not to be enjoined because it is already established. Thus he says: "bhāva... [and so on]. Nor is it correct to say that the scriptural passages such as "the most flavorful" (*rasatama*) serve merely to praise the injunction regarding meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*). The sense is that since it is possible for them to provide the object required by the injunction, they cannot be construed as mere praise (*stuti*).

One might ask: "Since forms such as the optative (*liṅ*) are used even in expressions of prayer, such as 'May the god do what I desire,' how can it be determined that words like 'one should meditate' (*upāsīta*) have the nature of an injunction? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*).

This [optative] suffix and so forth, by way of general rule (*utsarga*), would invariably be the indicator (*jñāpaka*)—that is, the mark (*lakṣaṇa*)—of the injunction known as "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) within the Vedas. However, when there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) such as a specific accompanying word (*upapada*), it has another purpose; this is the meaning.
This is what he says with the words "liṅ-ādi" (the optative suffix, etc.).

Furthermore, one should not be deluded into thinking that because the word "fifth" is mentioned in the verse, only five words possess the character of an injunction (*vidhi*), and not [words such as] "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) and so forth. For, by taking *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*—which denote action in general—as examples, it is intended to show that the optative suffixes and others, when colored by any verbal root whatsoever, possess the character of an injunction. The mention of the "fifth" word, however, is for the purpose of completing the meter relative to what has been stated.

Just as in the expression "Death runs as the fifth," although the verbal root *ḍukṛñ* (to do) alone— expressed by the word *karaṇa*— denotes the general action known as *bhāvanā*, while the other two roots (*bhū* in the sense of existence and *as* in the sense of being) denote different meanings; nevertheless, [this applies] to the act of becoming called birth and its fruit, which is existence.

Furthermore, because that which resides in the prompted agent is pervaded by the *bhāvanā*—which consists of the activity of the prompter—the convention of designating both as denoting action in general is maintained.

In this context, in the expression "one should do" (*kuryāt*), the *bhāvanā*, which is the meaning of the verbal root, is restated by the suffix; just as in the usage "two," the meaning of the root, namely duality, is restated by the suffix.
Similarly, by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the injunction known as its being a means to a desired end is made known.
However, since the agent is implied by that [efficient force], the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) with an implied agent has been illustrated.

Likewise, in the case of "it should be done" (*kriyeta*), the meanings of the verbal root and the suffix have also been explained; since the object is here primarily implied, the efficient force with an implied object has been illustrated.
The Mīmāṃsaka position is that since finite verbs (ākhyāta) lack the capacity for [denoting] grammatical factors such as the agent (kartṛ), the agent and the object are merely implied (ākṣepa).
In the expression "it must be done" (kartavyam), the object factor (karmakāraka) is expressed by the kṛtya suffix;
the distinction is that while the object is subordinate, the productive activity (bhāvanā) is expressed by the verbal root (prakṛti).

Likewise, one should provide examples such as *daṇḍī bhavet*, *bhūyate daṇḍinā*, and *bhavitavyam*; similarly, one should see that *syāt*, *bhūyeta*, and *bhavitavyam* are also examples of the root *as*,
because *as* is replaced by *bhū*.

By means of verbal suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like, which are colored by these three roots, a single injunction (*vidhi*)—consisting in the nature of being the means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) residing in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) as colored by the meanings of all the roots—is expressed.

Although there is a difference among the roots, the suffixes, and the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) such as the agent, there is no difference in the injunction; it is for the purpose of making this known that three examples are shown for each root. Thus everything is clear. Having thus explained in the Sūtra that "the efficient force (*bhāva*) is the injunction," he explains that "by the word *ca* [it means] the fruit (*phala*)" with the words "in each section" (*pratiprakaraṇam*).
The meaning is that this officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is capable of accomplishing the fruit through the singing of the *kāmaga* [hymns].

In this way, if even the meditations (*vidyā*) based on the constituent parts (*aṅga*) possess independent fruits, what need is there to mention the independence of the meditation on the Self (*ātmavidyā*), which is not a constituent part?
Since this inquiry regarding the independence of the meditation on the Self reaches its conclusion here, it should be understood as being connected to the [final] quarter [of the chapter]. //22//
END BsCom_3,4.3.22 START BsCom_3,4.4.23 4.
Section on the Pāriplava (The Wandering Narrative): Sūtras 23–24.
If it be argued that these passages have a merely discursive meaning, we say no, because they are specified as such.
[For example: "Now Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.1);
"Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, approached the beloved abode of Indra" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1).

Regarding the stories recited in the Vedānta such as, "Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man of faith, a giver of much, a provider of many cooked foods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.1), a doubt arises: are these for the purpose of the *pāriplava* ritual performance, or are they for the purpose of introducing the proximate knowledge (*vidyā*)? [The prima facie view is:
These scriptural accounts of stories are for the purpose of the *pāriplava*.
Because they share the nature of narrative (ākhyāna),
and because the application of narrative is enjoined for the purpose of recitation;
consequently, the Vedāntas would not have knowledge as their primary purport.
If it is argued that [the mantra] is subordinate to the ritual application because it possesses the characteristics of a mantra,
that is not so.
Why?
Because of the specific qualification.
For, having introduced the topic with "He should tell the *pāriplava*," certain specific narratives alone are qualified therein, such as "King Manu Vaivasvata" and so forth.
If there were a grasping of everything based merely on the commonality of being a narrative, then this specific qualification would be entirely purposeless.
Therefore, these scriptural accounts of narratives do not have the purpose of mere entertainment. // 23 //
"Pāriplava-arthāḥ" means "having the pāriplava as their purpose.

In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is prescribed that one should recite the pāriplava for the king surrounded by his sons and others; thus, the performance of the pāriplava is enjoined as consisting of the narration of various kinds of stories.

And so, because the stories found in the Vedānta share the common nature of being narratives and because they are situated in proximity to meditations (vidyās), he states the doubt with the words "What [is the case]? etc.

Previously, it was stated that the *vidhi* (injunction) is superior with respect to praise because it results in the attainment of performance; likewise, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the stories do not serve as praise for knowledge because they result in the attainment of the *pāriplava* recitation. Regarding this, he states the conclusion: "And therefore... (*tataśca*).

Just as in a mantra such as "devasya tvā savituḥ," because certain words possess a meaning inherent to the actual performance [of the ritual], the remainder of the mantra serves as an auxiliary to that performance; likewise, the narratives found within the Vedānta serve as auxiliaries to ritual performance.

Since all Vedāntas constitute a single syntactical unit with those [narratives] and are thus auxiliaries to ritual action, there is no primacy for knowledge (vidyā). This is the sense. [The opponent's position: By demonstrating the conduct between teacher and pupil through these narratives, they serve as auxiliaries to the proximate knowledge by way of facilitating the intellect; this is established by the indicative mark (liṅga) of their functional capacity. Therefore, considering the result to be the primacy of knowledge, he establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "That is not so" (tanna), etc.

The meaning is that since the specific stories are explicitly stated in the supplements for each day— namely, "Manu Vaivasvata" on the first day of the Aśvamedha, "Yama Vaivasvata" on the second day, and "Varuṇa Āditya" on the third day— it is appropriate to restrict the initial statement accordingly. //23//
And likewise, because they are connected as a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā). BBs 3.4.24.
And since it would be purposeless for the narratives to be merely a matter of wandering about, it is logical that they serve only to facilitate the presentation of the proximate knowledge (vidyā),

because they are bound together as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). For indeed, in those instances, a unity with the proximate [knowledge] is observed, by virtue of their utility for generating interest (*prarocanā*) and their utility for facilitating comprehension (*pratipatti*).

In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, for instance, there is seen syntactic unity with the knowledge [of Brahman] in such passages as, "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6); and in the Prātardana section as well, with such passages as, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious Self."
In this context as well, there are passages such as "Vāyu indeed is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1).
Just as the narratives found within the ritual scriptures (karma-śruti), such as "He cut out his own omentum," serve the purpose of praising the proximate injunctions, so it is here.
Therefore, they do not have the purpose of mere recitative narration (pāriplava). || 24 ||

Anticipating the question, "In what case, then, is there an application for these narratives? he says, "And so [it is]," indicating that they apply to the *vidyās* (meditative knowledges) due to their proximity. "Praising" (*prarocana*) means generating delight. For instance, the statement, "That Prajāpati cut out his own omentum and offered it," serves as a supplement to the injunction, "One should sacrifice a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati. In this same manner, the status of being a supplement to various respective injunctions is to be understood for the other narratives as well. //24//
END BsCom_3,4.5.24 START BsCom_3,4.5.25 5.
The Section Concerning the Kindling of the Fires and Other Duties. Sūtra 25.
For this very reason, there is no dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth.

Even though the sūtra "The purpose of man [is attained] from that [word]" (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.1) is separated by an interval, it is referred to here by the word "ataḥ" (from that), as it is possible [to do so].

And for this very reason—because knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of the human goal—it is concluded that the means belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*), such as the sacred fires and fuel, need not be required by knowledge for the accomplishment of its own purpose; thus [the author] summarizes the result of this very section with the words "for this very reason," intending to state further points. Having thus strengthened the principle of the independence of knowledge through three sections, he states the result of the first section: "for this very reason.

There is a doubt arising from the dispute among disputants as to whether the knowledge of Brahman requires ritual actions as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for the production of its own fruit, liberation (*mokṣa*), or not.

Since the attainment of liberation through the combination of knowledge and action is stated in such scriptural passages as, "Therefore, the knower of Brahman, the doer of good deeds, and the one who is radiant [attains the highest world]," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that action is required.

In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) maintains that because knowledge is the cause of liberation, there is no dependence on action for liberation known as the cessation of ignorance; this is stated in the words, "The human goal.
By the term "fire and fuel," the rituals accomplished by them are indicated.

The sense is that the scriptural passage—"The performer of meritorious deeds, becoming radiant and pure in essence, becomes a knower of Brahman and through that knowledge attains Brahman"—is to be explained in this way.

This concluding summary is stated to express further that, since actions have no efficacy regarding liberation (*mukti*), they are not required for that; however, they are required for knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of purifying the mind. Thus, he states the purpose of the concluding sūtra: "adhiketi.

Topic: The Requirement of All (Sarvāpekṣā). Sūtras 26–27. And there is a requirement for all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. (BS 3.4.26)
Now this is considered: is there an absolute non-dependence of knowledge upon the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma), or is there some dependence?

In this regard, since it was previously established that the duties of the stages of life—such as maintaining the sacred fires and offering fuel—are not required for the accomplishment of knowledge’s own purpose, and thus an absolute non-dependence had been reached, it is now said: "And there is dependence on all.
Knowledge does depend upon all the duties of the stages of life; it is not entirely independent.
Is this statement not contradictory—that knowledge requires the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) and yet does not require them?
We say: no.
For once knowledge has arisen, it requires nothing else for the accomplishment of its fruit; however, for its own arising, it does require [the duties].
Why? Because of the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifices and so forth.

For instance, scripture shows that sacrifices and the like are means for attaining knowledge: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Thus, it demonstrates the status of sacrifices and other practices as instruments of knowledge.
Furthermore, from their connection with the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), it is understood that these [works] function as means for its production.

As it is said: "Now, what people call 'sacrifice' is actually the praise of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) by means of sacrifice and so forth"; thus, the status of sacrifice and the other works as means is also indicated.
And: "That state which all the Vedas proclaim, and which all austerities declare..."

And such scriptural passages as, "I shall declare to you in brief that goal desiring which they lead the life of religious studentship" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.15), indicate that the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) serve as means for the attainment of knowledge.
Smṛti also states: "Ritual actions are the cooking of the impurities; knowledge, however, is the supreme goal."
"When the impurity has been ripened by actions, knowledge then arises"—such passages as these [are the source].
The phrase "like a horse" is an illustration of suitability (*yogyatā*).
Just as, by virtue of its suitability, a horse is not employed for pulling a plow but is employed for the movement of a chariot.
Thus, the duties of the stages of life (āśramakarmāṇi) are not required for the accomplishment of the fruit through knowledge, but they are required for its origination. // 26 //
He states the further [objection]: "dependence on all" (*sarvāpekṣā*).
