Just as there is no dependence on ritual action for the cessation of ignorance because it is the fruit of valid knowledge (*pramā*), so too, since knowledge (*vidyā*) is itself valid knowledge, and is accomplished merely by its instrument of valid knowledge, there is no dependence on ritual action; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In that case, the performance of ritual action for the sake of knowledge is not established.

The distinction is that in the Siddhānta, the fruit [is liberation] and its accomplishment [is the goal]. Here, in the case of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) or the knowledge being sought, the status of sacrifices and other rituals as causes is enjoined because it is something not previously established (*apūrva*).
This is possible because even valid cognition (*pramā*) can be accomplished through ritual action by means of purification known as the destruction of the evil (*durita*) that obstructs its arising.

Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural mention of the instrumental case (tṛtīyā-śruti) in the case of a mediated sequence; for even when the mediation occurs through the medium of a flame, one uses the expression "he cooks with wood," because the medium does not constitute an intervention.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for purity being the means [to liberation], for the Smṛti states:
"Knowledge arises in men through the destruction of sinful karma;
when the impurity has been ripened by actions, knowledge then proceeds."

He establishes the final position with the words "this [is it]," based on such scriptural passages as, "Having crossed over death by means of ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge," which state that the cessation of sin occurs through action and liberation through knowledge.

Now, an objection might be raised: here, by the use of the fifth lakāra (the optative) in the word *vividiṣanti*, it appears that the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) itself is the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), since the sense of the desiderative suffix (*san*) indicates that desire alone is what is to be brought about.

If, bypassing that [desire]—which is obtained through the natural beauty of the object—one says that knowledge (*vedana*) is the object to be produced, then why not bypass even that knowledge and say that liberation (*mokṣa*), which is its fruit, is what is to be produced by actions? To this, [the author replies:]...
He says: "And because of its connection with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

The meaning is that since knowledge (*vidyā*) is explicitly perceived as a fruit through the word [expressing] the object of desire, liberation (*mokṣa*), which is not heard [in the text], cannot be the fruit; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even in the sentence "he cooks with wood," the wood would be the cause of the fruit of cooking, namely satisfaction.
Regarding the fact that ritual actions serve the purpose of knowledge, he states the indicative marks and scriptural passages beginning with "Now" (*atha*).

He has stated that "all Vedāntas" [are concerned with this] because he considers that while some portion of the Veda directly declares the state called Brahman, others do so by means of ritual action aimed at knowledge.
The rest is clear. //26//

He should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth; nevertheless, because there is an injunction for those qualities, they too must necessarily be practiced as auxiliary elements of that [knowledge]. (BS 3.4.27)

If someone should think that it is not logical for sacrifices and the like to be means for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*) because there is no injunction [to that effect], one should consider this:

scriptural passages such as "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*) are of the nature of restatements (*anuvāda*), intended to praise knowledge rather than to enjoin sacrifices and so forth.

In this way, knowledge becomes highly exalted; thus, the seeker of knowledge—[as stated in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23: "Therefore, knowing thus, having become self-controlled, calm, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, he sees the Self by means of the Self alone"—is instructed.
Thus, because tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth are enjoined as means for the attainment of knowledge, and because what is enjoined must necessarily be performed;

[an objection is raised: "But even here, in the passage 'having become endowed with tranquility and so forth, he sees,' we find a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*), not an injunction (*vidhi*). We reply: "No."
Therefore, because the word "therefore" (tasmāt) refers back to the subject under discussion, it is understood as an injunction.
The Mādhyandinas clearly read the injunction in the form "one should see" (paśyet).
Consequently, even when there is no dependence on sacrifices and the like, tranquility (śama) and the other qualities must still be observed.
However, sacrifices and the like must also be performed, because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth.
Now, it was argued that in the passage "they desire to know through sacrifice and the like," no injunction is perceived.
True, this was said; nevertheless, since the connection [of these acts] is mentioned prior to the desire for knowledge, an injunction is inferred.

For this connection of sacrifices and the like with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) was not previously established such that it could be merely restated; rather, even in sentences where no injunction is explicitly heard—such as "Therefore Pūṣan has the ground portion, for he is toothless"—an injunction is postulated because of the novelty (*apūrvatva*) of the matter. Consequently, the investigation regarding whether "the grinding for Pūṣan is to be understood in the modified sacrifice" (*vikṛti*) and so forth was initiated in the first book (*tantra*) of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*.
And so it has been said: "Or [it is] an injunction, like the observance" (*Brahma-sūtra* 3.4.20).

Furthermore, in the *Smṛtis* such as the *Bhagavad-gītā*, it is elaborated that sacrifices and other rites performed by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) without aiming for their fruits become means for the attainment of knowledge.

Therefore, all duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*), including sacrifices and the like, as well as tranquility, self-control, and so forth, according to one's stage of life, must be relied upon for the arising of knowledge.

In that regard as well, it should be distinguished that because they are conjoined with knowledge (*vidyā*), the means of knowledge such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth are proximate; whereas because they are conjoined with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), sacrificial rites (*yajña*) and so forth are more remote. // 27 //
Having thus described the external auxiliary rites for the arising of knowledge, he states the internal ones with the word "śama" (tranquility).

Since it is possible for these to form a single syntactical unit for the purpose of praising knowledge, it is improper to assume an injunction by breaking the use of the present tense, as that would entail the consequence of separating them from the sentence concerning knowledge.

Therefore, having restated the opponent's view—that knowledge is obtainable through the mere words [of the Upanishads] such as "That thou art"—he accepts it, saying: "Even so, however... (tathāpi tu).

The meaning is that since tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities are necessary, knowledge is not obtainable through words alone. Because one who possesses such knowledge is not tainted by evil action, it is understood that there is an injunction stating: "Therefore, one seeking knowledge, having become endowed with tranquility and the rest, should investigate. Thus he says, "We say, 'No.

Here, by the word "withdrawal" (*uparata*), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is expressed; according to the view that renunciation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to hearing (*śravaṇa*), it is here enjoined that hearing—qualified by tranquility and the rest—is to be performed.

However, since renunciation (saṃnyāsa) has been established as possessing its own fruit in such scriptural and traditional texts as "Those desiring the world go forth [into homelessness]" and "One should renounce, placing knowledge at the forefront," it cannot logically be a mere subsidiary (aṅga) to hearing;

furthermore, if one were to enjoin multiple qualities such as tranquility (śama) and so forth by way of restating the hearing already enjoined in the rule "It is to be heard," this would result in the fallacy of sentence-splitting (vākyabheda).

Furthermore, because the word "should see" (*paśyet*) is used in its primary sense and because there is no defect in the characteristic of hearing (*śravaṇa*), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to hearing;

rather, even though it is to be performed prior to it, the view is that like hearing, it is for the sake of knowledge (*jñāna*). In that case, the injunction for the combination of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth for the sake of knowledge—namely, "one should cultivate knowledge through the combination of tranquility and so forth"—is beyond reproach.

He now abandons that previous acceptance of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth as being merely for the sake of praise—an acceptance made *ad interim* according to the maxim of the "sweetmeat on the tongue" (*guḍajihvikā-nyāya*) for the purpose of inducing the adoption of tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues—by stating, "even sacrifices and so forth.

Since the connection of sacrifices and the like with the means of knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*) is something not previously known (*apūrva*), an injunction is accepted through a syntactical split (*avāntara-vākya-bheda*);
the meaning is that there is a unity of purport (*ekavākyatā*) between the sentences concerning the knowledge of Brahman and the sentences concerning the injunctions.

Regarding the point that even in the context of the primary section (*prakaraṇa*) there is an intermediate injunction (*avāntaravidhi*), he cites the consensus of the earlier Mīmāṃsā system with the words: "Therefore, [the text] *pūṣā*...
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard: "Pūṣan has the ground portion as his share" (*pūṣā prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*).
In that case, neither Pūṣan as a deity nor a ground portion exists within the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Therefore, since the connection between the substance and the deity—understood through the compound and untouched by the three times—necessarily implies the injunction of a sacrifice, one must supply the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) for the sake of knowing the performance; thus, by being displaced from the context (*prakaraṇa*), the connection is established in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) as: "The portion of flour is to be made for Pūṣan."
The meaning is that this has been discussed in the Sūtra: "The grinding [of the grains] belongs to Pūṣan.
There are also Smṛti texts such as: "By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.

If ritual actions were causes for knowledge, they would have to persist until the dawning of knowledge—just like tranquility (śama) and the other qualities—and thus there would be no possibility of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). To this, he says: "In that case also..."

The sense is that because tranquility (śama) and the other qualities serve the purpose of knowledge by way of removing distractions of the mind, they continue [to be required]; however, ritual actions do not continue, because they serve the purpose of knowledge only through their unseen (adṛṣṭa) effects. //27//

Section on the Permission to Eat All Food (sarvānnānumati-adhikaraṇa), Sūtras 28–31. 7. [The Sūtra states: "There is no permission to eat all food, because of the non-universality of the scriptural statement. (Sūtra 28) [Commentary: It has been established that for one who has renounced the world, there is no such thing as eating food obtained through begging. Now, a further doubt arises: Is it permitted for him to eat any kind of food whatsoever, or is he restricted? Regarding this, the opponent maintains the following view: Since the scripture says, "He may eat whatever is offered," there is permission to eat all food. This is because the term "whatever" (yat kiñcit) denotes universality; therefore, there is no restriction. To this, we reply: There is no permission to eat all food. Why? Because the scriptural statement is not universal. The word "whatever" does not here denote all things without exception, but rather refers only to those things that are permissible to eat according to the rules of the *śruti* and *smṛti*. Therefore, the permission is limited to what is lawful, and there is no permission for what is forbidden. Thus, the conclusion is that even for one who has renounced the world, there is no permission to eat all food indiscriminately. [The Sūtra continues: "And because of the prohibition of meat-eating. "And there is no permission [to eat] anything except when life is at stake, because that is seen [in scripture].
Regarding this, it is heard in the *Chāndogya* in the dialogue on the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*): "Indeed, for one who knows this, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food" (ChāU 5.2.1).
Likewise, among the *Vājasaneyins*: "Indeed, for him, no food has been eaten, nor is anything non-food accepted as a gift" (BṛU 6.1.14).
The meaning is that everything indeed becomes fit to be eaten by him.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this permission to eat all food is enjoined as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of knowledge like tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, or is mentioned for the sake of praise (*stuti*), the initial position is that it is an injunction.

For such is the case: an instruction that produces a specific activity constitutes an injunction; therefore, because it occurs in proximity to the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), this cessation of restriction is taught as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that knowledge.
If this were so, would it not result in a contradiction with the scriptures that distinguish between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit?
This is not a fault,
because sublation is logically established through the relationship between the general and the particular.

Just as the prohibition against harming living beings is set aside by the injunction for the immolation of sacrificial animals; and just as, in the context of the Vāmadevya-vidyā, the scriptural rule distinguishing between permissible and impermissible sexual partners— which has a general scope— is set aside by the statement "he should not avoid anything whatsoever" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.13.2), which enjoins the avoidance of all prohibitions.

Thus, by this statement regarding the eating of all food within the context of the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), the scripture that distinguishes between what is fit and unfit to be eaten would be sublated.
This being the position reached, we reply: this is not an injunction permitting the consumption of all food.
For no injunctive word is found here; rather, it says: "Indeed, for one who knows thus, there is nothing whatsoever that is not food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1).
This is because it is stated as a description of a present state (*vartamānāpadeśa*).
Furthermore, even in the absence of a perceived injunction (*vidhi*), one cannot assume an injunction merely out of a desire for it to produce a specific activity.
Moreover, having stated that "the food of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) extends even to dogs," it is further said: "for one who knows this, there is nothing that is not food."
Furthermore, food as far down as dogs cannot be consumed by a human body;

however, it is possible to contemplate that "all this is the food of the vital breath" (prāṇa). Therefore, this explanatory passage (arthavāda) is for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the vital breath as food, and is not an injunction permitting the consumption of all food.
He shows this with the sūtra: "And there is permission for all food in case of life-threatening danger.
This is what is meant: only in the event of life-threatening danger—that is, in the most extreme calamity—is the eating of all food permitted, because that is what is observed in scripture.

For instance, the Śruti shows the sage Cākrāyaṇa engaging in the consumption of forbidden food when he was in a miserable state: "When the Kurus were struck by hailstones" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.1).
In this Brāhmaṇa,
it is said that the sage Cākrāyaṇa, having fallen into distress, ate some half-eaten groats belonging to a wealthy man;
however, he declined the accompanying drink on account of the fault of its being leavings.
And he stated the reason for this: "Indeed, I would not have lived without eating these," and "Water was my desire.
Furthermore, on the following day, he ate those very same stale kulmāṣa beans, which were the remnants of his own and others.

From the fact that the Śruti demonstrates this eating of remnants and stale food, its profound intention is perceived: that in the event of life-threatening danger, even what is unfit to be eaten may be consumed for the sake of sustaining life; however, in a state of health, it must not be done even by one possessed of knowledge—this is understood from the rejection of the accompanying drink.
Therefore, the passage "For indeed, in one who knows thus... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1) is a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
And so forth. // 28 //

And because there is no contradiction: "This being so, when the food is pure, the being is pure," and so forth; thus, the scriptural teaching on the distinction between what is fit to be eaten and what is not fit to be eaten will remain uncontradicted. (29)
The phrase "consent for all food" (sarvānnānumatiḥ) means that one who knows thus meditates on the fact that everything is the food of the vital breath (prāṇa). "Jagdham" means eaten.
A doubt arises because this is something not previously established (apūrvatva) and because no specific injunction (vidhi) is heard.

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that "it is an injunction (*vidhi*), because it is something not previously established (*apūrvatva*), like sacrifices and so forth"—with the word "injunction.

Here, the distinction is as follows: the result in the prima facie view is the establishment that the renunciation of the rules regarding what may and may not be eaten is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of knowledge; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is a glorification (*stuti*) of knowledge.
The scriptural injunction "one should not eat *kalañja*" refers to subjects other than those who know the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Just as the scriptural prohibition against another's wife applies to all except those who worship the Vāmadevya Sāman during ritual acts, so it was argued; however, the author shows the established conclusion (siddhānta) outside the sūtra itself: "This is not so. Because it occurs in proximity to the injunction for the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā), and because [the literal sense] is impossible, this is merely a praise and no injunction is to be inferred. The intention is that while an established injunction may sublate a general rule, an inferred one cannot do so, especially when it would contradict a prohibitory scripture.

Stating the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that there is no permission for a healthy person who knows the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to eat all kinds of food, he applies the Sūtra with the words: "He shows that.

When the crops in the land of the Kurus were destroyed by *maṭaci*—small red birds—and a famine had arisen, the sage, traveling to another region with his young wife, stayed in a village of elephant-drivers (*ibhya*). By that elephant-driver, [he was offered] half-eaten [roots], that is, those already partially consumed.
Having begged for loathsome beans, he ate them.

When the elephant said, "Take water," he refused, saying, "I would indeed be drinking what is left over by another. When the elephant asked, "Are the beans not also left over? he explained the reason for eating the beans and rejecting the water:
"In the matter of food, I am in a state of distress."

Since water for drinking could be obtained at will from ponds and other sources, he ate the beans and gave the remainder to his wife. She, though not herself in distress, learned of her husband’s misfortune and, having preserved the beans, gave them to him in the morning.

He, having eaten them, went to the king’s sacrifice, rebuked the *prastotṛ* and other priests, instructed them on the deities of the *prastāva* and other parts of the chant beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and remained there after obtaining wealth; such is the sense.

The sense is that, because there is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*)—consisting of avoiding what remains of another's leavings and the discarding of water—it is indicated that even a learned man, when not in a state of distress, must not consume what is unfit for consumption (*abhakṣya*), as established by Śruti. // 28 // // 29 //
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti: BBs_3,4.30.

Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti that even the eating of all kinds of food is permitted for one in times of distress, without distinction between the knower and the non-knower: "He who, having fallen into a situation where life is at risk, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Likewise: "A Brāhmaṇa [should avoid] liquor always... [and so forth].

The avoidance of food is prescribed by the Smṛti: "They should pour hot [liquor] upon a Brāhmaṇa who drinks *surā*," and "Those who drink *surā* become worms due to eating what is unfit for consumption. (30) [Note:
*Uṣṇām* means excessively heated.]
Fearing that one might continue to live even by drinking liquor, he says that it must never be done: "Likewise, [one should] always [avoid] liquor, O Brahmin.
The word "avoid" (varjaya) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Anticipating the question "Why?", he says "of the drinker of liquor," because a penance ending in death is prescribed for such a person.
"Hot" means excessively heated; the word "surā" (liquor) is understood as the object. For this reason as well, she says "those who drink liquor" to show that it must not be drunk. //30//
And for this reason,
there is a scriptural injunction regarding the non-performance of one's will. (BBs 3.4.31)

Furthermore, in the *Kaṭhaka Saṃhitā*, there is heard a scriptural statement prohibiting food unfit for consumption, which serves the purpose of turning one away from acting according to one's own whims: "Therefore, one should not drink *surā* [liquor] as a Brahmin.

That [prohibition] also becomes more appropriately justified as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the passage, "For indeed, there is no such thing for one who knows thus" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.2.1).
Therefore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) of this kind are not injunctions (*vidhi*). // 31 //
He states the source *śruti* for the aforementioned *smṛtis*: "And the word...

[referring to the passage] "kāmakāraḥ" (acting according to one's desire), which means acting as one pleases; that [freedom], as well as its prohibition, becomes even more appropriate because the passage "na ha vā evaṃvidi" is an *arthavāda*.

If this were also a mandatory injunction, then, because it would be both prescribed and prohibited, there would be an option regarding the drinking of *surā*—just as there is an option regarding the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; and that [option] is contradicted by all the *smṛtis* and by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
This is the intended meaning. //31//
Topic 8: The Section on the Duties of the Stages of Life (Āśrama-karma-adhikaraṇa) Sūtras 32–36 8.

Topic on the Duties of the Stages of Life (Āśrama-karma-adhikaraṇa) Sūtras 32–36 [The discussion concerns whether the duties pertaining to the various stages of life (āśramas) must be performed by one who desires liberation. Sūtra 32: "But [the duties] of all [stages of life] must be performed, because of the scriptural statement regarding the state of being a 'knower' (jñānitva). Sūtra 33: "[This is so] because of the connection with the purpose of the Self. Sūtra 34: "And because of the non-abandonment of the former [duties]. Sūtra 35: "But [this applies] only to those who have not renounced [worldly ties], because of the scriptural statement regarding the state of being a 'knower'. Sūtra 36: "And because of the non-abandonment of the former [duties]. [Note: This section establishes that while the seeker of liberation may perform the duties of any stage of life, those who have not yet renounced worldly attachments must continue to perform the specific duties of their respective stage, as these are conducive to the realization of the Self.]
"And because they are enjoined, the duties of the stages of life [are also means].
At [Brahma-sūtra] 3.4.26, "And there is need for all," it was determined that the duties of the stages of life are means for the attainment of knowledge.

Now, however, it is considered whether those [rites] are to be performed even by one who is not desirous of liberation (*amumukṣu*), who is devoted solely to his stage of life (*āśrama*) without seeking knowledge, and who does not desire knowledge; or whether they are not.

In this regard, since the duties of the stages of life are prescribed as means for attaining knowledge in such passages as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), they would not be to be performed by one who does not desire knowledge but desires some other fruit.

Now, if [it is argued that] these [rites] must also be performed by him [the seeker of knowledge], then they cannot be means for attaining knowledge, because of the contradiction between the obligatory and the non-obligatory.

To this position, the author replies: "The obligatory rites must indeed be performed even by one who abides merely in his stage of life (āśrama) and does not seek liberation, because they are enjoined by such texts as, 'As long as one lives, one performs the Agnihotra sacrifice,' and so forth. For there is no such thing as an 'overburdening' of a scriptural injunction. (Sūtra 3.4.32)
And because it is enjoined as a duty of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*):

since the duties such as the obligatory *agnihotra* are already enjoined, there is a contradiction between what has been assigned and what is being newly assigned; thus, in the face of this doubt, just as the statement regarding "eating all food" is a mere praise due to its conflict with other scriptures, so too the scriptural injunction regarding the application [of the sacrifice] toward the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) is a praise, because it contradicts the scriptural hearing that [the sacrifice] is permanently assigned [to the stages of life].
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

If ritual actions are performed out of a desire for knowledge, they are non-eternal and not mandatory; yet, because that [desire] is non-eternal, there is also eternality through injunctions such as "as long as one lives. Since this results in the occurrence of two contradictory properties, the result of the prima facie view is that the scriptural passage concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-śruti*) is merely a commendatory statement (*stuti*).
In the established conclusion (siddhānta), however, the result is the performance in both ways. //32//
Now, regarding what was said— that this being so, these [works] would not be means for knowledge— the following passage is recited as a reply:
And [they function] as auxiliaries;

for these [works] are auxiliaries to knowledge precisely because they are so prescribed by such passages as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
As it has been said: "There is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.26).

Nor should this statement regarding the auxiliary nature of the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karmāṇi) with respect to knowledge be understood as referring to the fruit of knowledge— like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—
because knowledge is not characterized by injunction (*avidhi-lakṣaṇatvāt*),
and because the fruit of knowledge is not something to be produced (*asādhyatvāt*).
For a means characterized by injunction, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, requires another auxiliary means due to the desire to achieve the fruit of heaven; knowledge is not like this.
And so it has been said: "And for this very reason, there is no dependence on the kindling of fire and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.25).
Therefore, the expression regarding their being "auxiliaries" applies only to their being means for the origination [of knowledge].
Nor should one suspect here a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal, because even though the action is the same, the conjunctions are distinct;

for in the case of the eternal [obligatory rite], there is one conjunction established by such scriptural injunctions as "as long as one lives," and that does not have the fruit of knowledge as its result.

However, the other connection is non-eternal; that which is established by such scriptural passages as "This very [Self] by the recitation of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) has knowledge as its fruit.

Just as the same quality of being made of *khadira* wood serves the purpose of the sacrifice through an eternal connection, yet serves the purpose of the person through a non-eternal connection, so it is here. // 33 //
"Cooperative actions" (sahakārīṇi karmāṇi) are those which, having come together, produce knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of purification;
"the state of being such" (*tattvam*) means their nature as such.
He rejects the notion that the capacity to produce the fruit [of liberation] exists simultaneously with knowledge—which would follow from the term "cooperative"—by stating: "And this is not so."
Since knowledge is not enjoined [as a ritual act], it has no requirement for auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

Therefore, enjoined rituals cannot be auxiliary factors for unenjoined knowledge; furthermore, because liberation is not something to be produced (*asādhya*), there is no possibility of rituals acting as its auxiliaries—this is the meaning.

There is no contradiction here, because there is a distinction of application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*) due to a difference in connection (*saṃyoga-bheda*) between two scriptural injunctions of equal force.
Even though desire is impermanent, there is no impermanence in the ritual acts, because their performance is permanent due to the permanent injunction.
When desire exists, the permanence [of the rite] is established precisely through the performance for the sake of that desire; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
This point was deliberated upon in the sūtra: "But when one [act] serves two purposes, there is a distinctness of connection."

Just as by the scriptural statement "the sacrificial post is made of khadira wood," the quality of being made of khadira serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*), while by the scriptural statement "for one desiring vigor, [the post] is made of khadira," it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*);
therefore, the meaning is that when two distinct sentences exist, there is no contradiction in the application of what has already been applied. //33//
In every way, they alone [are the cause], because of the twofold indicative mark. (BBs 3.4.34)

In every respect—both in the view that they are duties belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) and in the view that they are auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*)—those very same duties such as the *agnihotra* and so forth are to be performed.
By emphasizing "those very same," what does the Teacher exclude?
We reply: he excludes the notion that there is a difference in the nature of the action (*karma*).

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana sacrifice—wherein the statement "for a month he performs the Agnihotra" teaches a distinct ritual from the obligatory Agnihotra—there is no such difference of ritual here.
Why? Because of the two-fold indicative marks:
both from the indicative mark of Śruti and from the indicative mark of Smṛti.
First, the indicative mark from Śruti: "Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

This passage enjoins sacrifices and other rites—which already exist as established entities—toward the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*); it does not, like the injunction "he offers oblations," produce a previously non-existent form of these rites.
Furthermore, there is an indicative mark from Smṛti: "He who performs the duty that must be done without depending on the fruit of action" (Gītā 6.1).
Thus, [the scripture] shows that ritual action, whose duty is already known, is for the purpose of producing knowledge.

Furthermore, the well-known designation of Vedic rituals as "samskāras" (purificatory rites), as in the passage beginning "For whom these forty-eight samskāras exist," occurs in the Smṛti with the intention that knowledge arises for one who has been purified by them.
Therefore, this determination of non-difference [between the seeker and the knower] is indeed valid. // 34 //

[Objection: But surely, let the *Apūrva* sacrifices and so forth, which are indeed distinct from the obligatory (*nitya*) *Agnihotra* and other rites, be enjoined toward the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*). Why then is there an "enjoining of what has already been enjoined" (*viniyuktaviniyoga*)? To this he says: "In every way" (*sarvathāpi*). This means whether they are obligatory or optional. [This is so] because in the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*, regarding the statement "They offer the *Agnihotra* for a month," the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes a sacrifice that is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and thus the word *Agnihotra*—which has the same referent as that suffix—[denotes the same].

Since it is impossible for [the word "yajñena"] to refer back to an established Agnihotra that is separated [in context], it is logical that a different rite qualified by the attribute of "monthly" (māsa) is being enjoined;

however, in this case, because words ending in case-suffixes such as "yajñena" lack syntactic unity with the verb, they cannot serve as references to an established, remote rite. Therefore, the sense is that these very rites are enjoined for the purpose of knowledge.

He states—“yasyaita” (for whom these)—that even the well-known status of perfected actions as *saṃskāra*s (purificatory rites) is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the non-difference between actions intended for knowledge and those called *śuddhi* (purification), by way of the *saṃskāra* known as purification. //34//
And it demonstrates non-overpowering. (BBs 3.4.35)

This observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) serves as a corroboration of the very fact of cooperation; for the Śruti shows the non-overpowering [of knowledge] by afflictions such as passion in one who is endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), through passages beginning with, "For this Self does not perish, which one finds through celibacy" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.5.3).
Therefore, it is certain that sacrifices and the like, as well as the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*), are auxiliaries to knowledge. // 35 //

He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that actions such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) have knowledge (*vidyā*) as their purpose by way of destroying obstacles: "And non-overpowering" (Sūtra 3.4.35).
The section concerning the absence of instruments and so forth. Sūtras 36–39.
"But because it is seen even for those in between.

(BBs 3.4.36) Regarding the doubt as to whether there is eligibility for knowledge (*vidyā*) or not for those who are "in between"— such as Vidhura and others who lack the perfection of wealth and so forth, and who have failed to enter any of the stages of life (*āśrama*)— the initial position reached is that there is no such eligibility.

Since it has been determined that the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) are the cause of knowledge, and since these [householders] are incapable of performing such duties, this being the position reached, the author says this: "But even one who exists in the interval as a non-ascetic (*anāśramin*) is qualified for knowledge.
Why? Because that is seen."
For we find scriptural testimony that even such persons as Raikva, Vācaknavī, and others attained the state of Brahman. // 36 //

Moreover, it is recorded in tradition that Saṃvarta and others attained the status of great yogis through practices such as naked asceticism, even though they disregarded the duties pertaining to the stages of life (āśrama). This is recounted in the Itihāsas. (37)
But even for those between [stages], because that is seen;

since there is doubt as to whether the performance of recitation (*japa*) and other rites exists for those who are not in a stage of life (*anāśramin*), and because of the scriptural statement that the duties of the stages of life alone are the cause of knowledge and because of the condemnation of the non-staged state, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no entitlement [to knowledge].
In that case, it is established that the duties of those not in a stage of life are not causes of knowledge.
In the final system (siddhānta), its establishment is the result. // 36 // // 37 //

Now, an objection is raised: "Surely this indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the observation of *Śruti* and *Smṛti* has been set forth; what, then, is the actual basis for this conclusion? To that, it is replied: [the basis is as follows].
And there is also special favor (viśeṣānugraha).

Even for those such as the *vidhura* (the disabled), favor toward the knowledge (*vidyā*) is possible through specific dharmas—such as recitation (*japa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and propitiation of deities—which are not contradictory [to their condition] and are common to all human beings.
And thus says the Smṛti: "A Brāhmaṇa may indeed attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this."

"Whether he performs [the rites] or does not perform them, he is called a Brāhmaṇa by virtue of his mantra"—this shows that even those who are unable to perform the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) are qualified for the practice of recitation (*japya*).
Furthermore, the assistance of knowledge (*vidyā*) is indeed possible through the duties of the stages of life performed in previous births.
Thus says the Smṛti: "Perfected through many births, he then attains the supreme goal" (Gītā 6.45).
Thus, [the scripture] shows that even those who have accumulated specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births are not assisted in their knowledge [if they lack certain qualities].
Furthermore, since knowledge has a perceptible purpose, it qualifies one for hearing [the scriptures] and other practices by the mere absence of prohibitions.
Therefore, the qualification of widowers and others is not contradicted. // 38 //

He raises an objection, saying "But [the case of] Raikva and others," on the grounds that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of their possession of knowledge could be established otherwise through the performance of duties belonging to a stage of life (*āśrama*) in a previous birth; thus, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be stated to establish that even the duties of one not in a formal stage of life serve the purpose of knowledge.

He states the proof for the fact that duties pertaining solely to caste (*varṇa*), which are not inconsistent with being outside a formal stage of life, serve the purpose of knowledge, saying "And so it is":
"Maitra" means compassionate.

[Objection: Granted that for those who do not belong to any stage of life (anāśramin), ritual action may be a cause of knowledge; nevertheless, they lack the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth because of the absence of renunciation (saṃnyāsa). To this, he says: "And because its purpose is perceived. One who desires knowledge—which has as its fruit the destruction of the ignorance that binds—is qualified for hearing.
The point is that even if renunciation is performed at some time, it assists toward knowledge, since it is not an essential factor (aṅga) with respect to hearing. //38//
But the other [state] is superior to this, both because of the scriptural mark and because of logical reasoning. (BS 3.4.39)

Therefore, because it occupies an intermediate position, residing in the other stages of life (*āśrama*) is a superior means for the attainment of knowledge, as it is clearly seen in both Śruti and Smṛti.
This is also indicated by a scriptural sign (*liṅga*): "By this [path] goes the knower of Brahman, the doer of meritorious deeds, and those who possess splendor" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1).

And because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the Smṛti: "A twice-born man should not remain even for a single day without belonging to an āśrama; having remained without an āśrama for a year, he should perform one Kṛcchra penance. // 39 //
To the objection that the state of being an ascetic (*āśramitva*) would thus be in vain, he says: "Therefore, however" (*atastu*).

The meaning is that the one who performs meritorious deeds, who belongs to the realm of light (*taijasa*), and whose being is pure (*śuddhasattva*), proceeds by that path of knowledge and attains Brahman.

The sense here is that, because of the mark of being a performer of meritorious deeds (*puṇyakṛttva*), the state of being a forest-dweller (*āśramitva*) is superior; for through the accumulation of merit, one quickly attains knowledge, whereas the state of not belonging to any stage of life (*anāśrama*) is censured. //39//

Section on the Meaning of the Words Themselves. Sūtra 40.

"But for one who has become that [ascetic], there is no falling away from it, even according to Jaimini, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of those [other] forms. (BS 3.4.40).
It has been established that there are stages of life (*āśrama*) for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*).
However, a doubt arises as to whether or not there is a falling away from those stages for one who has reached them by some means.

"Or, even one who has fallen away—either through the desire to perform former ritual acts or under the influence of passion and so forth—might [return], because there is no difference [in the nature of the order].

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "But for one who has become that—that is, for one who has entered the state of an *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose semen is drawn up)—there can be no non-becoming-that, nor can there be a falling away from that state.
Why? Because of the restrictive rules (*niyama*), the absence of such a form [of activity], and [the scriptural] declarations."

For instance, such rules as "completely exhausting himself in the teacher's family" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1), "He should go to the forest; from there he should not return— this is the secret teaching," and "Permitted by his teacher, he should follow one of the four stages of life according to the rule until the liberation of the body," demonstrate that there is no possibility of falling away [from the stage once entered].

Furthermore, while statements of the nature of ascending are found, such as "Having completed the student life, one should become a householder" (Jābāla 4) and "One should renounce from the student life itself" (Jābāla 4), no such statements of the nature of descending are found.
Nor do such cultured persons (*śiṣṭas*) exist who follow this practice.

As for the claim that "descending" (*pratyavarohaṇa*) occurs out of a desire to perform the duties of one's previous caste, that is incorrect, because of the traditional teaching: "One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed" (Gītā 3.35).
And this is also due to logic:
for that which is prescribed for someone is his duty (*dharma*), not that which can merely be performed by him;
because *dharma* is defined by scriptural injunction (*codanā*).
Nor does there occur a falling away from [the state of knowledge] due to the influence of passion and so forth, because the rule of the restrictive scripture (niyama-śāstra) is more powerful.
By the word "also" in the phrase "of Jaimini also," he teaches the agreement between Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa on this point for the sake of strengthening the conviction. 40.

But for one who has fallen from the highest stage of life (uttamāśrama) and returned to a previous stage— such a person’s ritual action (*karman*) is also a cause of knowledge, just like the actions of those not belonging to any stage of life; this is the logical connection,
and it constitutes the result of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the Siddhānta, however, the result is that for one who has fallen away, ritual action (*karman*) is not the cause [of falling].
Because of the intensity of passion and the like, and because of the prohibition against falling away, they express doubt as to whether such falling away is authoritative or not.
He explains the restriction in the Siddhānta-sūtra with the words "For it is thus" (*tathāhi*).

"Excessively" (*atyantam*) refers to the rule of lifelong commitment (*naiṣṭhikatva*). "The forest" (*araṇyam*) signifies the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) characterized by solitude. "He should go there" (*tadiyāt*) means he should proceed according to the path of the scriptures; from that state of mendicancy, he should not return—that is, he should not fall away—this is the secret of the *Upaniṣad*.
He explains the absence of proof regarding the loss of that nature with the words "And as... (yathā ca). He states the absence of the conduct of the learned with the words "And not thus" (na caivam).
The sense is that, according to the Smṛti text, "Caṇḍālas are those who have fallen from their caste," the ritual action of those who have fallen is fruitless. //40//
