The Section on Qualification (Adhikārādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 41–42.
Nor can it be argued that [the rule] pertains to one holding an office, because of the inference of a fall from such a state, which would be inappropriate.

(BBs 3.4.41) If a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*) should, through negligence, break his vow of chastity, should he then be subject to the expiation prescribed by the rule, "One who has broken his vow of chastity shall sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti," or not?
It is said: no.

Furthermore, as for the expiation determined in the section on eligibility (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*)—namely, "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), just like that [of a householder], because the time for the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived" (Jaimini Sūtra 6.8.21)—that too cannot apply to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). What is the reason? "But he who, having ascended to the duty of a lifelong student, falls away from it... [is subject to the following].

"I see no expiation by which that self-killer might be purified"—because of this traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding a downfall that cannot be remedied, just as a remedy is impossible for one whose head has been severed, such an expiation is not applicable [for the lifelong student]. However, for the *upakurvāṇa* (the student who returns home), since there is no such traditional teaching regarding a downfall, that expiation is indeed possible. (41)
Nor does it pertain to one who holds an office (*adhikārika*).
"Would be defiled" (*avakīryeta*) means he would transgress.
One who has spilled semen into a womb is called *avakīrṇin*.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt as to whether or not there should be an expiation for one who has fallen [from the state of a twice-born], because it is both a minor offense (*upapātaka*) and because there are scriptural traditions concerning "falling" (*patana*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) argues that just as it was stated that sacrifices and other rites performed by one who has fallen are fruitless, so too should expiation be fruitless; thus he says, "It is said: No.

Here, the result is that for one who has performed expiation, ritual action does not become a cause for knowledge according to the prima facie view, whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it does.

Just as at the time of initiation (*upanayana*), the fire-oblation (*homa*) must be performed in the ordinary fire (*laukikāgni*)— because the formal establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), which is prescribed for the period after marriage, has not yet reached its proper time and thus the *āhavanīya* fire does not exist— at the same time, for the student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), the donkey, which is the sacrificial animal for penance, is to be offered in the ordinary fire; this is established in the sixth chapter concerning the characteristics of eligibility (*adhikāra*).

Having established that the prescribed expiation pertains only to the *upakurvāṇa* (the student who returns home) and not to the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong celibate), the author now sets forth the final conclusion. //41//
However, some maintain that even when preceded by the prefix *upa*, it denotes a state (*bhāva*), just like the word for eating; this has already been explained. (BBs 3.4.42)
However, some teachers consider this to be merely a minor offense (*upapātaka*).

They hold that when the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) breaks his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) with anyone other than the wife of his teacher and so forth, it does not constitute a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), because it is not enumerated among the mortal sins such as violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*).

Therefore, they maintain that like the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*), the lifelong student also deserves expiation (*prāyaścitta*), since there is no difference in their status as celibates and no difference in the fact that they have spilled their seed (*avakīrṇin*).
It is like [the case of] eating food:
just as for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), eating honey or meat results in the violation of his vow and necessitates a rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), so it is here.
For those who maintain that there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) at all, no scriptural basis (*mūla*) can be found.

However, for those who maintain that [the act] exists, the scriptural statement regarding no distinction between a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) and one who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*) is the basis.
Therefore, existence [of the act] is more logical.
As it was stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*: "The conflict would be equal" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.8).
"Or rather, those established in the scriptures [are authoritative], because they have that as their cause" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.9).
As for the traditional rule regarding the absence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), it has been explained that this is intended to produce a sense of gravity toward the effort required.

In the same way, for both the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) and the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), the forest-dweller, upon a breach of his initiation (*dīkṣā*), should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights.

A monk should increase his "great girdle" (mahākakṣa) like one in the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage, with the exception of the *soma* creeper and the sectarian marks (*liṅga*); he should also undergo the purificatory rites prescribed by his own scriptures.
In this manner, the traditional rules regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*) should be followed. // 42 //
Regarding the term *upapūrva*: it means that for which a secondary word (*upapada*) precedes the word *pātaka* (sin), that is an *upapātaka*.

Since the Smṛti statement "I see no expiation" is a record of non-perception, one must first assume it refers to the absence of an expiation; however, even before one can postulate a Vedic source (*śruti*) for that [Smṛti], the existence of an expiation is already established by a general Vedic text that has already been formulated.
The sense is that no such assumption arises because it would contradict established scriptural authority (*kḷpta-śruti*).

Although the existence or non-existence of a penance (*prāyaścitta*) might otherwise be considered equal [in terms of necessity], the establishment of its existence must be accepted because it is rooted in scripture; regarding this, he cites the consensus with the words "so it has been said.
In the case of the injunction "an oblation of barley" (*yavamayaś caruḥ*), some use the word *yava* for long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*), while others use it for *priyaṅgu* in certain regions.

Therefore, when a doubt arises as to for whom the *caru* (oblation) should be prepared, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—based on the similarity of usage among the elders—is that the understanding [of who should receive it] should be equal or identical, being a matter of option. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: the understanding rooted in the scripture (*śāstra*) must be accepted, because knowledge of dharma and so forth is caused by the scripture.
And thus: "When other plants wither, then these barley grains remain rejoicing."

Thus, the meaning is that because it is rooted in the authoritative scripture (*śāstra*), the practice involving long-awned grain (*dīrghaśūka*) alone is to be respected. He states the source for this Smṛti rule with the words "prāyaścitta" (expiation):

the meaning is that the venerable Atri said, "I do not see even a clear expiation," in order to make known that an excessive effort must be made for the sake of protecting one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

He states with the word "evam" (thus) that there is indeed an expiation for the breaking of celibacy through negligence even for the forest-dweller and the ascetic, just as there is for the lifelong student.
He should increase the *kṛcchra* penance known as the *prājāpatya* by providing water and other necessities to a large area (*mahākakṣa*) abounding in grass and wood;
however, the ascetic (*yati*) should increase it by [providing] everything except the *soma* creeper.
"Even one who is addicted to every kind of sin, by meditating for even a moment on Acyuta,
becomes once more an ascetic and a purifier of the assembly;
so it is with regard to the multitude of minor offenses and even the great sins."
Having entered the first quarter of the night, one should practice meditation on Brahman.

The meaning is that a monk must also perform the purifications such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) prescribed by his own scriptures. From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it follows: "The fire of yoga burns all defects born of mind, speech, and body—those arising from ignorance and those born of negligence—just as a flame consumes a heap of cotton."
"One should always perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas);
performed daily, they purify even the slayer of a fetus within a month"—such statements as these are to be accepted. //42//
12. The section concerning the external [sacrifice]. Sūtra 43.
But as for those outside [the fold], according to both [Smṛti and custom]:

whether the falling away of those who have taken the vow of perpetual chastity from their own stage of life constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or a minor offense (*upapātaka*), in either case they must be excluded by the learned.
"He who, having ascended to the duty of lifelong commitment, falls away from it again..."

"I see no expiation by which that self-killer might be purified," and "Having touched a Brahmin who has fallen after having ascended [to a high order], one who has been expelled from the [Vedic] circle, one who has hanged himself, or one bitten by worms, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance"— from such Smṛti texts expressing extreme censure,
as well as from the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas).
For the learned do not perform sacrifices, Vedic study, marriage, and so forth together with them. // 43 //

But as for those outside [the fold], even in both cases, there arises a doubt: whether the means of knowledge—such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth—performed together with them who have performed expiation (prāyaścitta) is valid or not. Since they have been purified, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it is a valid means.

However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that although they may be pure in the next world after expiation, because their state here [in this life] is not pure, it is not a valid means; thus he concludes: "If, however... (yady ūrdhvam).
The commentary is easy to understand. //43//
Section on Sovereignty (Svāmyadhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 44–46 13. [The section concerning] sovereignty. Sūtras 44–46.
"Because the fruit is declared for the master, so says Ātreya. Regarding the meditations on the subordinate parts [of the sacrifice], there is a doubt:
are they the acts of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or are they the acts of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That these are the acts of the sacrificer.
Why? Because of the mention of a fruit.
For a fruit is heard in such passages as: "It rains for him, and he causes it to rain, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in rain" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.3.2), and so forth.
And it is logical that this [result] should accrue to the owner,
because he is authorized for the performance together with its constituent parts,
and because such a category of action belongs to one who is so authorized.
Furthermore, the fruit of meditations is heard in scripture: "It rains for him who meditates," and so forth.

But is it not observed that even the officiating priest receives a fruit, as in: "Whatever desire he desires for himself, he obtains by singing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.28)? No; for that [fruit for the priest] is based solely on a specific scriptural injunction.
Therefore, the teacher Ātreya maintains that the master alone possesses the status of agent in those meditations that bear fruit.
Because the scriptural declaration of fruit refers to the master [of the sacrifice],

there arises a doubt regarding the meditations based on the subordinate members [of the sacrifice], since the possibility of both [the master and the officiating priest] being the performers exists therein.

This is because the general rule— that "one who has performed the penance is fit for social intercourse"— is set aside in the case of lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) and others by means of traditional texts (*smṛti*) expressing extreme censure.

He states the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view—that there is a sublation of the general rule by the scriptural declaration of the fruit for the agent—by asking "What [is the result]? The general rule is that when one is the agent of a subsidiary act (*aṅga*), he is the agent of that which depends upon it; however, this is sublated by the scriptural statement that the fruit belongs to the primary agent.

Here, the result is the co-location (*aikādhikaraṇya*) of agency and enjoyership; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the acts dependent on the subsidiaries are performed by the priests as agents.

If even meditations (*upāstayaḥ*) have fruits that belong to the sacrificer and are independent [of the ritual], what need is there to mention the independence of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) which resides in itself?

Thus, the fruit must be distinguished. Therefore, this is consistent with the [structure of the] chapter (*pāda*). The meaning of the scripture is that for one who meditates on rain within the fivefold *sāman*—consisting of the *hiṅkāra*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, and *nidhana*—the fruit is the abundance of rain.
To the question, "Why should the fruit of the *śruti* not belong to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)? he says: "And that" (*tac ca*).

Just as the fruit of the *godohana* vessel belongs to the person authorized for the sacrifice because it is subordinate to the qualified performer of the sacrifice with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-kratu*), so too the fruit of the meditation on the auxiliary (*aṅgopāsana*) belongs to that same person; this is the meaning.
To the objection, "Granted that its fruit belongs to him, why could the agent not be someone else? he says: "And the fruit" (*phalaṃ ca*).
Regarding what was stated—that the fruit accrues to the sacrificer—he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but surely).
The meaning is that [the Udgātṛ] accomplishes it by means of the *udgāna* (chanting).
The purpose of the resolution is that the general rule (*utsarga*)—that the fruit belongs to the sacrificer—is established unless there is a statement that serves as an exception (*bādhaka*).
Therefore, the meaning is: because of being the enjoyer of the fruit. //44//
"It is the office of the officiating priest," says Auḍulomi, for he is hired for that purpose. (BS 3.4.45)
This is not so; that these meditations are the duties of the patron is not the case.
The teacher Auḍulomi considers that these must be the duties of the officiating priests.
What is the reason?
For the sacrificer hires the officiating priests for that ritual action together with its ancillaries;

and since the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth fall within the scope of that performance, they are governed by the principle of "qualification based on what is already qualified" (*adhikṛtādhikāra*).
Therefore, like the rule regarding the *godohana* vessel and other such requirements, these meditations must be carried out by the officiating priests.

And likewise, the text "Baka Dālbhya knew him; he became the Udgātṛ priest of the Naimiśīyas" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.13) shows that the fruit of this knowledge belongs to the agent, namely the Udgātṛ.
As for what was said—that the fruit is heard to reside in the agent—[that is so].
This is not a fault;
because the priests act for the sake of another, and since there is no scriptural statement to the contrary, a connection with the fruit [of the rite] is untenable for them. // 45 //
And because of scripture:

"Whatever blessing the officiating priests invoke during the sacrifice, they invoke it for the patron alone," so he said. Therefore, an Udgātṛ priest who knows this should say: "What desire of yours shall I sing forth?
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.8–9).
This demonstrates that the fruit of the consciousness produced by the agent who has tasted that [juice] accrues to the sacrificer;
therefore, it is established that the meditations on the constituent parts (aṅga-upāsanās) are the work of the officiating priests (ṛtvij). // 46 //
Since officiating at a sacrifice (*ārlijyam*) consists of worship performed by a priest, he cites a Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*) to this effect: "And so it is" (*tathā ca*).

The meaning is that he meditated upon that *praṇava* called the *udgītha* through the vision of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and having meditated, he became the *udgātṛ* priest for the sacrificers (*sattrin*) of the Naimiṣa forest.

For, although the priests are the performers because they have been purchased by the patron (*yajamāna*) to carry out the ritual procedure with its constituent parts for the sake of the fruit accruing to him, it has been stated that they do not partake in that fruit, since there is no sublation of the general rule [that the fruit belongs to the patron].

The core idea is that through the act of purchasing [the body], the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of agency and enjoyership becomes logically consistent, just as one says "the king fights and wins" regarding a battle fought by his servants. // 45 // // 46 //

Section 14: The Topic Concerning the Injunction of Another Auxiliary (Sūtras 47–49) [The Sūtra: "There is an injunction for another auxiliary. (Sūtra 47) [Commentary: It has been established that the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to liberation, must necessarily be acquired. Now, it is being considered whether this acquisition of knowledge requires any further auxiliaries or not. In the context of the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the highest state" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), the text continues: "This, indeed, is the Brāhmaṇa’s instruction; this is the teaching; this is the secret doctrine" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.9). Following this, the text says: "One should meditate on the syllable *Om* as the Udgītha" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), and so forth. Here, a doubt arises: does the meditation on the Udgītha and other such practices serve as auxiliaries to the knowledge of Brahman, or do they belong only to the ritual acts? On the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), these meditations are merely parts of the ritual acts, because they are mentioned in proximity to the ritual injunctions. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: There is an injunction for another auxiliary. Just as the hearing of the Veda is an auxiliary to knowledge, so too are these meditations on the Udgītha and others enjoined as further auxiliaries to the knowledge of Brahman. This is because they are connected to the Self and lead to the same fruit—liberation—and because they are mentioned in the same instructional context as the knowledge of Brahman. Therefore, these meditations are indeed auxiliaries to the realization of Brahman. Thus ends the section concerning the injunction of another auxiliary. (Sūtra 47) [The Sūtra: "And there is no contradiction with the Smṛti. (Sūtra 48) [Commentary: Furthermore, this view is supported by the Smṛti texts. As it is said: "By the boat of the syllable *Om*, one crosses over the ocean of saṃsāra" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 260.10). Since such Smṛti passages confirm that the syllable *Om* and similar meditations are aids to crossing the ocean of worldly existence, there is no contradiction in regarding them as auxiliaries to the knowledge of Brahman. [The Sūtra: "And [the Smṛti] shows the same. (Sūtra 49) [Commentary: Moreover, the Smṛti itself demonstrates that these meditations are intended for the seeker of liberation. For instance, it is said: "Having renounced all duties, one should dwell in solitude, practicing the yoga of meditation on the syllable *Om*" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 260.12). Thus, the Smṛti clearly indicates that these practices are meant for those seeking the goal of liberation through knowledge. Therefore, the meditations on the Udgītha and other such elements are indeed enjoined as further auxiliaries to the knowledge of Brahman. (Sūtra 49) Thus ends the fourteenth section. (Section 14)
There is an injunction for another auxiliary means as a third [stage] for one who possesses that [first stage], like the beginning of an injunction; for it is heard in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*:

"Therefore, having attained proficiency through sacred learning (*pāṇḍitya*) regarding Brahman, one should remain in the state of a child (*bālya*); having attained both childhood and proficiency, one becomes a sage (*muni*); and having attained both non-sagehood and sagehood, one becomes a true Brahmin. (Bṛ. Up. 3.5.1)

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the state of silence (mauna) enjoined or not? For the moment, the prima facie view is that it is not enjoined, because the injunction is concluded with the words "he should remain in a state of childhood" (bālyena tiṣṭhāset).
For in the phrase "na hy atha muniḥ," no injunctive case-ending is perceived; therefore, this is properly an explanatory restatement (anuvāda).

If it is asked, "From where is its prior attainment?"—since the words *muni* and *paṇḍita* both have the sense of knowledge, the state of being a sage (*mauna*) is attained by the phrase "having fully understood scholarship" (*pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya*).

Furthermore, in the passage "having realized both non-silence and silence, then he is a Brāhmaṇa," the state of being a Brāhmaṇa is not being enjoined, because it has already been established previously.

Therefore, the phrase "then he is a Brāhmaṇa" is merely a commendatory statement; likewise, the phrase "then he is a sage (muni)" must also be understood as such, since the two cases are presented in an identical manner.
This being the position reached, we reply: it is an injunction regarding another auxiliary factor.

Since silence (*mauna*) is an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), its injunction must be accepted just like childhood and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), as it is something not previously established [by other means].
But has it not already been understood by the very word "scholarship"?
This is not a fault.
This is because the word *muni* signifies an excellence of knowledge, and the etymological derivation "a *muni* is so called because of reflection (*manana*)" is also possible;
as it is said: "Among *munis*, I am Vyāsa" (Gītā 10.37).
And because such usage is observed;

for instance, [one might object]: "But the word *muni* is also heard as denoting the highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*) in the passage: 'The householder's life, the teacher's family, the state of a sage (*mauna*), and forest-dwelling. [We reply: No, because deviation from this meaning is observed in cases such as "Vālmīki, the bull among sages" (*munipuṅgava*).

However, because of the proximity of the other stages of life (*āśrama*), the highest stage of life is understood there by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), since that highest stage has knowledge as its primary characteristic. Therefore, in comparison with childhood (*bālya*) and wisdom (*pāṇḍitya*), this third stage, characterized by an excellence of knowledge, is enjoined as "silence" (*mauna*).

As for the claim that the injunction concludes with childhood itself, nevertheless, because the state of being a sage (*munitva*) is something not previously established, it is accepted as an object of injunction, [expressed as]: "One should be a sage."
Furthermore, from the description of [the state] as being "not to be felt" (nirvedanīya), silence is understood to be something to be practiced, just like childhood and scholarship;
this applies to one who possesses that [silence], namely, the learned renunciant (saṃnyāsin).
And how is it understood that he is a learned renunciant?
Because that is the subject under discussion, [the text says]: "Having known the Self, having risen above the desires for sons and so forth, they then lead the life of a mendicant.

Now, one might object: "If one possesses knowledge (*vidyā*), excellence in that regard follows as a matter of course; what then is the purpose of an injunction for silence (*mauna*)? To this he replies: "As an alternative" (*pakṣeṇa*). This is what is meant:
In that case where [the result] is not attained due to the predominance of the perception of difference, this injunction applies;
it is like the beginning of an injunction (*vidhyādi*).

For example, in an injunction such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," the collection of subsidiary elements (*aṅga-jāta*) such as the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) is enjoined as a cooperative factor.
Thus, even though this statement concerning knowledge is not the primary subject, the meaning is that it prescribes the practice of silence. // 47 //
This is an injunction for another auxiliary practice.

Since ancient Brahmins, having known the Self, renounced and lived the life of a mendicant, therefore even the modern Brahmin who possesses the "pāṇḍitya"— the state of being a scholar consisting of initial knowledge— must, having become weary of that "pāṇḍitya," which is the act of hearing [the scriptures], renounce it.

Having attained certainty through the power of the knowledge born of hearing (*śravaṇa*) by means of childhood (*bālya*), one should desire to abide in reflection (*manana*)—which dispels doubt—or in the state of a child, which is the purity of mind; thus, having performed both reflection and hearing, one subsequently becomes a sage (*muni*) who practices meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). In this way, there is "non-silence" (*amauna*), which consists of the two states of childhood and wisdom other than silence, and "silence" (*mauna*), which is meditative absorption.
The meaning is that after having acquired the fullness of the equipment for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*), one who possesses the direct realization "I am Brahman" becomes a *brāhmaṇa*.
Since the word *mauna* is used both for the state of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*)—which is an accomplished fact—and for meditation (*dhyāna*)—which is to be performed—a doubt arises.

Just as in the supplementary passage beginning with "Baka [taught him]," it was determined that the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth pertains to the office of a priest (*ārtvijya*), so too, from the supplementary passage "then he is a *brāhmaṇa*" which lacks an explicit injunction, it is certain that *mauna* is not something to be enjoined.
Thus he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "It is not enjoined.
Here, the result is that meditation is not to be performed according to the prima facie view, whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is to be performed.

If *mauna* (the state of a sage) refers to the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), then it is merely restated as being already established by another scriptural passage, for the purpose of praising the injunction regarding childhood (*bālya*).

If it is knowledge, then that has already been obtained from the word *pāṇḍitya*; such is the meaning of the text of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). From the word *muni*, however, an excellence of realized wisdom (*vijñāna*) is understood, which is not obtained from the word *pāṇḍitya* as it denotes mere knowledge.
Nor does the word *muni* denote a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), since it is used in reference to Vālmīki and others.

Therefore, he establishes the final conclusion—that because silence (*mauna*) has not been previously established, it must be understood as an injunction—by means of the passage beginning with "Thus" (*evam*).
He explains the application of Āpastamba’s rule by saying "of the other stages of life" (*itarāśrama*).

Furthermore, he states that silence is something to be enjoined because of the scriptural statement, "Having become indifferent to both non-silence and silence," which indicates that it is to be practiced just like hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*); this is expressed by the phrase "because it is to be brought about through detachment" (*nirvedanīyatva*).

Nor is syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) a fault in the injunction of all three [meditations], because such a split is accepted, as in the case of the *uparidhāraṇa* (holding [the fire] above). This is the sense.
To the question "For whom is this meditation enjoined?", he says: "for one who possesses that" (*tadvataḥ*).
The meaning is that this refers to the renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) who possesses indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), as he is the subject under discussion by the words "having known the Self.

Anticipating the objection that meditation and the like might be obtained from worldly practice—since they are means for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of subtle objects such as the musical notes *ṣaḍja* and so forth—the author states a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) beginning with the word "nanu" (but/how then).

If it is asked: "In a sentence whose primary purport is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), how can [meditation] be a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of knowledge? the author replies: "Like the beginning of an injunction" (*vidhyādivat*). This is just like the injunction of subsidiaries within a sentence whose primary purport is a sacrifice that yields a specific fruit.
The procedure (vidhi) extends from the primary rite (pradhāna) down to its constituent parts (aṅga).
In this context, the meaning is that the primary sacrifice is the beginning of the procedure, and for that very reason, the subordinate elements are called the "end of the procedure" (vidhyanta).
Those who are ignorant of the intent of this Sūtra and its Bhāṣya claim that there is no injunction (vidhi) regarding such matters as hearing the duties of the renunciant stage (saṃnyāsāśrama).

For in the case of a ritual injunction, only the mere non-attainment [of the result] is required; and that has been demonstrated due to the intensity of the perception of difference—so say those who know the tradition. //47//

Since the stage of life characterized by solitude (*kaivalyāśrama*), distinguished by childhood and so forth and supported by scriptural authority, exists in this way, why is there a conclusion with the householder in the *Chāndogya* at the passage, "Having returned home, [he should live] in his family" (Chānd. 8.15.1)?
For by doing so, he demonstrates his respect for that subject.
Therefore, he recites the following reply: "But because of its totality, there is an inclusion [of the practice] by householders. (BBs 3.4.48)
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of specification;
its state of being "entire" (kṛtsna-bhāva) is specified.

For many duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma), such as sacrifices and the like, which involve great effort, are taught as obligations toward him, as are the duties of other stages of life—such as non-violence and restraint of the senses—as far as possible. Regarding him...
They do exist;
therefore, the inclusion of householders is not contradictory. // 48 //

The meaning of the objection is that since the concluding statement says, "Having remained in the household after the *samāvartana*, one attains the world of Brahman and does not return again," there is no such thing as renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

The meaning of the resolution is that the conclusion was made with reference to the householder because of the abundance of his duties involving great exertion, and not because of the non-existence of renunciation. //48//
The others [the other organs] are also [to be controlled] like the organ of speech, because instruction is given for them as well. (BBs 3.4.49)

Just as the stages of silence (*mauna*) and householdership (*gārhasthya*) are supported by Vedic scripture, so too are the other two—the forest-dweller’s life (*vānaprastha*) and residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukulavāsa*).

For the scriptural authority has been shown previously: "Austerity alone is the second [stage]; one who dwells in the teacher’s house after the period of studentship is the third" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1), and so forth.
Therefore, since there is no distinction in the instruction regarding all four stages of life, they are to be understood as being equal, whether practiced individually or in combination.

Regarding the phrase "of the others," it should be understood that the plural number refers to two stages of life (āśrama), either with respect to the diversity of their modes of livelihood (vṛtti) or with respect to the diversity of those who practice them (anuṣṭhātṛ). // 49 //

The author of the Sūtras has mentioned only two stages of life here: renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the householder's state (gārhasthya). To dispel the misconception that there might be no other two stages of life besides these, he says: "like the vow of silence" (maunavat); the meaning is "like the other two stages of life."

Although it should have been stated that [this applies] to the other two as well, the elaborate expression is used with regard to their internal subdivisions, which we have already demonstrated previously. //49//
Section on Non-Confession (Anāviṣkāra-adhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 50.
15. Anāviṣkārādhikaraṇam / Sū. 50. 15. The Topic Concerning Non-Disclosure.
"Because it is not manifested [as such] through the sequence [of the text]:
'Therefore, having discarded scholarship from that Brahman, one should remain in a state of childlike simplicity' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1)—
thus, childlike simplicity is heard in scripture as something to be practiced."

In this regard, since it is impossible to achieve the state or the action of a child— understood as "childhood"— in the sense of a specific stage of life or a particular desire, there arises a doubt: does "childhood" refer to the purity of disposition found among the behaviors of children (such as urinating and defecating wherever they happen to be), or rather to the non-development of the senses, or the absence of hypocrisy, pride, and the like?

What, then, is the prima facie view? It is reasonable to adopt that which is more well-known in the world as "childhood"—namely, acting, speaking, and eating according to one's desire, and voiding urine and excrement wherever one happens to be.
But is it not improper to resort to such arbitrary conduct because it entails faults such as moral degradation (*patita*)? No;
for the faults are removed by the scriptural injunctions and traditional codes (*smṛti*) applicable to the learned renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), just as in the case of animal sacrifice and similar acts.
This being the case, it is replied: No;

for there is no other possible interpretation of the statement. Indeed, when another meaning denotable by the word "childhood" (bālya) is available that is not contradictory, it is not proper to assume a contradiction with another injunction.
A subsidiary element (*aṅga*) is prescribed for the sake of assisting the primary element (*pradhāna*);
and here, the practice of knowledge (*jñānābhyāsa*) is the primary duty to be performed by ascetics.
Furthermore, if the entire conduct of a child (*bālacaryā*) were accepted as such a subsidiary, the practice of knowledge would not be possible.

Therefore, the internal distinction of states such as the non-maturity of the senses, which characterizes childhood, is what is intended here by the term "childhood. Thus it is said: "not manifesting [himself]"—meaning he should remain free from hypocrisy, pride, and the like, not proclaiming himself through his knowledge, learning, piety, or other qualities.
Just as a child, because his faculties have not yet matured, does not strive to reveal himself to others, so it is in this case;
for in this way, the conformity of this statement with its primary intended meaning is established.
And thus it has been said by the authors of the Smṛtis: "One who is neither virtuous nor non-virtuous, neither unlearned nor widely learned..."
He who knows neither the well-conducted nor the ill-conducted is a Brāhmaṇa.
The wise one, relying on the hidden Dharma, should conduct himself with behavior that remains unknown;
he should traverse the earth like one who is blind, like one who is dull-witted, and like one who is mute.
"Having unmanifested emblems and unmanifested conduct," and so forth. // 50 //
"Because it follows from the context, [the suffix] does not manifest [an action].

In this regard, concerning the word *bālya* (childhood), since it is impossible for the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) to have the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), one must accept the sense of "action" (*karman*). Then, because actions such as "urinating while standing" and the purity of disposition characterized by the non-development of the senses are both equally "actions of a child," he states a doubt:

"In that case. Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is that even acts such as urinating while standing must be performed as auxiliary parts of knowledge (*vidyā-aṅga*); whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is only the purity of disposition that is required.

Since the word *mauna* (silence) is well-known in the preceding context as referring to meditation (*dhyāna*) characterized by an excellence of knowledge, it was stated that meditation is what is to be enjoined.

Similarly, since the word *bālya* (childhood) is well-known as referring to acting according to one's desires and so forth, he states that this [word] refers to the injunction for that [state], asking: "What then is that? The meaning is: the state of one who acts, speaks, and eats according to his own desire (*kāmacāravādabhakṣaṇa*).

The sense is that, according to the rule of *bālya* (childlike conduct), the state of being one whose nature consists of urine and so forth—occurring as it arises and as it happens—is such that the scriptures concerning degradation (*pātitya*) apply to other subjects. This is because there is the possibility of enjoining a *bālya* known as "purity of disposition" (*bhāva-śuddhi*), which is not contradicted by the scriptural injunctions regarding rules for ritual purity, begging, and so forth—as in the passage: "But he who is devoid of knowledge, lacking a controlled mind, and always impure, does not attain that state, but enters into *saṃsāra*" and so on; therefore, this is not an injunction for acting according to one's own whims.
He establishes the conclusion with the word "evam" (thus).
He states that there is no injunction for that [childhood] because it is contrary to the primary [subject], using the phrase "pradhāna" (primary).

The construction of the Sūtra is as follows: since purity of being (bhāva-śuddhi) is connected as an auxiliary to knowledge (vidyā), the meaning of the injunction regarding childhood is that one should remain [in that state] without manifesting [one's spiritual maturity]. //50//

"Even that which pertains to this world [is attained] when there is no obstruction of what is not yet begun, for that is observed.
Starting from the sūtra *sarvāpekṣā ca yajñādiśruteraśvavat* (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.26), various means for the realization of knowledge (*vidyā*) have been determined.

Regarding that fruit, it is questioned whether knowledge, when being accomplished, is accomplished in this very life or perhaps even in another birth. What, then, is the initial position? That it is accomplished in this very life.
What is the reason?
For knowledge is preceded by hearing and so forth;
and no one engages in hearing and so forth with the intention, "May knowledge arise for me in the hereafter."
However, it is observed that one proceeds toward these [means] with the intention of producing knowledge in this very life;
for even sacrifices and the like produce knowledge only through the gateway of hearing and so forth, because knowledge is produced by means of valid authority (pramāṇa).
Therefore, the birth of knowledge occurs only in this world.
This being the case, we say: the birth of knowledge occurs in this life when there is no obstruction to what has been undertaken.

This is explained as follows: when no obstruction is placed upon the means for attaining knowledge that has been set in motion by some other karma whose fruition is imminent, then knowledge arises in this very life;
but when an obstruction to it is indeed created, then it arises in the next world.
The ripening of karma occurs through the convergence of specific place, time, and causal conditions.
It cannot be determined that the very same place, time, and causal conditions that ripen one karma will likewise ripen another,
because there are also karmas that possess mutually contradictory results.

The scripture also concludes merely by stating that this is the fruit of this action; it does not specify the particularities of place, time, or causal conditions. However, due to the specific power of the means employed, a supersensuous capacity manifests for one person, while for another, it remains obstructed. Furthermore, a desire for knowledge does not arise without distinction, because the intention—"May my knowledge arise either here or in the hereafter"—is unrestricted.
Even when knowledge arises through the means of hearing and so forth, it arises only in dependence upon the destruction of obstacles;

and thus the Śruti demonstrates the difficulty of realizing the Self: "He who is not obtained even by many through hearing, whom many, though hearing, do not know—he is marvelous as his expounder, skillful as his attainer, and marvelous as the knower instructed by the skillful" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.7).

Furthermore, by stating that Vāmadeva attained the state of Brahman while still in the womb, [the scripture] demonstrates the arising of knowledge in one birth from means accumulated in a previous birth;
for no worldly means whatsoever is conceivable for a being in the womb.
Also in the *Smṛti*: "O Kṛṣṇa, what goal does one go to who has not attained perfection in Yoga? (Gītā 6.37).

Thus questioned by Arjuna, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva said, "For no one who performs good deeds, my dear, goes to a miserable state" (Gītā 6.40), and after further declaring his attainment of the worlds of merit and rebirth in a virtuous family, he subsequently stated: "There he regains the mental disposition belonging to his former body" (Gītā 6.43), and so on, up to: "Perfected through many births, he then attains the supreme goal" (Gītā 6.45).
By this, he demonstrates exactly this:
therefore, it is established that the arising of knowledge—whether pertaining to this world or the next—depends upon the destruction of its obstacles. // 51 //

Having explained the collection of means beginning with renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and ending with childhood (*bālya*), which pertain to this life, the author now considers the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) that is to be accomplished by them. Stating the connection (*saṃgati*) in this way, he expresses the doubt—since the fruit of a means can arise in two ways—by the words "all" and so forth.

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that hearing and the other means are restricted to having fruits in this life, like the *Kārīrī* sacrifice, by saying "first of all" (*tāvat*). [An objection is raised: "But how can there be a restriction to this-worldliness for knowledge, which is accomplished through sacrifices and the like that have fruits in the hereafter? To this, he replies: "Even sacrifices and the like... [and so on].

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position holds that once purification through sacrifices and other means has been accomplished, and the direct causes of knowledge—such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth—have been engaged, a delay in the attainment of knowledge is not logical;

yet a delay is observed. Therefore, the result of this prima facie view is that the status of hearing and so forth as causes of knowledge is unestablished. The final conclusion (siddhānta), however, considers that even if there is a delay due to the influence of obstacles, the causal status [of hearing] is established. Thus, it concludes that hearing and so forth have an indefinite result, like the Citrā sacrifice, by stating: "In this way... (evam).

Now, one might ask: why is the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth obstructed by a specific *prārabdha* karma? Why could the ripening of karma not be obstructed by hearing and the like themselves? To this he says: "And because its ripening is imminent. The meaning is that karmas ripen through the power of place and other such factors.
To the question of why hearing and so forth do not themselves ripen [into full realization], he says: "And those which...
Ripening (vipācakatva) means being the cause for turning toward the fruit.
[Objection: "In that case, what is the nature of the place and other factors that ripen [the potential] for hearing and so forth? To this he says: "The scripture also...
The intention is that the knowledge of the place and so forth arises through the power of the result.
Nevertheless, regarding the reason why it is precisely karma that acts as an obstacle to hearing and so forth—and not the reverse—he states: "By means of the sādhana..."
The sense is that the power of obstruction (*pratibandhakatva-śakti*) must also be understood on the strength of the results [of experience].
He states the scriptural and traditional indicators (*liṅga*) for the existence of such an obstruction with the words "And thus," and so forth.
The establishment of the obstruction follows from the statement: "Even though they hear, they do not know."
One who speaks of the self as it truly is is also a marvel, like something extraordinary;
let alone one who has attained direct realization,
even one who knows it through indirect means is a marvel.
The meaning is: even though instructed by a virtuous teacher. //51//
END BsCom_3,4.16.51 START BsCom_3,4.17.52 17. The Section Concerning Liberation as the Fruit (Muktiphalādhikaraṇa) / Sūtra 52.
Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruits of liberation, because that state is not determinate; because that state is not determinate.

Just as for one seeking liberation who relies on the means of knowledge (*vidyā*), a specific determination regarding the fruit characterized by knowledge—consisting of the distinction between being a fruit pertaining to this life or the next—is observed due to the particular intensity of the effort in those means;
likewise, even in the case of the fruit characterized by liberation, some specific determination based on excellence or deficiency would [otherwise] exist.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruit of liberation.
Indeed, one should not suspect any such specific restriction regarding the fruit of liberation. Why? Because that state is definitively ascertained.
For the state of liberation is determined to be of one and the same form in all the Vedāntas.

Indeed, the state of liberation is Brahman itself, and there is no connection with multiple forms for Brahman, because it is determined to have a single characteristic, as stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "It is neither coarse nor subtle" (Bṛ. 3.8.8).
"This is that Self which is described as 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26);
"where one sees nothing else" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1);
"this immortal Brahman alone is before [one]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).

"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6); "Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25); "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
This is established by such scriptural passages as these.
Furthermore, the means of knowledge (vidyā-sādhana), due to its own specific potency, may impart some excellence to the knowledge itself, but not to liberation, which is the fruit of knowledge.
For we have stated more than once that liberation is unattainable through effort, being of an eternally established nature, and is merely realized through knowledge.

Furthermore, even in that [knowledge], an excellence consisting of superiority or inferiority is not possible; for that which is inferior lacks the nature of knowledge, since only that which is superior constitutes knowledge. Therefore, while an excellence in that [knowledge] might consist in its arising after a long or short duration, there is no possibility of any excellence whatsoever in liberation.
Furthermore, because there is no difference in the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), there can be no fixed rule regarding a difference in its fruits, unlike the case of ritual actions (*karman*).
For there is no differentiation in the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation, as there is in the case of ritual acts.
However, in the case of qualified knowledges (*saguṇavidyā*), such as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2)...

Since distinctions are established in these [meditations] through the addition or subtraction of qualities, a specific determination of their respective fruits is possible, just as in the case of the fruits of ritual acts (*karma*).
And there is a scriptural indication to this effect: "In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become.
This is not the case for the knowledge of the qualityless (*nirguṇa*), because of the absence of qualities therein.
And thus says the Smṛti: "For there is no higher goal for anyone; indeed, when a quality exists, they proclaim inequality.
The repetition of the words "because that state is ascertained" and "because that state is maintained" indicates the completion of the chapter. // 52 //

When there is no obstruction by *prārabdha-karma*, the arising of knowledge occurs in this very life, because obstructions consisting of accumulated sins have been removed by sacrifices and other such acts. But when there is an obstruction, it is removed through experience [in another life], and thus the rule regarding the distinction between knowledge being attained in this world or the next has been stated.

Similarly, one might think that even in the fruit, which is liberation (*mokṣa*), there might be some distinction such as superiority or inferiority; therefore, he says: "Thus there is no restriction regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is definitely determined, because that state is definitely determined."
Liberation (*mukti*) is the subject here.

Since liberation can possibly exist in both ways—whether there is a restriction of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-niyama*) in it as there is in knowledge (*vidyā*), or not—the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding this doubt with the words "as" (*yathā*):
liberation possesses specific qualities.
Therefore, because [liberation] is the fruit [of knowledge], the opponent holds that liberation is to be accomplished by ritual action; this is the prima facie view.

However, in the final conclusion (siddhānta), inference is sublated by scriptural texts which determine that Brahman is devoid of distinctions; thus, the fruit is that liberation is manifested solely by knowledge.

Furthermore, while one might admit some degree of excellence in knowledge due to the varying intensity of its means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth, he states—beginning with "Moreover, the means of knowledge"—that there is no excellence in the liberation obtained through that knowledge.

[Objection: Since Brahman is eternally established, if the cessation of ignorance were different from it, duality would result; yet if it were non-different, it could not be something to be accomplished, and thus it would not be the fruit of knowledge. To this, he says: "For that... [taddhi]. Because it is manifested by knowledge, the bliss of Brahman itself is the primary fruit; the manifestation, which is the cessation of ignorance, is accomplished by knowledge as the absence of the obstacle to the dawning of the nature of bliss, and that [cessation] is indeterminable (anirvācya).
There is no consequence of falling into dualism;
others, however, say that she (Māyā) is non-different from Brahman.
Nor should it be argued that spiritual knowledge (vidyā) would be futile there because of the impossibility of [Māyā] being something to be accomplished (sādhya).
The entire world proceeds from the knowledge that "in the absence of X, Y is absent," whereby X is established as the cause of Y.
For instance, in the absence of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is the absence of liberation in the form of the nature of Brahman; indeed, it is ignorance (*avidyā*) itself which constitutes this evil.
This is because the conventional expression "there is no liberation" refers precisely to this ignorance, and thus liberation is non-existent [as a distinct entity] in that context.

And thus, because of the certainty that there is no liberation without knowledge (*vidyā*), one acquires knowledge; and upon the arising of knowledge, one abides as the Self which is the bliss of Brahman—self-luminous and eternally free from all evils that are established by their own nature. This is beyond reproach.
Now, he abandons the acceptance of any excellence (*atiśaya*) in knowledge, saying "nor" (*na ca*).
The meaning is that in the case of a single form as an object, a gradation [of excellence] in valid cognition is untenable.
How then was a distinction regarding knowledge stated in the previous section? To this he says: "Therefore," etc.
The meaning is that even when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, a delay in knowledge has been mentioned, but not a gradation [of intensity].
To the objection, "In that case, why might there not be a delay in liberation even when knowledge is present? he says: "But not...

The point is that although there may be a delay in the production of a lamp due to obstructions such as wind, once it has been produced, no delay is observed in the cessation of darkness; likewise, when knowledge is present, there is no delay in the cessation of ignorance.
Furthermore, it is logical that there is a gradation of fruits corresponding to the gradation of qualities in ritual actions and meditations;

however, since knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā) is of a single uniform nature, its fruit is likewise uniform. This is stated in the passage beginning with "vidyābheda" and so forth. In the Smṛti, the meaning is "of a certain knower of the attributeless."
Therefore, it is established that liberation occurs at the very same time as knowledge. //52//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. // 4 //
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavat.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Internal and External Means for the Knowledge of the Attributeless (Nirguṇa)."
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Means," in the venerable Śaṅkara Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtras.
